title: ‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang on to the Burnham bounce? | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Conference delegates grateful ousting Starmer has paid off, but relief tempered by fiscal headwinds ahead
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Conference delegates grateful ousting Starmer has paid off, but relief tempered by fiscal headwinds ahead
Content: The slogan of Andy Burnham’s first Labour conference as leader has been ‘hope again’ but there is less hope around than two months ago.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe slogan of Andy Burnham’s first Labour conference as leader has been ‘hope again’ but there is less hope around than two months ago.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAndy BurnhamAnalysis‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang on to the Burnham bounce?Pippa CrerarPolitical editorConference delegates grateful ousting Starmer has paid off, but relief tempered by fiscal headwinds aheadUK politics live – latest updatesSun 27 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareEven Andy Burnham’s closest allies accept that deposing Keir Starmer to install their man as leader was a huge political gamble. But if the mood at the Labour party conference in Liverpool is anything to go by, it is one that – so far – has paid off.The contrast with last year, when Starmer retained his grip on the party and Burnham slunk away from Liverpool early, could not be more stark. Their relief at their turn of fortune is tempered only by the fiscal headwinds ahead.Cabinet ministers recount how at their political meeting two weeks ago, they were shown a series of charts showing the metrics behind the Burnham bounce. One in particular stood out to those in the room.‘Rip the plaster off’: Andy Burnham sets out vision for universal free social careRead moreIt was a graph showing whether the public felt the government was heading in the right direction. Until the end of June, it had been on a downward trajectory as public frustration mounted over Starmer’s leadership.But once Starmer announced his intention to step down and Burnham took over in July, the line suddenly rebounded and, while still in negative territory, has been moving definitively upwards since. “We’ve got a second hearing with the public,” one cabinet minister said. “We can’t squander it.”This time last year, just 14 months after coming to power, several were privately despairing about Labour’s electoral prospects. But with an energetic new prime minister and after a difficult summer for Nigel Farage, they now believe that a second term is winnable.It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that speculation about a snap election escalated in the run-up to the conference, to the extent that Burnham felt compelled to “knock that dead” and confirm a 2029 date instead.1:02Andy Burnham ‘prepared’ to deliver radical change despite economic challenges – videoSome of the prime minister’s closest advisers wanted him to rule out an early election from the off, pressing him to be explicit. “The polling isn’t good enough. We could end up being the biggest party but we could lose our majority,” one said. Another said: “Elections have to be about a choice, not a referendum on an alternative plan.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conferenceRead moreBut others inside No 10 felt he should go to the country while the polling was good, Farage was on the back foot, and before Burnham’s big plans for change ran headfirst into fiscal reality. “Right now the public is willing to give us the benefit of the doubt – that won’t last for ever,” one said.For his part, Burnham claims he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite the severe economic headwinds, by delivering tangible – albeit smaller – improvements in the short term while setting out a longer-term vision to transform things such associal careand youth unemployment at the same time.“There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them,”he told the Guardianat the weekend. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change.”The slogan of his first conference as leader has been “hope again” – but with the bleak global economic landscape there is less hope around than there was when he walked into Downing Street two months ago.The first crucial test for Burnham will be next month’s budget, at which he said the government would be “highly prudent” with the public finances, amid concerns that Labour needs to reassure the markets.But if the budget is about intent, next summer’s spending review is about proof, and as such, that could prove to be a make-or-break moment for this prime minister. It’s easy to make the promises, but much harder to deliver on them.With obstacles ahead, the relief felt by Labour MPs and ministers in Liverpool is heavily caveated. One cabinet minister quoted Alastair Campbell’s election mantra as a warning to colleagues who might be getting ahead of themselves: “Lots done, lots to do, lots to lose.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourLabour conference 2026Labour conferenceBudgetanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Does GLP-1 use result in significant hair loss? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Experts share what you need to know about GLP-1-related hair loss as the side-effect gets more attention from researchers
Author: Keren Landman
Headline: Experts share what you need to know about GLP-1-related hair loss as the side-effect gets more attention from researchers
Content: While GLP-1-related hair loss is often temporary and reversible, it’s significant enough that some patients hesitate to take weight-loss drugs.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhile GLP-1-related hair loss is often temporary and reversible, it’s significant enough that some patients hesitate to take weight-loss drugs.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesCall the doctorWell actuallyDoes GLP-1 use result in significant hair loss?Experts share what you need to know about GLP-1-related hair loss as the side-effect gets more attention from researchersKeren LandmanSun 27 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 20 million people across theUS,UK, and EUare taking GLP-1 receptor agonists like tirzepatide and semaglutide (Ozempic or Mounjaro are common brands) for weight loss and type 2 diabetes. As their use has surged, we’re learning more about their side-effects. One that’s been getting a lot of attention from researchers lately: hair loss.In one survey of people who take these medications,20%of respondents experienced hair shedding, although the lack of high-quality data from a randomized, controlled trial to assess this side-effect makes it difficult to know exactly how common it is.While GLP-1-related hair loss is often temporary and reversible, it’s significant enough that some patients hesitate to take drugs they would otherwise benefit from using. Here’s what you need to know.What kind of hair loss are people seeing on GLP-1s?Most people who take GLP-1 drugs don’t have hair loss. However, those who do often notice itwithin the first year, usually peaking a little before the 12th month.They’re usually experiencing one of two types of hair loss, says Lynn Petukhova, a geneticist at New York University who studies hair loss disorders. The most common type is a stress-related condition that dermatologists calltelogen effluvium, where a stressor pushes an unusually large share of hair follicles into theirresting phase. During this stage, the affected hair ceases to grow – and after two to three months, it falls out. This kind of hair loss is temporary; the growth interruption and shedding stops once the stressor does, and hair typically goes back to growing normally.A much smaller proportion of people taking GLP-1s experience new or increased pattern baldness, says Petukhova. That’s the genetically influenced, usually permanent hair loss that causes a receding hairline or thinning at the crown in men, and widening of the center part in women.In a recentstudyPetukhova led, men taking GLP-1 drugs were 7% more likely to experience this type of hair loss than men not taking the drugs. (The study was unable to assess the risk in women because their genes for the condition aren’t as well understood.)Hair loss may also manifest differently depending on hair type. In onestudy, white patients were more likely to report hair shedding and thinning, while Black patients more commonly reported hair dryness and breakage.What causes hair loss on GLP-1 drugs?Telogen effluvium has two possible causes in the setting of rapid weight loss: the shock of sudden and severe calorie restriction, and micronutrient deficiencies that result from dramatically reduced food intake.The type of drug and dosage is also relevant; people taking tirzepatide and semaglutide, especially at higher doses, had thehighest ratesof temporary hair loss.Women make up nearly90%of people who report telogen effluvium when taking GLP-1 drugs. Women also commonly experience it after giving birth, as a result of abrupt hormonal changes. It frequently follows weight loss surgery too; as many as60%of patients have hair loss after the procedure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPattern baldness on GLP-1s is less well understood but likely occurs because of some biological connection between the genes that make someone respond to GLP-1 drugs and those that cause this type of hair loss, says Petukhova. “Some people have a higher genetic risk” for pattern baldness, she says, “and the drug will unmask it.”Can you prevent or reverse hair loss on a GLP-1 drug?If you’re considering starting a GLP-1 drug, it’s worth discussing the possibility of hair loss with your doctor.Because hair follicles are extremely sensitive to certain nutritional deficiencies, eating enough protein and ensuring you’re consuming sufficient iron, zinc and biotin are sound strategies. However, these precautions are not guaranteed to prevent hair loss, especially if you’re losing weight rapidly. A lower dose and slower weight loss may also reduce your risk.If you are experiencing hair loss, consult your regular doctor or a dermatologist who can help you determine whether it is temporary or permanent, and thus how to treat it. As mentioned above, temporary hair loss is reversible with nutrition, time and patience. For pattern hair loss, medications like minoxidil and finasteride may be useful.If you have been prescribed a GLP-1 drug for health reasons and are concerned about side effects like hair loss, it’s important to talk to your doctor. The prospect of cosmetic changes alone shouldn’t discourage people from doing what’s best for the rest of their body, says Petukhova. “It’s more important for most people to get your metabolic health under control than to ensure that you have all the hairs on your head,” she says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCall the doctorWeight-loss drugsHealthHair lossWomen's hairMen's hairfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The PM oozes confidence and easy-going charm as he tells Laura Kuenssberg the hill he’ll die on is fixing social care
Author: John Crace
Headline: The PM oozes confidence and easy-going charm as he tells Laura Kuenssberg the hill he’ll die on is fixing social care
Content: You may struggle to pay your bills, you may fight to get a hospital appointment, but Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenYou may struggle to pay your bills, you may fight to get a hospital appointment, but Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamBurnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura showJohn CraceThe PM oozes confidence and easy-going charm as he tells Laura Kuenssberg the hill he’ll die on is fixing social careUK politics live – latest updatesSun 27 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIn recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that Andy Burnham would call an early general election. Speculation that existed largely in the heads of those writing the stories, as even the most favourable polls suggest Labour would lose its huge majority and become the largest party in a coalition government. But to stop the chatter dominating his party conference, Burnham made it clear therewould be no early election. His reward? Headlines in the rightwing press that he had bottled it. By not calling an election he had never planned to call. Sometimes you just can’t win.There again, you might call this a first-world problem for the prime minister. This time last year, Burnham had beenhanging around the fringes of the conferenceas he and his allies attempted one of the most half-arsed coups in living memory. One that fizzled out almost before it had started and became the butt of many jokes among Keir Starmer’s inner circle. Andy looked to have blown himself up on the runway, leaving Keir safe for the duration of the parliament.Fast forward a year and Burnham is in No 10, Reform UK’s lead in the polls has disappeared, andLabouris looking a lot more competitive than even the most rose-tinted party members could have reasonably expected in such a short period of time. Andy must be pinching himself. Unable to believe his luck. All that’s changed has been him. Energy prices are still sky high as a result of the war in Iran. The cost of living is still way too high. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch might have been a problem for Keir but they aren’t for Andy. You might even call them assets.No wonder then that Burnham was looking relatively chipper as hekicked off conferencewith the traditional lengthy interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg. Only relatively chipper, because you’d need to be a halfwit not to be a little wary. These interviews can go hideously wrong – Liz Truss’s at the Tory conference in 2022 is a collector’s item – and prime ministers generally regard them as exercises in damage limitation. To survive without generating the wrong kind of headlines is the dream.1:02Andy Burnham ‘prepared’ to deliver radical change despite economic challenges – video“You look like you’re loving the job,” observed Laura. Somehow biting her lip and refraining from adding that it is early days and we’ll see how much you’ve aged by this time next year. Andy smiled. He was, he said. Not because he had the job he had always coveted. But because now he had a chance to make a difference. To end the drift and division of the decade since Brexit – he could have gone back another five years and included austerity. To do politics differently. To bring back hope. You’re going to hear a lot of the H-word in the next four days. It’s plastered over every wall of the conference centre.And Burnham speaks as if he genuinely means it. He has the easy-going charm and self-confidence of a man who is comfortable in his own skin. He reaches parts that other politicians don’t get near. Nige has the same quality. Only, where he speaks to people’s fears and grievance, Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself. You may still struggle to pay your bills, you may still fight to get a hospital appointment, but somehow you can believe in better days ahead. The triumph of hope over experience.All of which is a much in demand – if not essential – skill for a politician. One that gives you a fighting chance of success. People feel both heard and seen by him. It’s almost uncanny. Burnham talks of being a different sort of politician, when the reality he is the archetypal career politician. You’d imagine he had spent years doing what he calls a real job as a hospital porter, but he’s been a politician almost all his adult life. Few understand the Westminster system better than him, he also suggests. You can’t escape the irony. Keir Starmer actually had a long and successful career outside politics, but he is the one who always sounded like the career politician. Speaking in soundbites and half truths. You’ve either got it or you haven’t.‘Rip the plaster off’: Andy Burnham sets out vision for universal free social careRead moreThe message Burnham really wanted to get across on Sunday morning was that social care was the hill he would die on. Other politicians had said they would tackle the issue but had recoiled when they realised how difficult it was. “I will grasp the nettle,” he said, opening his eyes still wider, hoping that viewers would fall into them. He would create a national care system that incorporated the NHS and social care. Old people were either paying through the nose for their own care, falling through the cracks or ending up bed blocking in hospitals. It was unsustainable and undignified.How this would be paid for would be laid out in due course. It would be what Labour would campaign on in 2029. But make no mistake, people were already paying for it. Here he was preaching to the converted. My sisters and I had to sell my mother’s house to pay for her care during the last seven years of her life as she suffered from Alzheimer’s. We didn’t mind so much, but my mother would have been gutted had she been aware. It had mattered to her that she could leave her house to the three of us. Paying a little extra in tax to make sure that other people – possibly even you – don’t have to burn through their assets seems the kind of thing any fair-minded society would do.Burnham ended by saying he very much hoped to work cross-party on all this. It was too important not to. This aspiration lasted all of five minutes. Because that’s how long it took the ever ridiculous Chris Philp – Kuenssberg’s next guest – to start going on about a “death and dementia tax”. Like clockwork. The Philpster becomes more and more a parody of himself. The Tory party’s very own Alan B’Stard. Venal, self-serving and not very bright. A man whose answer to everything is to cut the welfare bill still further, seemingly unaware his leader has already spent the cuts her party has proposed.It’s as if Philp regards getting dementia as a personal failing, just as he sees being on benefits as morally deficient. If you get dementia then you deserve to pay for your own care. Now is not a good time to be one of Chris’s relatives. If you find yourself in need of care then you’re very much on your own. There’s no way the Philpster is missing out on his inheritance.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchLabourLabour conference 2026Labour conferencenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s like the Scottish Upper East Side’: shame and snobbery as American students blamed for St Andrews classism | University of St Andrews | The Guardian
description: Online comments reflect class tensions at Scottish university between those from lower-income families and wealthier US undergraduates
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Online comments reflect class tensions at Scottish university between those from lower-income families and wealthier US undergraduates
Content: ‘It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianUniversity of St Andrews‘It’s like the Scottish Upper East Side’: shame and snobbery as American students blamed for St Andrews classismOnline comments reflect class tensions at Scottish university between those from lower-income families and wealthier US undergraduatesPatrick GreenfieldSun 27 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return to St Andrews University this academic year because of her experiences of classism on campus, she did not expect much of a response. But in the two weeks since she published her story on LinkedIn, it has resonated with hundreds of others.“Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” the former comparative literature and classical studies student wrote in alengthy post. “Arriving at a university ranked first in the UK at the time from a background like mine, I thought I was doing everything right.“I don’t mean for this to be a sob story but an explanation. I recognise the privilege of access to higher education, however I am also brutally aware of the hidden privilege of having unobstructed access to studying for a degree. There is a deep gap between the two, and it is never addressed.”For many responding, her comments touched on a growing tension at St Andrews, driven by the funding model of Scotland’s cash-strapped universities. Places for Scottish students, who study for free, are capped by the Scottish government and account for about 30% of students at St Andrews. Maintenance loans and bursaries cover basic costs, but those from lower-income families are still often left with less disposable income than their contemporaries – including wealthy international students who pay much higher fees.St Andrews,ranked secondin the Guardian’s university league table for 2026, accepts one of the highest percentages in the UK of privately educated students. The British aristocracy has long adored the medieval town’s cobbled streets, wind-swept beach and grand stone buildings: Prince William and the Princess of Wales met there.View image in fullscreenSophie Rose Jenkins’ comments have struck a chord with some other students.Photograph: noneBut the recent influx of wealthy US students has changed the dynamic on campus, students say. Americans account for around a fifth of undergraduates at St Andrews, the highest proportion in the UK, with each paying £33,250 for this academic year, more than three times what British students pay.“My parents were worried about me coming here. They didn’t want me to be left out,” said one Scottish fresher who is on a scholarship to study classics. “Most of the people I have met are international students. I didn’t grow up with tons of money. Maybe they can be a bit ignorant to the cost of things.”Another said: “There’s a Pret here. You have to ask yourself why that is in such a small town.”Aspects of fraternity and sorority culture have started to blend with the upper-class experience of British university, some students say. Regular black-tie dinners and balls are now rivalled by fashion shows and exclusive societies. A short walk from the student union bar, an interior design shop advertises luxury bed linen for students, while a popular coffee shop sells designer clothes and candles alongside speciality matchas.“I totally see her [Jenkins’s] perspective,” said one privately educated student from Edinburgh, who was returning from hockey practice with friends. “It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans. We knew lots of people from hockey already so it’s easy to feel left out if you’re not from that environment.“The American culture is coming in and it massively influences everything at the moment. They compete with each other. If you look at how they dress, people arrive in lectures as if they are going on a night out.”One student referenced a well-known student newspaper article published last year about how St Andrews hadturned intothe Scottish Upper East Side, which said: “Our beloved Scottish town is day by day turning into a microcosm of Manhattan’s elite world; complete with intrigue, privilege, and secrets that spread like wildfire.”Underlining the point, an American student walks past the student union loudly explaining to a friend: “Everyone is going to think you’re rich if you have a Ralph Lauren bag. But that doesn’t make you rich.”St Andrews said it had reached out to Jenkins to better understand her experience, but she had decided not to engage for now. It said it had a robust system for reporting complaints from students, and only a handful of complaints had been made in the last five years.“Yes, some students do arrive here in St Andrews, and at every other university, with immature, offensive and classist views. But they tend not to leave with them,” said the vice-principal Niall Scott.“This isn’t a St Andrews issue – it’s a societal issue. Classism begins in the home or at school, not at university. Universities like St Andrews have a crucial role to play in challenging these attitudes by bringing together people from different backgrounds, cultures and perspectives, encouraging understanding, respect and inclusion.”The debate around classism at Scottish universities is not new. In 2024, EdinburghUniversity offered guidanceon how students should treat one another after rising claims of discrimination and classism. “Don’t be a snob!” read the advice given out to students. At St Andrews, some students said the issue of classism was not only linked to the rise in American students.“It is generally an attitude thing. There is an idea that working-class students can’t speak about issues that are going on elsewhere in the world because they are not as well travelled,” said one science student. “At St Andrews, even for moderately wealthy people, it feels like there is an old money level above that you don’t even get to speak to.”Rasmus, a Danish student, said he was bemused by the social dynamics at the university.“It took two weeks for me to meet a Scottish person. They are surrounded by people here who have the money for international tuition, which is quite narrow. I can imagine that being quite a difficult experience,” he said.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of St AndrewsHigher educationScotlandClass issuesInequalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open  | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office
Content: Trump at the White House last year.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump at the White House last year.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpBad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into openPresident has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public officeRobert Taitin WashingtonSun 27 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing.“All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language.“Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.”Over the past decade,Donald Trumphas been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language.Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he wasmemorably reportedto have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second.He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally.A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn.Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025,when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.)Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April.“President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.”Civility in politicsTrump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies.In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”.View image in fullscreenPresident Lyndon Johnson meets Richard Nixon at the White House in July 1968. Both men had a taste for the profane.Photograph: National Archives/Getty ImagesTrump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, alive mic picked uphis description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”.A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard.These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through.Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem.“The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians.“Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.”In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics.Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”.View image in fullscreenJD Vance in Kansas City earlier this month.Photograph: Getty ImagesPete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.”Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity.Minneapolis mayor Jacob Freytold Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agentsto “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January.Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois,told a Washington thinktankshe was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.”A rhetorical maneuverWhile the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care.“The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.”Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language.“There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them.“It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.”View image in fullscreenBarack Obama with Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa in May.Photograph: Getty ImagesBenjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,”suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”.The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses.“I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.”But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.”In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics.“We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands.“Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’ | Books | The Guardian
description: Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novel
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novel
Content: ‘I’m proud of my resilience’ … Tomi Adeyemi.Photograph: Caroline FlissView image in fullscreen‘I’m proud of my resilience’ … Tomi Adeyemi.Photograph: Caroline FlissBooksTomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novelEmma LoffhagenSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing.Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her.“It was an intense choice, and I think it’s because I needed people to see me in this one,” she says. “I’ve had so much success, but it was also done in a way where so many people’s interpretations were put on to who I was.”The recent public fallout from the forthcoming film adaptation may have drawn attention, but the 33-year-old Nigerian American author had already spent much of her adult life being watched. Children of Blood and Bone, her 2018 debut, became a publishing phenomenon, netting a major seven-figure deal and debuting at No 1 on the New York Times young adult bestseller list. Its story of Zélie, a young woman fighting to restore magic to the kingdom of Orïsha, was inspired by West African mythology and offered something Adeyemi had craved as a child: a dark-skinned Black girl at the centre of an epic fantasy.The success brought its own mythology. Adeyemi was not merely a successful young writer; she became, she feels, a symbol of what the next generation of Black YA literature might be, something she felt the weight of acutely.double quotation markI felt pressure to be the perfect dark‑skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’“I felt pressure to be the perfect dark-skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’,” she says. “This was the biggest YA book deal in history, not just for a female or Black author. And so few of us are given a shot at all, so for the last 12 years there’s been this sense of carrying everyone.”Readers would tell her what the book had meant to their children. “You have no idea what this did for me,” they would say. Such responses were moving, but also difficult to know what to do with.Now, with The Siren, Adeyemi has moved from epic fantasy to something more contemporary. The standalone novel follows Emery, a Black student arriving at Dartmouth College determined to leave her troubled past behind. She is drawn into a mysterious sorority of “Sirens” and desperate to fit in. In some ways, Adeyemi says, the book is deeply personal. “[Emery] is my inner teen,” Adeyemi says. “I just want to give her a hug.”She may have found success, but in the beginning Adeyemi’s career never looked certain. She wrote her first story at five – a Parent Trap fan fiction because, she says, she “wanted a twin and a horse”. She then spent years trying not to become a writer. Her parents had moved to Chicago from Nigeria in their early 20s, and Adeyemi grew up with the ethos of relentless achievement that often comes with first-generation immigrants – one that does not take kindly to creative pursuits. She considered medicine, investment banking and consulting, but kept coming back to writing. “Being called to be an artist is terrifying,” she says. “It’s not a logical choice.”After studying English at Harvard, Adeyemi won a fellowship to study West African mythology and culture in Salvador, Brazil, an experience that would later inspire Children of Blood and Bone. She moved to California and began working part time at a film production company in Los Angeles, alongside writing her first novel.View image in fullscreenThat first attempt took four and a half years to write and received 63 rejections. She decided to drop the manuscript and wrote Children of Blood and Bone instead. When it was finally published in 2018 it quickly became one of the most talked about YA novels of the year. For a writer who had spent years being turned down, the speed and scale of what followed were dizzying. “I never really adjusted, because there was so much work still to do,” she says. “It’s been 12 to 14 years of intense grinding.”And then came the film. On paper, it was the stuff of a writer’s dreams: her novel was to be transformed into a major Hollywood production, with an impossibly starry cast including Viola Davis, Idris Elba, Regina King, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg and Cynthia Erivo, premiering in January 2027. Adeyemi co-wrote the screenplay, but as the adaptation progressed, she became increasingly unhappy with the process.In July, Adeyemi posted a five-minute video on TikTok in which she described the adaptation process as “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”. She said she had left the set “hyperventilating and sobbing”, and that afterwards she experienced severe physical pain and panic attacks. “I never want to hear about this project again,” she said.She says she had little hesitation about speaking publicly. “I understood that if I didn’t speak up, I couldn’t move forward,” she explains. “I can’t really worry about the response, because I don’t have to live with how people respond to me – I have to live with me, every day.”When I ask what exactly happened on set, however, Adeyemi hesitates. “I won’t go into the specifics,” she says carefully. “[But] the whole journey of the trilogy and the adaptation felt biblical … It took all of me.”There has, though, been public discussion around the film’s casting of Amandla Stenberg, who is mixed race, and questions around colourism: Stenberg’s character is described in the book as having “dark copper skin”. Adeyemi’s July TikTok also appeared to show messages she sent to Stenberg in February 2025, around the time Stenberg responded to the colourism backlash, telling the actor: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”When I ask Adeyemi whether she wants to clarify anything about the casting, she demurs. “With a film, the director makes every decision,” she says. “With my book I can talk about every choice down to the commas, because that’s truly in my hands. So there’s nothing for me to add, other than the clarity that these aren’t my choices.”She is clear, though, about one thing. When I ask her if she would ever adapt another one of her books for screen she responds simply: “Never.” She has no desire to watch the upcoming film either. “I still don’t plan to watch it, but it’s not really for me to watch,” she says.Instead, she is trying to leave the world of Children of Blood and Bone behind, and focus on what she has achieved. “I’m proud of my strength, resilience, and grace,” she says.She is also proud of what she believes her debut set in motion: the fact that she can now walk into a bookshop and see shelves of dark-skinned protagonists across fantasy, romance, thrillers and mysteries. “The girls who grew up after me will never have that experience,” she says. As her publisher told her: “You changed things.”The Siren by Tomi Adeyemi is published by First Ink on Thursday. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksYoung adultFantasy booksFilm adaptationsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Five arrested on terrorism charges after explosives found near RAF base used by US  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Counter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehicles
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Counter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehicles
Content: Five men have been arrested and three vans are being examined by army bomb disposal experts.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenFive men have been arrested and three vans are being examined by army bomb disposal experts.Photograph: BBCUK newsFive arrested on terrorism charges after explosives found near RAF base used by USCounter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehiclesJamie Grierson,Vikram DoddandHelena HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 14.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCounter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military.The Guardian understands that after five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans, with an initial view being they were consistent with improvised explosive devices.Images circulating on Sunday showed shirtless men being handcuffed in a dark country lane in the early hours of Sunday after police were called to reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which hosts US air force missions against Iran.The suspected plot appears to have been foiled by chance when a member of the public spotted unusual behaviour late at night in the countryside from a group of men and called 999.Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air baseDuring the major incident the residents of 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were rapidly evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre and a 400m cordon was placed around the white vans as robots from the army’s bomb squad examined them.Tests were ongoing to find out whether the suspected explosive devices were viable, with bomb robots deployed in the Gloucestershire countryside as investigations continued.View image in fullscreenArmed police maintain a roadblock close to RAF Fairford on Sunday evening.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesAfter their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act. The pictures of the men with their shirts off could point to a precautionary measure against the risk of suicide vests or concealed weapons.At least one van carried the logo of a fuel company and a phone number missing a digit. A real fuel company of the same name firmly rejected any connection to the incident and said: “We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission.” It said it was cooperating with the authorities.In a statement, counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am today (Sunday 27 September), police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase.View image in fullscreenPolice moved on the three vans after a 999 call from a resident who spotted them as she drove home.Photograph: BBC news“Armed officers responded and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.”The arrests come as the war between the US and Iran limps on. In July Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.Counter-terror police and the security services are searching for the motive. The circumstances of the arrest near the base and prior warnings from Tehran leave an Iranian motive high in the investigators’ and government’s thinking. But sources warn nothing is being ruled out, including a jihadist or other motive, and the UK threat level remains at severe, the second highest, meaning an attack is highly likely.location mapWhether there was any foreign involvement forms part of the investigation, and Iran’s ministry of intelligence and security has orchestrated attacks overseas before.Any proven link with Iran would be a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the UK and Tehran. While several recent incidents in the UK have been linked to the Middle-Eastern country, including theantisemitic arson attack on four Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, the alleged plot at RAF Fairford appears to be significantly more serious.And it raises urgent questions for the UK security services after it appeared the authorities had been unaware of the alleged plot, with police only moving on the three vans after a 999 call from a resident who spotted them as she drove home.View image in fullscreenRAF Fairford is a military base that hosts US air force bombers involved in the Iran conflict.Photograph: Getty ImagesThe US president, Donald Trump, claimed to have had the suspects under view for a “long time” and alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” – although the Guardian understands the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.“It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job,” Trump said.The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the incident.He said it was “deeply concerning” and the government will “always take every step necessary” to protect people.View image in fullscreenA B‑1B Lancer bomber parked at the RAF Fairford airbase, which hosts US air force personnel, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersFairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.In March this year, after then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases, four American bombers landed at RAF Fairford and the US started using British bases for “specific defensive operations”.There have been protests in recent months over the UK government’s decision to allow the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.At the time of Iran’s warning in July, a government spokesperson said: “Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.”Evacuated residents of Whelford spoke of “heightened tensions” in recent weeks around the base with more frequent, visible police patrols.Outside Cirencester leisure centre, Jason, a resident of Whelford who declined to give his surname, said: “There have been heightened tensions recently around the base, we are aware it is used by the USAF … It always feels pretty safe. Some residents have seen increased police patrols.”View image in fullscreenResidents of the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre.Photograph: Getty ImagesIt was unclear when people would be able to return to their normal lives; those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles (2.4km) north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.View image in fullscreenFairford youth football club.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersRichard Ocone, the assistant chief constable with Gloucestershire constabulary, said: “We appreciate the disruption this will have caused and would like to reassure them we are working as quickly as we can to get them back in their properties.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care service | Labour conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’
Content: ‘I realise it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me],’ Andy Burnham said of his social care plan.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I realise it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me],’ Andy Burnham said of his social care plan.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianLabour conference 2026Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care servicePM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’Analysis: can Labour hang on to Burnham bounce?Pippa Crerar,Alexandra ToppingandKiran StaceySun 27 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will fight the next election with a pledge to finally fix the broken social care system, acknowledging he is willing to expend political capital by asking taxpayers to cover the cost.As Labour’s party conference began in Liverpool, he pledged to “rip the plaster off” to radically transform care, setting out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everyone in England.The prime minister said the new NHS-style service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details on how his long-term plan would be paid for, indicating that a tax rise may be on the cards.One option could be to link reform of social care with looking again at the pensions triple lock, with government insiders not ruling it out in the future.He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks over “death taxes” would sink the policy.Burnham acknowledged there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement, although he rejected suggestions it could cost £18bn a year. “It’s not that high,” he told the BBC.“Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said. “I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].”But he said he would take his time to work out how it could be fairly funded. “The challenge in the public finances is real. So it has to be done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse. But I will bring forward proposals.”Labour’s annual gathering is intended to be an upbeat affair, with the prime minister wanting to restore hope that some of the country’s most intractable political problems can be solved despite severe economic headwinds.With political courage a theme of the conference, he said in aninterview with the Guardianat the weekend: “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”Burnham acknowledged the public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but he said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems.A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government with limited room for manoeuvre.On Sunday, Burnham said he did not want to focus on a “narrative of doom” about the UK’s economy but that he would show in his leader’s speech that he was prepared to take tough decisions.He acknowledged there was “real concern” in the financial markets about the state of the British economy, pointing to the “febrile” global backdrop. He said he was willing to cut government spending to balance the books, and he believed money could be saved by taking a more “productive” long-term approach to issues such as rough sleeping and youth unemployment.Amid concerns that the government could be hemmed in at the budget by the parlous state of the public finances, he said the chancellor, John Healey, would be “highly prudent” in running the economy. “I won’t do what the previous Tory government did and take risks with the economy that are actually still hurting us right now,” he said.Burnham suggested to the Guardian that a significant fiscal buffer would be necessary, with speculation that the Treasury could now consider £15bn acceptable.“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things,” he said. “But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances.”Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show | John CraceRead moreLouise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, and Healey are using the conference to stress the government’s commitment to boosting British manufacturing through procurement.Healey will tell the conference on Monday he plans to commission three new floating docks to service navy submarines, with the tendering process only open to British companies. The chancellor will promise “a new age of industrialisation”.Meanwhile, Haigh is using her speech to announce a £115m marine research vessel for assessing fish stocks, mapping the seabed, monitoring pollution and responding to marine incidents.Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said the “heavy lifting” on making the case for rejoining the EU needed to be done by the government now, after Burnham signalled that the move could be in the next manifesto.“The pitch rolling must be done now, explaining to the country the dis-benefits of being outside the European Union and the benefits of being part of this family,” Khan said.However, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, appeared to criticise Khan – and Burnham – telling Politico that the speculation “frankly cause[s] a lot of uncertainty for business”.Meanwhile, plans for a third runway at Heathrow are once again up in the air after Burnhamrefused to saywhether he backed the “contested” project, which is delayed by up to four years, saying it was “principally” a matter for London.Explore more on these topicsLabour conference 2026Andy BurnhamLabourLabour conferenceSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Failure to protect free speech could cost Labour votes at next election, says Liberty | Freedom of speech | The Guardian
description: Polling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effect
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Polling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effect
Content: Protesters at a ‘united not divided’ rally in London in September 2024.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters at a ‘united not divided’ rally in London in September 2024.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press/ShutterstockFreedom of speechFailure to protect free speech could cost Labour votes at next election, says LibertyPolling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effectHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 27 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFree speech will be a big concern for voters at the next general election, with the government’s current approach on the issue perceived by many to be bad for Britain, polling suggests.Three in five people said a political party’s position on free speech would affect how they voted at a general election. The human rights organisation Liberty, which commissioned the polling from More in Common, claimed the results showed that Labour’s failure to protect free speech could cost it votes.A significant proportion of those polled felt certain policies and rhetoric by politicians had been detrimental for free speech. For example, two in five said arrests of peoplefor holding signsin support of the banned group Palestine Action had had a negative effect on freedom of speech. That compared with one in five who said it was positive.Only about one in seven thought Andy Burnham cared more about protecting free speech than his predecessor, Keir Starmer.Akiko Hart, the director of Liberty, said:“The ability to express ourselves freely makes us all who we are, and free speech is of vital importance to the British public. These findings should serve as a stark wake-up call for the government, which has lost the public’s confidence on protecting this fundamental human right.“We’re fortunate to live in a nation shaped by many identities and perspectives, which means differences of opinion and sometimes uncomfortable views that could upset or offend others. This requires the government to adopt a consistent, non-partisan approach to safeguard everyone’s right to speak freely while protecting people from discrimination.”Graph on voter opinions on free speechThe polling, released ahead of a joint Liberty and More in Common panel event at the Labour party conference on Monday, also found that more than a third of people believe politicians calling for phrases to be banned at protests is bad for free speech, compared with just over a quarter who think it is positive.When asked about police getting greater powers to restrict protests or marches, a similar proportion – a third – believed it was good as thought it was bad. More than half of people polled said calling protests “hate marches” or “thuggery” had been bad.Starmercalled for “tougher action”against people who used phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – intifada is an Arabic word that translates as uprising or “shaking off” – at pro-Palestinian demonstrations, and therehave been arrests.Graph showing what voters think have been good or bad for freedom of speechThe Crime and Policing Act, which received royal assent in April under Starmer, gave police increased powers to restrict protests, including requiring them toconsider the “cumulative impact”of repeated demonstrations in the same area when imposing conditions. Many civil society groups were critical of the measure.Since Palestine Action became the first direct action protest group to be proscribed,in July last year, more than 3,600 people are believed to have been arrested for showing support for the organisation, most for holding placards saying “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”. Arrests have continued since Burnham entered office.The UK supreme courtwill hear an appeal against the ban in November, having decided it is arguable that proscription represents a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively.Both left and right have complained about so-called “cancel culture” in recent years, with each side portraying the other as the chief culprit.Hart said: “The prime minister must show urgent leadership on an issue that is dividing the country, and change course away from heavier restrictions and towards a principled defence of free speech.”A Home Office spokesperson said:“Freedom of speech and peaceful protest are fundamental rights that this government will always protect. But there is a clear difference between expressing a view and engaging in unlawful behaviour – such as inciting hatred and violence or supporting proscribed organisations. It is right that as a society and a government, we draw that line clearly.”The Labour party was also approached for comment.More in Common polled a nationally representative sample of 2,017 people in Great Britain between 11 and 15 September.Explore more on these topicsFreedom of speechOpinion pollsLabourProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossings
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Exclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossings
Content: Palestinians walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings at the Jabaliya refugee camp in Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersView image in fullscreenPalestinians walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings at the Jabaliya refugee camp in Gaza.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersImmigration and asylumUK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and PalestiniansExclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossingsUK politics live – latest updatesJessica ElgotandRajeev SyalSun 27 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood will announce a new legal route for refugees that prioritises Afghan women and girls and Palestinians, unfreezing a scheme that will put the most vulnerable refugees on a faster path to permanent status.The change marks a shift in Mahmood’s approach to asylum seekers after the abrupt closure of the Afghan resettlement scheme last year and changes that will keep refugee status under constant review for two decades.The home secretary is to say the changes will show there is fairness in the immigration system to support the most vulnerable refugees and that a balanced system will “unlock the inherent generosity of this country”.However, immigration experts and refugee charities have said the numbers who will be eligible are too small to deter asylum seekers crossing the Channel in small boats.The reopening of the scheme is likely to attract criticism from the right, especially as women and girls and people with disabilities are the most likely to be dependent on the welfare state.Reform UK and the Conservatives are also likely to raise questions about security checks – which theHome Officesays will be carried out – after the Sunday Times revealed that a former Hamas bodyguard had been granted asylum in the UK and was recently arrested on suspicion of being part of a terrorist plot.Mahmood will tell theLabour conferenceon Monday that she will reopen the UK resettlement scheme, which was in effect suspended for two years, though never formally closed.View image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood is to say the changes will help ‘unlock the inherent generosity of this country’.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAThe home secretary will say that a tougher migration system, combined with a new scheme for the most vulnerable, will be the best way to ensure there is still broad consensus for helping refugees.“Fairness is what unites us in this country. A fair society is what unlocks the very best of us. Because when people think this country is fair, they are more open and generous to others. When this country feels unfair, people turn inwards. They grow less willing to tolerate difference,” she will say.“I know the British people have not given up on their belief that we should be compassionate, live up to our international obligations, and save the lives of those fleeing war and persecution. But I also know this process must be capped and controlled, and communities must be ready and able to welcome those who come here.“This is what we can do and who we can be as we restore control to our borders, bear down on the small boat crossings, and unlock the inherent generosity of this country.”The Home Office expects about one in four arrivals to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, though numbers will initially be very small and capped each year. Under the scheme, potential refugees will undergo security and criminality checks.Those who arrive via the scheme will have a far more generous route to permanent settlement – granted indefinite leave to remain, which will give them a five-year path, in contrast to the constant review of status for those who arrive via irregular routes such as small boat crossings.The home secretary will also formally open another scheme announced earlier this year allowing community sponsors from next month to apply to bring refugees to build a new life in the UK. A sponsored work route for refugees is expected to follow in the spring.Home Office sources said the plan would be to begin with numbers in the hundreds and grow to the low thousands as levels of illegal migration fall. A cap would be set each year, sources said.Refugees will be identified by the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) and the International Refugee Assistance Project (Irap).The scheme had stopped taking any new referrals in December 2024. By that point, it was being used by only a tiny number. It will be reopened immediately, Mahmood will announce, with priority given to people with disabilities and for women and girls deemed to be vulnerable.Family units will be able to come together under the scheme, though not extended families because of a crackdown on family reunification introduced earlier by the government.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGovernment statistics show that almost 300 “legacy cases” arrived under the existing UK resettlement scheme over the first half of this year. Officials said they were people who had been referred under the scheme before it was suspended and who had taken time to arrive in the UK.View image in fullscreenPeople embark in a dinghy from the northern coast of France in an attempt to cross the Channel to the UK.Photograph: Jean-François Badias/APMahmood will also confirm two of three other settlement schemes that have previously been announced. Starting in October, charities and nonprofits will be able to apply to become sponsors, allowing communities and universities to host refugees. The first batch of arrivals on that scheme are expected to arrive by autumn next year.Applications for sponsors for a work sponsorship route, under which companies will host refugees, will open in spring 2027. Sponsors must provide accommodation, integration support and help finding work, with the aim of reducing pressure on local authorities.Numbers across all of the schemes are likely to be tightly limited, meaning the vast majority of refugees in the UK who arrive via irregular routes will still be subject to new and harsh restrictions on their status.Mahmood has previously announced that refugees will have their status reviewed every 30 months for up to 20 years, with the possibility of returning them to their home countries should those be deemed safe.Madeleine Sumption, the director of theMigrationObservatory at the University of Oxford, said the reopened route bore similarities to a scheme that was closed by Labour last year, and that its impact would depend on the numbers allowed to enter the UK.“It has been framed primarily as a matter of principle – in other words, the UK should be doing its bit, and not as a strategy to reduce unauthorised arrivals.“That is just as well, because there is no reason to believe that resettlement would have a large impact on unauthorised arrivals,” she said. Allowing in the “most vulnerable” in the resettlement part of the scheme would be a “trade-off” because of rising costs to the state, Sumption said.“On one hand, there is widespread political support for the idea of prioritising more vulnerable refugees who would not have been able to make it over on a small boat.“On the other hand, previous data suggests that these more vulnerable refugees, for understandable reasons, struggle more to support themselves in the UK, and fare considerably worse in the labour market, for example, than people who arrive through the asylum system,” she said.Responding to the announcement, Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “The government deserves credit for creating new safe and legal routes that will help refugees reach the UK without risking their lives. Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people-smugglers’ business model, but they only work if they operate at scale. That means thousands of places, not hundreds.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumLabour conference 2026MigrationShabana MahmoodLabour conferenceLabourRefugeesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Britain knew about the Holocaust as it happened. A new exhibition reckons with that truth | Holocaust | The Guardian
description: Research draws upon reporting and witness testimony, while a permanent memorial is planned for London
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Research draws upon reporting and witness testimony, while a permanent memorial is planned for London
Content: Children who survived the Holocaust stand behind barbed wire after liberation from Auschwitz-Birkenau.Photograph: Wiener Holocaust Library CollectionsView image in fullscreenChildren who survived the Holocaust stand behind barbed wire after liberation from Auschwitz-Birkenau.Photograph: Wiener Holocaust Library CollectionsHolocaustBritain knew about the Holocaust as it happened. A new exhibition reckons with that truthResearch draws upon reporting and witness testimony, while a permanent memorial is planned for LondonChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentSun 27 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 16.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe “complex and unsettling” story of what Britain knew during theHolocaustis being explored amid plans to create a new permanent national memorial.An exhibition highlighting how news of the atrocity reached Britain much earlier than is commonly understood will tour the country after being viewed privately by MPs at Portcullis House on the parliamentary estate at Westminster in September.The research draws upon newspaper reporting, broadcasts, academic scholarship, witness testimony and government archives. The exhibition is a sample of a more extensive, permanent exhibition for the nationalHolocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which is planned for a site in London.View image in fullscreenAdjaye Associates and Ron Arad won the design competition for the Holocaust memorial in London.Martin Winstone, the senior historical adviser to the Holocaust Educational Trust, said: “There’s a feeling today that Britain really only found out about the Holocaust at the end of the war. But in 1942, the year in which most victims of the Holocaust were murdered, you couldn’t really escape this information in Britain. It was in every newspaper. It was on the BBC.“The Manchester Guardian was the newspaper that reported most extensively on the Holocaust, taking a crusading position that there was more the British government and allied governments could be doing.”For years, the Manchester Guardian,which was banned from Germany in 1933for highlighting Adolf Hitler’s antisemitism, called for immigration restrictions to be lifted for Jews, lobbied for pressure to be applied to neutral nations to open their borders to refugees and for special rescue measures, realising that “the Nazis were aiming at the complete elimination of an entire group of people”.Much of the information about the Holocaust, including the locations of death camps, was smuggled out of Poland – where the murders were “happening in plain sight” – by couriers to the London-based Polish government-in-exile.Winstone said: “It was a challenging situation. There were lots of things the government had to deal with. And for much of that war, Britain was on the defensive.“On one level, the government’s response was always, ‘we’ll win the war, that’s how we stop this’; while critics said, ‘there’ll be nobody left to save, if that’s what you’re waiting for’.”During the second world war, the government commissioned reports on antisemitism in Britain, with agents opening people’s mail and recording conversations overheard in air raid shelters to gauge public opinion.In what Winstone described as a “complex and unsettling story”, Ministry of Information bulletins revealed that while there was mass public sympathy for Jews in occupied Europe, it contended with anti-migration and antisemitic sentiment.Winstone added: “Nearly everybody in Britain was disgusted about these mass murders, but at the same time you start getting more antisemitic discourse about Jews in Britain – that Jews were running the black market, avoiding military service and spreading panic.“Even before the mass murder began, during the 1930s, there was a significant body of opinion which felt Britain should not be admitting refugees.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWinstone said UK immigration laws in the 1930s were highly restrictive, in part because of antisemitism earlier in the 20th century. But after the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938,Britain relaxed restrictionsto some extent, allowing Jewish children to come from Europe without visas.
