The Manchester Guardian reported how Jewish communities and Quakers in the city set up organisations to support refugees.British women – from MPEleanor Rathbone, to grassroots fundraisers and those who found themselves interned alongside Jews in France – were at the forefront of humanitarian efforts, Winstone said.View image in fullscreenThe independent MP Eleanor Rathbone was at the forefront of humanitarian efforts.Photograph: Hulton Deutsch/Corbis/Getty ImagesA 2021 surveybyClaims Conferencefound 21% of the British public knew the UK government was aware of the mass murder of Jews as early as 1941.UK Holocaust Memorial Foundation is co-chaired by the broadcaster and former Labour politician Ed Balls and the Tory peer Eric Pickles, who said the exhibition would give an early insight into the work being developed for the forthcoming memorial.The exhibition will be at the Northern Ireland assembly from 30 October until 13 November; the Scottish parliament from 7 to 10 December; before travelling to Cardiff from 16 January to 4 February 2027, coinciding with Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January. It is also expected to visit Manchester, with a date and venue yet to be confirmed.The UK Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which would be at Victoria Tower Gardens, Westminster, does not have a confirmed opening date yet, as a planning application is being redetermined by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. TheHolocaust Memorial Act 2026received royal assent this year, granting legal clearance and government funding for the project.Explore more on these topicsHolocaustSecond world warLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Monty Don says he may have to let go of his gardeners after leaving BBC | Gardens | The Guardian
description: Presenter reveals corporation has been paying part of their salaries to keep his Herefordshire garden camera-ready
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Presenter reveals corporation has been paying part of their salaries to keep his Herefordshire garden camera-ready
Content: Monty Don in his garden. He said his current team of two gardeners, a propagation expert and a landscaper had been with him for 10 years.Photograph: Jason Ingram/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMonty Don in his garden. He said his current team of two gardeners, a propagation expert and a landscaper had been with him for 10 years.Photograph: Jason Ingram/The GuardianGardensMonty Don says he may have to let go of his gardeners after leaving BBCPresenter reveals corporation has been paying part of their salaries to keep his Herefordshire garden camera-readyHelena HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor 15 years, viewers have looked in amazement at Monty Don’s beautifulHerefordshiregarden, known as Longmeadow, as he hosted the show Gardeners’ World from his own back yard.But now the BBC presenter, who announced earlier this month that he wasleaving the show, has said he may have to let go of the gardeners who have kept the space beautiful and broadcast-ready.Speaking for the first time since announcing his departure, Don revealed that theBBChad paid part of the salaries of two full-time gardeners to tend to Longmeadow ever since he began hosting the show from his garden in 2011.“I have had two full-time gardeners, and have had them since I have been on Gardeners’ World, and from day one it’s been in my BBC contract that I have to have two full-time gardeners,” the 71-year-old said during an event at the RHS Malvern autumn flower show.Answering questions from the audience during a session hosted at Three Counties Showground, he said this was because the garden had to look camera-ready at all times. “If I’m off filming in the Rhine or India or somewhere like that, somebody has got to be getting it ready,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe presenter has said he would not open the garden to the public, as it is a private space.Photograph: BBC Studios“The BBC pays a contribution towards their wages. Not enough, but they do pay something, which is great. Obviously, that contribution is going to go.”His current team of two gardeners, a propagation expert and a landscaper have been with him for 10 years, he said. “They are a great team and we all work together really well. I will have to think of ways – I can’t afford it unless we earn money from it, so I am going to think of ways of earning something from the garden, but I can’t do that until the middle of next year at the earliest.”The presenter has said he would not open the garden to the public as it was a private space, and organising parking in the area would be too difficult.Don and his wife, Sarah, created the 2-acre garden in the village of Ivington in 1991, at which time it was a neglected field with one hazel tree.It is now split into four gardens: the cottage garden which is filled with shrub roses, the jewel garden with its bright, multicoloured flowers, the Islamic-inspired paradise garden, and the vegetable garden, which provides produce almost year-round.Don said he was leaving the show, which he has hosted along with his dogs, after 23 years because it was “the right time for a change”. He will continue working with the BBC on other programmes, as well as pursuing his own projects, such as writing books.The final series hosted by Don will continue to be broadcast from Longmeadow until later this year. It is understood he will shortly begin filming a travel programme for the BBC, named IslandGardens.Explore more on these topicsGardensHerefordshireBBCEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Late-night drive and a 999 call: farmer’s chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF base | UK news | The Guardian
description: Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight
Content: An officer at a roadblock outside RAF Fairford on Sunday.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenAn officer at a roadblock outside RAF Fairford on Sunday.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyUK newsLate-night drive and a 999 call: farmer’s chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF baseLocal people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnightJamie GriersonandHelena HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called 999 and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later.The resident, who asked not to be named but reportedly is a local farmer, told the Press Association: “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they [the men] were planning. A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the airbase is on high alert. I think it’s absolutely astonishing.”If there had been no 999 call, it appears the authorities would have been unaware of the vans and the potential threat they posed to nearby RAF Fairford.People living in the area have been used to disturbance from protesters and a heavy police presence ever since the decision to allow the US air force to use Fairford as a base for attacks on Iran.But in recent weeks they have noticed dramatically increased security measures, with the gates of the base newly barricaded.Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air base“In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy vehicles across all gates,” another resident said. She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously.”The resident said “great big concrete walls” had also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road.If local people had questioned the necessity of those steps, they may have been persuaded this weekend. In the early hours of Sunday morning, others in Whelford became aware of suspicious activity as the local WhatsApp group lit up with messages.Map showing location of RAF Fairford and Whelford in the wider areaOne resident of Whelford, named Jason, who declined to give his surname, said they were first alerted that something was happening at about 1.30am when people in the chat group started discussing the vans.Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said the 999 call had only come after an attempt to contact the airbase itself. “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.”A photograph published by the Daily Mail showed police arresting five shirtless men at night. Police later confirmed that five men had been taken into custody on suspicion of explosives and terror-related offences.Residents were then woken at 6am by police banging on their doors and telling them to leave immediately. People from 85 households were taken to a nearby leisure centre.Tudsbery said: “[The police] were banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown. There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.”View image in fullscreenUS air force military personnel tend to a Jdam precision-guided munition and a Rockwell B-1 Lancer heavy bomber on the tarmac at RAF Fairford in April.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThirty emergency vehicles were seen in the village, with the army, a bomb squad and counter-terrorism police all investigating at the scene. Explosives experts were seen examining three vans.The RAF base has come to prominence since March and the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran. From the perimeter of the RAF base it has been possible to see heavy bombs being loaded on to American aircraft.Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.Jason, 50, was evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre at 6am on Sunday with his family and 11-week-old puppy, Poppy, and friends who were visiting from London.“We went to bed [the previous night],” he said. “It was early the next morning when the doorbell rang. It was the police asking residents to evacuate as there had been a major incident.”Jason, who works in consulting, said there were about 40 to 50 people in the leisure centre, ranging from toddlers to elderly villagers, as well as a number of dogs. He said they had been given no more details than those that had been released publicly by police.View image in fullscreenA Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is stopped at a roadblock in Fairford.Photograph: Getty ImagesThe Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives. Those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.By Sunday afternoon, the cordon around the village had expanded so no one could get anywhere near it. Access to the village of Whelford remained closed. With RAF Fairford located along one side of the road, a single police vehicle acted as a blockade against further passage into the village.Tudsbery said he hoped he could get home soon. He had left his cat, Misty, behind.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tru – review: a five-star performance of a three-star script about the life of Truman Capote | Stage | The Guardian
description: Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s 85-minute monologue and Paul Farnsworth’s immersive set deserve better than a Broadway museum piece text on the Breakfast At Tiffany’s author
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s 85-minute monologue and Paul Farnsworth’s immersive set deserve better than a Broadway museum piece text on the Breakfast At Tiffany’s author
Content: Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s varied pacing and intonation is immaculately judged.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenJesse Tyler Ferguson’s varied pacing and intonation is immaculately judged.Photograph: Johan PerssonStageReviewTru – review: a five-star performance of a three-star script about the life of Truman CapoteMenier Chocolate FactoryJesse Tyler Ferguson’s 85-minute monologue and Paul Farnsworth’s immersive set deserve better than a Broadway museum piece text on the Breakfast At Tiffany’s authorMark LawsonSun 27 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTruman Capote’s core creative life was brief, peaking between the jolly novella Breakfast At Tiffany’s (1958) and the genre-influential “nonfiction-novel” In Cold Blood (1965).Blocked by drugs and drink, he spent two decades not writing asoi-disantmasterpiece, Answered Prayers, although magazine publication of early chapters led to ostracisation by socialites who found the novel not nonfiction enough.But, in the 42 years since his death, far more has been written about him than he wrote, including the movies Capote and Infamous, a much-toured solo show by Bob Kingdom and a season of the TV series Feud dramatising the fallout from the writer fictionalising rich friends.These authorial autopsies began with Tru, a 1989 Broadway show by Jay Presson Allen, now revived in London by Jesse Tyler Ferguson, familiar from 11 seasons of Modern Family on TV and a sparky recent Palladium turn as Herod in Jesus Christ Superstar.Paul Farnsworth’s design is less set than installation, making the whole Menier a convincing recreation – carpet, wallpaper, ceiling tiles, books and antiques – of Capote’s New York apartment. The audience sits on dining chairs or armchairs and sofas, with Tyler Ferguson speaking from a library ladder and singling out theatregoers for lines.The modern theatrical trend for rhetorical questions to be answered aloud results in Capote’s “Have you ever thought about killing someone?” receiving a vehement “Yes!”An 85-minute monologue – except for a few danced and spoken punctuations by Charlotte d’Amboise as various Capote women – is a feat of varied pacing and intonation that Tyler Ferguson immaculately judges.The title Tru has a silent e and question mark. Capote lied about his own life while publishing upsetting truths about others, issues more current than in his own life or this play’s. Here is a particularly frustrating example of an at least five-star performance of an at best three-star script. I’ve split the difference while wishing Tyler Ferguson a different text. A new play about Capote would require him to offer a stronger defence about treacherous use of others’ lives than a Broadway museum piece that sounds oddly light about addiction and betrayal.At theMenier Chocolate Factoryuntil 14 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreTruman CapoteImmersive theatreMenier Chocolate FactoryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Eva Longoria: Searching for France review – this lovely travel show radiates charm | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s light stuff with more than a touch of Emily in Paris to it, but the actor’s latest travelogue has enough passion to make it highly endearing TV
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: It’s light stuff with more than a touch of Emily in Paris to it, but the actor’s latest travelogue has enough passion to make it highly endearing TV
Content: Eva Longoria tastes French onion soup in Searching for France.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdView image in fullscreenEva Longoria tastes French onion soup in Searching for France.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdTV reviewTelevisionReviewEva Longoria: Searching for France review – this lovely travel show radiates charmIt’s light stuff with more than a touch of Emily in Paris to it, but the actor’s latest travelogue has enough passion to make it highly endearing TVHannah J DaviesSun 27 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’m Eva Longoria and I’m a SERIOUS Francophile!” So begins each instalment of the actor’s Gallic travelogue. France, says Longoria, “is my home away from home”, although she’s usually in the country for work, rather than to experience its abundance of “joie de vivre”. (She does, she notes, have some extracurricular experience with the French, having previously been married to the French-American basketball player Tony Parker for three years.) Now, though, she is on her own adventure, having returned tol’Hexagonefor something “deeper”. Cut to a clip of our intrepid guide in a vineyard, getting acquainted with cabernet sauvignon grapes (“That’s my favourite!” she whispers animatedly), before we segue to her floating gracefully past the Eiffel Tower.Eva Longoria: Searching for France follows the equally alarmist-sounding Eva Longoria: Searching for Spain, and sets up the exciting possibility of an extended Longoria televisual universe, where the Desperate Housewives star makes her way across the entire globe (Eva Longoria: Searching for Equatorial Guinea, anyone?). It’s all been done before on television, of course, but the passion and lightness of touch here make it an endearing proposition.View image in fullscreenDinner with Alain Ducasse and Lindsey Tramuta.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdTake the opening scene, as Longoria orders a baguette in a Parisian bakery, in French, only to be immediately addressed in English – an experience that even the most SERIOUS Francophiles must contend with. She is unfazed, concentrating on the “full sensory experience” of the bread, “from the smell, to the colour, to the crunch, to the warmth, to the taste”. It’s a little bit Stanley Tucci, then (he was the original Searching for … host, withSearching for Italyin 2021). And it’s definitely a little bitEmily in Paris.There’s asoupçonof French history laced through its eight episodes, though never enough for the programme to feel dry. An extravagant meal with the Michelin-hoarding chef Alain Ducasse and the US-born, Paris-based journalist Lindsey Tramuta leads to a gentle conversation about the origins of haute cuisine in the court of Louis XIV at Versailles. We also learn that the bohemian Belleville neighbourhood has strong working-class roots – stemming from the 1871 Paris Commune revolt. Longoria has lunch with Josephine Baker’s son, Brian, who gives a potted history of her life as an entertainer and resistance spy. But trivia is kept to a minimum: this is Searching for France, after all, not Searching for a PhD in French History. Plus, Longoria’s got important business to attend to, such as eating a delicious-looking take on thecroque madame, lovingly crafted by the Filipino-Australian chef Hanz Gueco. (“I thought it was a croque madame because the egg was a boob,” offers Longoria, lowering the tone of Gueco’s establishment.)A few minutes later, Longoria is threatening to lick herpomme pureeoff the plate at a fancy restaurant (Eva,non!). It’s a joke, of course, but there is definitely a sense that our permanently blowdried host plays up her fish-out-of-water qualities – and eating rich and saucy meals in white cardigans and dresses is surely asking for trouble. She’s chic, she’s elegant … she’s dangerously close to ruining her outfit withbouillabaissein Provence.Forget The Traitors: this is truly tense TV.Tucci in Italy review – Stanley works his magic yet again. Tutta bella!Read moreReally, though, Searching for France is a lovely series, unapologetically frivolous and filled with the finer things in life (Champagne! Caviar! Oysters! A whole pound of butter in thepomme puree, which shocks and excites Longoria in equal measure). It also serves as a PR-friendly showcase for some of the country’s buzziest restaurants, not least Mory Sacko’s MoSuke, where west African and Japanese cuisine are fused daringly. It occasionally decides to warm our hearts, too – see episode two, when Longoria visits a social enterprise-slash-restaurant in Marseille, which employs staff with disabilities and offers three-course meals to customers regardless of their budgets. Like Tucci, Longoria radiates easy charm, and – while she isn’t fluent – makes a big effort to conduct her interviews in French. It’s no easy feat, especially in an increasingly anglophone Paris where French conversation can feel more like ritual humiliation.It isn’t exactly meaty stuff, but maybe it doesn’t have to be? What’s more important anyway: learning about the various violent deaths of French kings and queens, or knowing how to make the perfect niçoise salad? Understanding the finer points of Haussmannian architecture, or finding out where to get a slap-up steak tartare? I know what I’ll find seriously useful on my next trip.Eva Longoria: Searching for France aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer now in the UK and on SBS and SBS on Demand in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: How did a solicitor who is the leader of the English Democrats and a Norwegian national fare on Brexit, surveillance and Ukraine?
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: How did a solicitor who is the leader of the English Democrats and a Norwegian national fare on Brexit, surveillance and Ukraine?
Content: Robin (left) and Aslak. All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRobin (left) and Aslak. All photographs: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa’How did a solicitor who is the leader of the English Democrats and a Norwegian national fare on Brexit, surveillance and Ukraine?Sam WollastonSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobin, 68, EssexView image in fullscreenOccupationSolicitorVoting recordAsleader of the English Democrats– an anti-immigration party that wants an English parliament – Robin votes for himself. Never successfullyAmuse boucheEvery year Robin and his wife do a cycle tour of the Netherlands. “There are separate cyclist lanes everywhere and it’s not hilly”Aslak, 55, LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationSoftware engineer and entrepreneurVoting recordHe has lived in the UK since 2010 but, as a Norwegian national, hasn’t been able to vote here. He votes Labour in NorwayAmuse boucheRuns an art gallery that will shortly unveil a controversial work featuring a Norwegian royalFor startersRobinI thought I’d be put with a full-on social justice warrior, but he wasn’t like that. I told him my father was in the army, I was born in Malaya, then sent off to boarding school when I was eight.AslakHe was dressed nicely, shirt and blazer. Almost a stereotypically British chap. We talked a bit about the Vikings because everyone loves to talk about the Vikings when they meet a Scandinavian. He didn’t seem that interested in me or my opinions.RobinI had a prawn starter, he had calamari, we shared a bottle of rioja. Apparently, they do karaoke there – not on this occasion, thankfully.AslakIf there had been karaoke, I would have done Seven Nation Army. I’ve sung in several bands. For main we both had lamb chops, so that’s one thing we agreed on …View image in fullscreenThe big beefRobinWe shouldn’t be involved in Ukraine. We need to focus on our own interests and not get involved in foreign adventures.AslakWhether we like it or not, we live in a globalised world, with international trade, migration, alliances. You can’t isolate yourself. If there’s a war somewhere in Europe, it affects everybody. My worry is if Russia takes Ukraine, or a part of it, they won’t stop. Then there’ll be much more to pay – in money and lives – than from giving some support now.RobinWhen the Soviet Union was dissolved there were promises that Nato wouldn’t expand to the east, promises that have been completely ignored. Most of Ukraine has been part of Russia since Catherine the Great. So from a historical point of view, you can see Putin’s argument.AslakEven if that was true, it isn’t today. A lot has happened in the meantime. Robin was happy for us to arm Ukraine, provided we charge for it. But he also said we should be willing to arm Russia at the same time, like a win-win situation. That sounds more like a business model than foreign policy.View image in fullscreenSharing plateRobinWe agreed people should be able to talk about things rationally. Once you think of another human being as an enemy, you’re not far off the next stage, which is that violence against them is acceptable.AslakWe agreed a bit on surveillance. I’m against the government collecting information on citizens without any suspicions. It creates a scary power balance and causes people to self-censor, which is bad for democracy.View image in fullscreenFor aftersRobinThe English Democrats campaigned for Brexit, and were obviously very pleased with the result. For a long time we have thought the British state, and its commitment to internationalist entities such as the EU, was against our interests. It hasn’t been a disaster economically; trade has continued to grow.AslakThe biggest problem has been alienating your biggest trading partners. And students aren’t coming to Britain to study any more because they don’t know if they can stay. And it’s now no longer people from Europe coming, but from all over the world. I don’t see how this aligns with what a lot of Brexiters wanted.View image in fullscreenDining across the divide: ‘He looked like a Green voter. As you get older you realise it’s unicorn politics’Read moreTakeawaysRobinAslak is a proper lefty, but he’s a proper lefty of the type I used to encounter years ago: rational about it, whereas one of the things we get with the culture wars is wild irrationality. We both said we’d enjoyed it.AslakWe disagreed about most things, but it was friendly and respectful. Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa. Not that I’m woke … Well, maybe a bit.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeAslak and Robin ate atZebranoin Brentwood, Essex.Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: Two helicopter pilots flew down low to wave to my three-year-old son – he was beside himself with joy | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: My son adores helicopters, so we waved as hard as possible as it flew past. Then it suddenly looped and came back around
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: My son adores helicopters, so we waved as hard as possible as it flew past. Then it suddenly looped and came back around
Content: ‘We had a lot of conversations about kindness that day. I told her how I had noticed a softer side to men since having a son.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘We had a lot of conversations about kindness that day. I told her how I had noticed a softer side to men since having a son.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyKindness of strangersAustralian lifestyleThe kindness of strangers: Two helicopter pilots flew down low to wave to my three-year-old son – he was beside himself with joyMy son adores helicopters, so we waved as hard as possible as it flew past. Then it suddenly looped and came back aroundRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesLydia, as told toKatie CunninghamSun 27 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy sister lives in Ukraine; I live in Australia. We had gone five long years without seeing each other when we finally reunited during a trip to Los Angeles. One day we took my three-year-old son to the beach and spent the afternoon catching up.We had a lot of conversations about people and kindness that day. I told her how I had noticed a softer side to men since having a son. As a woman, you’re often wary of construction workers, for example – what might they say to me when I walk past? But now when I pass a building site with my son, the workers often let him play with their radio, or beep a tractor to make him laugh. It was very heartwarming and gave me a whole new perspective on the other sex.The kindness of strangers: I was a ball of stress taking my four children on an international flight – then a passenger tucked a blanket around my sleeping sonRead moreAs I shared this observation with my sister, a coastguard helicopter flew overhead. My son adores helicopters and is always fascinated to see one, so we all waved as hard as possible as it flew past.But instead of carrying on up the coast, the helicopter suddenly looped and came back around. It began flying super low and circled around us twice, with both pilots – two men – waving at my son and mouthing “Hi!” from the cockpit. It was so close it felt like it almost landed right in front of us.We were shocked, as was everyone else at the beach – many people began filming. My sister burst into tears. My son was beside himself with joy. It was, simply, the coolest thing ever.It felt like an embodiment of what I had just been telling my sister – that having a little boy of my own had shown me how good men can be.After the helicopter flew away, we were left with the memory of those two pilots who saw a little kid and decided to do something to delight him, just because they could.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: Republic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over Israel | Nations League | The Guardian
description: First-half goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan gave Ireland a 3-0 win against Israel in a near-empty stadium in Debrecen
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: First-half goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan gave Ireland a 3-0 win against Israel in a near-empty stadium in Debrecen
Content: Troy Parrott gestures after opening the scoring for Republic of Ireland against Israel.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTroy Parrott gestures after opening the scoring for Republic of Ireland against Israel.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesNations LeagueRepublic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over IsraelPaul MacInnesat Nagyerdei Stadion, DebrecenSun 27 Sep 2026 17.24 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFootball and politics are inseparable in the modern world, no matter how many people wish they were not. But whether the beautiful game can ease the ills of our age is another matter. After a week in which the issue of Irish support for the people of Gaza had turned this fixture into a battle of conscience, the outcome of this underwhelming match ultimately felt inconsequential.In the end the result was indeed a walkover, just not because of a boycott. On Saturday night the question had been whether Heimir Hallgrimsson’s side would take to the field in Hungary at all. If they did, would their heads be in the game? It turned out that a week of internal angst had been enough to produce collective resolve among the Irish squad, or at least those selected to play. Strong and assertive from the off, their forwards each scored in the first half to settle the contest, with plenty of symbolic action to assure those back home of their feelings.Israel v Republic of Ireland, Norway v Portugal, Germany v Greece: Nations League – liveRead more“It’s probably been the toughest days of my coaching career,” Hallgrimsson said after the match. “But it’s not about me. It’s about the players and they’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them. They represented themselves on the pitch with dignity but also with the power of proud Irishmen. They’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them and hopefully they will have the support of the Irish people.”In a way the atmosphere in Debrecen was reminiscent of a match played during Covid. Every word uttered in the ground was audible and the nigh-on empty stands carried their own oppressive weight. As the nominal home side,Israelhad been allowed a small delegation of fans, about 150, who were doing their best to be excitable. Meanwhile, two blocks away were the Irish contingent, around a dozen people who had got into the ground despite the Football Association of Ireland’s decision not to bring an away allocation. They were all stood hands in pockets in a stairway.This odd, almost haunted mood was heightened further by Ireland’s mannered approach to the pre-match rituals. Irish staff faced away from the pitch when their national anthem was played. Ireland’s players, all wearing black armbands, stared at the ground during Israel’s. There was no exchanging of pennants and no shaking of hands, with both squads hurried away from the centre circle into their own huddles.The game had come close to being abandoned on Saturday, when the goalkeeper Gavin Bazunumade himself unavailable for selection, his decision prompting emotional exchanges among players and management. Hallgrimsson therefore picked a team with defender Jimmy Dunne nominally a third goalkeeper and also dropped the key forward Finn Azaz to the bench in one of five changes to the team that lost meekly to Kosovo. Azaz’s mother has Israeli citizenship and the Southampton forward was reported to have made an impassioned contribution to Saturday’s discussion. “Today we thought others would fit this game better than him,” Halgrimsson said.View image in fullscreenThe Republic of Ireland team bow their heads during the Israeli national anthem.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesAfter all the soul-searching, Ireland decided the contest in only 11 first-half minutes. Troy Parrott opened the scoring in the 14th minute, turning home a low shot through the body of Daniel Peretz after impressive work on the right by wingback James Abankwah. Two minutes later the lead was doubled when, running on the shoulder of the last defender, Adam Idah collected a smart through ball from Jack Moylan and wrapped a calm finish inside Peretz’s left-hand post.In the 25th minute Moylan got a goal of his own, his fourth in as many caps to continue a stellar start to his international career, driving 25 yards into the box before shooting low into the net. Moylan wheeled away to the corner flag, took off his black armband and kissed it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael raised their levels momentarily in the second half, with the substitute Dor Peretz drawing one excellent save from Caoimhín Kelleher. But ultimately the game deteriorated into just a series of scuffles, cheered on deliriously by the Israeli support who appeared to be chanting for the IDF as the final whistle blew.Their manager, Ran Ben-Shimon, was asked by Israeli media after the match if he would resign following the defeat, to which he answered no. “We didn’t handle the pressure well that is obvious, we failed mentally, we failed tactically,” Ben-Shimon said. “But in a few days there is another game we will have to find the energy to rise again.”Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueIsraelRepublic of Irelandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Thomas Tuchel resists ‘madness’ of calls to rest England players despite longer window | England | The Guardian
description: England head coach says it would not be right to allow his players or the clubs to pick and choose their matches during the elongated Nations League window
Author: David Hytner
Headline: England head coach says it would not be right to allow his players or the clubs to pick and choose their matches during the elongated Nations League window
Content: Thomas Tuchel said he was pleased with England’s performance against Spain.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said he was pleased with England’s performance against Spain.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEnglandThomas Tuchel resists ‘madness’ of calls to rest England players despite longer windowI don’t take calls from Premier League managers, he saysEngland play Czechia in Prague on TuesdayDavid HytnerSun 27 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel says it would be “madness” to allow his England players or the clubs to pick and choose their matches during the elongatedNations Leaguewindow as he promised to go full throttle for victory against Czechia in Prague on Tuesday.The manager did accept that Declan Rice needed to rest and could not be part of the squad in light of the Arsenal midfielder’s heavy workload across a number of seasons and well-documented fitness issues. Rice was at Wembley on Saturday to watchEngland lose 3-2 against Spainin their opening Nations League game.James Trafford’s England dream burns with No 1 spot finally up for grabs againRead moreBut now that Tuchel has his group, he says there is no room for compromise and certainly not to speak to club managers who might want to make deals over their players’ minutes. Tuchel does not want to rotate his starting personnel, although he does accept it could be impractical. After Prague,Englandgo to Rijeka to play Croatia on Saturday before returning to Wembley to face Czechia next Tuesday.“I don’t take calls from Premier League managers,” Tuchel said. “I never called any national team coach [when he was in club football]. I cannot manage [the minutes of] the players. It’s just impossible. I knew as a club coach … if I would call a coach in Brazil or Argentina, they would not know what I am talking about. The players would not know what I am talking about.“Why would I do this and start giving the players the impression that it’s OK to take a step back or share a half or to rest one match? I would never. It’s madness. We want to win the next match. I would love not to rotate but I am not sure if it’s possible. An ideal scenario would be to go again and go again and go again. With six or seven players minimum that start again – to put the responsibility on them and for them to feel the trust.”Tuchel accepted the Spain defeat had increased the pressure for the trip to Prague but he was unconcerned. “It’s nothing we can’t handle,” he said. “We need to be proactive and go for it. There is no room for managing [the players] or an economic style. It’s how the team want to play, how we want to play so let’s go.”Tuchel was asked whether Jude Bellingham, who was at his rampaging best against Spain, could sustain his all-or-nothing style for another three England games in quick succession. “It’s the only style he can play,” Tuchel said.“That’s just his game. It’s not an economic game. Let’s see. I would love to have him four times on the pitch. The concern is that he hasn’t done it this season in this tight period. We will need to check with the physios. We will not put Jude at any risk.”Bellingham created a game-high five chances against Spain, including the assist for Anthony Gordon’s equaliser for 1-1. He won the penalty thatHarry Kanemissed that would have given England a 3-1 lead. His running with the ball repeatedly stretched the world champions. There was also the moment on 35 minutes when he clashed with his Real Madrid teammate Marc Cucurella.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHarry Kane’s penalty miss was costly for England.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“Jude likes that, he gets better if that happens,” Tuchel said. “It’s better if he plays with a bit of rage. It’s what he does. I think sometimes he is looking for these moments to get his fire going. He doesn’t know any [Madrid] teammates [during an international game]. He is still friends with them but not for the 90 minutes.”It was a wild game against Spain. England conceded early and could have been four or five down by the 35th minute. Their defending was loose. They rallied to lead 2-1 at half-time and the match turned after Kane’s penalty miss in the 54th minute when he felt his standing foot give way. Tuchel insisted his team was not far away from beating the very best.“If Harry doesn’t slip we win the game,” Tuchel said. “If Harry doesn’t slip we go two goals up. We were clearly the better team until that moment. Of course, Spain never panic. How far away are we from that? One small slip from Harry.“If we had won, we would have deserved it but it wouldn’t have made us favourites for the Euros. We need to go step by step. They came with their strongest team. We had some key players missing. I am fine with this performance. We could have won the game and didn’t.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelHarry KaneNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Pulis says he and Stoke were ‘cheated’ in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdict | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Tony Pulis says ‘we won’t ever get that day back’ after Manchester City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Tony Pulis says ‘we won’t ever get that day back’ after Manchester City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules
Content: Ryan Shawcross (centre) of Stoke City is consoled by teammates after his side’s defeat in the 2011 FA Cup final.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRyan Shawcross (centre) of Stoke City is consoled by teammates after his side’s defeat in the 2011 FA Cup final.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty ImagesManchester CityTony Pulis says he and Stoke were ‘cheated’ in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdictManchester City won match 1-0 after goal by Yaya TouréClub deny wrongdoing and say ‘process is ongoing’Jamie JacksonSun 27 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Pulis has said his Stoke City team were “cheated” out of the 2011 FA Cup after Manchester Citywere found guilty on virtually all countsof breaching Premier League financial rules.Pulis’s Stokelost the 2011 Cup final 1-0after Yaya Touré’s goal. Yet following Friday’s news that City are guilty on all but one of the more than 100 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, Pulis feels serious discontent. City are expected to appeal and they deny any wrongdoing.Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict | Jonathan WilsonRead more“When do we get our FA Cup?” the 68-year-old wrotein his BBC Sport column. “That is what all Stoke fans have been asking me since the news broke on Friday. I thought exactly the same.“I don’t expectManchester Cityto offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners’ medals their players received. I don’t seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely.“But I still feel cheated. We won’t ever get that day back and the chance to celebrate around Stoke-on-Trent with the cup and medals we so honestly fought for. After breaking the rules, Manchester City got to do that instead. While the process is far from over because City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth.”Pulis pointed to City’s outlay on Touré, who was signed from Barcelona for £24m and earned about £180,000-a-week. He said: “Yaya Touré, who scored the winning goal, was reportedly earning 10 times what we were paying any of our players and, on his own, had cost more than our entire starting 11 when they had signed him from Barcelona in 2010.”View image in fullscreenManchester City’s Yaya Touré (left) scores during the 2011 FA Cup final.Photograph: Andrew Yates/AFP/Getty ImagesPulis underlined how his emotion has been changed by the verdict. “My disappointment was buried in the fact we had played a team full of superstars, and faced an elite coach in Roberto Mancini, and had just fallen short. Today, I feel very differently, as I am sure people connected with the other clubs affected by City’s successes in the same period, between 2009 and 2018 [will feel].“We lost, but to a team that have been found guilty of breaking the financial rules set out by the Premier League. In doing so, they did not just beat Stoke in an FA Cup final, they collected a stack of titles and went on to completely dominate English football for more than a decade. So, with those rules having been broken, what will the punishment be?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTony Pulis of Stoke City reacts in defeat.Photograph: Laurence Griffiths/The FA/Getty ImagesPulis believes action may be widespread. “I know all Stoke supporters will be demanding that City pass the trophy over and every club that has been affected by their actions will be considering their legal options,” he said.On Saturday, Khaldoon al-Mubarak,reiterated the club’s position. “There is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity,” said City’s chair.On Friday a City spokesperson had said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023. The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityTony PulisStoke CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derby | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Alyssa Thompson’s goal before half-time at Stamford Bridge proved enough to earn a precious win for the hosts against blunt opponents
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Alyssa Thompson’s goal before half-time at Stamford Bridge proved enough to earn a precious win for the hosts against blunt opponents
Content: Alyssa Thompson (left) slotted home a rebound to put Chelsea ahead of Arsenal at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Getty Images/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenAlyssa Thompson (left) slotted home a rebound to put Chelsea ahead of Arsenal at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Getty Images/Sportsphoto/AllstarWomen's Super LeagueChelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derbySophie Downeyat Stamford BridgeSun 27 Sep 2026 16.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal’s title chances were dealt a significant blow after a narrow defeat at the hands of Chelsea. Alyssa Thompson’s first-half finish was the difference on a competitive afternoon at Stamford Bridge but one that ultimately left Renée Slegers with more questions than answers about how to save their season.“Worried? No,” Slegers said. “Confidence is something that fluctuates. They know who they are and they know what they can bring. What’s important is that there’s always phases in the season and there’s different things you need to work on or focus on.Liverpool sink Everton and end derby drought after Olsson and Kapocs strikeRead more“It’s important that we keep any pressure and any complexity away from the players because we believe in them. It’s just really important that we keep that simplicity and clear minds for the players.”There is no game quite as eagerly anticipated in the Women’s Super League as the meeting between Chelsea and Arsenal. While other derbies and duels are in their early development, the London derby is the one year after year that brings the pressure, the drama and, of course, the eyeballs. While both sides clearly respect each other off the pitch, there is a distinct sense that once they cross the white line there is true competitive animosity there, one that lifts the levels of everyone in the vicinity.This edition was no different with expectation and apprehension buzzing around Stamford Bridge before kick-off and no shortage of new narratives. This was the first time Katie McCabe, 11 years a Gunner, would face her old team having moved in the summer. Would she help Chelsea to inflict more pain on Arsenal’s stuttering start, or could Slegers’s side put a pin in the pressure balloon and breathe new life into their search for a first title in eight years?Both teams came into this encounter having not yet hit form. Arsenal have created opportunities but have looked predictable in their buildup and lacked a finishing touch. In contrast, Chelsea have looked energetic and full of ideas but, excluding their win against Manchester United, have also struggled with ruthlessness in front of goal.View image in fullscreenChelsea’s Katie McCabe took on her former Arsenal teammates for the first time since her summer move.Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesSonia Bompastor was handed a significant boost before kick-off with the news that both Keira Walsh and Lauren James were available to start. Lexi Potter was given the nod alongside Walsh in midfield, a sign of how much trust the head coach has in the 20-year-old, while Melvine Malard was fit enough to begin up front.Slegers, meanwhile, rang the changes from Arsenal’s hard-fought victory against HB Køge during the week. Two who remained were Kyra Cooney-Cross and the goalkeeper Anneke Borbe, who kept out Misa Rodríguez.The visitors came out full of energy and looking to make an early statement. They dominated early on with 44.2% of the action happening in Chelsea’s defensive third in the first quarter and Arsenal looking to reap the rewards of their high press.Their biggest threat early on came from Lisa Baum. The 19-year-old has been one of the more positive aspects of their season to date and was given space down the right by Chelsea.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all of their control, however, it was much of the same old story for Slegers’s side, haunted by their inability to take their chances. Of the eight shots they created, they failed to register one on target and hit the woodwork twice through Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey.With every rattle of a post that reverberated around Stamford Bridge, Arsenal’s early confidence dwindled and Bompastor’s side started to find more joy. In direct contrast to their opponents, the Blues took their chance when it came when Malard pounced on Steph Catley as she played out from the back. Borbe made a good save to deny Walsh initially but the rebound fell perfectly for Thompson to hammer home.It was the ideal time to score and Chelsea went in ahead at the break with the momentum of the game having shifted significantly. They went on to create big opportunities of their own with Malard dragging a shot narrowly wide on two occasions.While Arsenal were able to create opportunities, the hosts looked comfortable in the circumstances and defended resolutely to see out the game and take home a valuable three points.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueChelsea WomenArsenal WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: The four minutes that lasted a lifetime as Wallabies won all-time chaos classic | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: One year out from a home World Cup, in circumstances comically heroic, this was the match Australian rugby needed
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: One year out from a home World Cup, in circumstances comically heroic, this was the match Australian rugby needed
Content: Harry Wilson of the Wallabies celebrates with the Mandela Plate after a win against South Africa for the ages.Photograph: Paul Kane/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Wilson of the Wallabies celebrates with the Mandela Plate after a win against South Africa for the ages.Photograph: Paul Kane/Getty ImagesRugby unionAnalysisThe four minutes that lasted a lifetime as Wallabies won all-time chaos classicJack SnapeOne year from a home World Cup, in circumstances comically heroic, this was the match Australia neededSun 27 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareWith four minutes to go, and four players down, Australia lead by two tries against the world champions in Perth. The Wallabies have been unbeaten in four matches under new coach Les Kiss, but they have not yet been tested against a rugby power. If they were looking for a test, this is now it.On the arena where the men’s rugby World Cup will begin in just over one year, Australia are showing promise. They had led South Africa 42-17 midway through the second half. Now, the score is 42-31.Wallabies hold off world champion Springboks in chaotic Test for the agesRead moreThe margin is 11, as is the number of Australian players on the field, after a rapid quartet of yellow cards. It’s the kind of proposition that has never happened before in elite rugby union: up by so much but with so few hands, with the time their only friend.The sight seems more appropriate for a quirky Japanese TV show, where 100 children take on three professional footballers, or bright-eyed office workers meet an army in foam suits. Or perhaps in a cheap video game, where a player disappears for each notch of increasing difficulty.This level begins at 76 minutes and 16 seconds. The Springboks have a lineout, 35 metres out. The announcer pleads with the 50,000-odd in attendance to show some faith. “Wol-ah-bees.”The home side’s backline is playing zone against the best side in the world, their loose chain of four covering the width of the field. A straight run from South African hooker Malcolm Marx draws the Wallabies’ utility back Harry Potter into the tackle. A defence that was threadbare now looks naked. “Wol-ah-bees.”The visitors spread it left and there is Australian fullback Tom Wright, 20 metres in from the touchline. Why? Rugby orthodoxy cannot explain it, but he appears to be trying to jam the Springboks attack. Instead, it swallows him like a tide. Towards the corner the green rushes, yet the fatiguing Wallabies scamper across, bringing down the Boks winger Ethan Hooker five metres out.View image in fullscreenAndré Esterhuizen of the Springboks is tackled by Australia players.Photograph: Paul Kane/Getty ImagesAustralia’s desperation means six in gold are committed to the breakdown. If a rugby field is 10,000-ish square metres, the Wallabies have more than half of their players in the corner 25, this postage stamp on a queen bed.Without delay, the Springboks send it right. Ten metres from the try line, Australia’s furthest defender on that side is the flanker Tom Hooper, not even as wide as the near goalpost. The clock ticks past 77 minutes.There are three Springboks unmarked to the right as Hooper grabs and clutches at the centre Canan Moodie, briefly slowing down the surge. But South Africa still have numbers. A try here would give the visitors another two minutes to find the winner. The contest teeters.Suddenly, there is Wright again. Last seen in the other corner, he has managed to cover half the field in seconds. With the trailing Hooper, Wright’s presence somehow compels Marx to ignore the two teammates to his right in the open field, and instead charge forward. Hooper is there again to slow him down.The Exeter player, who this year became the first Australian to be named to the Prem Rugby team of the season since before the pandemic, is not finished. South Africa’s bench scrum-half Morne van den Berg takes a step from the ruck instead of playing in one of four runners to his right. Hooper dives in to dislodge the ball, and its bouncing trajectory is diverted by Wright’s toe out to the 45m.The Australian chase numbers just two, and the Boks are back on the attack. Van den Berg finds the winger Edwill van der Merwe down the blindside, who chips into the open backfield. But his approach angle takes his kick too close to the touchline, and a fortuitous bounce hands the Wallabies a lineout.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe clock reads 77:28. It has been 72 of the most memorable seconds in Australian rugby history. The margin is still two tries. Two Australians are bent over with their hands on their knees. They look up to see the big screen tell them the final whistle is still two and a half minutes away.View image in fullscreenDesperate Wallabies players attempt to hold off Morne van den Berg.Photograph: Janelle St Pierre/Getty ImagesThe referee Andrea Piardi – who has spent much of the second half speaking to the television match official via iPhone after his radio malfunctioned – calls the players to get on with it.From the ensuring throw, the ball slips through the hands of Australian jumper Lachlan Shaw. The Wallabies recover, but only 20 seconds pass before South Africa wrench back control. A masterful piece of guile from Ox Nché, who feigns a tackle on Taniela Tupou just as the Australian prepares for contact. The 140kg prop – known affectionately as Tongan Thor – tumbles forward too far from his support, and Marx and Van den Berg snaffle the ball. Nché soon burrows over for the try.The Wallabies’ last outing was in Argentina,where they could not break a 28-28 deadlock in the final 10 minutes, despite their opposition being down to 13. Now they are the hunted, even if their 11 have become 13 after the return of the yellow carded pair Harry Wilson and Ryan Lonergan.Together, the 13 Australians survive. The suspense is ultimately eased by an obstruction penalty from a disjointed and clearly tired South Africa, who have spent three months on the road.View image in fullscreenHarry Wilson of the Wallabies celebrates the win.Photograph: James Worsfold/Getty ImagesThe finish may be an anticlimax for neutrals, but the victory is significant for Australia. The nation has cooled on union in recent decades. Butthis 42-38 win against the Springboks, one year outfrom the home World Cup, in circumstances comically heroic, is the match Australian rugby needs.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionAustralia rugby union teamSouth Africa rugby teamAustralia sportanalysisShareReuse this content

title: USA’s McNulty transcends chaos of Montreal road race to claim ‘miracle’ world title | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Brandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded him as world road race champion with an unexpected solo win in Montreal
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Brandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded him as world road race champion with an unexpected solo win in Montreal
Content: ‘Until the last 100m, I didn’t believe it’: Brandon McNulty celebrates as he approaches the finish line in Montreal.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Until the last 100m, I didn’t believe it’: Brandon McNulty celebrates as he approaches the finish line in Montreal.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesCyclingUSA’s McNulty transcends chaos of Montreal road race to claim ‘miracle’ world titleArizona rider first US champion since Lance ArmstrongPre-race favourite Evenpoel fails to add second goldJeremy WhittleSun 27 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded the Slovene as world champion with an unexpected solo win in the men’s UCI road race in Montreal.In the biggest triumph of his career, the 28-year-old American took his country’s first win in the UCI’s blue riband event since Lance Armstrong’s lone victory in Oslo in 1993.Vollering pips Niewiadoma to seal dramatic road race world titleRead more“I’m really at a loss,” McNulty said. “Until the last hundred metres, I didn’t believe it, I was so tired. I was just dying, but I kept pushing. We have said for weeks now that we had a super strong team. We talked about it, but I knew it would take a miracle. I guess miracles happen.”McNulty’s 50-second lead at the start of the closing lap of the hilly Montreal circuit was enough to hold on to the finish line, despite a last‑ditch attempt by Tom Pidcock to chase down the American that, at one point, reduced his advantage to only a handful of seconds.Australian Michael Matthews claimed silver while former world champion Mathieu van der Poel of the Netherlands finished third.Pidcock was one of the animators of the final hour of racing, which followed the same volatile and unpredictable pattern as the women’s road race on Saturday, which was won by Demi Vollering of the Netherlands. A gruelling race, ridden without the benefit of race radios, was at times chaotic, particularly within the Belgium team’s confused tactics, with the Olympic road race champion, Remco Evenepoel, left once again to ponder what might have been.With 90 kilometres to go, a select group of a dozen riders, including Pidcock’s British teammate Oscar Onley, went clear on the pivotal climb of the Voie Camillien-Houde. That group reduced to an elite six, including Van der Poel, and this year’s Paris-Roubaix winner, Wout van Aert.In the constant ebb and flow, the biggest loser, seemingly hamstrung by team tactics, was Van Aert’s fellow Belgian and pre-race favourite Evenepoel, who was seeking to add the road race title to the time trial gold medal he won seven days ago. With the leading group increasing their lead, Paul Seixas’s France team combined with Isaac del Toro of Mexico to lead a nine-man group in pursuit. But Van der Poel, recently the author of a successful 172km lone break in the Tour of Luxembourg, pressed on with Onley, the Slovene Primoz Roglic and Quinn Simmons of the US.View image in fullscreenBrandon McNulty (centre) flanked by the Australian silver-medalist Michael Matthews (left) and third-placed Mathieu van der Poel.Photograph: Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press/APRenewed accelerations from Van der Poel finally distanced Onley and split the peloton to an even greater extent. In a succession of regroupings the lead changed multiple times, until McNulty finally and definitively seized the initiative with just over 30km to race.Matthews won the sprint duel for second place, 13 seconds behind McNulty. The Canberra-raised rider previously won silver in 2015 and bronze in 2017 and 2022.“It’s not only the way I raced the race today, it’s after what I’ve been through the last two years with the embolism in my lungs thinking my career was done, to breaking both my arms at the start of this year and thinking my career was done,” the Australian said after the race.“Now bouncing back to being second in the world’s road race, I’m just speechless honestly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I said to my wife at the start today, ‘Let’s just leave it all out there and be proud of the ride and at the end of the day make sure I finish with nothing left’, and that’s exactly what happened today.”Matthewsbroke both wrists in a training crashin March that sidelined him earlier in the season.Twenty-four hours after Vollering’s last-gasp win in a brutal women’s road race, McNulty’s victory was equally enthralling. Vollering’s joy at her success was dampened by the UCI’s decision to fine her 1,000 Swiss francs and give her a points deduction and a yellow card for a “non-compliant” racing position. However, the results were not affected by the post-race ruling.Katarzyna Niewiadoma, second to Vollering in the Tour de France Femmes this year, claimed another silver medal, but the Dutch rider paid tribute to her rival’s efforts. “In the end, your greatest competitors are also your greatest motivation,” Vollering said.As the week of competition ended, the Spanish media revealed that one of the stars of the championships, the Spanish teenager Benjamín Noval, winner of the world junior road and time trial titles in Montreal, had escaped being sanctioned by the country’s anti-doping body Celad.El País reported that in 2024 Noval, who will race for Netcompany Ineos in 2027, had been found working with José “Pepe” Martí, banned for 15 years in the aftermath of the Armstrong doping scandal and prohibited from associating with athletes in any sport. Martí, who remains banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency until June, met Noval for physiological testing while under Celad surveillance, but Noval, who was only 15 at the time of the incident, was not subjected to any sanction.Explore more on these topicsCyclingUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Snedeker says Trump ‘gets all the credit’ after US complete huge Presidents Cup comeback | Golf | The Guardian
description: The United States made a stunning rally to capture an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup title on Sunday, completing a 17-13 victory over the Internationals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The United States made a stunning rally to capture an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup title on Sunday, completing a 17-13 victory over the Internationals
Content: Team USA celebrate their win on Sunday.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTeam USA celebrate their win on Sunday.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesGolfSnedeker says Trump ‘gets all the credit’ after US complete huge Presidents Cup comebackAmericans dominate final day singles contestsUS president gives speech before final dayAgence France-PresseSun 27 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States made a stunning rally to capture an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup title on Sunday, completing a 17-13 victory over the Internationals withDonald Trumpin attendance.Jacob Bridgeman secured the clinching point at Medinah by sinking a four-foot par putt at the 18th hole to defeat Australian Min Woo Lee 1-up.An embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as prop | Leander SchaerlaeckensRead moreThe Americans improved to 14-1-1 in the biennial rivalry after trailing 10.5-7.5 entering Sunday’s 12 concluding singles matches. The Internationals were poised to end a 28-year win drought but fell short once again.The Americans, boasting eight of the world’s 11 top-ranked golfers, won on the same suburban Chicago layout where Europe took the 2012 Ryder Cup with the famedMiracle at Medinah fightback.“These guys never lost faith,” US captain Brandt Snedeker said. “I told the guys last night that funny stuff happens here. Medinah’s got a history of funny things happening, and sure enough, they went out there and played their asses off. I’m so damn proud of those guys.”Trump, who attendedlast year’s US Ryder Cuploss, added tohis 2026 live sports viewing listthat has included the World Cup final, the NBA finals, college football, UFC and IndyCar events plus various golf events.“[Trump] told me I was going to bring some energy today for you guys. You guys need it,” Snedeker said. “And I told him if we did this, he gets all the credit. So thank you, President Trump.”Explore more on these topicsGolfUS sportsAustralia sportDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: England demolish Sri Lanka in ODI series decider as Banton bashes maiden ton | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Tom Banton scored his maiden international century as England thrashed Sri Lanka by 223 runs in the third and deciding one-day international
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Tom Banton scored his maiden international century as England thrashed Sri Lanka by 223 runs in the third and deciding one-day international
Content: Harry Brook lifts the trophy as England celebrate their 2-1 ODI series win over Sri Lanka.Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Brook lifts the trophy as England celebrate their 2-1 ODI series win over Sri Lanka.Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty ImagesCricketEngland demolish Sri Lanka in ODI series decider as Banton bashes maiden tonBatter hits first international century in one-sided winWill Jacks takes last wicket and named player of seriesAli Martinat the Kia OvalSun 27 Sep 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA dysfunctional summer ended on a brighter note for England as Tom Banton’s eye-catching maiden international century and some masterful finishing from Jordan Cox propelled them to a one-sided victory against Sri Lanka in this one-day international decider.The neurosis had chiefly centred around the Test team, in fairness, with Harry Brook’s white-ball sides on something of an upward trajectory in 2026. Hence Brendon McCullum was relieved of only half of his duties as head coach in July.England thrash Sri Lanka by 223 runs to win the deciding men’s ODI – liveRead moreNevertheless the sight of Banton, 126 from 105 balls, and Cox, 76 from 52, helping to put 355 for seven on the board, before Sri Lanka were derailed for 132 all out in 29.1 overs, said something about what is coming through. Had Jacob Bethell and Jos Buttler been fit, both would have been running the drinks in all likelihood.Brook provided a bit of ­inspiration himself, cracking 77 from 66 balls before overseeing Sri Lanka’s disintegration. The call to bat first in a match starting at 10.30am in ­September also went against the norm but ended up securing a 2-1 scoreline – ­England’s sixth bilateral series win in ­limited‑overs cricket this year.“Having not played too much 50-over cricket, you forget how long you have got to bat,” Banton said. “The tempo, hitting a few ­boundaries but going up and down the gears – there were periods they bowled well and I had to respect that.“It’s been an ­amazing few hours. I got close the other day [73 at ­Headingley] and got out at an important time. I came here today committed to what I have been doing. To finally get over the line with a hundred is difficult to put into words.”It was a raw team by the end. The loss of Buttler with a hamstring injury meant Joe Root was the only England player north of 50 one-day caps. And at the end of a long season that saw him thrust back into Test captaincy came the dismissal that has haunted his summer, trapped lbw by a medium-pacer in Janith Liyanage.But as much as Root will be pon­dering this glitch as he heads into a six‑week break before the white‑ball tour of Australia – nine of his 13 ­dismissals this summer have involved the ball thudding into his pad – perhaps it was for the best that England’s well-judged total was driven by the rookies learning 50-over cricket on the job.Take Banton, who before this match had played just three List A games in the past five years – two of which were last week. Not that you would have known it in a 150‑run third‑wicket stand alongside Brook during which the long-levered right‑hander matched his captain by way of aggressive 360-degree strokeplay.Banton ransacked 16 fours and five sixes overall, his half-century ­coming off 51 balls and three-figures just 44 more. Nerves were pretty ­nonexistent as the milestone came into view, Banton dancing down to the spinner Dunith Wellalage and ­creaming him through extra cover to trigger a deserved standing ovation.View image in fullscreenJordan Cox made an explosive 76 from 52 balls during England’s victory.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesWhat happens when Bethell is fit may not just be a question for the Test side and it was not a great day for Ben Duckett to endure a fifth‑ball duck. That said, even in a topsy‑turvy summer across formats that ended bowled by a ball from Dilshan ­Madushanka that swung away and nipped in, the left-hander was ­coming off a fluent 67 in Leeds and 141 against the might of India at Lord’s mid-season.Buttler remains a lock in the side, fundamentally, although Cox has seen his stock rise significantly this season. Arriving at 218 for three in the 35th over – Brook having ­mis‑timed his latest attempt to clear deep ­midwicket – he initially took a look, going at a run a ball to reach 30 before accelerating at the death. His half-century was also his first in List A cricket, this his 10th match in the format.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLike Banton, who had earlier shown his strong wrists with a reverse-swept six, Cox was full of innovation for his six fours and two sixes. The pitch was already offering turn but Cox was equal to it, while his wicketkeeping to the spinners also impressed later on – although he did risk undoing Jofra Archer’s direct hit to run out Pavan ­Rathnayake by ­disturbing the stumps before the ball hit the target.View image in fullscreenTom Banton shows his delight after reaching three figures in the win against Sri Lanka.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersThat incident was the main ­talking point as Sri Lanka crumbled under scoreboard pressure, not least since “Not Out” flashed up on the big screen initially. This was soon reversed, however, with the third umpire Adrian Holdstock clocking that Archer’s shy had knocked the stump clean out of the ground. All good,under Law 29.2.Otherwise it was a run chase that never really got going once Brook threw one of the two new balls to Sonny Baker ahead of Archer and he forced Pathum Nissanka to nick off with a beauty of a second ball. In for the rested Josh Tongue, Baker finally had his maiden ODI wicket after a shellacking on debut last summer.Gus Atkinson picked up two more wickets in the powerplay – Kamindu and Kusal Mendis both sent top edges high into the inner ring – before Liam Dawson, in for the dropped Rehan Ahmed, winkled out three for 26 from eight overs. Will Jacks picked up the final wicket and was named player of the series.A non-event? Slightly. But for ­England, having reached the finish line of a turbulent summer with five successive series wins across ­formats, this was very much welcome.Explore more on these topicsCricketEngland cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Labour is nostalgic for two-party politics. That cosy, simple time is over – let it go | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Our fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is key, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Our fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is key, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Andy Burnham travels on the new Royal Daffodil Mersey ferry on Saturday as the Labour party gathers in Liverpool for its annual conference.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham travels on the new Royal Daffodil Mersey ferry on Saturday as the Labour party gathers in Liverpool for its annual conference.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionLabourLabour is nostalgic for two-party politics. That cosy, simple time is over – let it goJohn HarrisOur fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is keySun 27 Sep 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTShareAsI wrote last week, whatever its current troubles, Reform UK has hardly disappeared. Meanwhile, those black-clad quasi-paramilitaries may well be another augury of a frightening immediate future. One more English settlement – the town of Barnham, in Norfolk – is seemingly poised to stage a pretend independence referendum in protest at plans to locally accommodate asylum seekers. Oh, and our new Labour prime minister has just held cordial talks with a US president who has not only brought a modern de facto fascism to his homeland, butwants to export it to Europe.But hold all those cheerful thoughts for a moment, and let us have a look at the Labour party as it gathers in Liverpool. The slogan plastered all over its conference is “Hope Again” – which, unlike last year’s dreadful “Renew Britain”, suggests that a few people at the top might have belatedly learned the basics of pithy political storytelling.The influence of the two slogans that are accepted modern classics – “Take back control” and “Make America Great Again” – is obvious. In Labour’s case, “again” not only implies how badly Starmer’s reign went, but looks back to a better past and implies that something comparable is eminently possible. You might take it as a reference to the best aspects of the NewLabourperiod, Harold Wilson in his pomp or the magical glories of the Attlee years.The slogan also echoessome of the pronouncements made by Andy Burnhamwhen he became leader, about the positive response of the voters of Makerfield to “the promised return of the Labour they once knew”. And it has to be said: those words and the conference tagline tap into his party’s ingrained nostalgia, and the idea that with enough effort, Labour might return to winning a commanding share of the vote, as it did back in the days when footballers chain-smoked and bowler hats were still a common sight (in 1951, although it lost to the Tories, Labour won a record 48.8%, and Wilson came very close to the same figurein 1966).Numbers aside, Labour still largely believes that by rights it should monopolise the progressive half of politics.
