The Tories have the same idea about the right of the spectrum, which has recently fed into a seductive notion held by both “main” partiesand many pundits: that withZack Polanski’s PR slip-upsand the trouble that has engulfed Nigel Farage, we may be witnessing the rebirth of comfy, cosy, simple two-party politics.What utter rot that is. The UK’s passage into a multiparty system is deeply rooted in a society and economy whose complexity can no longer be smothered by our ludicrous voting system. Look at what has happened where the electoral machinery is different. Labour recentlylost control of Walesto Plaid Cymru, attracting a mere 11% of the vote. The SNP’s dominance in Scotland may have weakened, but it is more than intact. Meanwhile, even with first past the post still creakingly in place, whole swathes of what used to be considered middle England – particularly in the home counties – haveswitched from the Tories to the Lib Dems.At the time of writing,the latest YouGov pollputs Labour on 23% (if that’s accurate, the “Burnham bounce” looks more like a modest bunny-hop), the Tories level with Reform at 21%, and the Greens and Lib Dems on 14% and 12% respectively. The same polling group has also done a multi-level regression and post-stratification – orMRP– that offers a picture of the House of Commons that would be elected if a contest were held today. It forecasts a hung parliament, with Labour dropping to 241 seats, and facing the inevitability of cross-party cooperation. Here, clearly, is further evidence of a fragmented model of politics that will endure for the foreseeable future. And in Liverpool, mostly at fringe meetings, it will be talked about, but not nearly enough.Before he became leader, Burnham seemed to be the only senior Labour politician positively responding to these shifts. He hasrepeatedly backed proportional representation(which he insists he still supports), and said that embracing it would pave the way “foragreement with other partieson wider reforms”. With that, he said, would come “amore honest and collaborativeway of doing politics”, a phrase that chimes withhis promisesof a lot less “finger-pointing” and “point-scoring”. Aside from his talks with the Tories and Lib Dems about social care, what this might look like is unclear; all we know is that Burnham’s drive for English devolution will definitely mean ceding power to other parties, and probably substantially change politics at a national level.And so to the really important bit. Eleven days after the start of Labour conference comes the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Publicly at least, Labour seems to be running a content-lite campaign, though it hasattacked the Greens’alleged fiscal impossibilism and sent members a communique framing the contest as a chance to “get our revenge” for Green triumphs in May’s local elections. The Green leader and candidate, Polanski, is aggressively accusing Labour of a miserable lack of solidarity with Palestine, while an ally also charged Burnham’s party with choosing its contender – the former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali – on the basis of opportunistic “identity politics”. It all looks like politics as usual – and as the far right gains more and more traction here and abroad, what is happening in this corner of London should make us feel very nervous about the next UK general election.The left-leaning cross-party pressure group Compass is about to convene the first meeting of a “council for the progressive majority”, which will bring together leading figures from each of the UK’s progressive parties – including Plaid and the SNP – to firm up how they might collectively defeat Reform. To quote froma recent Compass statement: “There is a progressive majority in this country … yet our outdated political system divides us … splitting the vote and clearing a path for extremist voices to win with little public backing.” This is the kind of urgent warning that will become very vivid in the buildup to the next election, amid campaigning – whatever the efforts of Burnham’s newNational Centre For Information Defence– festooned with lies, deepfakes and worse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA lot of us remain unsure of the exact solutions to a split left taking on a confident, tech-savvy and possibly united right. Electoral pacts tend to look like stitch-ups; parties agreeing to limit their campaigning in certain marginal seats can work much better. Whatever, millions of us – including, it seems, the new PM – increasingly feel that a cultural change is overdue, not least to stop the most basic civilisational values buckling before our eyes.Talking of which, it’s grimly ironic that the man still benefiting most from the fractured politics of the 21st century is Farage, a self-styled throwback permanently surrounded by a cloud of Rothmans smoke. Here, then, is a question for everyone gathered by the old Liverpudlian docks: how can he be comprehensively beaten, possibly when he may end up healing divisions on the right by striking a deal (pre- or post-election) with the Tories, and even Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain? By ludicrously insisting that people must vote Labour whatever their political circumstances? Or somehow cooperating with other parties to ensure his defeat? Those parties also need to change, of course. But the age of monopolistic Labour hegemony is over. Let it go. We need to fight today’s most important battles together, so the prospect of hope might actually start to feel real. Again.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionAndy BurnhamReform UKLabour conferenceLocal politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Surging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bind
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Surging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bind
Content: Andy Burnham (centre) with ministers during a cabinet meeting. He faces a tough autumn in terms of economic decisions.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham (centre) with ministers during a cabinet meeting. He faces a tough autumn in terms of economic decisions.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/EPAEconomics viewpointEconomicsBurnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic realityHeather StewartSurging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bindSun 27 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.11 EDTShareAs Labour heads to Liverpool this week, Andy Burnham haspromised to deliver “stability”in the public finances; but the economic backdrop is anything but stable.The longer the US-Israeli war on Iran persists, the more likely it is that UK consumers will have to swallow higher mortgage rates and energy bills – just as the government is wrestling with its own surging borrowing costs.We are only a few weeks into the three-month period tracking energy price moves that the regulator for Great Britain,Ofgem, will use as a basis to set the energy price cap in January – but it’s been a pretty bleak period so far, with the cost of a barrel of crude above $100 for much of that time.Based on the pricing in energy futures markets, the Bank of England reckonsOfgemcould increase the energy price cap, which sets the maximum energy rates paid by homes on standard tariffs, by an eye-watering 24% in January.At the same time, the Bank’s policymakers – from the governor, Andrew Bailey, down – have repeatedly signalled that while they are reassured high energy prices have not yet fed through into wider inflation, they can’t hold off from raising rates for much longer.“We’ve made it quite clear … that it’s going to be harder to maintain that stance, the longer we have high energy prices,” Andrew Bailey said on Friday.Or as his deputy, Sarah Breeden, who like Bailey did not vote to raise rates in September, put it: “The more sparks we’re throwing in the tinderbox, the more likely we might ​have to turn the hose on it.”Donald Trump made clear over the weekend thathe has no intention of staunching the flames himself,by bringing the conflict to a close.“I’m rejecting their deal,” he told reporters, after Iran made a fresh proposal. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly … we’re winning tremendously.”With UK inflationalready above 3%and likely to rise further, markets are expecting the Bank to raise rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.Such a situation almost certainly won’t happen – the economy would probably be clobbered into submission long before they got there, and inflation with it. But Bailey and his colleagues are widely expected to make a start in November, the week after John Healey’s first budget.Policymakers will also have to reckon with the impact on prices of what is expected to bethe most powerful El Niño weather system in 1,000 years, which as well as being devastating to human life, is likely to drive up the cost of important foodstuffs.Burnham has made offering the public a “breathing space” from higher costs a hallmark of his early weeks in power, with sensible but modest policies, such as the £2 bus fare cap. A new iteration of the Tories’ help-to-buy scheme for first-time homebuyers will follow at the budget,he announced this weekend.But while these offerings show a government keen to help, they risk being overshadowed by the wider picture. With the threat of a surge in energy bills looming, the government is keen to avoid announcing a large new support package, conscious of the cumulative cost of Labour’s interventions over the last year.“I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” Burnham said this weekend. These include the £2.3bn Rachel Reeves spent on lowering energy bills – including by shifting some green levies on to general taxation – and his own VAT cut on domestic electricity, which the Treasury has yet to explain how it will fund.Yet if, as Trump has hinted, the conflict continues until after the midterm elections in early November, global oil and gas prices could remain high for many more weeks – locking in a sharp rise in bills for UK consumers in the new year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEconomists are urging Healey to be bold on energy in the budget, rather than wait and hope. Experts at the research and innovation foundation Nesta arecalling for a gas price stabiliser, for example, that would cushion the blow of higher prices now, at the Treasury’s expense – but bring in additional revenue as market prices dropped in future.Any policy that cuts utility bills has the added bonus of bearing down on inflation, helping ease the pressure on the Bank to act.Adding to Labour’s woes, though, the government’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as the global bond selloff has gathered pace.It has been yet another harsh reminder of how exposed the government’s fiscal position is to the vagaries of global markets, with a knock-on effect for the budget forecasts.There are growing warnings, too, about the risks of market instability caused by the interaction of febrile bond markets and the AI mega-bubble.Labour was already in a tricky fiscal bind, given demands for higher defence spending – not least from Healey himself, who now has the job of finding the resources.The difficult decisions about how to do so – let alone fund Burnham’s wider priorities – look likely to be delayed until a spending review some time in 2027. It is very hard to see how that won’t necessitate a fresh round of tax rises.The plan had been for a relatively modest budget, focusing on plans for devolution, and filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced in the summer.This caution looked out of step with Burnham’s promise of a radical political reset and may be untenable if energy bills are going to soar. He and Healey face a tough autumn.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsEconomics viewpointEconomic growth (GDP)Economic policyEnergy billsEnergy industryUS-Israel war on IranInflationcommentShareReuse this content

title: What’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?  | Brian Logan | The Guardian
description: The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed, says the Guardian’s comedy critic Brian Logan
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed, says the Guardian’s comedy critic Brian Logan
Content: David Mitchell and Robert Webb on stage during Amnesty International’s Secret Policeman’s Ball at the Royal Albert Hall, London, October 2008.Photograph: Ian West/PA Wire/PA PhotosView image in fullscreenDavid Mitchell and Robert Webb on stage during Amnesty International’s Secret Policeman’s Ball at the Royal Albert Hall, London, October 2008.Photograph: Ian West/PA Wire/PA PhotosOpinionTV comedyWhat’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?Brian LoganThe deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changedSun 27 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTShare“Are we the baddies?”, asked the comedy double actMitchell and Webbin theirmost famous sketch, in which two uniformed SS officers look one another up and down and arrive at that inescapable conclusion. And lo, it turns out they are, if this week’s news about the supposed offensiveness of the duo’s back catalogue is to be believed.Their newfound unpalatability made headlines last Monday,when 11 of the pair’s sketcheswere pulledfrom the rerelease of That Mitchell and Webb Look on iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary – a move that led to loud condemnation from the keyboard cavalry in Britain’s never-ending, and never much fun, culture war.Was the BBC right to expunge the skits? There’s an argument that in this instance, a warning or disclaimer might have been sufficient. The sketches in question variously involve jokes about Jimmy Savile,Robert Webbplaying a rude Gandhi (seemingly wearing skin-darkening makeup) and two further scenes in which the comedians wear blackface. In neither sketch are they doing so to depict people of colour, but instead to depict white people (in one scene, re-enactors of historic battles having a go at an African skirmish) who themselves wear blackface. In both, they are alert to their own indelicacy: “Are you sure,” asks Webb repeatedly throughout one, “that this isn’t racist?”Some have argued that sketches such as these – satires on chauvinism, not examples of it – should therefore be spared the editor’s scissors. But that’s missing the point, which is that blackface (and indeed the N-word, which caused the standup comic Alfie Brownso much troublerecently when he used it in his own anti-racist routine) is considered beyond the pale, irreducibly hurtful to a portion of the BBC’s audience, regardless of context.Is it right that it is so considered? There’s no question these terms and behaviours are associated with very real harms. Perhaps the corporation focus-grouped that question – or perhaps it is pre-empting criticism, erring on the side of caution and care. Is it so outrageous that they should do so? The BBC is, as the comedy producer Jimmy Mulville statedthis weekin the most sensible comment yet made on the controversy, “in an impossible position”.For my part, I can’t get too exercised by the removal of a handful of sketches – one of them, which jokes about therecently deceased Bill Oddie, for reasons of common decency, and others on the same basis that 70s sitcomIt Ain’t Half Hot Mumhas long been withheld, without great controversy, from our screens. It feels important, mind you, that the episodes in question should be prominently marked as abridged, much as those Roald Dahl books adjusted for modern sensitivities were marketed as “updated texts”, in a move even more contested than this one. (Interestingly, David Mitchellresponded very cynicallyto Dahl’s “updating”.)View image in fullscreenStill from Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping, with Stevie Martin and David Mitchell.Photograph: Channel 4That act of bowdlerism felt more extreme because it affected (some would say diluted) the entire text, leaving readers uncertain what was Dahl and what was edited Dahl. (On the other hand, unlike in the case of Mitchell and Webb, the unexpurgated versions remained freely available.) In sketch comedy, by contrast, individual sketches can be removed wholesale, leaving the others unmolested. And yet in both cases, there’s a risk the public will be misled into thinking the past was just like the present, and a chance missed to consider that values – and the boundaries of the acceptable – are perpetually shifting and up for grabs.Do measures such as these give comedians the collywobbles? Mitchell and Webb themselves have apparently sanctioned the sketches’ withdrawal. In 2017,Matt Lucas disavowedhis sketch series Little Britain (“I wouldn’t make that show now. It would upset people”) and didn’t sound as if he were doing so just to stay employable; three years later, the show wasremoved from iPlayer and Netflixfor its egregious use of blackface. In my experience, comics don’t tend to consider anything sacrosanct, least of all old episodes of comedy shows. No one is more aware than a comedian of the shifting of social attitudes over time.But equally, comics are – or should be – constitutionally averse to piety. None would wish to see abridgements to vintage comedy become commonplace, nor for what is sayable to be any more strictly policed. All would defend the space for comedy to be uncomfortable, to tease at cultural faultlines, probing what we think and feel about ourselves, one another and the world.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI doubt many comics will expend outrage on this isolated instance of pruning that renders a well-loved series palatable on a mainstream, licence fee-funded platform in 2026. What they will, and what we should, care more about is that the BBC invests in new comedy. And empower it to explore and address the issues that define and discomfit our times as irreverently as Mitchell and Webb did theirs.Brian Logan is the Guardian’s comedy critic, and the artistic director of A Play, a Pie and a PintDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyOpinionComedyTelevisionDavid MitchellRobert WebbcommentShareReuse this content

title: Tony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he? | Tom Baldwin | The Guardian
description: The former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for all, says former Labour party adviser Tom Baldwin
Author: Tom Baldwin
Headline: The former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for all, says former Labour party adviser Tom Baldwin
Content: Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York this week.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York this week.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamTony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he?Tom BaldwinThe former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for allSun 27 Sep 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTShareTony Blair can, apparently, sound slightly wistful when he describes how he once had a cloak-and-dagger meeting withAndy Burnham, who wanted to talk to him about standing for the party leadership. Before anyone gets too excited, however, this wasn’t in the past few months, during which Burnham succeeded in landing the job. The story dates back to 2010. That was when he was a callow member of Gordon Brown’s cabinet and understandably wary of his boss discovering not only his ambition to take over if Labour lost the looming general election, but also from whom he wanted advice.Much has changed since then, not least Burnham himself.His journeyout of Westminster and back again – which in his telling has become an almost spiritual pilgrimage of personal redemption – enabled him to shed the New Labour baggage that proved so cumbersome during his previous, and unsuccessful, runs for the leadership. In common with Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer – all of whom tried with varying degrees of success to distance themselves from Blair – Labour’s latest leader now also wants to keep Blair at arm’s length, and certainly far away from his party conference in Liverpool this week.Their secret meeting long ago nonetheless underlines how often, since he left Downing Street in 2007, Blair has had a residual and sometimes illicit allure for those aspiring to fill his shoes. Part of that is because – with the exception of Starmer – those who came after him failed to win a single general election, let alone three. But it is also that this leader from the past still has a possibly unmatched ability to raise our sights, away from whatever the media tells us is most urgent, towards the colossal compound crisis now casting its shadow across the world and over Britain’s future.Blair does not, of course, always make it easy to agree with him. There was an awful lot to dislike about his5,700 word essayearlier this year, which said Britain had no power to stop either the AI revolution or Donald Trump. It led some to question once more the motives of a former PM whose proximity both to big tech firms and successive US presidents has so tainted his reputation. Burnhamswiftly respondedto the essay by saying Blair just didn’t get “what’s going on” with the impact of “40 years of neoliberalism” on working-class communities. He later promised that the interests of voters in Makerfield, where he was standing in a byelection, would be his test of what made good policy.View image in fullscreenTony Blair with his health minister Andy Burnham at a No 10 summit on reducing NHS waiting times, July 2006.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyIt was, however, a bit disingenuous for himto claimthat Blair agreed “our relentless focus now should be on domestic issues, and fixing our own underlying problems, rather than on re-running divisive arguments about rejoining the European Union”. Indeed, the bulk of the former PM’s essay was about the inability of this country’s politics to navigate an international landscape being churned at terrifying speed by forces far beyond Britain’s control.Conflicts in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have since put further pressure on government borrowing costs and household fuel bills. It is increasingly difficult to see how the inward-looking vision Burnham has painted so far, largely consisting of new powers for mayors and more regulation of privatised utilities, will deliver his promised “good growth in every postcode” any time soon. This week, his determinedly domestic focus relented and he acknowledged the government mustalso offer “resilience”in the face of global storms, before delivering aspeech to the United Nationsin New York on Tuesday night. The speech veered wildly from No 10 North in Manchester to Ukraine, Israel, Iran and China, briefly taking in the climate crisis, before setting out the need to create international safety standards on frontier AI and protect democracy from all kinds of Russian threats, including disinformation on social media.It didn’t go nearly far enough for Blair. On Thursday, his policy institute published a paper calling for Britain to set a course for re-entry into a “reformed European Union” over the next decade. Rather than re-run old arguments about Brexit, he would prefer to start a new one, saying the need for the UK and the EU to build capability in defence and capacity on AI is more pressing than it ever was in the past.Although Blair can point to polls showing a majority of the public and an even bigger slice of Labour voters would support rejoining, there is plenty of evidence to suggest relations with Europe have gone backwards under Burnham’s government. The prospect of Britain drifting alone on the tide of history felt closer to becoming reality last week when the annualstate of the unionspeech from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, made repeated references to Canada, a country about 3,500 miles away to which she offered an associate EU membership, while barely mentioning the UK at all.An EU-UK summit, originally scheduled to have taken place under Starmer’s premiership in May, was delayed until July and then to a yet-to-be confirmed date at the end of the year. What had been talked up as a “done deal” for a youth mobility scheme – by which young people from the EU and the UK could live, work and study in each other’s countries – risks being unstitched by new objections from some of Burnham’s newly appointed minsters that it fails his “Makerfield test”. There are similar claims that the EU’s “made in Europe” policy on supply chains will disadvantage British industry and bea further obstacle to an agreement, while progress that began in February to resolve the issue is said to have stalled.There are a lot of mixed messages on all this just now.Recent commentsthat it must be possible to get a deal agreed with Europe in “an amicable way that will add percentage points to our growth” perhaps made him sound too much like a regional mayor who had missed the past decade of Brexit mayhem in Westminster. But others believe Burnham is considering a big leap beyond the “red line” election pledges that prevented Starmer from rejoining a customs union, the single market or allowing freedom of movement. Over recent days some of those around him have dangled out questions about how, “purely hypothetically”, a case for re-entry could be included in his speech to conference this Tuesday, the 10-year plan later this year or, as Burnham himselfnotably failed to rule out this week, Labour’s manifesto at the next election (whenever that might be).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEither way, the freshly minted new PM will not want to be seen taking inspiration from a sometimes toxic old one. There has been no contact between them since Burnham entered Downing Street and a meeting – clandestine or otherwise – is not scheduled. That seems a shame because, on the issue of Europe at least, Blair really isn’t the worst person from whom Burnham could take advice.Tom Baldwin is a former assistant editor of the Times and a former senior adviser to theLabourparty. He is the author of Keir Starmer: The BiographyExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourTony BlairBrexitEuropean UnionForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: When a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships? | Bianca Denny | The Guardian
description: These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress
Author: Bianca Denny
Headline: These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress
Content: When a famous singer died, Jodie* experienced grief so strong that for weeks she struggled to attend work and was sleeping poorly, Bianca Denny writes.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhen a famous singer died, Jodie* experienced grief so strong that for weeks she struggled to attend work and was sleeping poorly, Bianca Denny writes.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty ImagesThe modern mindMental healthWhen a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships?Bianca DennyThese one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distressThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 27 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 19.13 EDTShare“It came as such a shock. I just can’t believe he’s gone.”Psychologists are accustomed to seeing bereaved individuals. But working with Jodie* presented a unique challenge – she’d never met the person she was grieving. Jodie was reeling after the recent death of a well known singer. Despite not knowing the singer personally, Jodie’s grief and loss seemed as palpable as other patients speaking about the deaths of family members or loved ones. Jodie reported that weeks after the singer’s death, she was struggling to attend work and was sleeping poorly, describing herself as consumed with thoughts of the singer.Jodie was experiencing grief related to aparasocial relationship. This is a social phenomenon in which a person experiences a one-sided psychological connection with a public figure or famous person. While an intimate and intense sense of friendship or connection is felt, the object of attention is oblivious to their admirer’s existence.Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI | Gaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughRead moreParasocial relationships are a normal part of modern life. Many of us are engaged in some sort of parasocial relationship – perhaps with a famous actor, sportsperson, musician or even a fictional character from a novel or television show. We feel we know these people and become invested in their lives. It’s an uncomfortable truth for some that the people we are focused on are, in fact, strangers. They have no reciprocal care for us, nor investment in our lives the way a friend or family members might have.At best, parasocial relationships allow us to tap into a brief fantasy of a life beyond our own, usually one of wealth and privilege. This daydreaming provides a break from the mundane and opens up space for creativity and lateral thinking for some people. But for others, such as Jodie, parasocial relationships can lead to emotional over-involvement and boundary-crossing behaviour. This can fuel psychological distress, especially when a celebrity dies or experiences a controversial or adverse life event.Despite my own general indifference about the singer’s death, I was mindful to not dismiss Jodie’s feelings. The loss was significant to Jodie; pointing out the crude fact that they were strangers would likely damage our therapeutic rapport and may have led to Jodie becoming further entrenched in the parasocial relationship.I attempted to relate to Jodie’s grief by tapping into my own experiences and observations of parasocial relationships: the anguish of many of my peers after Kurt Cobain’s death, the shock at Michael Jackson’s passing (and the complicated grief that followed), and the unprecedented public outpouring of sorrow following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. More recent examples of parasocial relationships also came to mind: fans’ unashamed obsession with Taylor Swift’swedding, and, on a different note, fierce debate about Ariana Grande’shealth and wellbeing.It was important to manage Jodie’s acute distress before we sought to understand why the singer’s death had been so impactful. We devised a plan to reduce exposure to information about the singer and his death, using a blocking app to taper social media scrolling and news consumption to 20 minutes per day. Together with encouraging a walk twice a day, limiting time online went some way to reducing Jodie’s rumination and improving her sleeping patterns.Jodie felt a strong connection to the singer. She listened to his music heavily during a difficult time in her own life, crediting the lyrics as “saving her”. She came to rely on his songs to lift her mood, providing a sense of company and comfort in an otherwise desolate period. These feelings had resurfaced upon hearing of his death. Allowing Jodie time and space to talk about her experience – of both her connection to the singer and the difficult time she had endured – helped alleviate her grief.double quotation markHer focus on other people’s lives had been to the detriment of her own.While our therapeutic work was prompted by the singer’s death, Jodie also detailed other parasocial relationships. She spoke about famous people as if they were in her own social circle, and expressed genuine delight at their personal and professional achievements.It seemed apparent that Jodie was lacking vitality in her own life and had attempted to fill this gap by investing in parasocial relationships. But her focus on other people’s lives had been to the detriment of her own. We set about bolstering Jodie’s real-life relationships and enriching social interactions, included reconnecting with old friends, trying a range of hobbies where she might meet like-minded people, and making new connections through meet-up groups and local community events.Why are we so obsessed with Taylor Swift’s wedding? | Dave SchillingRead moreFor Jodie, parasocial relationships felt safe. There’s little chance of rejection from someone viewed only from afar, and no need to navigate the usual difficulties and disagreements typical of real-life relationships. While parasocial relationships went some way to meeting Jodie’s fundamental need for affiliation and human connection, establishing genuine friendships brought reciprocity that parasocial relationships never could – people who Jodie cared about, who also cared about her.*All clients are fictional amalgamsIn Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.Dr Bianca Denny is a clinical psychologist based in Melbourne. She is the author of Talk to Me: Lessons from Patients and Their TherapistExplore more on these topicsMental healthThe modern mindHealth (Society)CelebrityHealth (Australia news)commentShareReuse this content

title: I have seen with pride how British overseas aid saves children’s lives. That is why I say cuts should be reversed | David Harewood | The Guardian
description: I understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground, says actor and Unicef UK ambassador David Harewood
Author: David Harewood
Headline: I understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground, says actor and Unicef UK ambassador David Harewood
Content: ‘UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end in December 2026, two years earlier than planned.’Photograph: Jonathan Porter/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end in December 2026, two years earlier than planned.’Photograph: Jonathan Porter/AlamyOpinionAidI have seen with pride how British overseas aid saves children’s lives. That is why I say cuts should be reversedDavid HarewoodI understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground. Our choices can do so much goodDavid Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassadorSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 03.33 EDTShareAs Labour party conference approaches, politicians will debate spending priorities, fiscal pressures and the UK’s place in the world. Before those discussions begin, I want ministers to picture a hospital ward I visited in Sierra Leone with Unicef (United Nations Children’s Fund).Inside the special-care baby unit at Makeni regional hospital were rows of tiny premature babies, some no bigger than my hand. Around them stood dedicated nurses and anxious parents, all willing these newborns to survive.Then I saw something that stopped me in my tracks. It was 2019, and I noticed a UK aid sticker fixed above a tiny incubator. Inside was a premature baby fighting for breath. Nearby stood oxygen equipment that staff explained had been funded through UK support. I learned that when power outages struck the hospital, as they often did, that equipment helped keep vulnerable newborns alive.Being in the presence of these sometimes inconceivably small children, seeing the UK aid sticker labelled across the incubators that were keeping them alive, emotion completely overcame me. It was not only sadness. It was pride. Pride that people in Britain, most of whom would never meet that baby or their family, had helped make survival possible. Seven years later, that moment remains one of the most impactful of my life.When you are standing beside a newborn fighting for every breath, politics feels very far away. But the truth is that babies live or die because of political choices.Since 2017, Unicef has supported Sierra Leone’s government to establish special-care baby units, providing sick and premature newborns with specialised treatment that was previously unavailable to many in the country.I met doctors and nurses doing extraordinary work despite limited resources. I saw community health workers connecting families with health facilities, and mothers receiving advice and support.One of them was Josephine, whose one-month-old daughter, also called Josephine, had been born dangerously premature at seven months. She told me she believed that without the special-care baby unit, both she and her daughter might have died during or after labour.That is what aid means. It is not charity, and it is not an abstract number on a government spreadsheet.The results in Sierra Leone show what that investment can achieve. Since the expansion of the special-care baby units began, annual admissions have risen from around 1,000 to 14,000, while survival rates had improved from 78% to 90% by the end of 2025.View image in fullscreenDavid Harewood visits Makeni regional hospital’s special-care baby unit in Sierra Leone, April 2019.Photograph: Unicef/Tom DymondBut those gains are now under threat. Since the start of 2025, global aid funding has fallen sharply as major donors have scaled back support. The UK has already reduced spending on overseas developmentfrom 0.7% of national income to 0.3%. Around the world, programmes that help keep children healthy, safe and in school are facing growing uncertainty. In Sierra Leone, those cuts are no longer a future concern. They are already being felt.I learned last week that the UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end this December, two years earlier than planned.I’m already hearing about the consequences. International paediatric support and specialist neonatal nurse training has ended. Reductions affecting the free healthcare programmes have also damaged the availability of lifesaving medicines for newborns, children and pregnant women.The danger is not just that units such as Makeni might suddenly close. It is that the foundations supporting them are gradually eroded. Medical equipment needs spare parts and trained technicians. Oxygen must remain available. Nurses need continuing training and clinical mentorship. Medicines must reach hospitals. Infection prevention, referrals, outreach and follow-up for small and sick babies all require sustained investment.Without that support, the progress I witnessed will be lost.Sierra Leone is building national capacity. But transferring skills and building resilient health systems takes time. Ending support prematurely risks pulling away the scaffolding before the structure is strong enough to stand alone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe scale of the unmet need makes that risk even more alarming. About 45,000 newborns in Sierra Leone require specialised care each year, but existing services reach only about 31%. Approximately 31,000 small and sick babies are still left without access to the essential care they need.This is not a programme that has finished its job. It is a programme that is working, but still reaches only a fraction of the children who need it. That is why I support Unicef UK’s No Choice But Childhood campaign.The Guardian’srecent reportsuggests that ministers are looking for ways to make a smaller aid budget work harder. That is an important discussion. But the question should not only be how aid is spent: it should also be who it is spent for. If children bear the greatest consequences of poverty, conflict and climate shocks, they should be a clear priority in how aid is allocated.The UK government should ringfence at least 25% of its overseas development spending for programmes that directly support children. The government must also set out a credible route back to spending 0.7% of national income on overseas development. Restoring that commitment will not happen overnight, but without a clear path, temporary reductions risk becoming a permanent retreat, with tragic consequences.I understand the pressures on public finances: governments must make difficult choices. But we should be honest about what those choices mean.In Makeni, they can mean whether oxygen is available when a premature baby cannot breathe. Whether a nurse has the training and equipment to act. Whether a mother goes home carrying her child.The special-care baby unit I visited remains open, for now, but declining support is making it harder to sustain its quality, while extending the same care to thousands of newborns who are still not being reached.No child chooses where they are born, and asLabourconference gets under way, I hope ministers think of children – like the tiny baby I saw in the incubator. That is what our choices can do.David Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassadorExplore more on these topicsAidOpinionUnited NationsSierra LeoneLabourAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: I spent a full hour watching Trump TV. It’s a digital pathway to hell | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull
Content: ‘Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionDonald TrumpI spent a full hour watching Trump TV. It’s a digital pathway to hellDave SchillingThe streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dullSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareAre you currently at an airport? Strapped to a hospital bed, with various tubes protruding from your body? Maybe you’re on a treadmill or visiting an elder care facility? Chained to a radiator in the basement from the Saw movies?If you said yes to any of these questions, you might be watching cable news while reading this column. Or maybe you’re one of the hundreds of people currently watching Donald Trump’s answer to cable news, Trump TV – a YouTube streaming channel that airs nothing but White House-sanctioned content 24 hours a day, seven days a week.Kudos to you for multitasking, and thank you for the click. I know Jacob Soboroff is hard to look away from, but at least finish this.I don’t typically watch cable news. Or broadcast news. I feel like the best way to consume vital information is through the glorious written word, full of context and detail, rather than various “experts” yelling at each other about which one is the harbinger of the antichrist. Instead, I can yell all I want at a newspaper or an internet article and no one can tell me not to. Except the people in the dentist waiting room with me.Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching. I gave myself the challenge of watching this neverending digital pathway to hell for one single hour, hoping I could capture whatever joy is being derived from this American horror story.When I first logged onto the stream, I was “treated” to a 11 March 2016 speech Donald Trump gave in Hebron, Kentucky – which Trump on more than one occasion pronounced “Keentucky”, presumably to mimic local speech patterns. That Donald Trump is just a good ol’ country boy, after all.I came in right smack-dab in the middle of the remarks, which very clearly were not prepared. As someone hyper-allergic to cable news, I don’t often witness the president’s speeches in full. I immediately felt as though I were succumbing to a form of intense psychosis, where reality had begun to melt before my eyes, like an ice cream cone that’s sat out in the sun too long.Trump was describing the stairs at the event, stairs he had to walk up and down. Stairs that he traversed despite his own natural sense of self-preservation. “I might slip, it’s soaking wet,” he said of the stairs. “They’re steel stairs. Four sets of stairs.” I immediately begin to imagine him counting the stairs. Slowly.From there, he played his greatest hits and mocked Joe Biden for falling down. But the big swerve was a backhanded compliment to Barack Obama for not falling down. “The only thing is how he bobbed down. He bobbed. I couldn’t believe that he made it without a major, noticeable fall.” The shock on his face that a healthy adult man would not trip on his descent from an airplane certainly made me wonder. You can tell this man has thought a lot about the best ways to not fall down stairs. Eventually, Dr Oz showed up, and I needed to mute my computer. My Uber Eats order had just arrived, and I didn’t want my neighbors getting the wrong idea when I opened the front door.We got a brief respite from Trump up next, with a re-airing of Melania’s ad … excuse me,speechabout how great artificial intelligence is, from 16 January. “The most powerful skill is knowing what to ask,” she declares. I realized the thing I should be asking right then was: “Why am I watching this?”I hung in a little longer for one more event: the National Prayer Breakfast from 6 February. Paula White-Cain, senior adviser to the White House Faith Office, opened the proceedings by saying: “No president in modern history or perhaps all of history has done more to elevate and protect religious liberty” than Donald Trump has. Except maybe George Washington, who presided over the ratification of the first amendment to the US constitution. The first amendment enshrined freedom of religion into the country’s laws. Also, awkwardly, freedom of speech and freedom of the press. You know, the press Donald Trump kicked out of the White House.Trump TV seems like the next escalation of the president’s obsession with and animosity toward cable news. I remain flabbergasted that someone could care about anything on television that much.At last census count, 342 million people live in the United States. Of that population, between 2 and 3 millionwatch cable news in a given day. The vast majority of those people watch Fox News. And the majority of that majority isover the age of 54.When I say “no one watches cable news,” I am only being mildly hyperbolic. To coin a term, I’m being “semibolic”. Just a “hint of bolic”.Yes, there are people who can’t seem to just turn their TV off out there, but MSNOW, CNN, and Fox News aren’t capturing the same level of enthusiasm as the latest episode of HBO’s Lanterns or your local bird-watching club. That cable news retains any significance in our daily discourse is a testament to how fiercely committed our nation’s leaders are to using it as a battlefield for their ideological warfare. And as aretirement community for ex-politicians.When Trump tried toban CNN, MS Now and the website Politicofor allegations of unfair, dishonest coverage of his administration, journalists had a reasonable fear for the state of freedom of the press in this country. Covering the goings-on at the White House is not, as Trump says, a “privilege”. It is a solemn duty. One that defines what’s left of our democracy. Maybe now, I’m being fully hyperbolic, but I’m a journalist. I should declare my own bias on this topic.Trump’s media blackout gambit backfired, as Fox News joined with their cable cousins to abandon coverage of the president’s activities, thereby ending the press pool that provided audio and video for news outlets. Without the press pool,no one can hear what Trump saysduring his speeches. Thankfully for those who use Trump speeches to calm their nerves before a midday nap, they can count on Trump TV to help them off to slumberland.Back to the Trump TV live stream. He was wearing the same purple tie at the prayer breakfast that he’d worn in Kentucky. If you were not an attentive viewer of Trump TV, you might think you were watching the same speech. I realized that just about everything on this stream is from this year, that we’ll probably never see anything from, say, 2020. But I couldn’t stick around long enough to find out, and Trump TV doesn’t seem to list its programming lineup anywhere.‘Literally state-run TV’: Trump launches YouTube channel amid boycott by US networksRead moreI left the house during the National Prayer Breakfast, just as Trump was getting going, declaring “something is wrong” with the Republican congressman Thomas Massie from … Kentucky. You know, the state Trump loves so much. I started to wonder if today’s Trump TV schedule was merely a troll directed at Massie, who lost his re-election bid in the Republican primary, to the former Navy Seal Ed Gallrein, whomm Trump endorsed. The absurdity of using a 24/7 YouTube stream to subtly mock a political rival for an audience of 800 people seems far more possible when you remember the person behind this project is Donald Trump.I took a 30-minute walk with my dog, and when I got back to my desk, I was shocked to learn that Trump wasstill talkingat the National Prayer Breakfast. Specifically about the size of our military budget, which I believe was a direct quote from 1 Corinthians 13:4–8. As Trump droned on (pun intended), the view counter kept going down. Even the die-hards were getting bored.The launch of Trump TV has been a fairly obvious disaster. Unlike cable news, YouTube has real-time data to tell you how many people are watching something.Multiple media outletstook aswipe at Trump for this folly, though in his defense, most YouTube streams get pitiful concurrent viewership unless it’s MrBeast or live footage of a police chase on an LA freeway. Trump TV was obviously never meant to be anything significant. No one in charge of this stream is trying, unless you count trolling Thomas Massie as “trying”. There are no graphics or lower thirds other than a number to text for “updates” from the White House. There’s no slick editing or editorial perspective outside of the purple tie/Massie element.But is this any worse than the ideologically minded focus of cable news – with the three major channels pointing their rhetorical ICBMs at each other all day long? Maybe Trump TV is actually the best way to consume our sitting president. Nothing else presents him in all of his repugnant glory: vain, myopic and worst of all, deeply, deeply dull. This holiday season, turn on Trump TV for your conservative family members. There’s always a chance that the uncut, unfiltered lethal dose of nonsense will break the spell for good.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsUS televisionUS television industryTV newsTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Bill payers should not fund another rescue for financiers of the water industry. Public ownership can end the cycle of extraction and failure
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Bill payers should not fund another rescue for financiers of the water industry. Public ownership can end the cycle of extraction and failure
Content: ‘A campaign to boycott Thames Water bills has sprung up in the Holborn and St Pancras constituency after repeated flooding caused by broken pipes.’Photograph: Jansos/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A campaign to boycott Thames Water bills has sprung up in the Holborn and St Pancras constituency after repeated flooding caused by broken pipes.’Photograph: Jansos/AlamyOpinionThames WaterThe Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopolyEditorialBill payers should not fund another rescue for financiers of the water industry. Public ownership can end the cycle of extraction and failureSun 27 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.26 EDTShareThis month, a cross-party parliamentary committee said Thames Water should beplaced in temporary state controland that any takeover by its creditors should be halted. The MPs were right. The “special administration” regime keeps the taps running while shareholders are wiped out, creditors take a haircut and the firm’s £19bn of debt is restructured. But it must not then be handed back to private hands. After Thames Water has failed its 16 million customers,polluted rivers,paid out billionsto shareholders and repeatedly demanded higher bills, a City-friendly reprieve would only reward the outrageous behaviour that the regulatory system is meant to deter. Ministers ought to seize the opportunity to nationalise Thames Water.In July, Andy Burnham agreed. On the campaign trail in Makerfield,he told reportersthat “there’s a very strong case for public ownership [for Thames Water] to sort out its problems”. Having entered parliament and become prime minister, Mr Burnham is instead looking at letting elected mayors “oversee” private water companies. There is nothing wrong with more democratic scrutiny. However, oversight without ownership and proper control seems like a sleight of hand.Voices from different wings of the partyrecognise this. Mr Burnham can’t kick the decision down the road for ever.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/AFP/Getty ImagesIn less than two weeks, water privatisation will be on the ballot in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when voters elect an MP to succeed Sir Keir Starmer. A campaign to boycott Thames Water bills has sprung up in the London constituency after repeated flooding caused by broken pipes. When asked by theCamden New Journalwhen the mains were last inspected, maintained or replaced, Thames Water gave “no answers”. IfLabourcannot take a failing private monopoly that ruins lives into public ownership,voters may ask themselveswho will?Polls suggestcomfortable majoritiesof Britons believe water companies should be run in the public sector. Under Sir Keir, Labour’s review of the water sector ruled out nationalisation. Some claim that new models of corporate governance could“subordinate” profits to the common good. But it’s hard to see how a failed regulatory regime will be fixed by more regulation. History has been turned on its head when British Rail is cited as proof that nationalisation is wrong. The state-owned rail firm hadproductivestaff working in an ageing railway starved of investment. By 2011,privatised rail cost 20%-30% more. Sound familiar? Mr Burnham called water “an industry where theshareholders never lose and the bill payers never win”. Deeds, not just words, are needed.England and Wales areoutliers: 90% of the globekeeps water in public handsbecause others understand that a natural monopoly in water offers no competition to raise standards and leaves households as captive customers for financiers eyeing easy profits. Nationalisation comes with a price tag. But, as theInstitute for Fiscal Studiesacknowledges, assessing the true cost to the state requiresvaluing the whole deal and future cashflows, not just looking at metrics that exclude most of what is being acquired. An efficient nationalised water industry should mean cheaper bills. Currently, Ofwat allows industry’s backers to recoup £22bn over five years. A Greenwich University study calculates thatnationalisation could save households up to £160 a yearby accessing low-cost state financing. The upshot of public ownership is that it puts an asset on the nation’s books, whereas privatisation puts the cost on customers’ bills.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterOpinionWater industryNationalisationWater billsAndy BurnhamPrivatisationUtilitieseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Manchester City: a strange kind of glory | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: If a guilty verdict on multiple counts of financial misreporting is upheld against the club, its achievements in the modern era will be forever tainted
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: If a guilty verdict on multiple counts of financial misreporting is upheld against the club, its achievements in the modern era will be forever tainted
Content: Sergio Agüero scores for Manchester City against Queens Park Rangers on 13 May 2012.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSergio Agüero scores for Manchester City against Queens Park Rangers on 13 May 2012.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianOpinionManchester CityThe Guardian view on Manchester City: a strange kind of gloryEditorialIf a guilty verdict on multiple counts of financial misreporting is upheld against the club, its achievements in the modern era will be forever taintedSun 27 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.33 EDTShareIn surveys ranking the Premier League’s greatest moments, football supporters regularly give pride of place to Sergio Agüero’s championship-winninggoalfor Manchester City in 2012. Scored in injury time on the last day of the season, Agüero’s strike against Queens Park Rangers delivered the first league title for City since the 1960s. Knocking their historic rivals Manchester United into second place, it also signalled a new era in which the club replaced United as the dominant force in the English game.“Aguerooooooo!” – the incredulous single-word response from the match commentator Martin Tyler – has entered football folklore. But an asterisk may now be needed at the end of all those Os.Reportsthat an independent panel has found Manchester City guilty of breaking Premier League rules between 2009 and 2023 cast a dark shadow over that day, and much else besides. During that period, the club won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Uefa Champions League, all while under theownershipof Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi ruling family. The inescapable implication of the apparent ruling is that those trophies were won unfairly.View image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan.Photograph: UAE Presidential Court/ReutersThe guilty verdict on more than one hundred separate charges against City has yet to be officially confirmed. It may be assumed that the club – which has consistently denied wrongdoing – will launch an appeal. But rivals are already taking advice over compensationclaimsand the Premier League, which began its investigation in 2018 after whistleblower leaks, must contemplate how tough it wants to be on the most successful English football club of the current era.If the verdict is upheld, the punishment should be exemplary and severe, given the threat to the integrity and credibility of the world’s most popular domestic football league. In essence, Sheikh Mansour and his board standaccusedof illicitly bankrolling the City men’s team’s ascent from Premier League also-rans to repeat champions, using inflated sponsorship deals and off the books payments to fuel the rise. The club hierarchy’s aggressiveresponseto scrutiny conveyed a sense that it seemingly thought extreme wealth – and the political heft of Abu Dhabi’s soft-power project – could confer a kind of impunity.The Premier League’s investigators should be congratulated for staying the course, and this extraordinarily long-running saga should now be brought to as swift a conclusion as possible. It is hard not to feel some sympathy forManchester Citysupporters, confronted with the likelihood that the greatest period in their club’s history will be forever tainted. On the pitch, City’s football during the Abu Dhabi era has at times been of a sublime quality, overseen by an inspired coach in Pep Guardiola. But off it, the biggest financial scandal in English football history is a reminder that the volume of money now washing about at the top of the game has been bad for its sporting soul.During the Premier League boom years, great footballing institutions have lost their spiritual bearings as dubiousbillionaires, debt-leveragingcarpetbaggersand petrostates have muscled in for a piece of the action. In the case of Manchester City, the Sheikh Mansour takeover delivered undreamt of success and that Agüero moment. But if it took persistent cheating to get there, it was a worthless kind of glory.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Facing up to the threat that Reform poses to our democracy | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by John Harris in which he urges Labour to offer hope and change
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by John Harris in which he urges Labour to offer hope and change
Content: A placard depicting Nigel Farage and questioning potential party donations near the Houses of Parliament in London.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenA placard depicting Nigel Farage and questioning potential party donations near the Houses of Parliament in London.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersReform UKLettersFacing up to the threat that Reform poses to our democracyReaders respond to an article by John Harris in which he urges Labour to offer hope and changeSun 27 Sep 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.18 EDTShareJohn Harris writes: “Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?” (Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen, 20 September). Because it is a cult, just as Maga is a cult. It is sustained by faith, not fact. It offers simple solutions to problems of such complexity that most of us are incapable of understanding them.Reform UK would not exist withoutNigel Farage. All his other “parties” only existed because of him. Its self-designation as outside “the establishment” is one of the few truths to be relied on – in the sense that it’s beyond the pale. It is an ethics-free zone. Farage is the tool of the US hard right in the UK. All that’s missing is the Christian end-times nihilism, and not many would be surprised if that clawed its way to the surface soon.Harris maintains that the next general election will be driven by emotion – all choices are. Our biochemistry sees to that before our prefrontal cortex even engages. And the choice will be stark. It will be about “me” or “we”. Do we each retreat to our own little “green zone” or do we hang on to that glimmer of hope and work together?I believeAndy Burnhamis sincere in his desire to do politics differently, but I am disturbed that he has said nothing yet about the systemic change necessary for a new, people-focused politics. The founding of a commission to inform a citizens’ assembly on voting reform would be a clear indication that he means what he says. I live in hope.Lyn DadeTwickenham, LondonThe threat that a Reform-led government poses to the UK is summed up in John Harris’s use of the phrase “munificently funded barbarism”. The rise of Reform and its ruthless rhetoric has helped generate the growth of violent racist militia-styled groups on our streets, whose increasing presence not only intimidates whole communities but creates an atmosphere of lawlessness and insecurity. Simultaneously, billionaires suddenly see an opportunity to buy influence in the UK’s democracy – loudly denied – and elsewhere tax exiles such as Jim Ratcliffe seem empowered to rant about Britain’s decline from when it was the greatest empire in the world.Barbarism, it seems, can attract both interest and vast sums of money from some of the wealthiest people in the world. That alliance of munificent funding and barbarism should alert Andy Burnham and hisLabourcolleagues and all of us who value and want to protect our increasingly fragile democracy.Peter RiddleWirksworth, DerbyshireJohn Harris mentions Aneurin Bevan, one of whose most famous quotes was: “The language of priorities is the religion of socialism.” This is something that many Labour MPs, and perhaps Harris, having read many of his opinion pieces, need to engage with. Their blanket kneejerk opposition, for example, to any justifiable scrutiny of the welfare budget is music to the ears of Reform. Hope and communities at ease with themselves will only follow from credible policy priorities married to fiscal competence.Roger WhitmoreBathHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The final whistle for the football booze ban?  | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Letters: The rushed law probably increases pre-match binge drinking, writes Prof Geoff Pearson; plus a letter from a concerned reader who lives near a football ground
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The rushed law probably increases pre-match binge drinking, writes Prof Geoff Pearson; plus a letter from a concerned reader who lives near a football ground
Content: ‘It is time that this outdated and ill-informed piece of panic law is subjected to evidence-based review.’Photograph: Dan Chung/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It is time that this outdated and ill-informed piece of panic law is subjected to evidence-based review.’Photograph: Dan Chung/The GuardianSoccerLettersThe final whistle for the football booze ban?The rushed law probably increases pre-match binge drinking, writesProf Geoff Pearson; plus a letter from a concerned reader who lives near a football groundSun 27 Sep 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.18 EDTShareThe prime minister is right to identify that the existing ban on alcohol consumption at football matches is viewed by fans as discriminatory (Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands, 23 September). However, the need for reform of this legislation goes much further.The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985was rushed through parliament, despite reservations at the time from the police and football authorities, and the absence of any evidence that it would reduce football-related disorder. Since then, no studies have indicated that the prohibition has reduced drunkenness or disorder at matches, but research has demonstrated how the ban can increase risks to public order and safety.Prohibitions on drinking in the stands probably increases pre-match binge drinking, as well as causing crushes at turnstiles and in concourses. And the equally important ban on alcohol consumption on chartered transport to matches pushes visiting fans who want to drink into town centres and on to already crowded scheduled train services.It is time that this outdated and ill-informed piece of panic law is subjected to evidence-based review.Prof Geoff PearsonUniversity of Manchester Law SchoolMarva Kreel (I love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern football, 25 September) fails to think about the impact on those living near football grounds when thousands of (possibly) inebriated fans spill forth into surrounding streets.I remember people urinating and vomiting against my wall, sporadic fights and being afraid to go out. Since the ban, things have been much more civilised. The rights of some fans should not be prioritised over those of long-suffering residents.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Formerly enslaved people in Guyana embraced collective action | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Letters: We should learn about emancipated people’s extraordinary capacity for mutual endeavour, writes Prof Kathryn A Monk, in response to an article in the Cotton Capital series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: We should learn about emancipated people’s extraordinary capacity for mutual endeavour, writes Prof Kathryn A Monk, in response to an article in the Cotton Capital series
Content: A coffee plantation in British Guiana in the early 1800s.Photograph: Granger Historical Picture Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenA coffee plantation in British Guiana in the early 1800s.Photograph: Granger Historical Picture Archive/AlamySlaveryLettersFormerly enslaved people in Guyana embraced collective actionWe should learn about emancipated people’s extraordinary capacity for mutual endeavour, writesProf Kathryn A Monk,in response to an article in the Cotton Capital seriesSun 27 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTShareYour report (British corporation continued trafficking of enslaved Africans to Guyana 40 years after abolition, 23 August)tells one important part of Guyana’s post-slavery history. There is another that deserves to be better known.In 1839, little more than a year after full emancipation in British Guiana, 83 formerly enslaved men and women pooled their savings to buy the 200-hectare (500-acre) Northbrook plantation. They renamed it Victoria. Other purchases by other groups followed, developing into what became known as the communal African village movement.These were not simply individual acts of property ownership. Many had kept their hard-earned savings buried for safekeeping; the first payment for Northbrook was reportedly carried to Georgetown in coins in a wheelbarrow. Formerly enslaved people went on to buy land collectively, establish villages and devise their own arrangements for managing roads, land and other shared resources. Victoria had established its own code of local government by 1845.Having worked inGuyana, I have always found this one of the most remarkable parts of its history. At almost the same moment that plantation interests were trying to perpetuate the old system, people emerging from slavery were demonstrating an extraordinary capacity for collective action, self-government and mutual endeavour.The history of emancipation is not only the history of what was done to formerly enslaved people, but of what they chose to build once they were free.ProfKathryn A MonkBristolExplore more on these topicsSlaveryGuyanaBritish empireColonialismAmericasSocial historylettersShareReuse this content

title: The pain of letting go of a loved one’s belongings | Bereavement | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Hudson’s article about disposing of her late mother’s possessions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Hudson’s article about disposing of her late mother’s possessions
Content: ‘I was determined to recycle as much as possible, feeding the good things through to charity shops.’Photograph: Jakovo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I was determined to recycle as much as possible, feeding the good things through to charity shops.’Photograph: Jakovo/Getty ImagesBereavementLettersThe pain of letting go of a loved one’s belongingsReaders respond to Polly Hudson’s article about disposing of her late mother’s possessionsSun 27 Sep 2026 13.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.19 EDTShareReading Polly Hudson’s account of clearing her mother’s house (My mum has died – and every decision I make about her belongings feels wrong, 20 September) made me think about my experience of doing the same. I sort of enjoyed the task, viewing it as the last thing that I could do for my mother, and seeing myself as a curator in reverse.I was determined to recycle as much as possible, feeding the good things through to charity shops and going back later to see what had and hadn’t sold. When one charity shop in the Welsh border town where my mother lived didn’t want her manual typewriter, on the grounds that nobody would have use for it, I took it to a charity shop in London, which snapped it up and put it in the window.I kept a number of things, including some clothes that I wear, a sideboard that had belonged to my grandparents and assorted kitchenware. Some things were offered to family and friends who needed them. Correspondence was kept, including a bundle of letters that I’d sent to my mother when I was at college in the early 1980s. Clearing a house can be a peculiar joy – the marking of a life well lived and lovingly remembered.Dorothy StannardLondonPolly Hudson’s final paragraph is spot-on. So long as you have the physical space, it’s not a “now or never” thing. I went through my mother’s things in waves. Many items that were impossible to throw out the first time around had became less so when I revisited them a few months or a year later. It was a gradual process that felt reliable.My sister and I evolved the concept of the “family archive”. So much that we as children were familiar with – such as what our parents looked like on holiday in their 40s – is fascinating to grandchildren who have only known them in old age, and the next generation will perhaps never have seen them at all.We don’t keep everything. Pictures showing 1960s clothing, some predecimal coins and notes, a photograph of the house that was our family home for 50 years. To coming generations, a paper-based diary will be a real curio. A 50s-era small cardboard suitcase will be a suitable home for the archive.Kersti WagstaffBillingshurst, West SussexPolly Hudson has my sympathy. My advice would be to take as much as you can to your own home before deciding. Every item holds memories not only of the person but of them in their home. Take any photos of where the items “lived”. Once removed, it can feel different and decisions may be easier.I am starting a little bit of “death cleaning” before this has to be dealt with by my daughter. It’s slow, because my thoughts are always about “would she like this, would she be upset by me throwing this out or by keeping it?” I still have some of my parents’ stuff. Anyone interested in my mum’s school reports from the 1930s?Jo BannonLondonSadly too late now, but maybe Polly Hudson should have persuaded her mother to downsize before she died. I am filled with guilt at the sheer amount of stuff that my daughter will have to deal with, but at least she won’t have the problem of disposing of the contents of six bedrooms and 18 bookshelves. I now make do with two of each.Margaret SquiresSt Andrews, FifeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
