title: Most of UK’s essential food supply grown in drought-risk areas, report warns | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Keys crops such as cereals, potatoes, sugar and oils grown in areas with moderate to very high risk
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Keys crops such as cereals, potatoes, sugar and oils grown in areas with moderate to very high risk
Content: Wheat waits to be harvested in a drought-hit field in Cheshire, EnglandPhotograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWheat waits to be harvested in a drought-hit field in Cheshire, EnglandPhotograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesFood & drink industryMost of UK’s essential food supply grown in drought-risk areas, report warnsKeys crops such as cereals, potatoes, sugar and oils grown in areas with moderate to very high riskJoanna PartridgeSun 27 Sep 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe vast majority of the UK’s essential foods, including cereals, potatoes, sugar and oil, are grown in areas ofEnglandrated as having a moderate to very high risk of drought.A very high proportion – 81% – of England’s fresh produce is concentrated in parts of the country that are already experiencing water stress, according to the analysis by the nature-focused investment fundRebalance Earth.Three-quarters of England’s wheat (77%), barley (75%) and oilseed rape (74%) grow in parts of the country rated as being at a moderate to very high drought risk, along with 70% of sugar beet and 67% of potatoes, it found.View image in fullscreenDying and undernourished sugar beet in drought-affected fields in Suffolk, England.Photograph: Si Barber/The GuardianIt said about a quarter of the country’s staple crops were grown in areas facing an acute risk of drought, including 30% of wheat and barley, 28% of oilseed rape, 27% of fresh produce and 21% of potatoes.“Drought builds slowly and quietly, and rarely gets the same attention as flooding, but its impact runs right through the economy: lower yields, strained supply chains and higher prices in all of our shopping baskets,” said Kirsty Wilman, the fund’s chief operating and financial officer.Some of England’s traditionally most productive agricultural areas – such as East Anglia, long known as the country’s breadbasket, and Kent, often described as the garden of England – are among those facing the greatest pressure from drought and have seen prolonged periods of dry weather in recent years.The yield from this year’s cereals harvest in England and Wales was described as disappointing in the final 2026 harvest report from the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), with volumes of wheat, spring barley and oats below historical averages across the UK.View image in fullscreenAndrew Blenkiron, managing director of the Elveden estate in Suffolk, next to a new reservoir called Summerpit.Photograph: Andrew BlenkironCrop yields are also significantly lower than normal on the Elveden estate in Suffolk, which is owned by the Guinness family and includes 9,000 hectares (22,000 acres) of farmed land.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“For three years out of five we have been in drought conditions,” said Andrew Blenkiron, who manages the farms on the estate in Breckland, an area on the Suffolk-Norfolk border known for its sandy soil. One of England’s largest commercial farms, they grow cereals including wheat and barley and root crops including onions and potatoes.“Water for food is key for us to function as a business and make sure we produce 100,000 tonnes of food here on an annual basis,” he added.Despite the challenges, Blenkiron believes the UK needs to better use its water resources to continue growing staple foods in productive areas. “If we didn’t grow on this land that is totally suitable for it, we would just import more and let other people deplete their natural resources.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryFarmingDroughtFoodWaterEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo | US news | The Guardian
description: Hurricane Nolo moving away from Hawaiian islands but the threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hurricane Nolo moving away from Hawaiian islands but the threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists
Content: Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday, near Naalehu, Hawaii.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APView image in fullscreenHurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday, near Naalehu, Hawaii.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APUS newsHurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane PoloHurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persistsAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19kph). But theHawaii county civil defense agencysaid a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph (165kph).Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach thePapahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, a national conservation area, early this week.Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center.Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APNear Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, National Guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation.Residents are still recovering fromHurricane Lala, which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.About a dozen people were in the water Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family.Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms are common, but hurricanes are rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact.“We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said.Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo.The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.View image in fullscreenYellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersMeanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds.Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph (205kph) and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph (19kph) about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph (19kph).Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, orSMN, said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday.Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas.The Mexican navy said in a statement that it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitucion.“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican Army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival.Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65kph) and was located about 300 miles (485km ) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.Explore more on these topicsUS newsHawaiiUS weatherHurricanesFloodingMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91 | Music | The Guardian
description: Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York
Content: The Calypso singer Mighty Sparrow. The performer, born Slinger Francisco, has died aged 91 after a brief illness.Photograph: Max Burkhalter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Calypso singer Mighty Sparrow. The performer, born Slinger Francisco, has died aged 91 after a brief illness.Photograph: Max Burkhalter/The GuardianMusicMighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New YorkAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSlinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.Mighty Sparrow: the king of calypso on freedom, Windrush and oral sexRead moreHis death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.View image in fullscreenMighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.Photograph: Frans Schellekens/RedfernsThe Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso fromTrinidad and Tobagoto the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.Explore more on these topicsMusicTrinidad and TobagoCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’
Content: Mike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN, speaks during a UN security council meeting on ‘Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine’ at UN headquarters on 23 September 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN, speaks during a UN security council meeting on ‘Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine’ at UN headquarters on 23 September 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesTrump administrationUN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end warWaltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’Edward HelmoreSun 27 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejectedIran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.Echoing comments byDonald Trumpon Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of HormuzRead moreIncomments to Axioson Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.”Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.“Our conditions are clear, ​and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for ​talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not ​accept “bullying or coercion”.“Iran is not seeking war, but will ​defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.Senate Republicans block Democratic effort to end US war with IranRead moreWaltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranUS politicsIranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Serbia’s populist president Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime minister  | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Vučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and election will test his grip on rule after widespread protests
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and election will test his grip on rule after widespread protests
Content: Aleksandar Vučić gestures to supporters in Belgrade after his resignation on Sunday.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersView image in fullscreenAleksandar Vučić gestures to supporters in Belgrade after his resignation on Sunday.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersSerbiaSerbia’s populist president Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime ministerVučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and election will test his grip on rule after widespread protestsAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue an attempt to become prime minister in an early parliamentary election that will test his firm rule in the Balkan country after nearly two years of protests.Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in the 25 October ballot.The governing populists face a major challenge from a youth-backed movement that led protests triggered bya train station canopy collapsein November 2024 that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad.University students demanded accountability for the tragedy.Their struggle for justice and against corruptionhas grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust the SNS after 14 years in power. Vučić has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.“I am resigning the duty of the president of the republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread discontent. His decision to run for prime minister is seen as an attempt to retain a top position and boost his party’s chances against the student movement.View image in fullscreenVučić supporters light flares outside the presidency in Belgrade after his resignation.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersVučić has toured the country in recent weeks with live coverage on pro-government media. He has opened new roads, offered assistance money and cheaper medicines and visited voters in their homes.The prime minister in Serbia is formally more powerful than the president, but Vučić still played a dominant role during his two five-year terms, sometimes presiding over government sessions and routinely announcing all important decisions and plans.Serbia’s independent Bureau for Social Research has filed a complaint alleging that Vučić has abused a public institution as president to promote his party, which he has dismissed. There has been no response from the anti-corruption authorities, which are under government control.The new acting president will be Ana Brnabić, a close Vučić ally and former prime minister who is the outgoing speaker of parliament. Once a new parliament is elected, the new speaker will take over from Brnabić, appoint the prime minister and schedule a presidential vote.Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including critical media. The SNS has gradually taken control of all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight corruption.The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life. Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign urging the rule of law and an end to corruption.Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling closelyin a referendum-like atmosphere. Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions, as Vučić, without offering evidence, has accused his opponents and critical media of intending to destroy the state under unspecified foreign influence.He told Serbia’s state RTS television on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country planned to stir unrest on election night.Serbia’s efforts to join the EU have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys | Animal welfare | The Guardian
description: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer
Content: The baboons’ presence has affected house prices on the Cape Peninsula, as they raid bins and kitchens and poo on properties.Photograph: Nic Bothma/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe baboons’ presence has affected house prices on the Cape Peninsula, as they raid bins and kitchens and poo on properties.Photograph: Nic Bothma/ReutersThe age of extinctionAnimal welfare‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeysTwo troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answerThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentGloria DickieSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming intorepeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A2025 censusfound that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.View image in fullscreenA community volunteer reminds drivers to slow down to protect baboons in Cape Town, May 2022.Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”View image in fullscreenA young boy at a protest outside the Urban Wildlife Centre near Simon’s Town on 13 September.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersInitially, the CBP’s2025 management planproposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.View image in fullscreenA baboon tries to open a car door. The animals often enter cars and buildings and take food.Photograph: Gallo Images/ShutterstockAnimal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, andsome scientistssay the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journeyRead moreHowever, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.View image in fullscreenA chacma baboon looking through a windscreen on the Cape of Good Hope.Photograph: Ryogo i Kubo/imageBroker/Shutterstock“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsAnimal welfareThe age of extinctionSouth AfricaAnimalsConservationAfricaUrban wildlifeWildlifenewsShareReuse this content
