title: Lime bike profits double as rider numbers surge in England  | Ebikes | The Guardian
description: US-owned firm says average monthly users at UK arm surged to nearly 700,000 with sales up by a third
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: US-owned firm says average monthly users at UK arm surged to nearly 700,000 with sales up by a third
Content: Dockless ebike schemes have fuelled a surge in cycling in London.Photograph: Alex MacNaughton/AlamyView image in fullscreenDockless ebike schemes have fuelled a surge in cycling in London.Photograph: Alex MacNaughton/AlamyEbikesLime bike profits double as rider numbers surge in EnglandUS-owned firm says average monthly users at UK arm surged to nearly 700,000 with sales up by a thirdSarah ButlerSun 27 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLove them or hate them, Lime ebikes are an increasingly common sight on England’s roads with new figures showing annual profits more than doubling thanks to a surge in riders.Lime’s average number of monthly users jumped 31% to approaching 700,000 as it added more than 4,500 ebikes and scooters to its fleet, taking the total to almost 38,000, the company’s UK arm, Lime Technologies, said in accounts filed at Companies House.Thousands of ebikes seized by London councils as anger rises over blocked pathsRead moreSales rose by a third to £148m in 2025 and profits more than doubled to £4.7m from £1.7m, as first reported by the Sunday Times. The progress followed expansion into new cities, including Oxford in 2024 and Nottingham in 2023, adding to its presence inLondon, Milton Keynes and Salford.Despite the surge in trade, Lime’s UK accounts show it employed just 54 people in 2025, up from 39 a year before, largely because it relies on self-employed contractors to shift and service its ebikes and scooters.The company, whose parent, Neutron Holdings, listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange last year valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn), is part-owned by US ride-hailing appUber. Lime was founded in 2017 in San Francisco, California, and now operates in about 230 cities across 29 countries, mostly in Europe.At the time of the listing, Wayne Ting, the chief executive of Lime, said the company was having “conversations with lots of other [UK] municipalities”.View image in fullscreenLime ebikes have become almost ubiquitous in London.Photograph: Melanie Major/AlamyThe English devolution bill, passed in April, gives local authorities inEnglandfresh powers to license rentalebikeoperators and set requirements around parking, safety and accessibility standards.London’s transport body estimated in 2024 that one in 10 of the 1.5m daily cycle journeys in the capital are made on dockless ebikes such as Lime, Forest and Voi.The schemes have fuelled a surge in cycling in London, helped by the patronage of celebrities such as Timothée Chalamet and most recently Kim Kardashian.However, there have been mounting concerns about safety forriders and pedestrians. Rented ebikes were reportedly responsible foralmost a thirdof cyclist collisions with pedestrians that required police intervention.Meanwhile, riders have been injured by defective ebikes while cycling or suffered fractures caused by the weight of the bicycle falling on them,a phenomenon known as “Lime bike leg”.Lime recently began introducing on the UK a new, smaller version of its ebikes, with batteries repositioned towards the back wheel, after safety criticism. More than 1,500 of the new models are now in operation in England.The company has said that more than 99.99% of Lime trips in London last year ended without a reported incident.Charities representing blind residents and people with limited mobility have also raised concerns about the difficulty in navigating parts of London amid chaotic parking of rental ebikes on pavements.London boroughs haveseized at least 3,000 ebikes this year, 2,000 of which were Lime ebikes, a Guardian investigation found, as hire companies face growing calls to stop bicycles littering streets and blocking pavements.Explore more on these topicsEbikesTransportLondonCycling (Life and style)TfLCycle hire schemesCycling (News)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’ve done everything by the book’: EU citizens left in limbo after UK government strips post-Brexit residency status | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Home Office faces legal action after 1,473 people living in UK before Brexit told settled status was granted in error
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Home Office faces legal action after 1,473 people living in UK before Brexit told settled status was granted in error
Content: Demonstrators call on MPs to guarantee the rights of EU citizens living in the UK after Brexit.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemonstrators call on MPs to guarantee the rights of EU citizens living in the UK after Brexit.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/AFP/Getty ImagesBrexit‘We’ve done everything by the book’: EU citizens left in limbo after UK government strips post-Brexit residency statusHome Office faces legal action after 1,473 people living in UK before Brexit told settled status was granted in errorLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSun 27 Sep 2026 08.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHome Officefaces legal action over a policy to strip residency rights from EU citizens who were in the UK before Brexit on the grounds that it gave them the status “in error”.It comes as a Home Office ministerrevealed that the government has contacted 1,473 citizenswith post-Brexit residency rights to tell them the original decision to grant them residency was made in error.The campaign group the3million, which is aware of at least 50 cases, has put the Home Office on notice that it is seeking a judicial review of the policy, which it enacted in late 2025 but has only recently come to light.“In many cases, the Home Office is actually wrong to say there was a mistake. So people whose status was properly granted are now fighting not to lose it – this is a clear breach of the withdrawal agreement,” it said in anappealto supporters to fund their case.Some of those who received notice were told they were not entitled to pre-settled or settled status because they did not submit passports with their original application.This includes a group of Brazilians and others with dual Italian nationality by birth whom the Home Office claimed were not Italian at the time of their pre-Brexit residency applications.Among them is a 33-year-old Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018, when he arrived for a PhD, and now has “settled status” – permanent residency granted after five years.View image in fullscreenThe3million campaign group is aware of at least 50 cases and is seeking support for a judicial review of the policy.Photograph: Kristian Buus/AlamyAs a consequence of the alleged Home Office error, he stands to lose withdrawal agreement rights to have his wife living with him, causing him great stress when he received the letter.“It was quite devastating for both of us. We have been here for a long time. We have done everything by the book, and we’ve always felt very welcome here and I always thought this is somewhere I could grow my career,”Fabio (not his real name) told the Guardianlast month.A woman working in the NHS and researching a PhD, who also received the “error” notification, saidher life had been turned upside down.“I can lose my job, I maybe don’t have the right even to rent the property that I’m living in now, because of course I have to prove my right to live here to the landlord to rent a place,” she said.The Home Office said those granted pre-settled status in error were “not withdrawal agreement beneficiaries” but could provide evidence to the contrary if they had it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“A person granted PSS in error can also make a further valid application to the EUSS [EU settlement scheme] which, if refused, will give rise to a right of appeal,” it said.The Home Office recently conceded it was wrong in one case that was taken to an administrative court. It agreed to withdraw its decision that the claimant’s pre-settled status had been “granted in error”, and that the receipt of a physical Italian passport after Brexit was not the date at which her Italian citizenship started.For Fabio, the case gives hope but the judicial review would give a determination for everyone in his situation.“Despite being hopeful, we are still in a limbo as we started an appeal process and haven’t received any communication from the Home Office regarding the fact that they are now conceding their mistake,” he said.He said he was concerned they would have continue with a costly court case to resolve the matter which could leave them with a bill of more than £5,000.Explore more on these topicsBrexitEuropean UnionForeign policyHome OfficeImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three in four UK GPs ‘too busy to talk to their patients in depth’ | GPs | The Guardian
description: Family doctors’ professional body finds the majority have no time to discuss preventative measures
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Family doctors’ professional body finds the majority have no time to discuss preventative measures
Content: GPs also be may be missing conditions that could be treated earlier, one expert said.Photograph: parkerphotography/AlamyView image in fullscreenGPs also be may be missing conditions that could be treated earlier, one expert said.Photograph: parkerphotography/AlamyGPsThree in four UK GPs ‘too busy to talk to their patients in depth’Family doctors’ professional body finds the majority have no time to discuss preventative measuresDenis CampbellHealth policy editorSun 27 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA friendly chat with your GP about your life, health and happiness was once a key part of the UK’s family doctor service.But mostGPsno longer have time to have pastoral conversations, because they are too busy dealing with the country’s rising tide of illness, research reveals.Three out of four family doctors are now too time-pressed to talk to patients in depth about how they might stop smoking, lose weight or get more sleep, the Royal College of GPs has found.Intense demands and 10-minute appointment slots mean they also miss opportunities to discuss taking more exercise or review their medications to see if they still need to be on them.The time to explore patients’ circumstances more fully and offer healthy living advice has been squeezed out of family doctors’ busy schedules, the head of the college said.An RCGP survey of 2,316 GPs across the UK found that 75% had too little time to offer preventative healthcare, such as offering lifestyle advice and giving advice on vaccinations. The results have raised concern about the government’s drive for theNHS– especially GPs – to do more to prevent people getting ill in the first place. One health expert called them alarming.The college’s president, Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, who is a GP in east London, said: “General practice is dealing with enormous demand, so in a busy consultation we inevitably have to prioritise the problems that most need our attention that day.“We will always act on symptoms or findings that need investigation or treatment. What can be squeezed out is the time to step back and look more holistically at how we can help that patient stay well in the long term.“That might mean having a proper conversation with someone who smokes. We will of course advise patients about stopping smoking. But in a busy consultation there may not be enough time to explore in depth whether they want to stop, what has made it difficult in the past, what concerns they have and what support or treatment might work best for them.“It is often the depth of those conversations, rather than simply identifying a risk and giving brief advice, that requires time.”GPs already deliver important preventative care every day, she said. But “the reality is that when you’re working in a busy surgery, with a long list of patients to be seen, there isn’t always enough time in consultations to go beyond the issue a patient has come in for that day”.The chief executive of the King’s Fund health thinktank, Sarah Woolnough, said: “With life expectancy in the UK among the lowest of most comparable countries, these findings are alarming as many GPs say they are too overwhelmed to carry out these important interventions, and may be missing conditions that could be treated earlier.“GPs are often frustrated that the increasing demands for appointments mean they don’t have time to provide the holistic care they were trained for.”The RCGP makes clear in its report that the NHS needs to employ more GPs and ensure they have more time with patients in order to fulfil the prevention ambition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe findings raise questions about ministers’ plan to make the NHS in England move “from sickness to prevention” in how it operates – one of the three “big shifts” outlined in the government’s10-year health planlast year.“Talk around shifting from sickness to prevention is meaningless if we cannot get these basics right first,” Woolnough said.“If the government is serious on prevention, then more action is needed to support and enable GPs to consistently catch conditions and ill-health early, keeping people healthier for longer, and reducing pressures on wider NHS services down the line.”A separate representative survey of 2,000 UK voters which the pollsters Censuswide undertook for the RCGP showed that 64% of the public trust family doctors to offer advice on healthy living. That was more than trust the NHS website (51%), pharmacists (38%), family and friends (22%), AI chatbots (7%) and social media influencers (5%).The Department ofHealthand Social Care did not comment directly on the RCGP’s findings, but a spokesperson said: “GPs play a vital role in our National Health Service, which is exactly why we’ve placed them at the heart of our 10-year health plan and our shift to community and neighbourhood health services.Noting an investment of £1.7bn into general practice and the recruitment of 2,000 additonal GPs, they said: “We know there is more to do and we will continue to work with the Royal College of General Practitioners and other partners as we rebuild and modernise the NHS.“We are already making progress, with record numbers of appointments being delivered, and 77% of patients now saying they have a good local GP service.”Explore more on these topicsGPsDoctorsHealthNHSHealth policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Houses can be built on floodplains despite failing safety test, says high court | Planning policy | The Guardian
description: Decision to allow 190 controversial new homes in north Somerset sparks campaign for change in the law
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Decision to allow 190 controversial new homes in north Somerset sparks campaign for change in the law
Content: Locals at the site of the floodplain in the village of Yatton, north Somerset.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLocals at the site of the floodplain in the village of Yatton, north Somerset.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianPlanning policyHouses can be built on floodplains despite failing safety test, says high courtDecision to allow development of 190 new homes in north Somerset sparks campaign for change in the lawAmelia HillSun 27 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouses can be built on floodplains even if they fail a crucial safety test, according to a high court judgment that will be of “immense interest” to developers acrossEnglandand Wales.The ruling clears the way for a highly controversial development of 190 new homes on north Somerset’s floodplains, despite the site being in “flood zone 3a”, the highest level of flood risk before land is considered a functional floodplain.Ministers and experts are so disturbed by the decision that it was agreed at a flood resilienceconferenceon Wednesday to campaign for a change in the law that would stop the ruling setting a national precedent.As a result, Tessa Munt, the chair of the flooding and flooded communities all-party parliamentary group (APPG), will now meet Matthew Pennycook, the housing and planning minister, to ask him to change the national planning policy framework (NPPF).“This is a dangerous and nationally significant exploitation of planning loopholes,” Munt said. “Tragically, we’ve lost the battle in north Somerset, but we need to change the framework as a matter of urgency, so this ruling doesn’t result in planners and developers across the country making similar speculative housing applications.”View image in fullscreenA sign in the village of Yatton, north Somerset.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianCharles Banner KC, who represented Persimmon Homes at the court case brought by the local council, agreed the decision was of national significance. His chambers, Keating Chambers, said the result was “hugely important”. “This decision will be of immense interest to the planning and development sector,” it added.Persimmon Homes won permission despite failing the “sequential test”, which is designed to be the ultimate barrier for floodplain development UK planning policy, after the inspector found 12 alternative sites at less risk of flooding.They also overcame heavy opposition from politicians, local and regional tiers of authority and locals – many of whom fear houses surrounding the site will be at increased risk of flooding.Munt said the high court judgment “flies in the face of everything insurers, lenders, Flood Re – a joint UK government and insurance industry initiative that makes the flood cover part of household insurance policies affordable – the Environment Agency and Defra are trying to do on a national policy level”.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of Yatton floodplain.Photograph: Peter SpeightThe Environment Agency objected to the development on flood risk grounds. But the high court agreed that even though the sequential test had failed, the inspector was entitled to consider the development’s wider benefits and whether it could be made safe for its lifetime when weighing the application.One in nine new homes in England built in areas of flood risk, study showsRead moreAnnemieke Waite, North Somerset council’s cabinet member for planning and environment, accused Persimmon of exploiting a legal loophole.“We’re not being nimbys, we accept we need to build these homes,” she said. “But we don’t accept the establishment of a highly controversial legal precedent whereby vital local environmental protections can be overridden to build on floodplains across England and Wales.”Local people living around the site are distraught. With just a few hours’ notice, 51 residents converged at the site earlier this week to meet the Guardian’s photographer, many leaving work early to be there – and one coming straight from a hospital bed.“We represent everyone living in areas at risk of flooding in England and Wales,” said Sue Gardiner, whose living room window opens out over the site. “This ruling massively increases the likelihood of developers building up near you, without having to answer for your increased flood risk.”View image in fullscreenSue Gardiner: ‘Our only asset could become a dangerous flood hazard.’Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianGazing over the fields, Gardiner broke down. “I’m petrified,” she said. “Persimmon claims we’re not at any significant greater risk of flood, but no one else agrees: we’ve been refused by three major house insurers on the grounds of increased flood risk on the back of these plans.“Without insurance, our home – the home we worked hard throughout our lives to pay for so we could leave it to our children – could become unmortgageable, and then unsellable,” she said. “Thanks to Persimmon, our only asset could become a dangerous flood hazard for us – and a worthless inheritance for our children.”Richard Croucher, whose home also abuts the site, agreed. “The value of our home was supposed to fund our care when we get old,” he said. “Now we’ve got nothing for when we’re old and in need: that’s terrifying.”View image in fullscreenLocal resident Richard Croucher.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianPersimmon Homes said: “Our proposals to deliver much-needed new homes in Yatton were subject to detailed scrutiny at a public planning inquiry before being approved by an independent planning inspector.“Flood risk was considered in detail through the planning process, including at the public inquiry by the inspector, before planning permission was granted.”Explore more on these topicsPlanning policyHousingLocal governmentSomersetEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would have curbed Nato cooperation | Switzerland | The Guardian
description: 70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: 70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia
Content: Give Peace A Chance by John Lennon, used in the campaign for tightening Switzerland’s neutrality rules.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPAView image in fullscreenGive Peace A Chance by John Lennon, used in the campaign for tightening Switzerland’s neutrality rules.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPASwitzerlandSwiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would have curbed Nato cooperation70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against RussiaJennifer RankinSun 27 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have requiredSwitzerlandto curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be ⁠written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amidincreasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’sdecision to mirror EU sanctionsagainst Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the UN.The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2m francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign.Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy”, leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate withNato.Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve,leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.Explore more on these topicsSwitzerlandEuropean UnionNatoEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: 61m tonnes of rubble: Gaza aid workers face delicate task of clearing ruins concealing up to 10,000 bodies | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Removal of war debris, in which lives, memories and unexploded Israeli bombs lie buried, is one of largest clearance operations in modern history
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: Removal of war debris, in which lives, memories and unexploded Israeli bombs lie buried, is one of largest clearance operations in modern history
Content: A child watches a bulldozer on Beirut street in Gaza City, once a busy area that now lies in ruins.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA child watches a bulldozer on Beirut street in Gaza City, once a busy area that now lies in ruins.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianGaza61m tonnes of rubble: Gaza aid workers face delicate task of clearing ruins concealing up to 10,000 bodiesRemoval of war debris, in which lives, memories and unexploded Israeli bombs lie buried, is one of largest clearance operations in modern historySeham Tanteshin Gaza CitySun 27 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt took all day to clear a section of road in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood inGazaCity. At the end of it, Ahmed Alyan, a UN engineer, was exhausted, surrounded by mountains of rubble despite the day’s work.“I feel as if we are holding a spoon and trying to empty the sea,” Alyan said, beads of sweat trickling down his forehead after a long, hot summer day.Alyan is part of a World Food Programme (WFP) team who have been working on Beirut Street, once a busy main thoroughfare lined with shops, offices and homes and filled with traffic and people. But now it is virtually deserted.The road was blocked by piles of rubble, stones and the wreckage of destroyed shops. Nearby, a tower stood tilted after some of its concrete foundations were damaged, while displaced families continued to live inside. In some parts of the road, sewage flowed from the ground after the drainage system was damaged and blocked by Israeli bombardment.The UN estimates that removing the bulk of the rubble in the Gaza Strip could take at least seven to 10 years and cost billions of dollars. That would make the removal of war debris in Gaza one of the largest rubble-clearance operations in modern history.View image in fullscreen‘I feel as if we are holding a spoon and trying to empty the sea,’ said Ahmed Alyan, a UN engineer working on Beirut Street.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian“The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” said Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative inPalestine.The task is being carried out in extremely difficult and hazardous conditions. The clearance teams are working in ruins containing countless dead bodies and unexploded bombs. So far, 580km of roads have been cleared, which has in turn made possible the movement of aid trucks, relief teams and residents.However, the reconstruction of Gaza is a huge challenge facing international and local organisations. After more than two years of work, about 907,000 tonnes of rubble have been removed and more than 300,000 tonnes recycled and reused. But this represents only about 1.5% of the total rubble.View image in fullscreenGaza has about 20 times the rubble generated in all wars over the last 18 years, according to the UNDP’s special representative in the territory.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianTo make things more difficult, the Israeli authorities have banned the necessary equipment from entering Gaza on the grounds that almost any aid that is not food or medicine could be“dual-use”and could somehow benefit Hamas.Initially, the WFP work was limited to removing debris from the roads and pushing it to the sides to create a passage for trucks. But the sheer quantity was overwhelming, and continuing Israeli bombardment during the nearly year-old ceasefire kept adding to the gargantuan task. Some roads had to be reopened several times.Widespread destruction across Gaza generated more than 61m tonnes of debris by July 2025Meanwhile, the so-called yellow line, a demarcation established at the start of the ceasefire last October,keeps creeping forwardas Israeli troops seize more of the territory. The area still accessible to people and aid workers is barely 30% of the whole Gaza Strip, making the problem of what to do with the rubble even more acute.“One of the ways we have tried to address this problem is by recycling and reusing the rubble in different ways,” Cilliers said.The UNDP has begun managing five rubble-crushing sites across Gaza, where debris collected from roads and damaged critical infrastructure is processed for reuse. The rubble is first sorted to remove non-concrete materials, including metal and steel rods. The concrete is then crushed into smaller pieces, eventually down to roughly the size of a marble or a very small rock.UNDP relies on seven crushers across Gaza, all of which were already in the territory before the war. Two of the seven were reconstructed by local engineers in Gaza over the past year, based on models they had available, as they were unable to bring new machinery into the strip.View image in fullscreenOne of the UNDP’s concrete crushing sites in Deir al-Balah, where debris is processed for reuse.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianAt one of the crushing sites, a large space that had previously housed UN warehouses, piles of rubble are stacked across the yard. Trucks arriving with large amounts of debris stop on a weighbridge before tipping their cargo on to the piles.There is a constant roar in the area as the mechanism breaks the concrete into smaller pieces, and the air is thick with dust.View image in fullscreenCrushed rubble is used for repairing roads. ‘These solutions have been imposed on us by the reality we are living in,’ said a WFP team member.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianThe condition of the machinery poses a big challenge for the teams carrying out the work. Most of the equipment available in Gaza has become severely worn out. The machinery frequently breaks down during operations, partly because of the acute shortage of spare parts, engine oil and other resources needed to maintain and operate it.In July 2025, 8m tonnes of the debris created in Gaza was potentially hazardousWith major restrictions on the entry of construction materials still in place, engineers are reusing the crushed rubble for a number of essential purposes. Much of it is used to repair roads and fill potholes, while some is placed beneath tents and shelters to raise them above rainwater and sewage.Nehal Abu Hassan, a member of the WFP team, said: “These materials cannot be compared with the natural materials normally used to build roads. Their quality is lower, and they are difficult to work with. But there is no alternative. These solutions have been imposed on us by the reality we are living in.”Removing some of the rubble has already had a big impact. “The road has become wider, the problem of rodents and insects has decreased and cars can pass through more easily,” said Ibrahim Daradona, a displaced man from Jabaliya who is living in the Tel al-Hawa area of Gaza City. “The rubble was even a danger to children playing here.”View image in fullscreenIbrahim Daradona said the rubble was a danger to children.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianMore than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters, as dire humanitarian conditions persist after nearly three years. Rubble has become part of the environment in which they live every day.The removal of rubble has also helped revive Gaza’s local economy by creating space for people to start new activities and reopen shops and small businesses. “One of the things we have seen is that when we clear rubble in front of damaged shops and businesses, many of them reopen within around 20 days,” Cilliers said.Despite all the efforts to remove rubble and restore access to residential areas, the remains of homes carry a particular sensitivity. Every metre of rubble may conceal things that cannot be seen from the outside.“Rubble in some areas does not represent just debris to people; it represents their entire life and memories. In some cases, there may be bodies still under the rubble. That is why removing it is a very sensitive issue for families and communities,” said Abu Hassan.View image in fullscreenNehal Abu Hassan, a WFP engineer, said the debris represented people’s lives and memories.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianThe presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian issues in Gaza. According to estimates cited by the UNDP, between 8,000 and 10,000 bodies may still be buried.UNDP has said it is working with organisations including the International Committee of the Red Cross to identify locations where human remains may be buried and prioritise them during rubble-removal and recovery operations.“We are also working on a forensic process to identify remains, [to] ensure that they are handled properly and that religious burial rights are respected, and [to] provide the necessary documentation and certificates for families. This is extremely important for families in Gaza,” Cilliers said.Unexploded ordnance in rubble and on roads is a serious challenge for teams clearing the debris. UNDP and WFP teams coordinate with the UN mine-clearing arm, Unmas, the British charity the Halo Trust and other organisations before beginning clearance work, to identify unexploded ordnance and protect workers and returning families.Given the limited capacity to remove explosive ordnance in Gaza, these organisations cannot disarm or remove all unexploded items. But they can identify hazardous areas and mark them.View image in fullscreenClearing the debris is a dangerous task, with unexploded ordnance and asbestos amid the rubble.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianAlongside the danger from explosives, rubble may contain other hazardous materials, including asbestos, which can pose a serious health risk when its fibres are inhaled.Partly standing damaged buildings pose another risk. Some families return to their homes believing they are safe, only for the structures to collapse suddenly. Assessing the safety of damaged buildings before residents return is therefore an important part of the recovery process.“The progress in early recovery is slow, we are trying to do what we can despite the limitations on bringing in the equipment and services we need,” Cilliers said.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsGazaPalestineHumanitarian responseAidInternally displaced peopleIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in France | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
Content: Pope Leo waves from a popemobile in Lourdes.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPope Leo waves from a popemobile in Lourdes.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesPope Leo XIVPope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in FrancePontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’Jennifer RankinSun 27 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit toFrance.Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday,Pope Leo XIVcalled on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.Leo met seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy privately on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.The survivors said the pope had listened to them, was informed of their cases and said more work was needed to respond to the scandal.Five of the seven held a press conference in Lourdes. Jean-Marie Delbos said he never thought the day would come when he would meet a pope. He asked Leo to bless a photo of his grandmother, which he did. “It was extraordinary,” he said.View image in fullscreenPope Leo celebrates a mass in Lourdes.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersDuring a homily to the faithful, the pope also attacked medically assisted dying as immoral “false compassion” in a staunch articulation of the Catholic church’s teaching that all human life must be defended from conception until natural death.After years of debate, France formally adopted legislation last monthallowing incurably ill adults the right to “aid in dying”, joining a small number of countries with similar laws, including Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Canada.The pope said: “It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral.”The pope was due to take part in six events while in Lourdes, including a meeting with staff and patients at the shrine’s care centre.Lourdes has drawn millions of sick and disabled believers seeking a cure from its spring waters since the Catholic church officially recognised visions of the Virgin Mary reported by a local girl in 1858.Arriving there in a white popemobile on Saturday night, however, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing women over three decades.Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court,accused by more than two dozen womenof having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.View image in fullscreenLeo’s is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty ImagesRupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.Among the survivors who met the pope was a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram. Former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to bethe biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn an interview published last year, the pope spoke of a crisis of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.Thefirst official papal visit to France in 18 yearsfollows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in ParisRead moreFrance’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation aftera landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abusedover seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.View image in fullscreenCarmelite nuns attend mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV in Lourdes, France.Photograph: Valentine Chapuis/AFP/Getty Images“You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération.The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines InternationalExplore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVChild protectionThe papacyChildrenCatholicismChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation | Bill Gates | The Guardian
description: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
Content: Bill Gates in New York City on 8 May 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenBill Gates in New York City on 8 May 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersBill GatesBill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulationMicrosoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on SundayRamon Antonio VargasSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Gateshas called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropistsaidto Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”Another portion of the interview –excerptsof which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AIRead more“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similarwarningsby a wide array of tech and political figures.Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.His fellow tech moguls includingSam AltmanandElon Muskhave joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some expertstheorizecould precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.Meanwhile,Microsoftitself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to aGuardian essaypublished on Friday.The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure tomonitor, arrest and deport immigrantsen masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeoverRead moreAn external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in Julydeterminedthat he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the hostaskedhim: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”Explore more on these topicsBill GatesAI (artificial intelligence)MicrosoftUS politicsComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
Content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The company said it would resume training its latest models ‘only when we are confident that we have addition safeguards’.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenOpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The company said it would resume training its latest models ‘only when we are confident that we have addition safeguards’.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyOpenAIOpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogueDecision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected waysAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 21.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in whichOpenAIagents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.Last week Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese,revealedan OpenAI agent had breached the government’s national healthcare system – but saidno sensitive informationhad been compromised.AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropichave called for a slowdowntoo.OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemmaRead moreIt is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attacktargeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.In a meetingwith Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: London’s investment bankers and lawyers make more than £1bn in takeover frenzy | Banking | The Guardian
description: Bumper fees paid in the year’s mergers and acquisitions spark anger over high City pay during cost of living crisis
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Bumper fees paid in the year’s mergers and acquisitions spark anger over high City pay during cost of living crisis
Content: The value of mergers and acquisitions of UK-listed companies surged to about £100bn in 2026, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets for bankers, lawyers and accountants working on the deals.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe value of mergers and acquisitions of UK-listed companies surged to about £100bn in 2026, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets for bankers, lawyers and accountants working on the deals.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesBankingLondon’s investment bankers and lawyers make more than £1bn in takeover frenzyBumper fees paid in the year’s mergers and acquisitions spark anger over high City pay during cost of living crisisLauren AlmeidaSun 27 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon’s investment bankers and lawyers have made more than £1bn from a frenzy of takeover deals this year, sparking anger over high City pay during thecost of living crisis.The value of mergers and acquisitions of UK stock market listed companies has surged 175% in 2026 to $132.9bn (£100bn), according to theLondon Stock Exchange, as overseas buyers snap up British companies at record pace.Fees paid to investment bankers, lawyers and accountants working on these deals topped £1.2bn, official filings suggest, helping drive multimillion-pound pay packets.The bumper fees were fuelled by a string of corporate takeovers driven by a flood of private equity cash and acquisitive American buyers targeting undervalued British businesses. The spree of acquisitions of listed companies has led to concerns over thefuture of the London stock market.The takeover frenzy has fed advisory business at the biggest banks and law firms in the City. Bankers atJP Morganhave been the busiest, advising on more takeovers involving UK companies than any other bank this year – a total of 14 deals worth a combined $89.4bn (£67.6bn), according to the LSE. The leading law firm was Slaughter and May, it found.UK bankers have also benefited from soaring bonuses, after the government scrapped a rule capping bonuses at two-times annual salaries in late 2023. Each bank now sets its own upward limit. Big investment banks such as Goldman Sachs now allow performers tobe paid up to 25 times their annual salary.The surge in business comes while the banking sectorlobbies against paying higher taxes in the UK.Jamie Dimon, the billionaire boss of JP Morgan, has issuedseveral warningsto Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget on 28 October. The industry body UK Finance echoed the view this week.Lenders in the UK currently pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets.The most lucrative deal in the City this year wasthe £10.6bn takeoverof the lab testing group Intertek by the private equity firm EQT, which is expected to generate more than £370m in fees. Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Deutsche Bank are working on the deal for EQT, while Intertek paid Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Cazenove and PJT Partners.Lawyers at top City firms have started to out-earn some bankers. Partners at the “magic circle” firms Linklaters and Clifford Chance were paid an average of £2.5m and £2.3m respectively in the year to April, their highest ever. A&O Shearman partners were paid £2.2m.View image in fullscreenThe Clifford Chance building at Canary Wharf, London. Partners at the firm were paid an average of £2.3m in the year to April.Photograph: Robert Evans/AlamyAt the boutique bank Evercore, which the LSE said had advised on five deals in the UK stock market this year, the firm’s “members” – senior managing directors who are dealmakers – were paid an average of about £2m. Its best-paid member collected £16.2m this year.Overall, dealmaker fees are likely to be even higher this year as the figures do not include deals which did not complete, were rejected or for which documents have not been published – including the £5.7bn takeover of the FTSE 100 airline easyJet by the private equity firm Apollo Global Management,agreed last month.While pay continues to climb in the City, millions of UK households are struggling with the cost of living.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCharlotte Brumpton-Childs, the national secretary at the GMB union, said financial brokers were paid huge sums “while the people who keep this country moving struggle to make ends meet”.“The UK needs to seriously re-examine what we value and hold dear – is it the people who build, who create, who look after us and our loved ones in their hour of need? Or is it a bloated financial sector?” she asked.Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress,repeated his call for a windfall taxon lenders’ profits asinterest rates have risen, saying that “if banks can afford bonanza payouts for their top brass, they can clearly afford to pay more tax”.“People up and down the country are struggling, and things could get a lot worse with energy prices set to shoot up,” he said.Earlier this month figures from the Office for National Statistics showed that average growth in total earnings, including bonuses, slowed to 3.9% in the three months ended in July, down from 4.1% in the three months ended in June.There are fears that, while dealmakers’ pay is rising on the takeover boom, investment banks could lose out on revenue from their sell-side research and work on flotations as more companies leave London’s stock market and fewer line up to join.Despite hopes that 2026 could spark a revival on the UK stock market, there were just seven listings in the first half of the year, raising £577m in total, according to data from the professional services company EY. However, this week, Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, said it wasplanning one of the biggest UK listingsin years.Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
