title: Korea review – a nirvana of wild beauty shattered by the 20th century | Art | The Guardian
description: The staggering resourcefulness and fantastic originality of bygone artisans is showcased in earthenware so exquisite it will soothe your soul. But a lurch into the modern breaks the spell
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The staggering resourcefulness and fantastic originality of bygone artisans is showcased in earthenware so exquisite it will soothe your soul. But a lurch into the modern breaks the spell
Content: A glorious responce to Korea’s landscape … Jeong Seon, Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang, 1751.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaView image in fullscreenA glorious responce to Korea’s landscape … Jeong Seon, Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang, 1751.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaArtReviewKorea review – a nirvana of wild beauty shattered by the 20th centuryBritish Museum, LondonThe staggering resourcefulness and fantastic originality of bygone artisans is showcased in earthenware so exquisite it will soothe your soul. But a lurch into the modern breaks the spellJonathan JonesSun 27 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan they do it again? The runaway success of theBayeux tapestryhas put the British Museum in a league of its own, perhaps making it, at this moment, the leading museum on earth – and it’s rapidly following up with Korea, a survey of “2,000 years of creativity” in a land that, before its sufferings in the 20th century, enjoyed millennia of calm, at least to judge from its art. But it’s a blockbuster with a tragic flaw, a lovely broken vase badly stuck together.You are lured at first into a nirvana of beauty. A giant bronze bell from a Buddhist monastery, cast in the eighth century AD and bulging with dragons, flames and flowery embossments, strikes the tone. It calls you to meditation. A gong adds to the harmony (and if you need that underlining, there are bells and gongs on the now obligatory exhibition soundtrack). I was held rapt by this Buddhist period in Korea’s history, when the contemplative religion from India interacted with the artistic influence of China to inspire ecstatic hand-copied sutras (spiritual scriptures) and slender little statuettes of bodhisattvas (Buddhist saints who have achieved enlightened holiness).View image in fullscreen‘I was held rapt by this period in Korea’s history’ … Avatamsaka Sutra (The Flower Garland Sutra),  The Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra, 1341-67.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaYet even before Buddhism brought its ethereal aesthetic, the resourcefulness of artisans in the Korean peninsula was staggering. Intricate stoneware objects from as early as the fifth century include a horse standing on a circular plinth with a drinking horn balanced on its back – a practical object of wild beauty.Ceramicscame to Korea from China but took root in creations of fantastic originality. The kingdom of Goryeo, which unified the peninsula from 918 to 1392 and made Buddhism the state religion, sponsored superb courtly ceramics. Potters adopted the green glazed stoneware, celadon, from China’s Zhejiang province and perfected it in smooth pale green bowls and vases that soothe your soul.View image in fullscreenSuperb ceramics … Gourd-shaped ewer with chrysanthemum design, 1200-1300.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaA flair for exquisite earthenware continued under the neo-Confucian Joseon dynasty, which ruled from 1392 until, astonishingly, 1897. The most captivating pot from this era is a huge, white, near-spherical moon jar made in the 18th century. It’s an intoxicating blend of scale and geometry created by throwing two semi-circular bowls and joining them together. You can see the imperfect, dimpled join, cherished in Korean culture, which adds to its uniqueness, its personality.And then the spell is broken. The show shifts forward suddenly, brutally, into some so-so early 20th-century Korean art. Modern pastiches of traditional art mix awkwardly with European and American-style modernism from the 1900s to 1950s. Why this lurch, just as you were starting to grasp the subtle shift from Buddhism to neo-Confucianism and how their aesthetics differ? The blockbuster cultural history of Korea falls apart. It’s just a collection of things, after all.In fact, this is, with a few additions, the collection of Lee Kun-hee, who was the chair of Samsung – the exhibition’s “corporate partner” – until his death in 2020. It’s a fine collection. Several works here, now owned by South Korea’s leading museums, are national treasures of unique significance. But a collection comes with its owner’s idiosyncrasies, and cannot be taken as an objective history of a people’s art and beliefs. It is not very insightful about the modern history of Korea: where are the photographs, news stories, popular imagery, if you want to tell that story? Instead the show shrinks into a display of elite art. Fair enough if it was simply presented as one collector’s taste.The 20th century was a brutal period for Korea: from 1910 to 1945 it was colonised by the Japanese empire but the cosy modern paintings here say nothing about that. More mention is made of theKorean warthat killed three million people. A desperate, cartoon-like pastel by Lee Jung-seop of a fisher being welcomed home by his family is an unfulfilled dream: this artist became a migrant in the war and died before ever seeing his family again. Another roughly drawn work by him shows naked bodies tied up in a chilling glimpse of the horrors of that time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPast beauty and modern violence … Do Ho Suh, Self-portrait, 2019.Photograph: Trustees of the British MuseumThat grief, chaos and cultural loss – with Korea still divided today – is only slightly evoked. What stays with you is the lost harmony of the past, when scholars and monks meditated on nature and its beauties. The work of art that most gloriously responds to Korea’s landscapes is Jeong Seon’s hanging scroll Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang. Done in ink on paper in 1751, this more than metre-wide view takes you into a fresh, atmospheric encounter with nature: a dark mass of mountain hangs over the scene while trees are evoked as rapid moist blurs. It is not idealised but spontaneous. You wonder what Jeong and his faraway contemporary Thomas Gainsborough might have made of each other.Perhaps the broken feeling of the show, in which there is no link between past beauty and modern violence, tells us a tragic truth. The very last object implies this.Do Ho Suh’s 2019 self portrait, owned by the British Museum, depicts the artist as a tiny figure under a cascade of multicoloured threads streaming down from a floating image of a traditional Korean house. The grace of this world holds you in this exhibition and you feel its vanishing as a personal loss, wherever you come from.At theBritish Museum, London, 1 October-31 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArtSouth KoreaNorth KoreaBritish MuseumCeramicsIllustrationPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream review – Munya Chawawa bewitches in lovingly juiced-up 90s rave | Stage | The Guardian
description: A narcotic, orgiastic woodland party clashes with the traditional values of John Major’s Tory party in Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss’s exuberant production
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: A narcotic, orgiastic woodland party clashes with the traditional values of John Major’s Tory party in Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss’s exuberant production
Content: Showstopping … Munya Chawawa as Bottom in A Midsummer Night’s Dream at Chichester Festival theatre.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenShowstopping … Munya Chawawa as Bottom in A Midsummer Night’s Dream at Chichester Festival theatre.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewA Midsummer Night’s Dream review – Munya Chawawa bewitches in lovingly juiced-up 90s raveChichester Festival theatreA narcotic, orgiastic woodland party clashes with the traditional values of John Major’s Tory party in Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss’s exuberant productionMark LawsonSun 27 Sep 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Shakespearean canon contains the term “love juice” twice, both in A Midsummer Night’s Dream. So, though purists might be furious, that druggy usage – and Fairie King Oberon’s access to potions that “make eyes roll” – offer textual justification for Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss staging the play around a narcotic, orgiastic woodland party in the summer of 1994.At that time, prime minister John Major was introducing legislation to ban “illegal raves”. Egeus (Henry Everett), an Athenian courtier in the source, becomes Chief Constable of West Sussex, surnamed Anderton, an allusion to Sir James, a Thatcher ally whose Bible-inspired policing saw him called God’s Copper. Duke Theseus becomes MP for Chichester, a seat held by the Conservatives for a century from 1924. With one character wearing Major rosettes on her breasts, a PM often derided as dull is becoming a theatre star: the National next year stages a James Graham bio-drama, Major.High-concept Shakespeare risks bits not fitting, a jeopardy increased in A Midsummer Night’s Dream by a plot divided between courtiers, artisans and faeries. But, in this version, the substances consumed by the first two groups may lead them to hallucinate the third: reports of a woman snogging a donkey or Technicolor creatures filling forests can be attributed to the pharmacopeia of Oberon (David Sturzaker), here a DJ running a rave-based cult.View image in fullscreenRaving crew … Eve Ponsonby (centre) as Titania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.Photograph: Manuel HarlanWhile it’s unclear if he and his followers are from a higher sphere or merely high, the conceit, with word changes and some new speeches, accommodates most of the narrative. A hard part of the play to sell to modern audiences is the “law of Athens”, by which a woman who refuses her father’s choice of husband must opt for death or the convent. But this religious misogyny seems plausible enough amid the moral hardening in the 90s Tory party that led to three Labour terms and Conservatives defecting further right. Lysander becoming Lysanda (Ellie Larkin), adding bisexuality to the youthful romantic quadrangle, increases the moral jeopardy at this Tory court.The “rude mechanicals”, who have taken over the local Tory party’s am dram group, are the new working-class Tories of the era, including Nick Bottom, a video shop owner, bewitchingly played, in his full theatrical debut, by comedian Munya Chawawa. He is verbally (“prologue” mispronounced prow-log-wee) and physically energetic: his slapstick gymnastics in the often lumberingly unfunny Pyramus and Thisbe playlet stop the show with earned applause.Female characters are given additional agency, sometimes violent. Kieran Taylor-Ford’s swaggering Demetrius is regularly doubled over in pain after being thumped in the crotch by Hermia or Helena, potentially interchangeable characters who Angela Sant’Albano and Freya Parks make vividly distinct. Hippolyta (Celeste Dodwell) keeps guys in line with a riding crop.A play that can become tedious through repertoire regularity is lovingly juiced up by Audibert and Joss with resonances local and national. Chichester is now Liberal Democrat, while this production’s Bottom, Theseus and Egeus, you suspect, would have defected to Reform or Restore, a period when mainstream Conservatism seemed extreme now feeling like a dream.AtChichester Festival theatreuntil 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreA Midsummer Night's DreamChichester Festival theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A joyful place’: a new museum coaxes Austrians to embrace The Sound of Music | Musicals | The Guardian
description: Sixty years after the film’s release, Salzburg is embracing a Hollywood classic it once kept at arm’s length
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Sixty years after the film’s release, Salzburg is embracing a Hollywood classic it once kept at arm’s length
Content: ‘A few of my favourite things’: The Sound of Music was not a big hit in Salzburg, where the film is set. Photograph: GRANGER/Historical Picture Archive/AlamySixty years after the film’s release, Salzburg is embracing a Hollywood classic it once kept at arm’s lengthByDeborah Colein SalzburgSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLet’s start at the very beginning – famously, a very good place to start.Just two decades after the second world war, a Hollywood crew descended on Salzburg with stars, show tunes and a compelling, essentially true story of love and opposition to Adolf Hitler: The Sound of Music.The Austrian city, still economically and morally devastated from the Nazi period, wasn’t quite ready to receive them.Although director Robert Wise was free to make use of the glorious Alpine settings and the old town’s historical facades, scenes such as soldiers marching across the central Residenzplatz under swastika flags made municipal authorities deeply uneasy.When the film premiered in 1965, it ran for a couple of weeks, closed for lack of ticket sales and largely disappeared from local memory. That is until the tour buses started coming.View image in fullscreenKym Karath, Debbie Turner, Angela Cartwright, Duane Chase, Heather Menzies, Nicholas Hammond, Charmian Carr andJulie Andrewsin The Sound Of Music.Most Austrians – and Germans – still have never seen the five-time Oscar-winning film starring Julie Andrews and Christopher Plummer.But a new museum in Salzburg dedicated to the movie and its real-life anti-Nazi family of singers now aims to reconcile the global cultural touchstone with its long ambivalent home town.The road to Austria’s growing embrace traversed dramatic hills and valleys only the budding nun Maria and her cherubic band of charges could properly serenade.“Beneath all the kitsch, this is also a film about resistance,” co-curator Matthias Bergsmann said on a tour through the exhibition. “It was about saying no to national socialism. And about a family who said: if we stick together we will abide, and music will save us. For all its beautiful images and songs, the film has depth.”View image in fullscreenCurator Matthias Bergsmann in the Sound of Music museum , Salzburg.The nearly three-hour opus was rarely shown on Austrian television until a special screening last Christmas for the 60th anniversary. The dubbed film, known asMeine Lieder – meine Träume(My Songs – My Dreams), remains obscure in Germany as well.The 1959 Broadway musical and subsequent film were based on a popular memoir by Maria von Trapp. In it she described how as a spirited young novice, she was hired by Georg von Trapp, a widowed father who had been a submarine commander in the Austro-Hungarian navy, to care for his seven children.Trying circumstances and proximity soon gave way to love.The Nazi annexation of Austria led the family, who had already started performing together in the 1930s, to flee their homeland. Moved by fierce opposition to Hitler as well as financial concerns, they left everything behind to begin new lives in the US as professional troubadours.View image in fullscreenThe von Trapp family in The Sound of Music, 1965.Bergsmann said the reasons for the cold shoulder in Austria were not as simple as embarrassment over the Nazi period, particularly considering the glut of second world war films produced in German in the ensuing decades.“At the time, it was perhaps simply too early to tackle this subject in this way seen as sentimental. Perhaps the wounds were still too deep, or the process of coming to terms with the past was only just beginning.”He said Salzburgers also quibbled with Hollywood scrambling their landmarks and the von Trapps’ story for the sake of the script, such as having them flee Austria on foot to Switzerland when they actually left for South Tyrol by train.View image in fullscreenThe glass gazebo that inspired the set of the Sixteen Going on Seventeen duet between Liesl and Rolf, as well as Maria and Georg’s first declaration of love.Days after the opening, the museum was packed with international visitors and a few locals. “It was top of my bucket list, my dream location since I was a kid,” said Jemimah Daniel, 29, a youth librarian from Christchurch, New Zealand. Her partner Rhys Harris, 30, said many parents used to turn off the television during the movie “when the Nazis come”. “So I never knew about that part until when I was an adult and I thought, wow, OK, they actually touch on some real things.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: vintage memorabilia, framed photo of Von Trapp family in the US, family photos on the wall and illustrations.The exhibit is in the coach house and hunting lodge of the majestic 17th-century Hellbrunn Palace, whose grounds were used in the “I Have Confidence” scene in which a euphoric Maria leaves the abbey to become a governess. It also boasts the glass gazebo that inspired the set of the Sixteen Going on Seventeen duet between Liesl and Rolf, as well as Maria and Georg’s first declaration of love.The building work cost €4.6m (£4m) in public funds, while another €1.8m went into the exhibition, including original costumes, film posters and private Super 8 films recorded on set.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Sound of Music posters from around the world, a still of Christopher Plummer and Julie Andrews from the film and a visitor takes a selfie by the gazebo.A reconstruction of the gazebo inside shows a restored copy of the playful “Do-Re-Mi” scenes shot at Mirabell Gardens on a loop, and visitors are invited to sing along. Access to the real pavilion outside had to be restricted after too many guests danced in it, causing damage.View image in fullscreenA reconstruction of the real gazebo.Upstairs are von Trapp family relics including a winter dirndl worn by the real Maria, Georg’s naval uniform complete with a sabre, and a journal from the von Trapps’ flight to the US.Caroline Dolley, 55, a companion for elderly people from Chester, England, called the museum “a joyful place”: “I only recently watched The Sound of Music in its entirety for the first time ever. It’s stood the test of time really well.”View image in fullscreenIt’s ‘a joyful place’, said Caroline Dolley.Helmut and Margarete Zoufall, native Salzburgers, wanted to learn more about the film after decades watching giddy tourists “hop around” on the city monuments. “I remember in the 1970s Americans coming into a record shop and asking for the Austrian national anthem – they thought it was ‘Edelweiss’!” Margarete, 73, said, laughing.View image in fullscreenMargarete and Helmut Zoufall.Helmut, 81, remembered seeing the movie crew at Nonnberg’s hilltop abbey as a young man. “It was always said that the film was made too soon after the war. People were starving and didn’t want to be reminded of that period,” he said. “But time has passed.”Dutch child psychotherapist Weeke von der Kooi, 66, said she loved the movie for its “romance and hope” but never knew it was based on a true story. With rightwing extremism on the rise again, she said, “it’s like history repeating – it’s awful”.View image in fullscreenElisabeth von Trapp.Elisabeth von Trapp, a granddaughter of Georg and his previous wife Agathe, divides her time between Vermont and Salzburg, where she offers guided tours. Although the movie made her family world famous, she said it irked them that their story got warped by Hollywood. “When they saw the film, they were going, ‘that’s not how I experienced it’,” von Trapp, 72, said, citing for example the captain’s inaccurate portrayal as harsh and remote. “I’m so thrilled that they have a section in this exhibit that tells their true story.”She is grateful Austrians are restoring the von Trapp legacy in their homeland. “I just hope this museum will help say, ‘look, this family was from your own back yard’,” she said, describing their story as a “wake-up call” in a fraught political age. “They returned in 1950 and sang three major concerts in Salzburg. They had a clarion call saying it’s time to rebuild and that whatever happened during those years shall not happen again.”Elisabeth von Trapp sings at opening of Sound of Music museum in SalzburgSocial media has recently ignited interest in The Sound of Music among younger audiences, particularly in southeast Asia, Bergsmann said. The timeless Rodgers and Hammerstein songs fly on YouTube, and a scene in which Georg rips down the Nazi flag and tears it in half becamea go-to giffor opponents of the far right.Plans for the museum date back to the 1980s. Beyond finding the right spot, lining up government financing and resolving copyright concerns took decades. The museum will cater to the estimated 300,000 people who come to the city each year primarily for its associations with the film – roughly holding its own with native son Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart in terms of local attractions, Bergsmann said.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsJulie AndrewsAustriaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Eva Longoria laps up butter on a French foodie tour | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The actor sets off on a culinary adventure, starting in Paris. Plus: ridiculous but addictive reality show Apocalypse. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The actor sets off on a culinary adventure, starting in Paris. Plus: ridiculous but addictive reality show Apocalypse. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Know your onions … Eva Longoria: Searching for France on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdView image in fullscreenKnow your onions … Eva Longoria: Searching for France on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Eva Longoria laps up butter on a French foodie tourThe actor sets off on a culinary adventure, starting in Paris. Plus: ridiculous but addictive reality show Apocalypse. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hannah J Davies,Ali CatterallandPriya ElanSun 27 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEva Longoria: Searching for France7.15pm, BBC Two“Don’t you have any wine in this joint?” Even if Eva Longoria’s foodie tour of France sometimes feels stylish at the expense of content, she doesn’t hold back and her relish carries the day. The actor begins in Paris, where she tries an Asian version of the classic croque madame, enjoys a sit-down with the don of French cuisine Alain Ducasse, and discovers the secret of truly decadent cookery: basically, nothing isn’t improved by a few (dozen) cubes of butter.Phil HarrisonThe Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down7.45pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenCracked it? … Fatiha El-Ghorri on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down on Channel 4.Photograph: Channel 4The formula may be very familiar at this point but this pottery challenge is still a warmly good-natured indulgence. From Paul Merson’s bumbling charm to Lucy Beaumont’s eccentricity, the contenders all bring something welcome to the table. This time, it’s raku week and the newbie potters attempt animal sculptures – with inevitably mixed results.PHThe Split Up9pm, BBC OneMore of the hammy (if highly watchable) spin-off from Abi Morgan’s ratings hit The Split, centred on a British-Asian law firm in Manchester. Aria (Ritu Arya) deals with a demanding client, while also wondering what secrets her boss and dad Dhruv (Sanjeev Bhaskar) is hiding.Hannah J DaviesWilderness With Simon Reeve9pm, BBC TwoReeve explores Mexico’s extraordinary Sea of Cortez, nicknamed the “aquarium of the world”, where he joins conservationists striving to restore its fragile ecosystem. Diving with endangered sharks delivers some truly heartstopping images: a whirling mass of hammerheads results, as Simon says, in “a moment of almost ethereal beauty”.Ali CatterallThe Blame9pm, ITV1The addictive Line of Duty-ish six-parter continues, as Emma (Michelle Keegan) and Tom (Douglas Booth) attempt to solve the case of Sophie, the murdered 16-year-old figure skater. Convinced it’s an inside job, can they obtain enough evidence to get the case under the nose of the chief superintendent and, even better, find a motive?Priya ElanApocalypse9pm, Channel 4As watchable as it is ridiculous, this challenge show, which attempts to maroon its participants in an end-of-days thriller, continues to generate its own cheesy plotlines. This time, a fragile peace is on the horizon after the incident with the chickens. But a gun has gone missing, which could mean a resumption of hostilities.PHLive sportOne-Day International Cricket: England v Sri Lanka, 10am, Sky Sports Main EventThe final match from the Oval.Women’s Super League Football: Liverpool v Everton, 2pm, Sky Sports Main EventChelsea v Arsenal follows at 5.15pm.Uefa Nations League Football: Denmark v Wales, 4.45pm, BBC OneWales v Norway is on Thu at 7.30pm on BBC Two.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Godzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streak | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
Content: A still from Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: Courtesy of GKidsView image in fullscreenA still from Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: Courtesy of GKidsFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewGodzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streakNew York film festival:The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effectsJesse HassengerSat 26 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 20.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago.Godzilla Minus One, the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in aseriesof Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn’t just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Now. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and theToho-made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. Arguably the artsiest, brainiest of the major fall fests is playing unexpected host to a truly spectacular monster battle royale, packaged alongside some of the same thoughtful historical context that informed the previous film.‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new filmRead moreWriter, director and VFX maestro Takashi Yamazaki returns for the sequel, bringing his lead characters back with him. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience withGodzillato overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to “zero”, hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to “minus one”. Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn’t seen directly in trailers, this isn’t a spoiler; he’s featured from the very first scene of the film.)Ghidorah’s appearance obviously sends off alarms in the disaster-response agency that now employs Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), also from the previous film. Noda is joined by Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist who introduces less artillery-heavy defense mechanisms for this new threat. Of course, there is a natural Ghidorah deterrent last seen disintegrating into the sea but known for his adaptability – if only the big guy could be called upon and steered in the right direction.In the older Godzilla films, Ghidorah-Godzilla battles can sometimes make whatever humans who might fit into the picture seem all the more insignificant; the monsters are so fearsome and, in their way, charismatic, that they level anything else in their way. In the tradition of its emotionally involving predecessor, Godzilla Minus Zero grapples more directly with humans’ attempts to assert some control over forces that initially seem impossible to harness. It’s no accident that one of its new heroes attempts to predict the weather – and has faced natural disasters despite her accurate predictions. The characters wield technology that is more science-fictionally advanced than in the previous movie while still relying on a sense of impromptu can-do scrappiness and determination to protect their country. With decreased puny-human helplessness comes greater dangers and new dilemmas.View image in fullscreenMasami Nagasawa in Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: Courtesy of GKidsThe film’s version of the US military, for example, is willing to provide planes but not troops to aid in the fight, which is partially how Kōichi and Noriko are drawn back into the conflict despite the pleading of young Akiko. The partners’ skill sets make them valuable assets, perpetuating some of the previous film’s questions about what kinds of sacrifices might be expected or required when sending citizens into the thick of battle. There’s also an element of body horror used intriguingly, but perhaps not to its fullest potential, given the shiver of anticipation that shoots through the audience when it’s introduced.There’s some value in sidestepping expectations; Yamazaki mentioned at a NYFF press conference that he sought to avoid conforming to any fan guesswork about how various kaiju business in a sequel to Minus One might proceed. True to his word, the movie seems determined to stay true to the human melodrama that proved so surprisingly effective in the previous film, rather than going into all-out monsters-attack mode. That approach works well for the film’s new characters as well as for Noda (Yoshioka is especially good reprising the role), but sometimes falters when it comes to the family-soap parts of the story, which manage to be both more tearful (onscreen) and less (in the audience, though obviously some mileage will vary). The restrained relationship between Kōichi and Noriko made sense last time; in a movie two years later, their nominally romantic partnership seems weirdly glum, even anti-sexual, in a state of co-parenting stasis. There’s little sense of time’s passage for this makeshift family.The Love Hypothesis review – hit BookTok romcom lacks spark on screenRead moreThat’s not to say that the monster-attack stuff falls by the wayside in favor of the humans. In fact, the movie’s extended climax features some of the most majestic CG monster action put to film; if the fun American MonsterVerse series tends toward pro-wrestling kaiju, Godzilla Minus Zero cross-breeds its fight-to-the-death grappling with disaster-movie scope and horror-movie teeth. Yet it also doesn’t go in for the overkill; like its predecessor, the movie favors quality of visual effects over quantity. Little-yet-huge details like Ghidorah’s lightning-like attack beams have a jagged beauty that makes them both cooler and scarier than so many obligatory effects-movie laser shows.It’s a fittingly judicious use of computers, given that the world of Godzilla Minus Zero often appears perched on the verge of a post-war technology boom, and on the precipice of the further global disasters that could be invited by the collision of humankind’s supposed innovations and unknowable forces of nature. (Minus One came out the same year as Oppenheimer; was this one, like Nolan’s The Odyssey, conceived in its wake?) If Yamazaki’s previous Godzilla movie ultimately allowed crowd-pleasing thrills to punch through its mid-century anxieties, this one lands a bit more ambiguously. Maybe that’s why the melodrama stuff isn’t quite so satisfying this time around; attentive as the movie is to its human cast, it’s increasingly clear that we’re living in a world of monsters.Godzilla Minus Zero is screening at theNew Yorkfilm festival and will be released in Australia on 5 November and in the US and the UK on 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewGodzillaAction and adventure filmsNew YorkFestivalsVisual effects (VFX)JapanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Eminem’s Lose Yourself is my anthem for getting the kids out of the house’: Kimberly Wyatt’s honest playlist | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The Pussycat Doll went roller skating to the Beach Boys and is ‘completely over’ Gangnam Style. But what song makes her cry every time?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Pussycat Doll went roller skating to the Beach Boys and is ‘completely over’ Gangnam Style. But what song makes her cry every time?
Content: ‘The best song to have sex to? The Bad Touch by Bloodhound Gang’ … Kimberley WyattPhotograph: Anna FowlerView image in fullscreen‘The best song to have sex to? The Bad Touch by Bloodhound Gang’ … Kimberley WyattPhotograph: Anna FowlerHonest playlistPop and rock‘Eminem’s Lose Yourself is my anthem for getting the kids out of the house’: Kimberly Wyatt’s honest playlistThe Pussycat Doll went roller skating to the Beach Boys and is ‘completely over’ Gangnam Style. But what song makes her cry every time?As told toRich PelleySun 27 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withWhen I learned to drive and got my first car, I felt this real freedom. I’d put the windows down, blare out Ghetto Supastar (That Is What You Are) by Pras, featuring Ol’ Dirty Bastard and Mýa, and sing at the top of my lungs.The first single I boughtEvery Friday night we’d go to the roller skating rink, and I couldn’t wait for them to play Kokomo by the Beach Boys, from the Cocktail soundtrack. So I bought it on cassette from Best Buy in Warrensburg, Missouri.The song I do at karaokeI Wanna Dance With Somebody (Who Loves Me) by Whitney Houston. It’s a classic – everybody joins in, so you know you’re in for a good time.The song I can no longer listen toI’m completely over Gangnam Style by Psy. Everybody was doing the dance and singing it. My kids certainly overdid it in my house. Now I feel a sensory overload the moment I hear it.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toI DJ loads and always play I Love It by Icona Pop, featuring Charli xcx. Everybody in the audience loves it and together we sing every word.The best song to have sex toThe Bad Touch by Bloodhound Gang.The song that changed my lifeFreedom Dance (Get Free!) by Vanessa Williams was the music for my first dance competition as a soloist for the Junior Miss Dance of America when I was 14. I only entered for the experience and to learn, but I ended up winning. It sparked a real belief in myself. I was contestant number 12, so 12 has remained my lucky number ever since.The song that gets me up in the morningI’ve got three kids, so I have to get up super-early to make snacks and breakfast, and get everybody changed and out of the house. I need an anthem to push me through and get me to the gym afterwards, so Lose Yourself by Eminem.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe song that makes me cryMy eight-year-old daughter Maple does dance competitions to Human by Christina Perri – which is about being brilliant, but you’re only human so you can only go so far. She reminds me so much of myself when she’s on stage. To see that little human go up and do superhuman things – but tell the world that she’s got her limits too, and that’s OK – makes me cry.The song I’d like played at my funeralI walked down the aisle to Beneath Your Beautiful by Labrinth, featuring Emeli Sandé. It’s my anthem, so I’ll have it when I say goodbye, too.ThePussycat Dollstour the UK and Ireland29 Septemberto 13 October; tour starts Birmingham.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockHonest playlistPussycat DollsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: LPO/Edward Gardner review – Britten’s pacifist War Requiem lands with a bitterness and snarling irony | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Three fine soloists were joined by the excellent Tiffin Boys’ and Girls’ Choirs alongside the London Philharmonic Choir and the London Symphony Chorus whose pianissimo singing left us with a much-needed glimpse of hope
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Three fine soloists were joined by the excellent Tiffin Boys’ and Girls’ Choirs alongside the London Philharmonic Choir and the London Symphony Chorus whose pianissimo singing left us with a much-needed glimpse of hope
Content: An edgy charge … Edward Gardner conducts the London Philharmonic Orchestra performing Benjamin Britten’s War Requiem at the Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenAn edgy charge … Edward Gardner conducts the London Philharmonic Orchestra performing Benjamin Britten’s War Requiem at the Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Andy ParadiseClassical musicReviewLPO/Edward Gardner review – Britten’s pacifist War Requiem lands with a bitterness and snarling ironyRoyal Festival Hall, LondonThree fine soloists were joined by theexcellentTiffin Boys’ and Girls’ Choirs alongside the London Philharmonic Choir and the London Symphony Chorus whose pianissimo singing left us with a much-needed glimpse of hopeAlexandra CoghlanSun 27 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘All a poet can do today is warn,” Wilfred Owen wrote in 1918. TheLondon Philharmonic Orchestra, launching their new season In Search of Purpose, find it in Owen’s words, just as Benjamin Britten did in 1962 with the premiere of his War Requiem – a pacifist manifesto that doesn’t just mourn the dead, but rages at the senseless conflict that killed them, and cautions of “greater wars” yet to come.View image in fullscreenFinding the humanity … baritone Benjamin Appl.Photograph: Andy ParadiseIt’s a curious starting point, a piece that stresses the limits of art as well as its capacity, but one depressingly, perennially pertinent. Originally cast to reflect the three main warring nations, the three solo roles once again reflected this topicality in Ukrainian-Welsh soprano Natalya Romaniw, American tenor Paul Appleby (replacing an indisposed Allan Clayton), and German baritone Benjamin Appl.ConductorEdward Gardnerhas form with this piece. His reading has shed some of its cushioning grandeur over the years and now lands with a bitterness and a snarling irony to equal its solemnity and prayerfulness. The LPO caught the edgy charge, embedding it in the machine-gun rattle of the trumpets in the Dies Irae and those mocking fanfares of the Sanctus, anticipating the shocking punchline of Owen’s The Parable of the Old Man and the Young in the chamber orchestra’s sardonic commentary.High up in the hall’s rear balcony, the excellent children of the Tiffin Boys’ and Girls’ Choirs felt – deliberately – a long way from the action: an angelic chorus remote and unconcerned by human struggles below. A copy-bound Romaniw conveyed the same impression, bell-clear but impassive in the Benedictus, oddly aloof through the Lacrimosa.It was left to Appleby and Appl to find the humanity, both mining the text with lieder-singers’ sensitivity, each devastating in the slow-burn horror of Strange Meeting. But it was Appleby’s face you watched even as Appl delivered that climactic moment of revelation – “I am the enemy you killed, my friend” – embodying the drama without reservation.The War Requiem is big enough to need a little help from friends, and the London Philharmonic Choir joined forces with the London Symphony Chorus to powerful effect: consonants bullet-clean, fortissimos blazing. But it was the pianissimo singing that left us with a much-needed glimpse of hope, floating that final cadence – whose resolution seems dropped from heaven itself – with unearthly delicacy.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicBenjamin BrittenLondon Philharmonic OrchestraEdward GardnerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Catherine Bohart: Borrowing Trouble review – obsessive compulsion to overshare is captivatingly funny | Stage | The Guardian
description: This latest bulletin from the Irish standup’s fraught life delves deep into her OCD and dismay at her own foibles
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: This latest bulletin from the Irish standup’s fraught life delves deep into her OCD and dismay at her own foibles
Content: Irrepressible … Catherine Bohart in Borrowing Trouble at Soho theatre, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIrrepressible … Catherine Bohart in Borrowing Trouble at Soho theatre, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStageReviewCatherine Bohart: Borrowing Trouble review – obsessive compulsion to overshare is captivatingly funnySoho theatre, LondonThis latest bulletin from the Irish standup’s fraught life delves deep into her OCD and dismay at her own foiblesBrian LoganSun 27 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople talking about their mental health is boring, saysCatherine Bohart. Even listening to herself do so frays the patience. So how to justify Borrowing Trouble, a new standup hour from the Irishwoman delving deep into her OCD? Well, the justification here is the humour, rich and hard-won. But it also comes down to Bohart’s trademark candour. This is a condition so all-consuming, on this evidence, that to not address it might feel like dishonesty – which, for the 38-year-old, would be intolerably off-brand.In this latest bulletin from Bohart’s fraught life, we find her fulfilling an ambition close to all Irish hearts, she tells us, and buying her first home. This entails moving in with her girlfriend too, a process that applies pressure on her compulsion to control. But what’s a girl to do? Move on to her fifth therapist, after the underachievement of the preceding four? Try coming off antidepressants? Her doctor’s response to that suggestion does not inspire confidence. Seek refuge with her family? Well that won’t work, as illustrated by an ill-advisedly long visit home to her parents – AKA her symptoms. Here we see mum fret intrusively on Catherine’s behalf and (in one eye-opening anecdote) dad display the type of behaviours that might, just might, suggest that obsessive compulsions run in the family.This all comes at us in a torrent from the irrepressible Bohart, who channels real-world neurosis into a wonderfully uptight and oversharing stage persona. Her dismay at her own foibles is matched only by alarm at the inexplicable conduct of others – see her routine about disliking lesbian weddings, or the later one in which it dawns on her that her girlfriend’s masculine stylings are underpinned by no practical domestic skills whatsoever. Then there’s the section on women’s health, which argues, amusingly contrary to the received wisdom, that we all need to know and hear a lot less about it.You might think the same of comedians’ neurological disorders; Bohart certainly does. But Borrowing Trouble proves that, in the right hands, even the most tormenting of mental afflictions can be captivatingly funny.AtSoho Theatre, London, until 3 October;then touringExplore more on these topicsStageComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)Soho theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: I’ll Be Seeing You review – Simon Russell Beale’s Liberace is a life force too great to be tamed  | Stage | The Guardian
description: Martin Sherman’s meta new work sees Fra Fee’s writer struggling to turn out a play about the flamboyant pianist while despising everything the showman stands for
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Martin Sherman’s meta new work sees Fra Fee’s writer struggling to turn out a play about the flamboyant pianist while despising everything the showman stands for
Content: Milking it … Simon Russell Beale as Liberace in I’ll Be Seeing You at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tiu MakkonenView image in fullscreenMilking it … Simon Russell Beale as Liberace in I’ll Be Seeing You at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tiu MakkonenStageReviewI’ll Be Seeing You review – Simon Russell Beale’s Liberace is a life force too great to be tamedPitlochry Festival theatreMartin Sherman’s meta new work sees Fra Fee’s writer struggling to turn out a play about the flamboyant pianist while despising everything the showman stands forMark FisherSun 27 Sep 2026 06.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSimon Russell Bealemakes his entrance in mid-air, appearing some way above the stage in a heavenly haze of smoke and light. He flashes a voluminous silver cape and spangly waistcoat, his eyes wide and imploring as if he cannot believe it either. It is flashy and flamboyant and it is a problem for Fra Fee.In this headily meta new play by Martin Sherman, still provocative and unexpected at the age of 87, Fee plays a writer commissioned byPitlochry Festival theatreto turn out a play about Liberace. The only thing is, he despises everything the American showbiz pianist stands for.Russell Beale has smashed into designer Tim Hatley’s previously orderly front-room set with the kind of over-the-top flourish that onlyLiberacecould pull off. And that is what infuriates the writer.As a young gay man, he is embarrassed by the innuendo, the materialism and the deceit. He is hung up in particular by the entertainer’s successful 1959court action against a Daily Mirror columnistwho had implied he was a homosexual (more precisely, a “quivering, giggling, fruit-flavoured, mincing, ice-covered heap of mother love”).View image in fullscreenEmbarrassed by the innuendo … Simon Russell Beale and Fra Fee in I’ll Be Seeing You.Photograph: Tiu MakkonenNot only the young writer but also, it would seem, Sherman himself is dismayed by Liberace’s willingness to lie on oath, denying his sexuality just as he would deny the HIV diagnosis at the end of his life.But the more the writer obsesses about that lie, the less Liberace’s court-room denial seems to be the issue. Sherman, the elderly playwright looking back on his life – and making his stage debut to do so – sees in Liberace the frivolous opposite of himself.The man who made his name withBent, a play about gay persecution during the Holocaust, has nothing in common with the pianist’s rhinestone-and-candelabra escapism. Yet, in a merrily wayward production co-directed by Ben Occhipinti and Alan Cumming, Russell Beale keeps barging in, demanding the limelight, milking the applause.Liberace’s life force is too great to be tamed. In a struggle between the earnest and the ephemeral, he might well be the victor. By the end, the pianist is spoon-feeding ice-cream into the mouth of the playwright, a man infantilised by a hopeless battle.AtPitlochry Festival theatre,until 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreSimon Russell BealeLiberacePitlochry Festival theatreMartin ShermanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Doors Down review – outrageously sharp, joyously sweary return of the Latimer Crescent favourites | Stage | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the sitcom’s new series in 2027 the full TV cast reunite for a masterclass in comfort comedy, adding musical interludes to the familiar suburban bedlam
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: Ahead of the sitcom’s new series in 2027 the full TV cast reunite for a masterclass in comfort comedy, adding musical interludes to the familiar suburban bedlam
Content: Amped up absurdity … from left, Jamie Quinn, Kieran Hodgson, Arabella Weir, Doon Mackichan and Jonathan Watson in Two Doors Down, at OVO Hydro, Glasgow.Photograph: Ian Georgeson/Ian Georgeson PhotographyView image in fullscreenAmped up absurdity … from left, Jamie Quinn, Kieran Hodgson, Arabella Weir, Doon Mackichan and Jonathan Watson in Two Doors Down, at OVO Hydro, Glasgow.Photograph: Ian Georgeson/Ian Georgeson PhotographyStageReviewTwo Doors Down review – outrageously sharp, joyously sweary return of the Latimer Crescent favouritesOVO Hydro, GlasgowAhead of the sitcom’s new series in 2027 the full TV cast reunite for a masterclass in comfort comedy, adding musical interludes to the familiar suburban bedlamArusa QureshiSun 27 Sep 2026 05.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may have started as a one-off special in 2013, but seven series and five Christmas specials in, Two Doors Down has become a Scottish institution of sorts. Created and written by Simon Carlyle and Gregor Sharp, the BBC Scotland sitcom set in aGlasgowsuburb is comfort comedy at its very best, with endlessly quotable quips and characters that are masterfully crafted – simultaneously far-fetched and remarkably familiar.The premise of every episode is essentially the same: longsuffering couple Beth and Eric Baird (played by Arabella Weir and Alex Norton) spend their days being hassled by their eccentric neighbours, who continuously abuse their hospitality and turn trivial moments into drama-fuelled bedlam. While the story follows the same structure in this stage adaptation, we soon learn that big changes are afoot, which threaten to upturn the entire ecosystem of Latimer Crescent as we know it.View image in fullscreenProsecco o’clock … Kieran Hodgson, Doon Mackichan and Alex Norton in Two Doors Down.Photograph: Ian Georgeson/Ian Georgeson PhotographyThe beauty of Two Doors Down is that very little ever happens in a single episode, so the question of how this translates to the mammoth stage of Glasgow’s OVO Hydro is a fair one to ask. But the intimacy of Simon Higlett’s suburban set design, with the addition of some creative and extravagant touches, transports you seamlessly to Beth and Eric’s living room, with its pressure cooker-like atmosphere amplified by the arrival of each guest.The entire cast are on fine form and their camaraderie and clear synergy is what allows this adaptation to work so well. Elaine C Smith is predictably, and gloriously, ludicrous as the ever-critical and no-holds-barred Christine, and Jonathan Watson and Doon Mackichan amp up the absurdity with each glass of prosecco as the unfiltered and highly inappropriate couple Colin and Cathy. Playing the usually polite and eager-to-please Gordon, Kieran Hodgson is finally let loose and elicits some of the biggest laughs of the night, while Graeme “Grado” Stevely’s deadpan Alan offers up a barrage of terrific one-liners.There are nods to the TV series throughout: callbacks to fan-favourite lines (“I’ll tell you who does a nice paracetamol – Morrisons.”) and memorable moments from episodes, including Cathy and Colin’s cringe-inducing wedding dance, but it never feels stale. Instead, the addition of musical interludes and purposely exaggerated Scottish cliches and in-jokes makes this production feel like a warm hug from someone you’ve missed. There is no expectation of anything profound occurring, but there are snippets of tenderness in the gentle reminder of the power of community and the strong pull of home. Ultimately though, with its outrageously sharp punchlines and joyously sweary cheek, this version of Two Doors Down is a great way to tide everyone over until the series returns in 2027.AtOVO Hydro, Glasgow, 9-11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageGlasgowTheatreComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m an everythingist’: How Es Devlin became the go-to for Beyoncé gigs, fashion runways and the Olympics | Es Devlin | The Guardian
description: The Londoner is the set designer big names turn to for eye-popping spectacle. As a new retrospective opens, she gives the Guardian a glimpse at her studio
Author: Dale Berning Sawa
Headline: The Londoner is the set designer big names turn to for eye-popping spectacle. As a new retrospective opens, she gives the Guardian a glimpse at her studio
Content: The Londoner is the set designer big names turn to for eye-popping spectacle. As a new retrospective opens, she gives the Guardian a glimpse at her studioByDale Berning Sawa; photographs byKate PetersSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour years ago, the V&A East Storehouse in east London got in touch withEs Devlin. The museum’s curators wanted to invite the British artist and designer to respond to a 100-year-old theatrical backdrop by the Russian artist and designer Natalia Goncharova. For a 1926 London production of The Firebird by the Ballets Russes, Goncharova had painted a fortified Muscovite cityscape festooned with onion domes and spires, rust-red and golden against a deep-blue sky. Devlin didn’t know much about Goncharova. But alighting on the term she had favoured for describing her kaleidoscopic approach to art-making, Devlin realised she’d found a kindred spirit. “She called herself an ‘everythingist’,” Devlin says, a smile in her eyes.View image in fullscreenWorks in progress in Devlin’s studioView image in fullscreenTrawl through Devlin’s own outsized CV and you’ll see immediately why she felt the label fit her too, and why she chose The Everythingists as the title of the large-scale sculptural work she made in response.In the 30 years since she won the Linbury prize for stage design in 1995, Devlin has established herself as a go-to set designer for highbrow theatre, international opera, global pop (Bad Bunny, Lady Gaga, Beyoncé), official celebrations (two Super Bowl half-time shows, two Olympic ceremonies), fashion runways and public sculpture. She has three honorary doctorates, multiple Oliviers, Tonys, Emmys and Critics’ Circle awards, the LondonDesignMedal, an OBE and a CBE. Much of this has been for services to design. But Devlin’s ability to pair drawing and intricate handicraft with arena-level spectacle and sociopolitical relevance has also routinely caught the eye of contemporary art curators (Hans Ulrich Obrist, Ekow Eshun) and theoretical physicists alike (Carlo Rovelli is a fan).View image in fullscreenA workdesk in Devlin’s studio“I’ve been like this since I was very young,” Devlin says from her garden in south London, where we meet ahead of her forthcoming retrospective, Es Devlin: Other Worlds at the Design Museum in London. “When I was at school, the teachers used to say: ‘You’re a jack of all trades and master of none,’ and it’s only recently that I learned that phrase actually has another couplet, which is, ‘But oftentimes better than a master of one.’” To her mind, “it’s an injustice to the condition of being alive to seek only depth at the expense of breadth. I think you actually achieve greater depth if you expand your line of inquiry.”Devlin wears a Barbie pink T-shirt under a knitted vest of a slightly different bright pink, workers’ blue trousers, bright coral-red Crocs and sculptural pendants on long silver chains. Two floor-to-ceiling mirror doors separate her studio rooms from her home, with a light-filled open-plan kitchen and living area beyond them. Two ginger cats mosey about between giant vessels of turned wood on wide marble surfaces and a pair of even bigger sculpted hands, roughly the height of a person. These are maquettes for the floating 25 metre-tall set Devlin designed for Carmen at the Bregenz Festspiele in 2017. The right hand stands guard by the sofas. The left perches in one of the studio rooms out front, surrounded by a sea of materials, works and models. “I’m actually quite excited about moving everything from that studio into the Design Museum because I’ll have every space clear and nothing on the walls. And then I just need to sit in there and make stuff.”View image in fullscreenA bookcase at Devlin’s homeThe retrospective maps out 30 years of Devlin’s practice in sculpture, film and installation, with an expansive display of archival drawings, paintings, collages, diaries and prints that give an insight into how she gets things done. At the show’s core is a large circular piece that combines several milestone projects including the 2021 mirror-maze piece Forest of Us; the rotating glass box-based set designed in 2018 for The Lehman Trilogy, directed by Sam Mendes; and the union jack stadium-floor covering designed for the London 2012 Olympics closing ceremony.In 2023, Devlin published a monograph titled An Atlas of Es Devlin, which comprised a double fold-out list, detailing more than 120 projects she had worked on over 30-plus years. A revised edition now adds 30 new projects to the list, evidence of an unrelenting workflow. Recent collaborations have included the set for a production of Rajiv Joseph’s Archduke at London’s Royal Court theatre; a retrospective at Futura Seoul, South Korea; and London Oratorio, a one-night production at the South Bank, in collaboration with musician Jacob Collier, composer Kieran Brunt and scores of the capital’s choristers. She is designing Olivia Rodrigo’s forthcoming arena tour. She’s writing a book, planning a ball, setting up a new studio in Sussex. When does she sleep? “I get plenty of sleep. But I do have quite a lot of things …” She gestures to the tree above her. “I wouldn’t be able to do what I’m doing today if I hadn’t done what I did yesterday. It’s an accumulation. It’s a tree that’s growing.” The most important thing is to keep feeding the trunk of it, she says, “to be alone in the studio”.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenDevlin in her studio, with some of the tools of her tradeEsmeralda Devlin was born in Kingston upon Thames in 1971. Her father was a journalist and her mother a teacher – to Devlin’s mind, both artists. When she and her three siblings were all under 10 years old (she’s one of the middle kids), her parents took in three of their cousins for a year, seven children fitting into a three-bedroom house. “Any time there was a Christmas or a birthday, you know, my mum would just say: ‘Well, you can’t buy anything. Make something,’” she says.Beyond gifts, Devlin would invent systems, follow instructions in craft books to make a periscope, say, with her mother’s makeup mirror, and devise complicated games. “My dad, who’d always take us quite seriously, would say: ‘You know, maybe we should send this to Waddingtons. Maybe this could become a game.’” Every Tuesday night there was a mad rush to find and return the library books they’d each got out for the week. “Mine were always under a pile of yoghurt pots, and cardboard boxes and toilet rolls because I’d be making some elaborate run for the gerbils.”double quotation markI think I was insufficiently intimidated early on ... there was a lot I wanted to expressWhile she was still little, her family moved to Rye, on the East Sussex coast. She recalls the theatricality of church services there, where she would help to set out the wafers and wine for holy communion and ring the bell during the Kyrie Eleison, plus the altogether more pagan celebrations of the town’s bonfire pageants. She remembers routinely taking any visitors down from London to see the Rye Town Model next door, asonetlumièrerecreation of the town and its history, replete with lighting and a recorded narration. Nearly 50 years on, Devlin can tell you exactly what was in it: “There was a story about a monk and a nun who got bricked up in the walls for having an affair. There was a story about a butcher murdering somebody.” What really stuck in her mind, though, was that each house would light up as it spoke. Hers told of a wool merchant and a writer, the daughter of a poet. She found it mesmerising that “a building that I lived in was small enough for me to hold. I could look down on my house and think: ‘Oh, I can pick it up.’ But also, I would go next door and I’d be in my house and my house would be holding me.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenSketchbooks in Devlin’s studioAlong with the power and presence of objects, music has woven a golden thread through Devlin’s life. She took all her grades in violin, clarinet and piano before realising, as a teenager, that her path would be, as she puts it, “something that fused my knowledge of music and my practice of music, with other things”. After a BA in English literature, a foundation course at Central Saint Martins and a year on the Motley theatre design course atTheatreRoyal Drury Lane, that path lit up. She won a job to design Marlowe’s Edward II at the Octagon theatre in Bolton. That led to a piece at London’s Bush theatre, which was seen by Trevor Nunn, artistic director of the Royal National Theatre, who promptly hired her for a production of Harold Pinter’s Betrayal. Then came the Rambert Dance Company’s Four Scenes, the show with which the new Sadler’s Wells was inaugurated in 1998. Devlin had just turned 27. “It was a very rapid baptism of fire,” she says.Was she intimidated, working at that level with established directors so early on in her career? “I think I was insufficiently intimidated,” she says. “By then, I had been in education a long time and there was a lot I wanted to express.”This unflappable nature, this gung-ho “yes, please!” attitude, has since taken her everywhere – Compton, the Louvre, Morocco’s Agafay Desert, Malawi – collaborating with everyone from Rosalía and Kendrick Lamar to Max Richter. In 2013, shetold the Guardianthat a low point of her career had been sending groundplans to Shakira while in labour. Young artists, in particular, often ask how she holds on to her identity when collaborating with powerful people. “The best answer I’ve given to this question is: I actually am not too afraid to lose my identity. By being prepared to lose it, you encounter other aspects that are probably more interesting.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen(Clockwise from top left) Devlin’s 2026 installation Sou o Outro do Outro in São Paolo; Library of Light in Milan from 2025; Congregation at St Mary le Strand in London from 2024; The Lehman Trilogy at the National Theatre, London from 2018That doesn’t mean that she ever actually loses herself in someone else’s world, which, you sense, is exactly why these big names seek her out. “What I’ve observed about powerful people is, it’s unfortunate, but a bit like barnacles on a great whale, there are peripheral structures that accumulate around power and fame. And to the powerful person and the famous person, those structures are really uninteresting.” She looms, instead, like an octopus, tentacles in every direction, drawing the world in an indelible ink that is hers alone. Viewers at the Design Museum will note the coherence, the very Es Devlinness, of her work, regardless of whom it is for. Leitmotivs (the line of light, the glowing box, the map, the tree-lung, the egg that opens) recur. Her conceptual imperatives are clear, too. She has no interest in decoration, everything has to have meaning. The audience must have agency. Materiality matters. And portraiture is fundamental. “Everything is both a portrait of the collaborator and a self-portrait at the same time.”My second visit, two days later, is to Devlin’s other studio in Peckham, south London, where design associates sit at computers rendering 2D and 3D visualisations for set designs: Olivia Rodrigo’s forthcoming arena tour; the Design Museum show floorplan. The latter will contain multiple maquettes of previous large-scale works. Downstairs, a model-maker is adding finishing touches to a tiny maquette of Devlin’s installation Library of Light, an 18-metre revolving cylindrical bookshelf containing 3,200 books, designed for the Salone del Mobile in Milan in 2025. Beside her are reused takeaway boxes filled with tiny fake books: she reckons she’s made about 1,800.View image in fullscreenArtworks around Devlin’s studioDevlin appears in bright yellow and bright white. Sitting down to lunch, she says: “I was speaking with William Kentridge about the way he labels his projects, and he has ‘urgent’, ‘desperate’, ‘emergency’ and ‘SOS’. That’s definitely how we could label our projects.”What is SOS right now? “The Design Museum is SOS,” she says. So too, the 2026 British Museum Ball in October, for which she is the artistic director. She and a member of her team went on a tour of the museum and met “six people who’ve worked there, a combined number of 137 years; profound knowledge, profound understanding of objects which tell our history and explain who we are”. What she wants her design to communicate, she says, is the museum’s staff, all 1,000 of them. She sees them as protagonists, much like the 50 refugees of whom she did portraits for her UNHCR installation Congregation in 2024, or the 55 million adults invited to take part in her A National Portrait project for London’s National Portrait Gallery.U2 review – an utterly astonishing, admirably raw Vegas extravaganzaRead moreThat people and real lives are central to what Devlin does is tangible in the way she includes her team in our chat. She wants their perspectives. She clearly treasures their work. One associate tells me she trained as an architect but, on graduating, thought: “There’s got to be something else out there. This is surely not it.” Devlin’s studio is a haven for like-minded seekers, who are interested in everything and want more.Over coffee and dark chocolate, Devlin shows me her rings. She is testing intriguing prototypes of kinetic silver with her designs: an iris, a spinning cube, a minute Venus of Willendorf, an egg that opens up to reveal a tree or a lung. “I’m writing a book called The Compass of Es Devlin,” she says, “which is sort of elucidating various practices that have helped me. And these are to help me remember them. It’s almost like they’re little cues.”To watch her manipulate these tiny sculptures, or draw her signature into a book, is to see what she must have been like as a small child – utterly engrossed in the creative task at hand: Es Devlin, the everythingist.Es Devlin: Other Worldsis at the Design Museum, London, from2 Octoberto 4 April.
