title: Does avoiding misery make you happy? | Books | The Guardian
description: It might seem like self-preservation, but the results aren’t necessarily what you’d expect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It might seem like self-preservation, but the results aren’t necessarily what you’d expect
Content: Illustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianThe big ideaBooksDoes avoiding misery make you happy?It might seem like self-preservation, but the results aren’t necessarily what you’d expectGeorge LoewensteinSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInDr Seuss’s Green Eggs and Ham, the relentlessly upbeat Sam-I-Am spends the entire book badgering a grouchy, nameless narrator into tasting the eponymous dish. He cycles through one inventive but futile pitch after another – in a house, with a mouse, in a box, with a fox, on a train, in the rain – until the narrator, caving just to get some peace, tastes the dish and discovers he loves it. When my son was growing up, “Green Eggs and Ham” was my shorthand for telling him he was avoiding something he’d love if he only tried it.Of course, not every experience we fear or dread turns out to be a delicious surprise. Misery is an inescapable part of the human condition. We can’t avoid it, yet people try their hardest anyway. We cling to hope even when a situation is hopeless. We push painful thoughts out of mind rather than confront them. We struggle to control things that cannot be changed. And we go to sometimes self-destructive lengths to protect our pride from even the tiniest pinprick. These strategies may sometimes spare us pain in the moment. But while they are intended to promote (or at least preserve) our happiness, over time they have the perverse result of making us much more miserable.Consider relationships. Declining to chat with the talkative person sitting next to you on a plane avoids one obvious downside – getting stuck in a boring conversation you can’t gracefully exit. But as psychologist Nicholas Epleyshowsin an extensive body of research, doing this again and again quietly robs us of interactions we might have found genuinely rewarding, though we’ll never know what we missed.The same instinct to protect ourselves can become more destructive in close relationships, when the misery that we fear is rejection. People who are “rejection sensitive” tend to expect the worst and see signs of the coming apocalypse even in ambiguous behaviour, like an unanswered text message. When they think they see rejection coming, they try to avoid it by rejecting first – responding with hostility or pulling away from their partner in a self-defeating effort to protect themselves. As a result, behaviour that was meant to ward off rejection ends upprovokingit.In my own research, Isurveyeda large sample of adults, asking whether they take too many risks, too few, or roughly the right amount – both overall and across key areas such as work, health and relationships. The results were striking. About half felt they took the right amount of risk. But among the rest, the overwhelming majority felt they took too few – and the reason they gave, again and again, was a desire to avoid miserable emotions like fear and regret.double quotation markWe reach for distraction, numbing, and busyness to keep from thinking about what causes us painOne of the great engines of misery is “counterfactual thinking”: our mental habit of imagining how things might have gone differently. While we have the capacity to imagine better and worse outcomes, research shows that we are much more likely to dwell on how things could have been better than to consider how they could have been worse. Such “upward counterfactuals” – the job offer we didn’t take, the romantic connection we didn’t pursue – tend to leave us feeling regretful and dissatisfied with the reality we actually have. This asymmetry punishes those who assiduously avoid every opportunity that might result in pain or heartbreak, because such avoidance inevitably creates a stockpile of upward counterfactuals, all the roads not taken. Psychologists distinguish regrets of commission from regrets of omission; it’s the latter – the things we could have done but didn’t – thathaunt us longest.We don’t only avoid misery by avoiding risky behaviour; a whole separate category of avoidance happens purely in the mind. We reach for distraction, numbing, and busyness to keep from thinking about what causes us pain. But you cannot anaesthetise sadness without anaesthetising everything nearby. Emotional systems don’t come with a dial that turns down grief while leaving joy untouched; suppress one and the whole range tends to flatten.The practised avoider often ends up not happy, exactly, but flat – free of acute suffering, perhaps, but also missing the intensity, curiosity, and aliveness that make the good parts of life feel good. This flatness is easy to mistake for equanimity, since it doesn’t announce itself as pain. The protagonist in Stefan Zweig’s story Fantastic Night lives this numbness for years, until one reckless act cracks it open – and what rushes back in isn’t relief but a flood of feeling, the discovery that his calm had been an absence, rather than peace.Research onphysical painfinds, surprisingly, that focusing on pain can diminish its intensity more effectively than trying to distract from it – and there are parallel, if somewhat more mixed, findings for negative emotions generally. One line ofinquiryshows that “affect labelling” – simply putting feelings into words – dampens neural reactions to distress. Another set ofstudiesfinds that people instructed to accept a negative emotion, rather than suppress it, recover faster, both emotionally and physiologically.None of this is an argument for deliberately courting misery, or for treating pain as good in itself. But unhappiness-avoidance, adopted as an organising life principle rather than an occasional and reasonable caution, is self-undermining. It reduces the kinds of experiences available to us, including those of the “Green Eggs and Ham” variety that may prove incredibly meaningful.My father, born a German Jew, spent part of the second world war in a French prisoner of war camp. He and the small pack of close friends he made there were hungry enough to dig up worms for food and chew on shoe leather. But he once told me that, due to the companionship and challenge of that ordeal, it was the peak experience of his life. Avoidance of misery rests on a false premise about how happiness actually works. The person who spends a life dodging unhappiness does not arrive, in the end, at a life free from misery. Unhappiness avoided is not happiness gained, but more often just misery in disguise.George Loewenstein is university professor of economics and psychology at Carnegie Mellon, and author ofThe Opposite of Happiness(William Collins).Further readingBetter in Every Senseby Norman Farb and Zindel Segal (Yellow Kite, £20)The Antidoteby Oliver Burkeman (Vintage, £12.99)Full Catastrophe Livingby Jon Kabat-Zinn (Piatkus, £24.99)Explore more on these topicsBooksThe big ideaHappinessNeuroscienceMental healthHealthPsychologyHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children | Roblox | The Guardian
description: Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data
Content: Roblox says that to avoid scams, users should always go through the official app or website, and ‘never click through links or download anything from unknown senders or websites’.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoblox says that to avoid scams, users should always go through the official app or website, and ‘never click through links or download anything from unknown senders or websites’.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersScam watchRoblox‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting childrenCriminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal dataShane HickeySun 27 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 02.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour 10-year-old son has started playingRoblox, when he realises all of his in-game currency, Robux, is gone.When you try to find out what happened, he says he was recently promised extra Robux if he followed a link on YouTube. When he signed on at the site link, he was taken to the Roblox site as usual but there was no sign of the extra currency.He has fallen victim to a fraud where Roblox users – many of whom are children – are being targeted for their login details. With those details criminals can steal the virtual currency and players’ personal data.Within Roblox, players use Robux to buy virtual items, such as skins or animations for their avatar. You can earn the currency within the game, but it can also be bought. At Roblox’s online store you can buypackages costing up to £199.99.Using ready-made kits bought on the dark web, fraudsters create a fake login page that is identical in appearance to the legitimate Roblox site.View image in fullscreenA screengrab of a scam webpage targeting young Roblox usersPhotograph: Screengrab“The kid will enter their details and the fake website will actually redirect them to a legitimate Roblox page,” says Gerald Kasulis, the vice-president of global affairs at the cybersecurity company NordVPN. “So ultimately, the kid will get to where they want to go.”By that stage, however, the criminals will have the details they need for defrauding.Researchers from NordVPN say that over a seven-day period they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages that provided the tools to defraud Roblox users.What it looks likeOften the links to the phishing sites are in comments on YouTube or TikTok videos or in chats on Discord, the chat app for gamers.The message might say there are free Robux available if a player clicks on the link provided. Like many scams, there will often be an element of urgency attached, such as the offer apparently only being valid for a few hours, to encourage the victim to act without fully thinking through the consequences.From that link, the child will be taken to a fake sign-in page that will probably be identical to a legitimate Roblox site in appearance. The address will usually contain the name Roblox, for example “Roblox-verify” or “login-Roblox”.View image in fullscreenA screengrab of a scam webpage targeting young Roblox usersPhotograph: ScreengrabWhen they are on the scam site, the child will be asked for their username and password but may also be told to put in two-factor identification codes, says NordVPN. But then the child is taken to the legitimate Roblox site so they can play their games as normal, leaving little indication that anything is amiss.Once they have the login details, the fraudster may sell them on or use them to transfer Robux to another account.What to doTalk to children about scams.“One of the simplest habits is to encourage children to open Roblox directly through the official app or website rather than logging in through links they are sent,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN.“Two-factor authentication remains an important protection, but authentication codes and backup codes should be treated just like passwords and never handed over to somebody else.”If your player has lost their Robux to a hacker, it seems unlikely that they will get it back. Roblox says that it is under “no obligation” to assist people whose accounts have been compromised, unless it is required to do so by law.“Roblox does not guarantee that an individual’s account will be restored to its previous state, or that Roblox will be able to recover lost virtual items or virtual currency,” it says.In “very limited circumstances”, Roblox says it may recover lost items or the value of them.A spokesperson for Roblox says there are security measures in place to prevent phishing, such as two-factor authentication and a feature that stops criminals logging into your account from elsewhere.“We continue to work on new ways to minimise the risk of account theft and actively encourage Roblox users to follow security best practices, including not clicking on links or downloading anything from unknown senders or websites,” the spokesperson adds.Explore more on these topicsRobloxScam watchScamsConsumer affairsGamesInternet safetyCybercrimeChildren's techfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rapper and actor Eve looks back: ‘I was the only girl in the boardroom in major label meetings – that Philly girl had to come out’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The Grammy-winning artist on ​d​estroying egos in school, the dealers who looked out for her, and learning from early failure
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The Grammy-winning artist on ​d​estroying egos in school, the dealers who looked out for her, and learning from early failure
Content: FlashbackMusicRapper and actor Eve looks back: ‘I was the only girl in the boardroom in major label meetings – that Philly girl had to come out’The Grammy-winning artist on ​d​estroying egos in school, the dealers who looked out for her, and learning from early failureHarriet GibsoneSun 27 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEve in 2000 wearing a red sleeveless top, red trousers and belt, and red heels, reclining on some white stairs with her thumbs in her pockets, and recreating the image in 2026Eve in 2000 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian. Styling: Andie Redman. Archive image: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesBorn Eve Jihan Jeffers in Philadelphia in 1978, rapper Eve released her debut album, Let There Be Eve … Ruff Ryders’ First Lady, in 1999; it entered the Billboard 200 at No 1. She followed its success with the platinum-selling Scorpion, which went on to win a Grammy for the single Let Me Blow Ya Mind. As an actor, she appeared in the Barbershop films and starred in her own sitcom, Eve. She married London-based entrepreneur Maximillion Cooper in 2014; together they have a son, and she is stepmother to his four children. Eve will tour the UK and Europe in 2027.This was taken in Miami, where I was recording Scorpion.I was obsessed with red because of its astrological affiliation with Scorpio – everything had to be that colour. My hair is short because I convinced my hairstylist to put both a perm relaxer and colour in, which you’re not supposed to do. All my hair fell out, but thankfully it looked good. I felt powerful and sexy.I knew I wanted to be a rapper as far back as 15. I was that kid at school who tried her hand at everything, whether it was tap dance or violin. I started rapping at 11, and four years later I said to my mum: “I know you probably want me to go to college, but I really want to do music.” I thought she would be upset, but she wasn’t. There was only one plan B, and that was special-effects makeup. Some days I still think about retraining in it.Coming from Philadelphia definitely shaped the rapper I went on to become. Philly girls are known for being feisty, for not taking no for an answer. It’s the underdog city – close to New York, but people usually skip over us to get there – and as a result Philly people are used to working their asses off. Growing up, it was a lot more dangerous than it is now, so I saw a lot of drugs and guns, but the dealers were also guys who looked out for me – they were friends. I still knew I wanted to get out. I had a sheer determination that things would turn out different for me.double quotation markI loved words, and when I wasn’t in a battle trying to destroy someone’s ego, I was also obsessing over poetryMy rap battles started at school.I was battling the boys, often in patois, which is so ridiculous, because I’m not even Jamaican. I would talk about their dick size, but also how they lived with their mum and were broke and taking the bus to school, ignoring the fact that I was, too. I loved words, and when I wasn’t in a battle trying to destroy someone’s ego, I was also obsessing over poetry.In my late teens, I met Ma$e. Like a birdie on my shoulder, he started telling me I should take rap seriously. After that, I got signed to Dre’s Aftermath. At the time, I was calling myself Eve of Destruction, because I really was that girl – I had an attitude. Eight months later, I got dropped. It was devastating to have my dream taken away, but if I hadn’t experienced that initial failure, I probably wouldn’t have had the success I had next. After I had spent a month depressed on my mum’s couch, Jimmy Iovine called and said I should meet Ruff Ryders [a hip-hop label and collective that included DMX, the Lox, Jadakiss, Swizz Beatz].Ruff Ryders were my safe place. I’d gone through a lot of haunting experiences trying to get my music out there previously – the kind of bullshit that all women go through in most industries. I’d go to New York to play my demo to some producer, and instead of taking me seriously he’d hit on me and say, “Let’s go for dinner.” By comparison, Ruff Ryders were the opposite. If anything, they were trying to cover me up, as I loved to wear little heels and shorts and tube tops. They were like: “Here, put this vest on! Get these Timberlands on!” They also taught me how to format a song. At the start, I was just a battle rapper, but working with them was a hip-hop boot camp.All of which led to the success of Scorpion.I was a huge fan of all genres of music, from Biggie Smalls to No Doubt, and when I wrote Let Me Blow Ya Mind I knew we should get Gwen Stefani to feature on it. I was the only girl in the boardroom in those major label meetings and that Philly girl often had to come out. They were initially resistant because I was a rapper and she was a rock star, but I said: “Guys, this will work. Trust me.”Even though I won that particular fight, the response to a lot of my suggestions was often: “Oh, that’s cute. We’re not doing that.” I felt I couldn’t be my full, excited self because there were so many miserable motherfuckers around me in those boardrooms. The atmosphere made me feel like I had to suppress myself and stay small. Decades later, my old A&R actually called up and apologised. He said: “I really wish we listened to you a little bit more – you had some good ideas.” That was validating.When things took off, there was no time to celebrate. I was on to the next studio, on to the next show. But I remember hearing my voice in an SUV on Hot 97, one of the biggest hip-hop radio stations in New York, and thinking, “This is it. This is the moment.” I’d meet young women with the same paw prints tattooed on their chest as mine, who would tell me it had gotten them in trouble with their parents. “This is amazing,” I’d say, “but I did not tell you to do that!”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElkie Brooks looks back: ‘Before I went on stage I used to drink Guinness and a few shots of brandy’Read moreThe grind was gruelling, and in the aftermath of Scorpion I was burned out. I struggled with anxiety and depression, but nobody talked about mental health back then. Instead, I was encouraged to drink and get on with whatever we had to do that day. Like every young artist, I was definitely tortured. I hung around the wrong people, did the wrong things to try to cope, and went down the path of self-medicating. There were many moments when I would call home and cry to my mum and tell her: “I can’t do this any more.” I was sad and lonely and my friendships were breaking up. I was always thinking, “Wait, who changed? Did I change? Did you? Did we change?” I’d lost a sense of belonging that I’d always had.I realised that being a musicianwasa gruelling ass life,and had a period of time where I straddled the disciplines of being a rapper and actor and a TV personality. But that was exhausting, too. I would go to the club, get in at 2am, and have to be on set at 9am, all of which was unsustainable. One day I looked at myself and thought, “What life do you really want? I just want to be happy and healthy.” I started implementing things like therapy, acupuncture and healing work. I still have days where I am overwhelmed – life is not perfect – but at least I have the tools to cope.Rapping in my 40s is a different act than it was in 2001. What remains is my feistiness – it still comes out when it needs to. But this time I am present. I don’t have anybody breathing on my neck, saying: “We’ve got to sell these records.” I also have a total sense of wonder about my life, that it’s taken me this far. I wake up and think, “Damn. How did a girl from Philly get here?”Explore more on these topicsMusicFlashbackPhotographyRapHip-hopPop and rockTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d like to explain why I was such a monster back then’: six writers on the apologies they wish they’d made | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: From making life hell for a young teacher to doubting the motives of a caring foster mother, Olivia Petter, Derek Owusu, Annie Lord and other writers repent for past bad behaviour
Author: Olivia Petter
Headline: From making life hell for a young teacher to doubting the motives of a caring foster mother, Olivia Petter, Derek Owusu, Annie Lord and other writers repent for past bad behaviour
Content: Illustration: Pâté on Toast/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Pâté on Toast/The GuardianHealth & wellbeing‘I’d like to explain why I was such a monster back then’: six writers on the apologies they wish they’d madeFrom making life hell for a young teacher to doubting the motives of a caring foster mother, Olivia Petter, Derek Owusu, Annie Lord and other writers repent for past bad behaviourOlivia Petter, Derek Owusu, William Rayfet Hunter,Poorna Bell,Annie LordandNikesh ShuklaSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlivia Petter: ‘We hid in cupboards behind Ms Hill’s desk and jumped out to frighten her halfway through lessons’View image in fullscreen‘‘I really regret the way my friend and I behaved.’Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianAt school, I was not a good girl. Actually, that’s putting it mildly: I was an emotional terrorist hellbent on inflicting torture and humiliation on my year 6 teacher, Ms Hill, one whoopee cushion at a time. That’s how it began, anyway, but like all crimes, mine followed a strategic pattern of escalation, carefully executed alongside my best friend and accomplice.We started small: bringing spiders into Ms Hill’s classroom; writing silly notes on the whiteboard; replacing her precious chocolate digestives with stale biscuits from the dining hall. Then we took things further, hiding in cupboards behind her desk and jumping out to frighten her halfway through lessons, and, on one occasion, exploiting the bathroom’s faulty taps to flood the entire thing over lunchtime.None of this was OK. In fact, it was downright awful, a symptom of reckless malevolence fuelled by boredom and entitlement. We were just unhappy kids who wanted to watch the world burn – an operation that poor Ms Hill bore almost all of the brunt of. To be clear, we never did anything that would constitute harassment, but our pranks were consistent and cruel.Looking back on them as an adult with several friends who work as teachers, I can’t help but feel a deep sense of shame and guilt. I owe Ms Hill a proper apology. And, while I won’t attempt to justify my 11-year-old self’s behaviour, I’d like to offer an explanation as to why I might have been such a little monster back then.Like so many other kids, I was being bullied, as was my best friend. I can remember one breaktime when she was pushed up against a wall by one of the older girls, who threatened to physically hurt her. Then there were the other classic things girls do to one another: leaving people out, spreading malicious rumours, and generally finding new and innovative ways to put people down to make others laugh. Neither one of us felt as if we fitted in, and so we stuck together.There were issues going on at home – my parents divorced and my dad was living between London and the US. And I wasn’t really sleeping, either; I had bouts of insomnia as a child. In other words, I was struggling, and doing poorly at school as a result. A newly qualified twentysomething teacher in charge of our class, Ms Hill was the one often reprimanding us for not getting the grades we should have been – it was a highly competitive school, so I suspect she was under pressure to make sure her pupils were meeting certain standards. Again, as kids, we didn’t know that. All we saw was a young teacher telling us we weren’t good enough, and being mean to us in the process. So we decided to be mean back.I really regret the way my friend and I behaved back then. Because, even though on the surface this might have looked like innocuous mischief, I can imagine it took a toll. Nobody deserves to be humiliated in their place of work, especially not by obnoxious children with far too much time on their hands. So, Ms Hill, if you’re still around, please accept my apology. I’m sorry for all the whoopee cushions, for stealing your biscuits, and for attempting to embarrass you to mask my own feelings of inadequacy. Ultimately, I hope my behaviour made you laugh more times than it made you frown. And that you are living a happy, fulfilled life somewhere with unlimited supplies of McVitie’s and absolutely no spiders.Olivia Petter is a journalist and author ofGold Rush.Derek Owusu: ‘Why did you foster us – why not other children, lighter in tone and burden, closer to those you had brought up?’View image in fullscreen‘I wish I had let you be, returning your compassion with some form of empathy.’Photograph: Kate PetersMum, why don’t I remember more about you? So much is missing. I had 10 years with you: seven before I was returned to my biological mother, and three broken up into Christmas visits, with photos I have since lost and sweets sometimes arriving in the post. I tell myself you died when I was 10, but maybe it was later. Maybe you were kept from me to help me move on, just like your death was kept from me until I turned 14.The last Christmas visit I remember well enough: the huge stocking with socks and satsumas at the bottom, imitation Game Boys, all surrounded by chocolate gold coins that sometimes cut you before they revealed the goods. Then, 10 of us around the kitchen table, crackers pulled and hats donned, jokes read to straight faces or a quick “oi” and glance down the table from you, and then, finally, the wait. Everyone had to be finished before we could run to the tree, and whoever was last received Christmas knocks on their head when you weren’t looking.These are the images I come back to. So many children running around your house, so much noise, so much joy and, of course, so much lost. Because each child was away from their parent(s), long‑term or short-term, but each child called you Mum, regardless of duration, regardless of difference.And weweredifferent. All black children living with a very white mother, from dressing us up for Remembrance Day – flat cap and shoe polish – to awkwardly cutting our afros with scissors and never worrying about moistening our scalps. So I ask why. Why did you foster us – why not other children, lighter in tone and burden, closer to those you had brought up? You had seven children of your own, I think, and grandchildren who surely could have allowed you to relive those years.View image in fullscreenDerek Owusu with his adoptive mother.Photograph: Courtesy of Derek OwusuI never got to ask, so I grew up speculating. Were you a white saviour, I asked myself. Was it Christian virtue? Was there more going on, more that I can’t remember, or choose not to?It could have simply been about the money. You had retired, and perhaps you needed the income, though I remember your husband working. Perhaps it was greed, the four-bedroom house with a garage and garden not enough. I asked myself all this and more, fictionalised you and then questioned you, tried to uncover something suppressed.Until, with time, with differing perspectives, I turned the why on myself. Why must there be something more? The money – the fee charged for private foster care that my biological mum paid monthly – you took a quarter of it and put it into a secret account, which became mine when I turned 16. Our race wasn’t your choice; it was more that private foster care was the safest alternative for west African immigrants, ones anxious about sending their children back to where they started, even if they struggled to find footing on the troubled ground of Britain.You were no saviour, because you were imperfect and made no attempt to hide it. You taught us lessons but presented them harshly, maybe too harshly, the cane by the window sill evidence of your impatience. But you apologised when you were wrong, acknowledged when we had done right. And kept going even when sick, when dying, trying to fight for the last of us.There is a story I remember, of one of the foster kids almost being deported with his family. And the person they immediately called was you. You drove to the airport, in that beat-up van we loved to pile into, picked up the child, and said you’d keep them safe for as long as was necessary.I need to let kindness be. I wish I had let you be, returning your compassion with some form of empathy. So, Mum, I am sorry. I’m sorry I failed to see you and I am sorry for my doubt.Derek Owusu is a writer and poet. His third novel,The Recovery House, is out now.William Rayfet Hunter: ‘I don’t think I dated you because I wanted to deceive you. I fell for you because I wanted to deceive myself’View image in fullscreen‘I already knew I was gay. Or rather, I knew in the strange way people know the things they cannot yet afford to admit.’Photograph: Courtesy of William Rayfet HunterIt’s a fresh spring afternoon, but inside the hermetically sealed corridor of the students’ union, the air is thick with body heat and desperation. Through clouds of Lynx Africa and BO comes an incessant thrum: whispered soliloquies, hummed arpeggios, the rustle of photocopied scripts. Next to me, a boy repeats his own name over and over as though, faced with the impatient stare of a third-year student cosplaying as a theatre director, he might forget this most elementary fact about himself. When my turn comes, I summon the confidence I’ve been trying to assemble over the previous six months.The theatre society was full of extraordinary talent, but all of the best performances happened off the stage. University offered all of us the same irresistible bargain: here, finally, we could become whoever we wanted to be. New friends. New politics. New haircuts. We dressed like people we had seen in films, smoked because interesting people smoked, half-read Judith Butler, and spoke with the unique certainty of bright 19-year-olds.That was the backdrop to our meeting. You were the rosy-cheeked girl in the director’s chair and I was your leading man. And from there we both played our parts perfectly until everything fell apart. Three months together at university felt like three years anywhere else. We rehearsed together, got blind drunk together, and learned each other’s childhood stories with the urgency of people convinced life was already slipping away.I’m sorry that when we met I couldn’t really see you. You were funny and warm and emotionally fluent in a way I wouldn’t be for years. You were trying, with remarkable generosity, to know me. The trouble was that I was entirely invested in remaining unknowable.I already knew I was gay. Or rather, I knew in the way people know the things they cannot yet afford to admit. It was my Big Secret: a stolen penny burning a hole in my pocket.I walked into that audition room full of false and careful bravado, and saw what I thought might be my salvation in your smile. I don’t think I dated you because I wanted to deceive you. I fell for you because I wanted to deceive myself. I imagine the distinction matters far less when you’re the one who gets hurt.If there was ever a moment, afterwards, when you wondered whether there had been something lacking in you, then I am deeply sorry. There wasn’t. The thing that wasn’t whole was me, and I mistook that incompleteness for a problem that could be solved by somebody else filling in the gaps.Growing up has involved many apologies. Some I’ve made. Some I’ve only rehearsed. This one sticks in my throat because it asks me to admit something I still find uncomfortable: that becoming yourself is not, by itself, a virtue. It matters how you do it, who gets caught in the machinery. I was so intent on becoming someone I could live with that I forgot you were living through it, too.People often say university is where you find yourself. That wasn’t quite true for me. University was where I finally stopped pretending it was possible to be somebody else. The irony, of course, is that I had joined the one society statistically least likely to cure me of being gay. Somewhere between Annie Get Your Gun, the Sondheim medley and the cancelled production of Rent, the evidence was mounting.Auditions are strange things. You spend two minutes pretending to be somebody else in the hope that someone will finally see who you are. I spent much longer pretending. I’m sorry you had to watch.William Rayfet Hunter is a writer and author ofSunstruck.Poorna Bell: ‘I went into a diatribe about how that woman was such a phoney. “I’m standing right behind you,” a voice said’View image in fullscreen‘I was in a really unhappy place in my life, and while alcohol should never be an excuse, it made me a nastier version of myself.’Photograph: Courtesy of Poorna BellAs nicknames go, Foghorn Leghorn – inspired by the oversized cartoon rooster with a booming voice – isn’t particularly agreeable to me, but it has been fairly accurate. When combined with alcohol, this tendency can create a toxic cocktail, and leads to me saying obnoxious things at a high volume, often about someone as they stand undetected, mere feet away.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI haven’t drunk alcohol for 16 months, primarily because it was making my body feel like a garbage pail, and with newfound sobriety comes a reckoning about some of the things I did and said while under the influence. It’s not exactly a 12-step list of amends, but it’s close.About 11 years ago, I was going to a press awards ceremony held at the Grosvenor hotel in London. I didn’t particularly want to go as it required a late night and an early start the next day, and it was this bedrock of grumbling that was my undoing. Sometimes I can be a cheerful drunk, but other times it taps into some unexpressed reservoir of resentment, and it was this that flowed into my bloodstream along with a lot of white wine.Early in the evening, a woman in her 20s came up to say hello. We didn’t know each other well, but I remembered her from an internal work event a couple of months prior. We made small talk at the bar, which then turned slightly awkward as we ran out of things to say, so I made my excuses. Around halfway through the evening, our team hadn’t won anything, and the mood of the table had turned slightly sour. It was at this point that the young woman came over to chat again. Through a haze of wine, I remember feeling irritated.Finally the ceremony ended, and we shuffled out to the cloakroom, where she and I encountered each other for the third time. Again, a sense of overfamiliarity lingered as we said our goodbyes. As my colleagues and I were heading to the door, one of them asked me who she was. I went into a diatribe about how that woman was such a phoney, pretending that we knew each other well. I overegged it entirely for the benefit of my audience. “I can’t stand her,” I finished dramatically.“I’m standing right behind you,” a voice said. I turned around, and there she was. When such a moment occurs, adrenaline floods your body alongside a cold dread, and then you just have to sit in the murk of what you have created. I opened my mouth to apologise but nothing came out.Although this is someone whose name I don’t remember, and who I am unlikely to recognise if I saw them again, I think about this moment with surprising regularity. I think about what it must have been like to hear someone talk about you like that, but I also wonder what possessed me to say all of those things that weren’t even real, or true.I wish I could tell her I’m sorry, and that I was probably saying all of those things about myself, and it was definitely not about her at all. That, actually, I was in a really unhappy place in my life, and while alcohol should never be an excuse, it made me a nastier version of myself. I wonder how many of these apologies I owe to people.Poorna Bell is a journalist and author. Her latest book,She Wanted More, is out now.Annie Lord: ‘I gave it about a day, then I dumped him. I thought I was rotten, so if someone liked me there must be something wrong with them’View image in fullscreen‘I hope it didn’t make him scared of intimacy, or trap him in a pattern.’Photograph: PRWe were in year 8. I don’t remember much about him. Only that he was covered in freckles and was very bony, all elbows and knees. To me he appeared quite conventionally attractive with his well-proportioned face, but he was in the nerdy group so that wouldn’t have counted for anything. He came back from a holiday with malaria, which I thought was pretty exciting back then.Around him, everything else seemed to fade into nothing. My throat would go dry when we spoke, and it was hard to get my words out. I realised after a while that this must be what fancying someone felt like. Eventually, he fancied me, too, and asked me to be his girlfriend. Well, he asked someone to ask me, as was customary back then.It wasn’t long after I said yes that something started to shift. What was once light and uncertain was now concrete: he was myboyfriend. Now there were rules we had to follow. People would expect us to kiss, hold hands, be together all the time. The intensity that I had once enjoyed now felt suffocating.When people found out, there wasn’t much of a commotion because I wasn’t a very notable character. I was Vicky’s best friend, the blond girl who went bright red when anyone spoke to her. But I remember sitting on the field during PE and one of the popular girls saying to me, “Oh, how sweet, Pete’s finally got a girlfriend.” It was immediately horrifying. Her comment seemed to confirm all my deepest fears. There must be something wrong with him – that’s why no one else wanted him.I gave it about a day and then I dumped him. He would have seen Vicky coming across the field and known what was coming. He took it well. He wasn’t horrible to me, like some men I’ve rejected. I felt an instant dizzying relief, but then alongside it, digging its nails in, this fear that maybe I’d made a mistake.I’d go on to repeat this pattern over the course of my life with lots of different men. Liking them and then having a feeling of terror when they started to like me. I would watch them move on to other women, look at their photos together on Instagram and think, why were you so scared of that being you?‘People treat each other as disposable’: dating columnist turned novelist Annie Lord on love and sex in the age of appsRead moreIt’s only in the last year, through therapy, that I have fully unpacked what was going on. I was going through puberty, my body was changing, and a deep feeling of wrongness sunk down into my very tissue. I thought I was rotten, so if someone liked me there must be something wrong with them. That girl’s comment during PE confirmed this.We can be so imaginative when it comes to love. But when it comes to rejection we can’t imagine all the million reasons a person might not want to be with you: there’s just you and why you’re not good enough. I hope he knows it was nothing to do with him. I hope it didn’t make him scared of intimacy, or trap him in a pattern.When I see kids in love, I think about how lucky they are. It must be so incredible to love that young, to feel it that much, to enter into intimacy slowly and safely with someone you trust. We could have had that, but I ran from it. I ruined it for both of us. I’m really sorry for him because I robbed us of that experience, but I’m also really sorry for myself.Annie Lord is a writer and author. Her latest book,The Project, is out now.Nikesh Shukla: ‘I grew up in fear of being told off, not really understanding what I did wrong in the first place. And I don’t want you to feel like that’View image in fullscreen‘None of those situations are because you actually did anything that bad. They were all me.’Photograph: Abi BansalDear kidsI don’t know what came over me. I’m sorry. That’s all I can say. I know it’s not nice to  be shouted at. And, look, I think you and your sister could take a little responsibility for waiting until I’m concentrating to start bickering. Why did you wait until I sat down at my desk to work on my novel before getting into a fight about the big green Lego tile? Seriously? We have two of them! I know one of them is supersize, but stick them together and you get a mega-tile! Imagine the house you could build on a mega-tile! Just stop bickering!I think I have let this apology run away from me somewhat. It’s almost as pompous as what I said to you at the time. When I relayed this story to a friend later on, she howled with laughter and called me a pretentious [redacted swear word]. I believe I said – well, shouted, at the top of my voice: “I don’t have a regular job. I am in that room creating universes and moving characters around them. And when you pull me out of that universe and back into this boring home because you can’t remember who used the green Lego tile last, that universe dies. Just a little. But it dies.”Oh God, typing that out you can really hear how ridiculous it sounds. How high-minded. You’d really have to think what you do is special in order to shout that. What you don’t know is, at the time, I was writing a scene in a comic book about a man tripping over a discarded apple while running for the bus. Put that in your imagined universe and smoke it.I used to think a lot about what sort of parent I would be. Of course, you only ever really have your parents as the first example. My own mum and dad made me feel as if they were never in the wrong. If they told me and your aunt off, they didn’t ever really explain themselves. I grew up in fear of being told off, not understanding what I did wrong in the first place. And I don’t want you to feel like that. Because there have definitely been times when I’ve been cross with you because I was tired, or stressed by work, or interrupted having a gossipy text exchange with a friend and thought, hold on a minute, I’m the blinkin’ adult here! I must regain control.None of those situations are because you actually did anything that bad. They were all me. And so I have tried my best to apologise when I realise that the telling off that upset you was because of something else. I didn’t apologise to you that day, about being Mr Universe-Creator. As soon as I sat back down at my desk, I realised how ridiculous I had been. And you were both quiet again, playing away, creating your own universes. When I checked back in on you later, I saw that you had ended up working together, using all the green tiles to build a mega-structure. Which I suppose was a good thing, but I hated myself for making you do it because of my anger.That comic book is out now. And it’s about a dad who can’t really control his anger. And, it turns out, the call was coming from inside the house the entire time. I am so sorry I shouted something incredibly pompous at you, and, to be honest, apology aside, there is no way of telling this story without looking like a complete pilchard.Love, DadNikesh Shuklais an author and screenwriter.Some names have been changedExplore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingFamilyRelationshipsBullyingFosteringSexualityChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I may have turned into a sausage by the time you read this’: the best casserole dishes for stews and pasta sauces – tested | Kitchen essentials | The Guardian
description: With autumnal comfort food in mind, it’s time to find the perfect pot for pies, gratins and roasting. Our chef put nine casserole dishes, from Le Creuset to John Lewis, to the test
Author: Sophie Wyburd
Headline: With autumnal comfort food in mind, it’s time to find the perfect pot for pies, gratins and roasting. Our chef put nine casserole dishes, from Le Creuset to John Lewis, to the test
Content: Potluck: our writer looking decidedly un-sausage-like, but thrilled with her findings.Photograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPotluck: our writer looking decidedly un-sausage-like, but thrilled with her findings.Photograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterKitchen essentialsReview‘I may have turned into a sausage by the time you read this’: the best casserole dishes for stews and pasta sauces – testedWith autumnal comfort food in mind, it’s time to find the perfect pot for pies, gratins and roasting. Our chef put nine casserole dishes, from Le Creuset to John Lewis, to the testThe best frying pans for every kind of cookSophie WyburdSun 27 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe are now firmly in slow-cooking season. Each weekend, you’ll likely find me tinkering over a pot in the kitchen, glass of wine in hand, tunes on, before retiring to the sofa to watch a film while the scent of beef shin ragu wafts through the house. A good casserole dish is essential to bring this vision into reality.Many of my favourite meals emerge from them – from stews and lasagnes to gratins and pasta sauces. The quality of your casserole dish plays a vital role in how pleasurable the process of cooking such things is, so I’ve put some to the test.As with many others, I’ve long been a Le Creuset loyalist, an allegiance so strong that I’ve never owned another casserole dish. Can these tests challenge my faithfulness?At a glanceBest casserole dish overallLe Creuset26cm cast-iron casserole dish£225.12 at AmazonBest budget casserole dishHabitat5.3l cast-iron casserole dish£29.99 at Sainsbury’sBest casserole dish for slow roastingStaub28cm round cast-iron cocotte£299 at ZwillingBest lightweight casserole dishOur Place6l ceramic nonstick perfect pot£135 at Our PlaceWhy you should trust meI’ve cooked professionally for a decade, in restaurants and, in more recent years, as a recipe developer. I am all about comforting, relaxed home cooking. My cookbook,Tucking In, is packed with recipes for lasagnes, pies and pastas. I am not known for proteinmaxxing or nutritious salads; I’m a cook who loves sausages, butter and potatoes, and my style lends itself to cooking with casserole dishes. So I do, multiple times a week, professionally and for my own enjoyment.I have cooked hundreds, probably close to thousands, of meals in casserole dishes. So while I wouldn’t proclaim to be an expert in much, I would say that making a cosy dinner in a casserole dish is as close as I’d get.How I testedView image in fullscreenAbsolute banger: Sophie’s test recipe, sausages with squash and beans.Photograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianThis test has seen me cook many sausage stews (mysausages with squash and beansfrom Feast, to be specific) in nine different pots. I may have turned into a sausage by the time you read this, but it will be worth it for you to know which pans are worth your salt, dear reader.I studied many things. How evenly did the pans conduct heat? How well did the coating hold up over multiple cooks? How well did they retain heat? Would you have to take out a small loan to buy one? How pretty does it look on your hob?Because they can be pricey, you want a casserole dish to last years. I haven’t been able to road test these over multiple years, alas, but after a couple of cooks, I got a good sense of which ones should stand the test of time.The best casserole dishesView image in fullscreenStirring stuff: writer Sophie in the kitchen testing our lineup of cookware.Photograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianBest casserole dish overall:Le Creuset 26cm cast-iron casserole dishLe Creuset26cm cast-iron casserole dishfrom£225.12£375 at Le Creuset£225.12 at AmazonWhat we loveExceptional quality; maintains heat wellWhat we don’t loveThe priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The Guardian£375 at Le CreusetFrom £225.12 at Amazon★★★★★The most famous brand is in fact the best, even in light of the price. These enamelled cast-iron casseroles are beautifully made and finished, and available in a range of colours, shapes and sizes, to suit whatever vibe you are after.Why we love itAs you would hope with a pan in this price range, it’s a joy to cook with. Sausages browned beautifully, and onions softened evenly in the enamelled cast-iron base, even after multiple cooks.The pot maintains heat magnificently, too, with temperatures still sitting at 73C after 30 minutes off the heat. Food caught a little in hotspots on the base of the pan during browning, but these easily lifted off when deglazed. Le Creuset offers a lifetime warranty for faulty workmanship and materials, although wear and tear is not covered.Even so, I’m confident that if you opt for Le Creuset, you’ll be investing in many years of happy cooking.It’s a shame that …it comes in on the pricier side, as it is otherwise a fairly faultless pan.Le Creuset26cm cast-iron casserole dishfrom£225.12£375 at Le Creuset£225.12 at AmazonWhat we loveExceptional quality; maintains heat wellWhat we don’t loveThe priceBest budget casserole dish:Habitat 5.3l cast-iron casserole dishHabitat5.3l cast-iron casserole dishfrom£29.99£29.99 at Sainsbury’s£46 at ArgosWhat we loveBrilliant heat retention at an excellent priceWhat we don’t loveLid could fit betterView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The Guardian£29.99 at Sainsbury’s£46 at Argos★★★★☆I was pleasantly surprised by how well this pan performed, especially as it’s considerably cheaper than its Le Creuset competitor.Why we love itIt’s a reassuringly heavy enamelled cast-iron pot with a sleek look, and is oven safe up to 260C. It comes in a few colours, too, from cream to red.Sausages built up an impressive crust, and the brilliant heat retention meant that it bubbled easily on low heats. It also kept food hot for a long time after cooking. And it managed to do all that while keeping the handles relatively cool compared with others on my stovetop tests, which is handy for when you need to stir.It’s a shame that …the lid didn’t fit snugly enough, so there was some water dripping down the sides of the pan during cooking. There was more onion sticking on subsequent cooks, too, but otherwise I was impressed.Habitat5.3l cast-iron casserole dishfrom£29.99£29.99 at Sainsbury’s£46 at ArgosWhat we loveBrilliant heat retention at an excellent priceWhat we don’t loveLid could fit betterBest casserole dish for slow roasting:Staub 28cm round cast-iron cocotteStaub28cm round cast-iron cocottefrom£299£299 at Zwilling£389 at John LewisWhat we loveBeautiful; clever lid helps food stay moist during cookingWhat we don’t loveThe dark interiorView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianFrom £299 at Zwilling£389 at John Lewis★★★★☆For me, the most beautiful pan in the test, and available in an array of colours and finishes.Why we love itThe dappled interior of the lid stops food from drying out by dripping condensation back into the pan, a useful design mimicked by some of the cheaper pans in this test to maintain moisture in your cooking.The black enamelled cast-iron surface allowed sausages to brown marvellously. Although it’s the weightiest pan of the bunch (7.12kg), it had similar heat retention to some of the more lightweight pans, so this heft is potentially unnecessary. There is a lifetime warranty available for Staub pans – though it covers defects in manufacture and materials, not normal wear and tear – that may help ease the pain of the eye-watering price.It’s a shame that …there was sticking even on the first cook, and the dark surface makes it a harder pan to clean (and harder to tell when it was clean).Staub28cm round cast-iron cocottefrom£299£299 at Zwilling£389 at John LewisWhat we loveBeautiful; clever lid helps food stay moist during cookingWhat we don’t loveThe dark interiorBest lightweight casserole dish:Our Place 6l ceramic nonstick perfect potOur Place6l ceramic nonstick perfect potfrom£135£135 at Our Place£135 at AmazonWhat we loveEven nonstick cooking; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveHarder to build crust on meat than with cast iron surfaceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The Guardian£135 at Our Place£135 at Amazon★★★☆☆A stylish Japandi-esque pan, with a built-in strainer and beechwood spatula included.Why we love itThe Our Place pot heated up quickly and cooked onions evenly on the ceramic nonstick base, but this also meant it was harder for the sausages to get the good grip they need to form a nice solid crust.I found that food cooled down faster than in the more traditional cast-iron pans, too, perhaps unsurprisingly because of the lighter weight (2kg) and aluminium body. The sheen of the pan’s nonstick surface did mean it was a breeze to clean, though.It’s a shame that …cooking performance can’t compete with its heavier competitors due to the lightweight design, though this makes it easier to handle in the kitchen.Our Place6l ceramic nonstick perfect potfrom£135£135 at Our Place£135 at AmazonWhat we loveEven nonstick cooking; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveHarder to build crust on meat than with cast iron surfaceThe best of the restJohn Lewis 24cm cast-iron round casserole dishJohn Lewis24cm cast-iron round casserole dish£65£65 at John LewisWhat we loveSolid heat retention; good lookingWhat we don’t loveHotspots resulted in some stickingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The Guardian£65 at John Lewis★★★☆☆A good one for fans of the Le Creuset look, but on a budget. This John Lewis dish has an attractive, deluxe finish. I found its heat retention to be pretty solid, though it took some effort to lift off caramelised sausage juices, and onions cooked unevenly on subsequent cooks owing to hotspots in the pan.It does have a 10-year warranty, which for a pan at this price is handy, though, again, it’s against faulty workmanship and/or material failure, not wear and tear.It didn’t make the final cut because…I wasn’t convinced by the quality of its interior surface.John Lewis24cm cast-iron round casserole dish£65£65 at John LewisWhat we loveSolid heat retention; good lookingWhat we don’t loveHotspots resulted in some stickingM&S large cast-iron casserole dishM&SLarge cast-iron casserole dish£42£42 at M&SWhat we loveExcellent heat retentionWhat we don’t loveUneven cookingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The Guardian£42 at M&S★★★☆☆Another enamelled cast-iron dish, though clunkier-looking than some of the others in the test. The M&S large cast-iron casserole dish shares the self-basting lid design of the Staub pan, which is great for keeping your food moist.I found that fat pooled around the edge of the pan on the first cook, and onions stuck a fair bit on the second use. It retains heat well, though: the sausage stew was still 75C after 30 minutes off the heat. I tested the 5.2 litre size, which would be a great pan for cooking dinner for a big crowd where you’d need the food to stay hotter for longer.It didn’t make the final cut because …the pan didn’t cook food as evenlyas I would have hoped, even on the first cook.M&SLarge cast-iron casserole dish£42£42 at M&SWhat we loveExcellent heat retentionWhat we don’t loveUneven cookingProCook 30cm oval cast-iron casserole dishProCook30cm oval cast-iron casserole dish£60£60 at ProCookWhat we loveGood nonstick coatingWhat we don’t loveHeat retention after cooking is so-soView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianFrom £60 at ProCook★★★☆☆An attractive pan that comes in several chic colours, though the black interior meant it was harder to see what was happening to the food or when it was clean. That shiny enamelled interior did, however, act as a good nonstick coating and made cooking onions a breeze.It maintained a simmer even on low heats, which I’m putting down to the weighty (6.5kg) design, although I was surprised that didn’t translate to better heat retention when off the stove.It didn’t make the final cut because …despite the heaviness, it didn’t retain heat as well as I would have hoped when off the heat.ProCook30cm oval cast-iron casserole dish£60£60 at ProCookWhat we loveGood nonstick coatingWhat we don’t loveHeat retention after cooking is so-soWhat I learnedView image in fullscreenYou gotta ‘role with it: how you cook and who you cook for should be a factor in how big a dish to go for.Photograph: Sophie Wyburd/The GuardianThe price disparity between different casserole dishes is slightly bananas and can make the shopping experience feel confusing. Ultimately, all of the casserole dishes I have tested here will cook your dinner. Some will retain heat for longer, some will cause ingredients to stick more, but none of the ones I have recommended would render what you cook inedible. You can expect any of them to stick a little after multiple uses, and some will last you longer than others, but there are still reliable options in each price category.Here are a few things you should consider before making your chunky purchase.Your budgetWhile the best-performing pan sits on the pricier side, lots of cheaper pans were still solid performers. My budget pick, the Habitat dish, performed so well against the big cheeses that I’d happily recommend it to anyone who isn’t looking for an investment piece.The warrantyLots of casserole dishes have warranties that cover enamel cracking, warping and pinholes developing in the cast iron, which is worth factoring in when deciding your budget, as it may prevent you from having to repurchase sooner than you’d wish. The cheaper pans tend to have smaller (if any) warranty periods, whereas the pricier ones, from the likes of Le Creuset and Staub, have lifetime warranties (though not for normal wear and tear).The appearanceAesthetics are a major factor in our buying habits. Some of us like to surround ourselves with pretty things, and as with many items in the modern day, a casserole dish has become a status symbol of sorts. A Le Creuset or Staub will look beautiful on your hob and could even attract the envy of your friends, but whether it is worth the price is down to your priorities.The sizeHow you cook and who you cook for should be a factor in deciding how big a dish to go for. Casserole dishes come in tiny sizes suitable for cooking for one, or enormous pots better suited for crowds. If you regularly host massive get-togethers or love batch-cooking a big pot of bolognese, consider getting a 28cm casserole. For most people, a 24cm pan that cooks for four to six people will do the job.Sophie Wyburdis a cook and food writer specialising in simple, hearty comfort food, and finds herself cooking in casserole dishes multiple times a week.
