title: The ‘elixir of long life’: how the elusive Chartreuse quietly became the trendiest drink around | Alcohol | The Guardian
description: With its garish ‘grellow’ colour, mythological origins, secret recipe and limited supplies, the herbal liqueur made by French monks is now the coolest thing to order at the bar
Author: Morwenna Ferrier
Headline: With its garish ‘grellow’ colour, mythological origins, secret recipe and limited supplies, the herbal liqueur made by French monks is now the coolest thing to order at the bar
Content: Morwenna Ferrier with a bottle of green Chartreuse at the wine cellar La Cave de Belleville in Paris.Photograph: Magali Deporte/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMorwenna Ferrier with a bottle of green Chartreuse at the wine cellar La Cave de Belleville in Paris.Photograph: Magali Deporte/The GuardianAlcoholThe ‘elixir of long life’: how the elusive Chartreuse quietly became the trendiest drink aroundWith its garish ‘grellow’ colour, mythological origins, secret recipe and limited supplies, the herbal liqueur made by French monks is now the coolest thing to order at the barMorwenna FerrierSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s just after 9pm in drizzly Belleville, Paris. Too late for cocktails, too early for bedtime, but up the steep hill that straddles the 19th and 20th arrondissements, digestif hour is in sight.In the past few years, more and more Parisians have been reaching for a glass of Chartreuse, an intensely green/yellow herbal liqueur with a folkloric backstory involving Carthusian monks, cholera and a recipe of omertà-like secrecy.There are several types, of varying strengths, colours and prices, but none are that easy to find. At La Commune, a cultish leftwing hangout in Belleville, where tequila shots cost less than €4, they finished the Chartreuse the night before. A few doors down at Les Triplettes de Belleville, I spot a third-full bottle of the cheaper yellow stuff sandwiched between the gins. Hugo Césard, the 19-year-old bartender, pours me a €7 shot, my third of the night. On first taste, it behaves like ouzo: sweet, fennelly, cloyingly thick. Then you hit the more complex notes, which are closer to an Alpine meadow. This one is a navy-strength 40% ABV, while the green version is about 55%. In theAlps, you’re more likely to drink it in hot chocolate.To down it at room temperature is sacrilege, unless “you want to get very drunk”, says Césard. For me, alas, that ship has already sailed.View image in fullscreenHugo Césard pours a shot of Chartreuse for Morwenna Ferrier at Les Triplettes de Belleville in Paris.Photograph: Magali Deporte/The GuardianRound the corner at Combat, an edgy-cool bar run by women and frequented by thoughtful students and dressed-up boomers, they mostly serve it cold in a crystal-cut sipping glass or a cocktail called The Last Word, mixed with gin, lime and a maraschino cherry. I try both. Combat bartender Marie-Paule Corby, 30, loves its “complicated flavour”, though outside, a customer called Nour (also 30) is not a fan. “I only ever drank it in the Alps. Too sweet for me,” she says, and sticks out her tongue in disgust.You’ll find Chartreuse in most ambitiously stocked bars, but interest among younger drinkers shot up mostly after the pandemic, says Theo, who works in La Cave Pigalle, a small chic wine shop in Pigalle in the 9th arrondissement. The same thing happened in the US, where it became a “sleeper” ingredient during the giddy era of the craft cocktail movement of the early 00s. Then came lockdown, and a taste for the weirder, top-shelf stuff grew further still, particularly here.View image in fullscreenBrother Laurent, a Carthusian monk, making the liqueur in a factory near the Grande Chartreuse monastery in Dauphine, south-eastern France, in 1953.Photograph: Bert Hardy/Getty ImagesAt the award-winning, taxidermy-filled bar Satan’s Whiskers in east London, it appears in various cocktails. The Pig on the Beach on Dorset’s Jurassic coast sells five different types, one of which – the Eau de Vie from 1941 – costs £50 a measure. It’s always been pricey, though disaster hit in 2021 when the Carthusian monks suddenly announced plans to cap production in order to “protect their monastic life and devote their time to solitude and prayer”. In aletter in 2021, they said: “Making millions of cases does not make sense in today’s environmental context and will have a negative impact on the planet in the very short term”, though rumour has it the decree came from the Vatican, which pointedly reminded the monks“that they were monks, not businessmen”. Today, according to a spokesperson for Chartreuse, the brand is shifting its focus back toward herbalism.Back in Paris, at the beloved bottle shop La Cave de Belleville, Chartreuse is scarce. “We have an allocation – 24 bottles of green and 24 bottles of yellow, but that’s for a year”, says Remy Pousse-Vaillant, 46, a knowledgable liquor expert with a Kandinsky tattoo. There are currently five on the shelf, but that’s it until the next order. Under French consumer law, any item displayed with a visible price is considered sellable, which is partly why somecavesstash the good stuff in the basement. The brand won’t divulge the numbers, only to say that they keep half and export half to the US, Japan, Australia, and “countries surrounding the Alpine arc”. They only make what they need to sustain the order, though Pousse-Vaillant thinks it’s not much over 1m bottles worldwide. Like most wine shop staff, he will neither confirm nor deny if he’s got Chartreuse in the basement.View image in fullscreenChartreuse is popular at spots such as Les Triplettes de Belleville in Paris.Photograph: Magali Deporte/The GuardianStill, if we’ve learned anything fromBirkin economics, it’s that few things sharpen our appetite like the prospect of scarcity. Is that why Chartreuse is back on the map? “Yes, partly,” he says. The stuff that creeps on to cocktail menus – espresso martinis, negronis, cosmos – “used to come from TV shows like Mad Men or Sex and the City”. Now it’s aggressive advertising campaigns meticulously engineered by savvy publicists. Take Campari, which turned Aperol into a global aesthetic, and M&S’s Clemencello, which, according to the supermarket, will be the most in-demand drink this Christmas, despite the fact that most of us have never heard of it. Chartreuse has a much lower profile. I only know about it because Jay Gatsby kept it in his secret cocktail cabinet – and from Bruce Springsteen’s memoir, in which he reveals he got hooked on the stuff when he first started drinking. Tom Waits is also a fan.The story of Chartreuse began in earnest in 1605 when the Carthusian monks – herbalists, scholars and expert alcohol distillers – were entrusted with the recipe by Duke François Annibal d’Estrées. His manuscript outlined a 130-ingredient “elixir of long life”, which contained plants, barks, spices and roots and took the monks over a century to decipher. Finally they landed on what they call the “élixir végétal”, which is the base of today’s Chartreuse. The monks continued to develop the elixir while also trying to create a liqueur that was easier to drink. The first version was created in 1838 and was white, but variations in green and yellow followed in 1840, the green being more herbal in taste and the yellow sweeter. The green “health elixir” version of the recipe was even given to cholera patients – while it clearly wouldn’t have treated the disease, it may have provided some pain relief.View image in fullscreenBottles of yellow and green Chartreuse in the bottle shop La Cave de Belleville in Paris.Photograph: Magali Deporte/The GuardianToday, just three people in the world know the recipe, and they’re all monks. It’s thought that the original two monks only shared the recipe with the third because one of the two was considering retiring. They are helped in the distillery by five lay people, who are also anonymous.It’s a fine story and, as social media weasels its way into everything we eat or drink, perhaps it was only a matter of time before it landed on Chartreuse. The majestic labels, the photogenic shade of “grellow”, the mythological origins – and now the sheer dearth of the stuff. It all feels perfectly suited to the trend-fatigued in 2026, says Pousse-Vaillant. “In this era of AI, of Meta and of constantly [being online] I think people want something real, something authentic, something unchanged.” And the brand agrees. “As the monks say: ‘the cross stands firm while the world turns,’” a Chartreuse spokesperson said. “It is a good motto because the world is difficult right now. So what else can we do?”Explore more on these topicsAlcoholFood & drink industrySpiritsFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make cornbread – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: While it’s ideal for mopping up chilli and soup, this Southern US staple can be made substantial enough for a main meal with a few simple additions
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: While it’s ideal for mopping up chilli and soup, this Southern US staple can be made substantial enough for a main meal with a few simple additions
Content: Felicity Cloake’s cornbread.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s cornbread.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make cornbread – recipeWhile it’s ideal for mopping up chilli and soup, this Southern US staple can be made substantial enough for a main meal with a few simple additionsFelicity CloakeSun 27 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike banana bread, a rather less ancient North American creation, cornbread isn’t a loaf in the conventional sense. Though it’s perfect for soaking up chilli, brothy bean soups and the like, it’s actually substantial enough to be the main event, rather than something you might reach for to mop the plate after it. (It’s also gluten-free, should that be a consideration.)Prep10 minSoak2 hrCook25 minServes6200g coarse cornmeal, or polenta, preferably stoneground240ml buttermilk(see step 3)2 tbsp bacon grease, or butter or oil½ tsp salt2 eggs, beaten1 tsp baking powder¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda2 tsp soft light brown sugar(optional)1 A note on the cornmealThe best, most flavourful cornmeal is stoneground but, depending on where you’re based, it may not be that easy to find, so you may have to compromise on the stoneground element of things. Coarse cornmeal is often found in the world food sections of larger supermarkets, usually from Caribbean brands, but if you do see stoneground polenta, grab that.View image in fullscreen2 Toast the cornmealEither way, you can enhance the flavour of your cornmeal by toasting it before use. Put a large, dry frying pan on a medium-high flame and, when it’s hot, add the cornmeal and toast, shaking constantly so it doesn’t catch and burn, until fragrant but not browned; this should take only a couple of minutes.3 Soak half the cornmealTip half the cornmeal into a large bowl and add the buttermilk (if you can’t find buttermilk, use the same amount of milk instead, and add a teaspoonful of lemon juice or vinegar in step 6). Leave to soak for at least a couple of hours, if possible (though you can use it immediately), or overnight if you’re making this for breakfast.4 Get everything else readyView image in fullscreenOnce you’re ready to cook, get all the ingredients ready, because, once the bicarb meets the buttermilk in step 6, it’ll get straight to work. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. For a really crisp base, you’ll need a roughly 20cm ovenproof frying pan, though you could use a (not loose-bottomed) cake or tart tin, greased with hot fat in step 7.5 A note on the fatIf you eat pork, cornbread is particularly delicious cooked in bacon fat, so it’s worth saving drippings or even wiping a piece of fat from a rasher of bacon around the warm pan to grease it before adding another fat. Put the drippings, butter or oil in the pan and heat until sizzling and, in the case of butter, browning.View image in fullscreen6 Finish the batterMeanwhile, stir the remaining toasted cornmeal into the bowl of buttermilk-soaked cornmeal, then mix in the salt, beaten eggs, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda and sugar (that last is sure to horrify those from the American South, but,according to Serious Eats, corn used for milling is traditionally ripened for longer, which makes it sweeter and more flavourful, so unless you have some really good cornmeal, a pinch of sugar will help replicate that).7 Add the fatStir the hot fat into the batter bowl, then turn up the heat under the pan. Pour in the batter – it should sizzle as it hits the pan (or quickly grease a tin and pour the batter in there instead) – level it out, then bake for about 20-25 minutes, until golden and firm. Serve warm. Cornbread reheats well in a moderate oven; it’s good to freeze, too.8 Or flavour with chilli and cheese …View image in fullscreenThis is a very adaptable recipe. Try stirring 70g grated cheddar or red leicester cheese and two-thirds of a chopped jalapeño chilli into the batter in step 7, then sprinkle 10g more cheese on top, plus the rest of the chilli, before baking (you can also use another variety of mild chilli or jarred pickled jalapeños, if you prefer).9 … or bacon, beans or vegOther good things to include: cooked drained beans, crumbled fried bacon, chunks of feta, cured chorizo, drained tinned corn, chopped chives, spring onions or caramelised onions, cooked peppers – if it goes with corn, it’ll probably work here. I especially like to serve mine with room-temperature butter whipped with hot honey (two to four teaspoons per 100g butter).Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassBakingBreadVegetablesAmerican food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sebb’s, Glasgow G1: ‘A delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: Little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, from a chef who wants to deliver maximum joy
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, from a chef who wants to deliver maximum joy
Content: Sebb's, Glasgow: ‘The distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSebb's, Glasgow: ‘The distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewSebb’s, Glasgow G1: ‘A delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns’ – restaurant reviewLittle bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, from a chef who wants to deliver maximum joyGrace DentSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSebb’s is a basement restaurant on Miller Street in Glasgow with a door that’s perilously easy to miss, even though it’s bright red. The first time I tried to find it, I waltzed past and almost ended up in the pants department of TK Maxx. I was luckier the second time around, and soon found myself descending a set of stairs into a room with the distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley: there’s no natural light, there are booths that are perfect for conspiring in, a DJ playing psychedelic rock and food served in brown paper bags. The13th Floor Elevatorsat noon on a Thursday?! Absolutely – as well as the globally ranging delights of sobrassada and ancho honey pitta, tandoori pork belly with tamarind chutney, barbecued squid withzhougand preserved lemon aïoli, and trout ceviche with habanero, mango and tequila. It’s as ifthe Big Lebowskitook up cooking.Sebb’s opened in late 2024, and just over a year later, head chefDanny Carruthers’ food had already snagged the place a Michelin bib gourmand – to my mind by far the most interesting part of the whole tyre company’s advertising hoopla. Bibs are designed to reward places just like Sebb’s: odd, informal, intriguing – the type of place where you can pop out to for lunch without needing four spare hours, a booking months in advance and a decorative Patek Philippe watch on your wrist.View image in fullscreen‘The best pakora in Britain’: Sebb’s are served with piccalilli and grated sheep’s cheese.Instead, I’m a solo lunchtime walk-in on a summer’s day. And they treat me beautifully, settling me at my table with an alcohol-freeCrossipcooler cocktail – bitter, long and with an olive in it, this is the kind of no-alcohol build that makes you forget to miss the gin – and a round of pakoras with cheese and piccalilli. I order coronation cauliflower, aware it sounds like the sort of thing with which Mrs Dooms-Patterson might torment Jerry onThe Good Life. And it turns out this cauliflower is an absolute stonking triumph: tiny, nutty florets, blackened but still sweet and crunchy, in a slick of silky, cashew-based sauce that’s fragrant with coconut and scattered with plump sultanas. As it happens, directly above Sebb’s, at street level, isMargo, a smarter, more composed restaurant that, like Sebb’s, is run by Scoop, the team also behind the city’sOx & FinchandKa Pao. Which basically means that Margo Leadbetter is upstairs, while downstairs is where the people who actually enjoy themselves are.Sebb’s menu is a delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns, and the dishes are a testament to a chef who has learned little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, and who wants to deliver maximum joy. Atom dip arrives first: sweet, smoky, mashed aubergine, red pepper, earthy hazelnut dukkah and strained yoghurt, with a warm pitta served unceremoniously in a brown paper bag. The humble aubergine, elevated.View image in fullscreen‘An absolute stonking triumph’: Sebb’s grilled coronation cauliflower with cashews and raisins.Then those pakoras: will I make friends by declaring that the best pakora in Britain is in a Glasgow basement, even though the place reminds me of nothing so much as turning up mid-soundcheck for some sort of music event? These pakoras are thoroughly crisp outside with a gloriously squidgy interior, paper-thin onion that’s properly fried through, and all dotted with creamed piccalilli and blanketed in grated sheep’s cheese.Rump fillet comes seared yet blushing pink, sliced thinly, beautifully arranged and served with cowboy butter – a Glasgow spin onbeurre maître d’hôtelthat features shedloads of garlic, herbs, mustard and chilli – sweetness, sharpness and umami. For me, this dish pretty much sums up Sebb’s, because it’s a riot of unbridled tastiness with a huge nod to French gastronomical technique. You can have spiced fries with garlic and herb aïoli alongside, or Isle of Wight tomatoes with urfa pepper, capers and pine nuts, which, on a menu this far-ranging, lands like a postcard from somewhere unexpectedly close.View image in fullscreen‘One of the best things I’ve eaten all year’: Sebb’s chocolate sorbet.Mimicking just about every Maccy D’s from Land’s End upwards, Sebb’s soft-serve machine is broken the day I go, so instead they offer me chocolate sorbet, which remains one of the best things I’ve eaten all year: a culinary sleight of hand, andsowithout the bad stuff that it’s practically a health tonic.I ate lunch with one of my favourite people (me, on a day off) and enjoyed myself so much that I found myself recommending Sebb’s to random people at Glasgow Central Station, and again later on my travels in Leeds, Birmingham and London. Nowthatis the sign of a properly good little spot.Sebb’s68 Miller Street, Glasgow G1, 0141-739 9381. Open all week, noon-9.45pm (last orders). From about £30 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsFrench food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks’ | Food | The Guardian
description: It has taken me decades to get over the vegetarian cookbooks of my past
Author: Ruby Tandoh
Headline: It has taken me decades to get over the vegetarian cookbooks of my past
Content: Illustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianFood‘I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks’It has taken me decades to get over the vegetarian cookbooks of my pastRuby TandohSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt would be unwise to overstate things, the world being as it is, but what happened in the UK with stuffed peppers is a tragedy. You know the ones I mean: traffic light bell peppers stuffed with a cupboard raid of rice, breadcrumbs, lentils, nuts and veg – 70s stuffed peppers. The kind you might find in a wholefoods cookbook, cheerfully distended and jaunty of cap, with the physiognomy of PC Plod. I used to make them at university sometimes, my sensibilities being, as ever, several decades out of touch. I think I was trying to channel the vegetarian cookbooks my parents once had – in the years before discovering pesto, these peppers were the vegetarian’s lot. The recipes I concocted bore things like buckwheat groats, curly leaf parsley and yeast extract. To this day, I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks to such peppers and their generous cargo of junk.It’s a shame, because stuffed vegetables so obviously do not have to be this way. Takechiles rellenos: think about what it takes not just to stuff a poblano, but to blacken it over flame, then to peel off its skin, fill with cheese, secure the seam with a toothpick, coat in flour, dip in fluffy whisked egg, and fry until the batter is crisp and puffed.I recently decided it was time for me, too, to get on the stuffed vegetable beat. (It only took a couple of decades of recovery post my vegetarian spell.) It was late summer, and I was running out of ways to cook squash. Any allotment tender will know the feeling: the delight of the first little speckled courgette, the beauty of the flowers, the wonder that the earth could provide such riches. Then, the second wave of courgettes, then the third, then the panic of stewing, souping, roasting, baking, and pickling through the glut. You end up grating courgette into dishes it has no business being in; smuggling it into cakes, or, as I found myself thinking: “stuff these courgettes”.So, partly because I wanted to learn how to honour nature’s bounty, and partly because aubergines were yellow-stickered in the shop, I applied myself to the stuffed vegetable arts. For help, I went cap in hand to the cookbooks of the dolma belt – an area of stuffed-vegetable excellence, which maps nicely on to the contours of the Ottoman empire, from the Balkans across Turkiye and Palestine, through West Asia and to Iran. Calling this a region doesn’t exactly make sense – it spans time zones, languages and continents. But across this swath, there has been a Cambrian explosion of stuffed peppers, aubergines, summer squash, courgettes, cabbage and vine leaves. It makes the British stuffed pepper seem like a half-formed thought.So, I learned a little about texture, construction and contrast. I fried onions and minced beef, and mixed them with spiced maftoul, then spooned this into halved, hollowed-out peppers. I repurposed a few little globe squash, the size of closed fists, and filled them with lamb, bulgur and handfuls of soft herbs. I learned from Palestinian cookbooks (nowhere does stuffed vegetables quite like Palestine) that a specialmanakra– a long, curved blade, great for coring things and much easier to use than a knife – provides a first line of defence against mid-cook meltdowns. And crucially, I learned that no matter the fateful and seemingly inherent vegetarian-ness of stuffed vegetables over here, meat is probably the best stuffing you can use. So much pain could have been avoided, I think, if the ancestry of British stuffed veg came through the dolma belt, and not through macrobiotic cookbooks.The downside of all this, of course, is that such dishes take for ever. But now that the evenings are longer and summer FOMO is thankfully done, it’s a good time for such kitchen projects. In previous years, it’s been starting on the Christmas cake or ill-advisedly trying to reverse engineer a Mr Kipling fondant fancy. This year, it’s the seemingly modest – and actually momentous – challenge of stuffed veg dishes which, under ideal circumstances, require an entire production line of volunteer peelers, corers, rollers, folders, idlers, pot watchers and gossipers to produce.Top of the list: Kurdishyapraxi silq– the Noah’s ark of stuffed vegetables: an elaborate layering of simmered, translucent, onion layer sheaths; tiger-striped and hollowed out courgettes; aubergines and tomatoes, their bellies gouged; and rolled up swiss chard leaves. I found the recipe in Pary Baban’s delightfulNandên. I’ve already made one of her other yaprax (stuffed vegetable) recipes: aubergine and cucumber filled with rice and minced lamb, then – gorgeously, surgically – sewn shut with needle and thread. This is the level we’re at. I will report back when I have finished constructing this yapraxi silq, in this lifetime or the next.Explore more on these topicsFoodVegetablesEastern European food and drinkBritish food and drinkVegetarian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I turbocharged my career then pressed eject’: why couples are getting divorced later | Divorce | The Guardian
description: Financial pressures, legal changes and shifting attitudes may help explain why couples are staying married for longer
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Financial pressures, legal changes and shifting attitudes may help explain why couples are staying married for longer
Content: The median length of a marriage before it ends in divorce reached 13 years in England and Wales in 2025.Illustration: Guardian Design / Anaïs Mims/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe median length of a marriage before it ends in divorce reached 13 years in England and Wales in 2025.Illustration: Guardian Design / Anaïs Mims/Getty ImagesThe Sunday readDivorce‘I turbocharged my career then pressed eject’: why couples are getting divorced laterFinancial pressures, legal changes and shifting attitudes may help explain why couples are staying married for longerAmelia HillSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 01.03 EDTShare“We don’t know anyone whose marriage hit the skids after just a few years,” Celia said, reflecting on her divorce. “Everyone seemed to cling on to their relationships for as long as they possibly could.”It took Celia two years to initiate divorce after realising her 12-year marriage wasn’t going anywhere – and the latest figures show this experience is increasingly common, with marriages that end in divorce now lasting longer than at any point since records began.“I approached it very methodically,” the AI analyst said. “I knew that women almost always end up financially worse off after divorce, especially where there are children concerned, so I took the time I needed to turbocharge my career before pressing ‘eject’.”It helped, Celia said, that she and Martyn, her former husband, had been in their 40s when they got married.“Because we were older and wiser, we took the time to try to mend our relationship instead of rushing off to start a new life,” she said. “When that didn’t work, Martyn was mature enough to know it was best for the children, me and us that he subtly left me alone to get to where I needed to be before we formally called time on the relationship.”According tofigures from the Office for National Statistics(ONS) released this week, the median length of a marriage before it ends in divorce reached 13 years in England and Wales in 2025. The figure for opposite-sex marriages has risen from 12.7 years in 2023 and a low of 8.9 years in 1985.At the same time, the proportion of couples divorcing during their first decade of marriage has fallen sharply. Among couples who married in 2015, an estimated 16.3% had divorced by their 10th anniversary, compared with 24.7% of those who married in 1995.The ONS research does not give any answers as to why marriages are ending later. But it does suggest several hypotheses, including that couples may delay the legal end of their relationships until they can afford what comes next.Prof Emma Hitchings, the deputy head of the University of Bristol law school, who led the Fair Shares project, a nationally representative study in England and Wales examining how divorcing couples divide their money and property, said: “Divorce may have become legally easier, with the advent of no-fault divorces, but separating one household into two has not.”She said that the longer a couple stayed together, the more tightly entwined – and harder to untangle – their finances became.“Every financial aspect of divorce is harder,” she said. “From higher tax and mortgage rates, childcare and school fees – as well as the general cost of living. Then throw in the cuts to legal aid for almost all private family law proceedings in England and Wales, and you can see why couples need to spend more time trying to calculate how they can feasibly afford to separate – which may well account for why marriages are lasting longer before divorce.”Celia said she and Martyn had a number of friends who also broke up after marriages of similar lengths. “It was the oddest thing. But we have three groups of friends, across Europe and in the US, who went through divorces after marriages of a decade or more.”The research bears out Celia’s experience. In the US, the Pew Research Center found that the median length of marriages ending in divorce rose from 10 years in 2008 to 12 years in 2023.Germany’s federal statistics office put the average length of marriages ending in divorce at 14.6 years in 2025. In the Netherlands, the figure was 14.7 years. Belgium’s statistics office recorded a median of 12.03 years in 2024.The figures are not directly comparable as countries collect and present divorce statistics differently. But the broad pattern of marriages lasting longer before divorce is not solely a British phenomenon.Anne Barlow, professor emeritus of family law and policy at the University of Exeter, said there was a curious feature of the British figures. “No-fault divorce, introduced in 2022, made the legal route out of marriage more straightforward – but there has been no corresponding rush into divorce,” she said.One possibility was that knowing you could leave made it easier to wait, said Dr Alexander Maine, a senior lecturer at the City law school who leads a research project called: “Queer families and the law after ‘I do’.”“Another is that no-fault divorce could allow couples to work through a separation without the acrimony that previously accompanied assigning blame,” he said. “If there is no need to prove fault, there may be less pressure to bring the marriage to an immediate legal end.”Greg Ceely, the ONS’s head of population life events, emphasised that until more research was done, these all remained hypotheses. “The change can’t definitively be attributed to any one thing – or any number of things – because there are so many social and economic factors that could also affect the trend,” he said.Certainly, experts find no problem in pointing to other possible reasons for marriages lasting longer before divorce, from disruption to the family courts affecting the timing of divorces in the years around Covid, as well as influencing the duration figures, to the 2022 changes introducing a minimum 20-week period between the start of proceedings and application for a final order.Julia Carter, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of the West of England, Bristol, who is researching couples living together after divorce or separation, said wider global and environmental uncertainty was also having an impact.“I hear people saying that even if their marriage isn’t great, they don’t want to introduce uncertainty into their homes as well, especially if there are children in the relationship who are having to negotiate this unstable world outside their family homes,” she said.Carter pointed to the fact that women remain overwhelmingly the main instigators of divorce. “So if we’re saying that people are waiting later to get divorce, we’re actually saying that women are waiting longer in order to get divorced. So you’ve got to look at what’s changed for women,” she said.In the 1990s and 2000s, she said, “society was all about female empowerment, girl power, Sex and the City, and ‘let’s go out and grab our opportunities’. But there’s been a rolling back from that kind of positioning, especially for women, because we’ve been through so many crises since then: economic, environmental, political, jobs.“I think we can see the impact of that in intimate family lives where there’s an embedding of marriage as a kind of refuge, a place of long-term stability and security for couples – and especially for women,” she said. “That has reignited a reluctance to go through divorce.”The ONS’s same-sex figures give a different set of questions. The median duration of same-sex marriages ending in divorce was 7.5 years for male couples and 6.6 years for female couples in 2025. The figures need to be treated cautiously because same-sex marriage was introduced in England and Wales only in 2014, meaning the pool of marriages that could have reached divorce is still relatively young.But the ONS says the 6.6-year figure for female couples is nevertheless the highest recorded since the first same-sex divorces in 2015.Maine suggested that same-sex couples might have particular reasons for taking marriage seriously. “Marriage equality was something many gay people spent so many years campaigning for very hard,” he said. “Because of that, divorce in the LGBT community sometimes carries an additional sense of having failed not just the relationship but the whole community.”Brienna Perelli-Harris, a professor of demography at the University of Southampton and director of the UK Generations and Gender Survey, suggested a more fundamental change that might underpin the change: the rise of cohabitation.More than 90% of people in Britain cohabited before marrying, said Perelli-Harris, whose research across 10 European countries found that an increasing proportion of first partnerships were ending before marriage.“Marriage may therefore be becoming a more selective institution,” she said. “Couples who move in together and discover that the relationship does not work can separate without ever marrying. Those who stay together and eventually marry are, my research shows, the couples who are happiest.”

title: This is how we do it: ‘As a sexual abuse survivor, I’ve had to relearn how to have healthy sex’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Miranda felt intimacy and love with Ishan right away, but sex was more awkward to navigate
Author: Elena Angelides
Headline: Miranda felt intimacy and love with Ishan right away, but sex was more awkward to navigate
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘As a sexual abuse survivor, I’ve had to relearn how to have healthy sex’Miranda felt intimacy and love with Ishan right away, but sex was more awkward to navigateHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toElena AngelidesSun 27 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiranda, 30double quotation markWhen you spend time talking about repressed memories, it brings up a lot of shame and complicated feelingsIshan exudes a sense of safety. His presence makes you feel as though you can just take a big, deep breath. I have a history of sexual abuse, which has made our sex life complicated at times. Before Ishan, I was in a strange auto-pilot self-protection mode, because once I fell in love with someone, I would find it hard to have sex with them. I would become scared and physically freeze up, and so I relied on one-night stands and fleeting encounters.With Ishan, the intimacy and the love was there right away – and that made it hard in a different way. When you are a survivor of abuse, sometimes the safest relationship can be the most challenging one, as you have to relearn how to have sex in a way that feels healthy.I have recently started a new type of talking therapy for people with a history of sexual abuse. My first session completely knocked me and I haven’t felt like myself since. I told Ishan I needed a week or two where we didn’t have sex – he is always very understanding. When you spend time talking about repressed memories, it brings up a lot of shame and complicated feelings. The memories that come back are so fragmented, you start to question them, and that uncertainty can be draining.double quotation markFor me, there is a fine line between Ishan trying not to trigger me but also not treating me as a victimWe met when we were 24, and Ishan hadn’t had a lot of experience. He was more nervous about sex. Our sex was more awkward at the start – we didn’t know each other’s bodies or ourselves very well. For me, there is a fine line between Ishan trying not to trigger me but also not treating me as a victim. I am often the leader in exploring new things in sex. I am happy to take charge. He often uses toys on me to start, and brings me to a certain level of arousal. I prefer doggy or being on top, as missionary can be triggering.Nowadays, Ishan is definitely out of his head a lot more. I feel most comfortable having sex in the flat we share, when we are both in the moment – sweaty, feral and connected.Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreIshan, 30double quotation markIn the past, I have often overthought whether I’d get an erection, which affects my ability to get oneWe haven’t been intimate in a couple of weeks because a lot of Miranda’s history of trauma comes through during sex. I don’t feel disappointed or rejected by how long she needs to take off. I am just thinking about how we can get her back to feeling more connected with her body.I can tell she wants to, but is just scared. I want her to know I still desire her and signal that urge to her. Previously, I was so conscious of trying to not trigger her during sex that it impacted my ability to be in the moment, but we have spoken about it a lot, and overcome that hurdle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markWhen I met Miranda, she was so open to talking about sex, whereas I can feel anxious talking about itThis is how we do it: ‘As a Catholic monk, I was celibate. But sex with Orla feels so natural’Read moreIn the past, I often overthought whether I’d be able to get an erection – which affects my ability to get one. I was also stuck in my head, thinking about whether my partner is enjoying it. I became a bit avoidant and Miranda was the one to take charge. Recently, I went to the doctor to get medication to help with erectile dysfunction. We have had sex a couple times without it, but it’s a good thing to lean back on.I think I repressed some of my sexual desires in my younger years. As a teenager, I remember feeling turned on when I saw Trinity from the Matrix in a full leather suit. As I got older, I would worry that if I was turned on by something, it was misogynistic or derogatory to women. When I met Miranda, she was so open to talking about sex, whereas I can feel anxious talking about it.I am so often in awe of Miranda. She is incredibly funny, intelligent and empathetic. She can command a room very easily – you can find her laughing loudly at the centre of a group. When we’re at home, she embraces this introverted part of her personality and really values our quality time together. She’s so go-go-go, I think I slow her down – we balance each other out that way.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My husband never stops working, but he won’t discuss it. Should I leave him? | Family | The Guardian
description: You really need to find a way to talk about this and explore the underlying issues – for both of you
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: You really need to find a way to talk about this and explore the underlying issues – for both of you
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyMy husband never stops working, but he won’t discuss it. Should I leave him?You really need to find a way to talk about this and explore the underlying issues – for both of youAnnalisa BarbieriSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 03.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince thestart of our relationship,more than 20 years ago, I was awaremy husbandhad a strong work ethic.But I am beginning to resent the time he spends working, which often includeslate nightsand weekends when an emergency happens.It has a big impact on our family life, and my daughter is often let down.When I try to discuss the effect of this on our family life Iam toldI have to accept it. I am feeling less willing todo so as time goes on.I also have a demanding job, yet I manage this as well as running the house.Often I think I would feel happierif it was just me and my daughter. He’s not a bad person. I just wonder if life would be better on my own.Having witnessedbreakupswith friends the same age, it seems so hard to do, but perhaps it’s the right thing.Or maybe the grass is always greener. And we made a commitment to each other. I’m chasing my tail around in the circle of morality.You did make a commitment – to each other, ie he also made a commitment to you. You ask if you would be better off alone, but it seems youarealone a lot of the time. You didn’t tell me what your husband does, nor how truly credible it is that he “often” needs to work so late and at weekends. I can only hope and presume he’s a doctor and he’s saving lives. Nor did you tell me what he’s like when all three of you are on holiday.I went to psychotherapist Chris Mills, who pointed out that your husband’s commitment to his work “may be how he feels most effective in contributing to the stability and welfare of his family”. But it seems excessive, and sometimes when people spend that long at work it’s because they are avoiding something. Or – I have to say it – they have a whole other, secret, life.Being told you have to accept it is not acceptable. If you’re not allowed to bring up points of unhappiness, then this isn’t a partnership. But Mills said, “If the challenges [you make] always come across as criticisms, without any respect being shown, his defensiveness is not surprising.”double quotation markIf you do still love him then you should seek outside professional help with learning how to communicate around differenceI would add that if he has never let you discuss these things then he’s not showing you respect either.Mills said: “When you describe your husband as ‘not a bad person’ this suggested to me that you no longer have any significant feelings of love for him, in which case a separation would probably be the kindest solution for both of you. But if you do still love him then my recommendation would be to seek outside professional help with learning how to communicate around difference and difficulties.”Our children may be surprised by what’s in our will – should we tell them now? | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreYou sound very down about this and I’m not surprised. Mills and I discussed your point about morality. He said: “I’m not sure any moral purpose is served by staying with someone you no longer love and don’t particularly like [if that is the case]. But I wonder if framing the issue around how hard your husband works is a way of trying to find moral justification for some guilt you may feel about no longer wanting to hold to the commitment you originally made to him.”I note the use of the term “mydaughter” – that to me suggests a splitting off of the two of you. I realise vows and commitments are serious, but they are not shackles. With the caveats mentioned, if this is no longer working for you it’s really OK to say so.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. title: With turbulence all around, Armani plays it safe and easy in Milan | Armani  | The Guardian
description: The late designer’s niece echoes his sense of relaxation, as the house seeks to prove itself to potential buyers
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: The late designer’s niece echoes his sense of relaxation, as the house seeks to prove itself to potential buyers
Content: A model walks the runway during the Giorgio Armani collection show, part of Milan fashion week.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model walks the runway during the Giorgio Armani collection show, part of Milan fashion week.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesArmaniWith turbulence all around, Armani plays it safe and easy in MilanThe late designer’s niece echoes his sense of relaxation, as the house seeks to prove itself to potential buyersChloe Mac DonnellSun 27 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA year after the death of Giorgio Armani, the Italian fashion house he founded in 1975 is facing increasing uncertainty about its future ownership.In his will, Armani, who ruled over the business for 50 years,instructed his heirsto sell an initial 15% stake of the company within 18 months of his death. If a private sale does not materialise, an IPO is mandated to take place. Now there are reports the group is readying itself for formal talks with the French conglomerate LVMH, the beauty giant L’Oréal and the eyewear group EssilorLuxottica – three of Armani’s preferred acquirers – over the possible sale of a minority stake.Against this backdrop, pressure is mounting for the company to prove to potential buyers the continued allure of Armani. In 2025,its revenue fellfor a second consecutive year, dropping 2.8% to €2.19bn.In a turbulent luxury market, the question now is if Armani can remain a powerhouse without its founder – who turned it into an empire – at the helm.So far during this era of upheaval, Armani’s niece Silvana Armani, who took over as creative director of womenswear after his death, has chosen to play it safe by leaning into continuity rather than any dramatic design shake-up.Her latest show on Sunday – which closed outMilan fashion week– reflected this with a collection that further cemented her uncle’s legacy.View image in fullscreenModels present creations from Armani’s women’s spring/summer 2027 collection at Milan fashion week.Photograph: Matteo Bazzi/EPARelaxed suiting echoed Armani’s approach to tailoring. He famously did away with heavy shoulder padding and stiff linings. This sense of ease was boosted further by whisper-thin silk shirting and cardigan-like delicate cashmere jackets. In a recent interview, Silvana, who only wears trousers, jackets and shirts, said: “My woman inevitably ends up looking a bit like me.” The biggest changes she has implemented have been ditching her uncle’s beloved hats, adding more pockets to pieces including dresses, and using cotton, a material Armani disliked.A double-breasted, black tailored suit styled with white gloves was inspired by a photo Silvana found of a young Armani at his communion. Another look included a sparkling printed bomber jacket featuring a printed portrait of the late designer.Key to Armani’s success was his dominance of the Hollywood red carpet. From Diane Keaton in a greige menswear jacket at the 1978 Oscars to Julia Roberts in an oversized suit at the 1990 Golden Globes, Armani spearheaded the fusion of fashion and Hollywood.More recently, a younger cohort of A-listers has been delving into the Armani archive, including Zendaya who wore a webbed dress from a 90s collection to the recent premiere of Spiderman in Italy. A series of liquid black slinky gowns and shimmering champagne tasselled looks showed the sustained capability the brand has when it comes to creating red-carpet drama.Dolce & Gabbana mixes it up as pressure mounts for turnaroundRead moreHowever, there are hints greater change may be afoot at the company. Last week, it appointed Dario Vitale as creative director of Emporio Armani, making him the first external designer to lead an Armani line. The Italian designer has been tasked with revitalising the diffusion line launched by Armani in 1981. Aimed at a younger customer, it accounts for almost a third of the group’s revenue.Vitale will also oversee the accessories offering at Giorgio Armani. He previously worked at Miu Miu, where he has been crediting with shaping its viral success, before landing the top job at Versace afterDonatella’s departure. Despite widespread acclaim, his tenureended abruptly last year. It is widely expected that Vitale will eventually take over the creative role at Giorgio Armani too, which for prospective buyers could add further enticement.View image in fullscreenKendall Jenner during the Bottega Veneta collection show at Milan’s fashion week.Photograph: Piero Cruciatti/AFP/Getty ImagesElsewhere, on Saturday night, Sunderland-born Louise Trotter showed her third collection for Bottega Veneta. The brand famously createdIntrecciato, a distinct handwoven leather technique in 1966, which Trotter has now reimagined across everything from giant bags to trench coats. Chunky crochet and handmade lace further added to the homespun mood. Trotter also secured one of the starriest moments of Milan fashion week.The model Kendall Jenner closed the show, while her boyfriend, the Wuthering Heights actor Jacob Elordi, who has been an ambassador for the brand since 2024, snapped a photo from the front row. He sat alongside the musicians Tyler, the Creator, Solange and the actors Lauren Hutton and Julianne Moore.Explore more on these topicsArmaniIPOsLuxury goods sectorMilan fashion weekFashion industryWomen's suitsFashion weeksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s problematic’: concern as weight-loss jab maker sponsors Vogue World event | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Critics say partnership between Mounjaro maker Eli Lilly and fashion giant suggests thinness is an aspiration
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Critics say partnership between Mounjaro maker Eli Lilly and fashion giant suggests thinness is an aspiration
Content: Gigi Hadid walks the runway during Vogue World 2026.Photograph: Stefania M D’Alessandro/Getty Images for VogueView image in fullscreenGigi Hadid walks the runway during Vogue World 2026.Photograph: Stefania M D’Alessandro/Getty Images for VogueFashion‘It’s problematic’: concern as weight-loss jab maker sponsors Vogue World eventCritics say partnership between Mounjaro maker Eli Lilly and fashion giant suggests thinness is an aspirationChloe Mac DonnellSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fifth iteration ofVogue World, overseen by Anna Wintour, took place in Milan on Tuesday night. Gigi Hadid and Jennifer Lopez provided theatrics on the catwalk, but it was one of the event’s backers that caused the biggest stir.Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical company that manufactures a wide range of medicines, including weight-loss jabs Mounjaro and the Foundayo pill, was listed in the event credits as one of its “fashion adjacent” sponsors.The pharmaceutical company also sponsored the 2025 Vogue World in Hollywood, as well as the Met Gala livestream earlier this year, which includeda promotional videostarring the actor Patrick Schwarzenegger and the fashion brand Public School.While the ongoing partnership did not explicitly link Mounjaro or Foundayo withVogue, the marriage of high-profile fashion events and a weight-loss drug manufacturer has attracted fierce criticism from eating disorder charities and academics.These groups have long believed that the fashion industry promotes thinness by habitually casting very thin models in catwalk shows, editorials and advertising, and warned of the negative impact this could have.“It suggests that thinness is once again being positioned very explicitly as something important that we should aspire to – and now something that can potentially be medically achieved,” said Charlotte Markey, a professor of psychology at Rutgers University and author of The Body Image book series.View image in fullscreenJennifer Lopez walks the runway during Vogue World.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images for VogueMarkey found the merging of fashion marketing with pharmaceutical marketing particularly troubling as she said it suggested that prescription medication was now part of an aspirational lifestyle. “For an audience already exposed to intense appearance pressures, that can normalise the idea that changing your body medically is simply another beauty or wellness choice,” she said. “I would like to see publications such as Vogue thinking very carefully about the broader psychological and cultural consequences of that message.”Lauren Downing Peters, an associate professor of fashion studies at Columbia College in Chicago, and author of books including Fashion Before Plus Size, said the sponsorship showed “how normalised GLP-1s have become within the fashion industry and within culture at large”.Tom Quinn, director of external affairs at the eating disorder charity Beat, found the partnership alarming. “We’re concerned by the widespread use and advertising of GLP-1s, particularly as they can be very attractive for those with eating disorders,” he said.“Given that the fashion industry has at times been known to idealise and promote unrealistic body ideals, this event being sponsored by the manufacturer of Mounjaro is a problematic association.“We would encourage both the fashion industry and pharmaceutical companies to consider how they can promote healthy body types and lifestyles to the public.”Included in the Milan Vogue World partnershipisa video published on the Vogue websitetitled Portrait of Progress. Produced by Vogue with Eli Lilly, the video compares pharmaceutical technologies to fashion manufacturing.“For 150 years, Lilly has been revolutionising health,” says a voiceover as a montage of fashion and health related clips play. “The future has always been handmade, discovering, creating, and moving forward. Everything begins with health, and everything else is up to you.”Downing Peters said that while the video didn’t directly mention thinness or weight-loss drugs, it “links health as a precondition for creativity”.In August, the UK became the first country in Europe to approve Lilly’s weight loss pill. In the US, the company holds over 60% of the diabetes and weight-loss drug market, with a trillion-dollar valuation.Many have felt that the fashion industry has recently seen a reverse in its progress towards size inclusivity, with a worrying return of ultra thinness on and off the catwalk.Last year,a report by Vogue Businessfound that out of the 9,038 looks presented across 198 shows in the womenswear collections in September 2025, 97.1% were shown on straight-size models who measured between a US size 0-4 (the equivalent of a UK 4-8). Only 0.9% of models were plus-size, also known as curve (UK 18+), while 2% were mid-size (UK 10-16).The widespread use of GLP-1s, especially for aesthetic weight loss rather than for medical reasons, is believed to be a contributing factor.View image in fullscreenAshley Graham who took part in the Vogue World show in Milan.Photograph: Daniele Venturelli/WireImageThis week’s Vogue World show featured the plus-size models Paloma Elsesser and Ashley Graham, and none of its promotional materials made reference to thinness or weight-loss drugs. However, Felicity Hayward, a plus-size model who advocates for size inclusivity in fashion, viewed the presence of plus-size models in the showas “box ticking.” She described the casting as “size diversity cosplay” by Vogue and said the choice of sponsorship was “advocating for thinness with a fog horn”.A Condé Nast source said the partnership was focused on Eli Lilly’s overall brand and did not focus on one particular drug.An Eli Lilly spokesperson said: “This sponsorship is part of our 150th anniversary – 150 years of putting health above all. Health is what gives all of us the freedom to move, explore, and be present.“We partner with cultural platforms like Vogue because that is where conversations about bodies and health take place. Lilly is working to shift the conversation about weight from aesthetics to health and to challenge the stigma people with obesity face every day.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
