Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsFashionVogueWeight-loss drugsHealth & wellbeingPharmaceuticals industryFashion industryEating disordersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Camo’s back: noughties pop’s military style is on the march again | Fashion | The Guardian
description: A look evoking memories of All Saints and Destiny’s Child has fashion editors, Brad Pitt and the high street all blending in
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: A look evoking memories of All Saints and Destiny’s Child has fashion editors, Brad Pitt and the high street all blending in
Content: Destiny’s Child in 2001, part of an era now being viewed with nostalgia.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenDestiny’s Child in 2001, part of an era now being viewed with nostalgia.Photograph: Zuma Press, Inc/AlamyFashionCamo’s back: noughties pop’s military style is on the march againA look evoking memories of All Saints and Destiny’s Child has fashion editors, Brad Pitt and the high street all blending inLauren CochraneSun 27 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiscussing their style while in All Saints, Nicole and Natalie Appleton saidearlier this yearthat some things don’t change: “Army trousers and combat trousers will always be a staple with us.”If, for a long time after All Saints’ noughties heyday, the sisters would have known this look was not the height of fashion, things have changed in 2026. Judging by those attending shows at London fashion week this month, camo is very much back.Worn with heels, beaded flats, camisoles and shirting, camo trousers became a standout front-row trend, one that had first been spotted at Copenhagen fashion week in August. Voguedescribed it as“a clear winner among the trends we spotted outside the shows”. Fashion editors aren’t alone either: celebrities including Alexa Chung and Iris Law have worn camo recently. And Brad Pitt, promoting his new survival movie Heart of the Beast, looked the part wearing camo trousers and matching jacket this month.View image in fullscreenBrad Pitt at the Heart of the Beast premiere in Tennessee last week.Photograph: Jason Davis/Getty Images for Paramount PicturesHetty Mahlich, a brand editor at Burberry, was photographed wearing her army surplus camo pants at fashion week. She likes the way they can give a sense of contrast to an outfit: “They go with a vintage nightdress or a white baby tee, but they’re also great with a heel as I never like feeling too dressed up.”View image in fullscreenA guest wearing camouflage pants during New York fashion week.Photograph: Christian Vierig/Getty ImagesCamo is becoming more popular beyond those in the front row. Searches have increased 108% on the resale app Depop since April and brands ranging from Zara to Marks & Spencer and Adidas are selling it on the high street. Maharishi, the label that dressed All Saints in their camo pants, has enjoyed a revival: it collaborated with Arsenal in 2023 on a popularcamo-tinged collection.Most of the wearers of camo now are looking to the last moment it was fashionable – with bands such as All Saints and Destiny’s Child in the early noughties. AGrazia articlepost-Copenhagen described camo as “a trend I’ve buried in the place in my mind where Facebook photo albums and concealer lips live”. However, with a generation born at this time now coming of age, the era is being looked at with nostalgia.This was when camo went mass market, said Andrew Groves, a professor of fashion design at the University of Westminster. “By the noughties, camouflage had become completely normalised,” he said. “You could wear camo trousers without consciously making a military statement. It had become comparable to tartan or leopard print.”Of course, the history of camo – or camouflage – begins with the military. It was first used extensively in the first world war. By the time of the Vietnam war in the 1960s, camo was also being worn as a statement – by those in the US opposed to the war. In the 80s, the pattern moved across to high fashion – after Andy Warhol’s camouflage paintings were used in a collection by Stephen Sprouse in 1987. “By then it wasn’t simply military clothing any more,” said Groves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFast forward nearly 40 years and the trend for camo comes with a backdrop of wars around the world. Groves said even with the now-established place in fashion, the military connections remained – but this might be part of the appeal: “It carries associations with warfare but also protest and counterculture. That ambiguity is perhaps why fashion keeps returning to it.”View image in fullscreenAll Saints setting the trend.Photograph: Tim Roney/Getty ImagesFor Mahlich, the wearers of camo since the 60s mean the military element fades into the background. “I think of it more as a universal pattern,” she said. “Military uniforms have been co-opted by subcultures and on the runway for so long that now they have new meanings and associations.”Explore more on these topicsFashionAll SaintsnewsShareReuse this content

title: 15 great cottages and cabins for an autumn escape in the UK | Cottages | The Guardian
description: Get inspiration for your next short break with our pick of self-catering accommodation, from a sleek Highlands retreat to a cabin with a hot tub on a Somerset vineyard
Author: Rhiannon Batten
Headline: Get inspiration for your next short break with our pick of self-catering accommodation, from a sleek Highlands retreat to a cabin with a hot tub on a Somerset vineyard
Content: A cabin at Thornfalcon Winery in SomersetView image in fullscreenA cabin at Thornfalcon Winery in SomersetCottages15 great cottages and cabins for an autumn escape in the UKGet inspiration for your next short break with our pick of self-catering accommodation, from a sleek Highlands retreat to a cabin with a hot tub on a Somerset vineyard15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UKRhiannon BattenSun 27 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 04.57 EDTSharePen BoncMoelfre, Ynys Môn (Anglesey)View image in fullscreenAs close to the sea as you can get without setting sail, this newly renovated cottage is moored up between a little shingle beach and the village of Moelfre, with its lifeboat station, pub, fish and chip shop, cafe and parlour serving locally made ice-cream. A former fisher’s cottage, it’s decorated in nautical blues and whites, their cool tones warmed by antique chests and an inglenook fireplace once used for smoking herring. An unusual circular garden spins out towards the sea; hop over its low stone wall and you’re right on the Anglesey Coastal Path, soaking up cinematic views of Puffin Island, and Eryri beyond.Sleeps eight, twonights from £746,boltholesandhideaways.co.ukHeronden LodgeEastry, KentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Nathan ShepherdThis doll’s house-like, red-brick cottage sits sheltered by trees in a quiet corner of the Kent countryside, 10 minutes’ drive from Sandwich and 20 from Deal. Newly spruced up, it’s restfully low-key, with buttermilk walls and wooden floors. Upstairs are two bedrooms (one a king, the other a twin) and a bathroom with a tub: perfect for dunking mud-splattered children after days at the beach or trailing along footpaths. Downstairs, there’s a simple country kitchen, a double-windowed dining room and a sitting room with an open fireplace. Walks lead straight into the surrounding farmland and to the village pub, 20 minutes’ away. There are also two farm shops within 10 minutes’ drive.Sleeps four, twonightsfrom £472,keeperscottages.co.ukTy BachBeulah, PowysView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kayleigh DoyleMid Wales is at its moody best in the autumn, the hillsides glowing auburn beneath squally skies. If your walking boots are calling, this recently launched holiday cottage just north of Llanwrtyd Wells is a good base for exploring the trails of the Cambrian Mountains or the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons). The smaller of two cottages on a site that was once a busy village school, it had been empty for more than three decades when the current owners took it on. It took them eight years to restore it, and now it’s a vision of flagstone-floored, putty-walled, slate-roofed comfort, cosied up with a plush raspberry sofa and copper kitchen appliances. This is a place for being rather than doing. Add-ons range from gourmet grazing boards to massage treatments.Sleepsfour, twonightsfrom £260,tosholidayhomes.co.ukBasecamp North LakesTroutbeck, Lake DistrictView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ruth BurgessA few miles west of Penrith, this farm shop, cafe, community garden and wetland restoration site juggles more plates than a Barcelona tapas bar on a Saturday night. It’s also home to a charitable enterprise,Alpacaly Ever After, which rescues llamas and alpacas and offers meets, walks and even camping experiences with them, accessible to all. This summer it added one more item to the menu, launching seven smart new cabins beside the site’s lake. Kitted out with glossy green-tiled shower rooms, galley kitchens, wood-burning stoves and private outdoor baths, they each have one bedroom but can sleep two more on a sofa bed in the lounge.Sleeps four,twonightsfrom £300,basecampnorthlakes.co.ukPeatlands RetreatBallybogey, County AntrimView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gareth AndrewsSitting in the countryside between Ballymoney and Portrush, the two restful shepherds’ huts here come with en suite shower rooms and king-size beds. You’re within easy reach of Old Bushmills Distillery, the Giant’s Causeway, Dunluce Castle and a string of some of the most stunning sandy beaches in the UK, but many guests don’t venture beyond the site’s gardens, meadow and woodland, staying to spot resident hares and light wood-burning stoves. The owners also run an artisan micro-bakery on site; Saturday sourdough workshops can be booked (£90pp), bakery breakfasts can be delivered to your door (£16pp) and twice a week there’s a hyper-local pizza-to-hut delivery service (£15 each).Sleeps two, twonightsfrom £320 (discounts for solo stays),peatlandscausewaycoast.comPippin CottageBude, CornwallView image in fullscreenRun by a former Vogue producer, her chef partner and their farming family, Pippin is one of three cottages set on a working orchard outside Bude. Mixing heirloom pieces with Studio Ore taps and Hay lighting, it’s a lesson in understated, soulful style. Works by local artists cheer the walls (many are for sale) and in the kitchen you’ll find apple juice pressed straight from the orchard’s trees. This autumn, the site has opened a new custom-built sauna and cold plunge, and guests can book add-on wellness experiences such as yoga and sauna sessions that end with hot cocoa around a fire pit.Sleeps four, twonightsfrom £256,cannorchard.comMontagu CottageDrumlanrig, Dumfriesand GallowayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alix McIntosh PhotographyBuilt in the 19th-century as the laundry for the Queensberry estate, Montagu Cottage has been scrubbed up for modern-day guests. A peppermint cream colour scheme cosies up its lofty living area and three bedrooms, there’s a clawfoot bath for post-hike soaks and a double-aspect wood burner blazes in the cottage’s heart.Drumlanrig Castleis easily reached on foot (guests get free access to the gardens and adventure playground until the end of October); spectacular woodland and valley walks lead out from the door; and you’re close to the village of Thornhill for pubs, bakeries, shops, cafes and, if you time it right, a live gig or film screening at theOld School.Sleeps six, three nights from £750,drumlanrigcastle.co.ukMolly’s CabinSutton Bonington,NottinghamshireView image in fullscreenTucked into the field-woven gap between Nottingham and Leicester, beneath the approach to East Midlands airport, Bonington Farm’s four distinctive holiday cottages include a blackened timber cabin with sociable, dorm-style bedrooms, a circular grain store, a pretty brick farmhouse and a corrugated former hay barn. The latter, Molly’s Cabin, is a gallery-walled, salvage-speckled hideaway that’s about to undergo a gentle refurb. Single-night Sunday stays include a private movie night in the farm’s cute grain silo cinema. Or, stay for the whole weekend and go leaf-crunching along the trails ofThe Outwoods, a 110-acre woodland around 20 minutes’ drive away.Sleeps two, onenightfrom £200,boningtonfarm.comFjordUllapool, the HighlandsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lukas RambousekA minimalist counterpoint to the rugged maximalist scenery beyond, Fjord is one half of Corylus Retreats, the twin self-catering apartments opened just outside Ullapool in May. Conceived and run by the team behind nearbyEcotone Cabins, it was designed sustainably with stripped-back timber walls, and floor-to-ceiling windows maximise natural light and have views of neighbouring Loch Broom. On clement days, the pretty harbour and restaurants of Ullapool are easily reached, and there are craggy hikes around Assynt, Coigach and the Summer Isles. If it rains, hunker down inside, enjoying the luxury of underfloor heating or curling up on the covered deck to watch scudding clouds.Sleeps four, threenightsfrom £661,premiercottages.co.ukHafod GwylltCwmystwyth, CeredigionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lou ArchellIts name translates as “wild summer dwelling” but this renovated cottage deep in the Cambrian mountains is equally good for an autumn escape. On the Hafod Estate, deep in the Ystwyth valley, it has no neighbours besides ponies, and has easy access to hiking and wild swimming. Newly available as a holiday rental, it’s stylishly understated inside, with whitewashed walls, slate and wood floors and a collection of ruffled lampshades, tapestry blankets and old pine dressers in soothingly subdued shades. Outside, there’s a wood-fired hot tub with rugged mountain views and the owners can arrange dark skies photography sessions or visits to local potters.Sleeps four, threenightsfrom £690,sandandstoneescapes.comCae’n y BwlchTalsarnau, Eryri (Snowdonia)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Polly LovegroveGetting away from it all is a given at this newly launched cottage in a secluded mountain setting north-east of Harlech. Owned by a ceramicist and an artist, its slate floors and limewashed walls are warmed by glowing fires and a colourful collection of antique dressers, jaunty art, textiles and carved wooden love spoons. While you could drive down the hillside for a windswept walk along the beach at Black Rock Sands, or to explore the legacy of Clough Williams-Ellis at Portmeirion and Plas Brondanw, it would also be tempting to arrive fully supplied and squirrel yourselves away, soaking up the views or hiking straight out into the rugged wilds of Eryri national park.Sleeps six,threenightsfrom £509,underthethatch.co.ukRiders LodgeBallycastle, County AntrimView image in fullscreenStay Lagom is a small estate set around a Georgian rectory on the fringes of Ballycastle. With bike hire on site and a new programme of add-on wellness experiences (think yoga and seaside saunas), it’s popular with visitors coming to hike, surf or cycle the Causeway Coast. Hotel-style bedrooms and boutique dorms can be booked and there are two self-catering cottages, including Riders Lodge, where a sofa-bed stretches capacity to six. Popular with families and small groups of friends, it’s a sociable space with surfboards and bikes suspended on the walls, its own courtyard hot tub and a stash of board games for evenings around the wood burner.Sleeps six, twonightsfrom £524,staylagom.comHoolet BothyBeauly, the HighlandsView image in fullscreenIf Mrs Tiggy-Winkle retrained as an architect, she might come up with something like Hoolet Bothy. A remote, off-grid farm cottage in the hills above Beauly, 12 miles west of Inverness, it’s the epitome of cosy, with timber-panelled walls, a log-burning stove, a double bed tucked into the eaves and a wood-fired Rayburn for cooking and supplying hot water to a small cast iron bath. Guests have access to a fridge and a charging point down at the farm, three minutes’ walk away, and a cool box is supplied for essentials, but there’s no electricity on site so hunker down for days of walking among deer-speckled hills and red kite-dotted skies, and evenings spent storytelling by candlelight.Sleeps two, threenightsfrom £477,airbnb.co.ukLabour in Vain CottageWest Bexington, DorsetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: National TrustSet back from the 18-mile swoosh of shingle along Chesil Beach, this semi-detached rental (there’s another next door for holidaying apart together) has been newly renovated by the National Trust. Its name, like the lane beside it, is thought to refer to a year of crop failures in the middle ages – but there won’t be much labouring, in vain or otherwise, while staying here. Hike a stretch of the South West Coast Path, go swimming or fossil-hunting, watch the skies for migratory brent geese and head into nearby Bridport for shops, cafes and pubs. As well as a snug ground-floor lounge, the attic has been converted into a games room with a TV, telescope and space to spread out jigsaws or toys.Sleeps four, twonightsfrom £561,nationaltrust.org.ukThornfalcon WineryTaunton, SomersetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Felicity MillwardOne of two wooden cabins on a working vineyard (there’s also a more spacious barn conversion suitable for families), the Vine Hut blends rustic timber walls with apple green paintwork and a red gingham sofa to give a cheery, gingerbread cottage feel. It comes with its own outdoor copper bathtub and firepit, plus access to the neighbouring swimming lake and Finnish sauna (pictured). Earlier this year the owners of Thornfalcon renovated a barn on site and have launched a wine school there, plus a series of monthly supper clubs, pairing the vineyard’s wines and juices with seasonal menus; October’s is a culinary caper through the hedgerows, fields and waves via pheasant, hake, mussels, squash, radicchio, puntarelle and quince (from £65pp).Sleepstwo, twonightsfrom £340,thornfalcon.comPrices are for October-November and were correct at time ofpublication

title: Readers reply: Which leader from history does the world need now? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: Would David Attenborough make a better leader than a politician?Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAView image in fullscreenWould David Attenborough make a better leader than a politician?Photograph: Victoria Jones/PANotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: Which leader from history does the world need now?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical conceptsThis week’s question:Is it possible that 3 is the most common number in UK street addresses?Sun 27 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 09.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s clear that the world as it is – considering the climate crisis, the rise of nationalism, geopolitical tumult, the possibility ofAI killing us all by the end of the decade– could do with some more ethically astute and capable leadership. If you could time warp them into the present day, which leader from history could the world do with now – and why?Bernard, MachynllethSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyNo one from history. The climate crisis, technology challenges and the power concentrated within a group of several billionaires are unprecedented in human history. The leader we need is probably a woman, already an activist, someone who does not care to be a politician, but does care about making the planet livable and safe, for current and next generations. And she or he can get things done. We don’t need someone who is “just” wise and has the right worldview, we need someone who acts, despite all the bureaucracies and dependencies we have created in the world. The right people are already there. Only we have not noticed yet, glued to the old template and old perspectives.LundskaneMikhail Gorbachev. He recognised that the game was up, and managed to end the cold war (at that time) without it becoming hot. It is a great shame that the west’s leaders were more interested in triumphalism than mutual development.ArthurOPoddDeganawida, otherwise known as The Great Peacemaker, a little known (in the west) leader of the Iroquois nations. He brought five tribes together, under the law of peace, getting all the warriors to bury their weapons under a white pine. It takes a far braver (wo)man to pursue peace among warring nations than one who sends thousands to their deaths in the name of their own egos.slojdarePerhapsNelson Mandela. He has so much respect that the world would listen and act accordingly.RattandyMichael Collins, a strong but realistic leader who wasn’t afraid to make tough decisions. He was a tough, resourceful, clever military leader and a realistic politician who wasn’t afraid to compromise.SunShineEileJacinda Ardern – and she’s available!chrisstarlingWe just need the United Nations to have full control, setting targets for countries’ governments, judging disputes, redistributing wealth, protecting all things vulnerable, and taking the lead in things single nations can not. It is already there, it just needs a full mandate and no more vetoes.Essay1970I think a leader who can lead the world through all the present insanity is already here:Mark Carney. He clearly possesses a moral courage that is spreading across the globe, and an international vision that is being followed and implemented by an increasing number of countries.JacintoBocaSirDavid Attenborough? His respect for living things and joy in the lives of all manner of creatures would enfold us all and permeate our collective unconscious.MyfavouritememoryisJesus Christ.Alison SwanI suggest Theodore Roosevelt. Well educated, fiercely intelligent and productive, an unhealthy youngster who developed into a physically robust man, a wealthy man who could see the problems of the lower classes and empathise with them, courageous against the powerful class, of which he was one. He fought corruption, personally led the fight at San Juan Hill during the Spanish-American War, started the US national parks programme, and fought against corruption. He was our equivalent of your Churchill. Alas, are there any men (or women?) of this stature and ambition in the US?Lawrence BakerQueen Elizabeth I.janet coxErnest Shackleton. He put people before achievements. Trapped in the ice off Antarctica, he set off at great personal risk to save his men. Although he could have been a great national hero, when he got home the world had changed and was at war. Who knows, if he had the opportunity to develop his philosophy as a national figure sanity may have prevailed. Even if it didn’t, a people-centred postwar settlement might have prevented the rise of the Nazis. A model which we need today.John SommerJimmy Carter. He was a far better president than he was assessed by Americans. He just arrived at the wrong time, with the Arab oil embargo and the revolution in Iran. When gasoline was in shortage and there were fights at gas stations, he was blamed. When the attempt at rescuing the Iran hostages went disastrously wrong, he was blamed, when the true fault was with an incompetent military. He was unfairly made to look weak because, behind his back, Reagan was making deals with Iran to keep the hostages until he was elected. The best part was that during his entire presidency the US was at peace, and he was a leader who withdrew support for the South American dictators the US had worked to install. He was elected to decontaminate the US administration, and he could do it again.BoguilleMargaret Thatcher. Despite all the hate directed at her memory, she is the only PM since the second world war to get the public finance straightened out. She played a crucial role in the first climate treaty restricting refrigerants. No doubt she could bang heads together over carbon emissions. Had she not disappeared from the scene, our relations with Russia would undoubtedly be in a better place. There is a long list of achievements which people conveniently forget. Yes, she oversaw the “destruction” of many old industries. But they were already twitching corpses when she came to power. Who now would want to work in the mines or shipbuilding, or any of the other old extremely dangerous occupations? Even though the City of London may not be quite the force it was, our service industries which she encouraged are still a source of high revenue returns for the state. The creation of the single market had much to do with her drive to get something useful from our EU membership. Her mistakes are well known. Taking her eye off the ball over the Falkland Islands. Not using council house sale money to build more social housing. Right now we need someone as strong as Thatcher to keep Nato focused and stand up to the tech bosses etc.Colin NealNo past leader would cope. No present leader is coping. Is it time to do away with leaders altogether?DrivantestigoExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesEthicsClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Anatomy of an inferno: inside the push to map, predict and prevent spread of increasing UK wildfires | UK news | The Guardian
description: Scientists are racing to understand how fires behave as hotter summers turn green landscapes into tinderboxes
Author: Linda Geddes
Headline: Scientists are racing to understand how fires behave as hotter summers turn green landscapes into tinderboxes
Content: Homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, severely damaged by wildfire.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHomes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, severely damaged by wildfire.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesUK newsAnatomy of an inferno: inside the push to map, predict and prevent spread of increasing UK wildfiresScientists are racing to understand how fires behave as hotter summers turn green landscapes into tinderboxesLinda GeddesSun 27 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the scorched heathlands of theNew Forestto the smouldering valleys ofsouth Walesand burned-out homes inStourbridge, an extraordinary summer of wildfires has left its mark across Britain.To most of us, these charred landscapes may look like pure devastation, but to a trained wildfire investigator they are full of clues. Heat-scorched leaves can become frozen in position, preserving evidence of the wind direction as the fire passed through. Soot or staining on rocks, the pattern of fallen grass and bracken, and even how those stems have burned, provide further information about how the fire itself moved.By combining such clues, investigators can work backwards through a fire, progressively narrowing their search to a likely area of origin, then to a smaller patch within it. “At this point you’re on your hands and knees, looking in great detail,” said Andy Elliott, the UK’s only serving fire officer trained in specialist wildfire origin. “If, for example, somebody has used a match, or if a firework was the cause, the chances are you’ll find it.”Yet, surprisingly few people are trained to read a burnt landscape in this way. While fire crews routinely record a probable cause, a2023 Forestry Commission reportwarned that these judgments were generally made by personnel with limited or no specialist training, leaving their accuracy “open to scrutiny”.More serious or complex fires may be referred to specialist fire investigators, but their expertise is generally in structural fires, rather than burning vegetation. “Wildfire investigation is a different discipline, almost a completely different world,” said Rob Gazzard, the Forestry Commission’s wildfire contingency planning adviser, who co-authored the report.Elliot said: “At the moment there is no capability for wildfire fire investigation in the UK, full stop.” He spoke to the Guardian in his capacity as founder of the wildfire training and consultancy business WildfireTaC.View image in fullscreenA wildfire rages in Merthyr Tydfil during one of the summer’s heatwaves.Photograph: Ethan Fowler/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThat knowledge gap is growing more problematic as the UK faces hotter, more fire-prone summers. Researchers and wildfire specialists are racing to develop the tools and skills to identify what starts wildfires and predict what will happen once they do.Without specialist investigation, the Forestry Commission warned, preconceived ideas about what starts wildfires can influence investigators’ conclusions, potentially misdirecting prevention efforts. Take discarded cigarettes: despite UK campaigns often focusing on them, “research undertaken by wildfire scientists has determined that the cigarette as a cause is extremely unlikely and has been debunked by most eminent wildfire investigators”, the report said.Similar uncertainty surrounds disposable barbecues,which various organisations have called on to be banned. While Elliott does not dispute that they can start fires, the existing data cannot reliably establish how often this happens – or what other causes may be going undetected.View image in fullscreenThe remains of a disposable barbecue left next to the Jubilee River in Dorney, Buckinghamshire.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock“If we knew that 40% of our wildfires are caused by portable barbecues, you could ban them – though people may light another kind of fire – or you could educate people in how and where to use them safely,” said Elliott. “We’ve got three common causes of wildfires in the UK: men, women and children. Beyond that, we don’t know.”The Forestry Commission is seeking to address this, with plans for two courses teaching people how to preserve evidence at wildfire scenes, and how to investigate wildfire origins and causes. Both are awaiting funding.For Gazzard, understanding the cause of wildfires is fundamental to prevention. England alone experiences roughly 30,000 vegetation fire ignitions each year, and while most quickly fizzle out, understanding where, when and why they occur could reveal patterns, and prevent more from developing into major incidents.“Preparedness and prevention is where you win the wildfire,” said Gazzard. “It’s not about response.”The need for such prevention is only likely to grow, as hotter, drier conditions make it easier for such ignitions to catch hold and spread. This year’s summer was the UK’shottest on record, coupled withextreme and persistent drought. “The UK basically has been a tinderbox,” said Prof Stefan Doerr, a wildfire researcher based at Swansea University.Although last year set a record for land burned by wildfires, by mid-August this year firefighters in England and Wales had already attendedmore wildfiresthan in the whole of 2025. “Fires are starting to become much more difficult to control. They’re also starting to destroy people’s homes, businesses and vehicles,” Elliott said.View image in fullscreenSmoke engulfs Dunwich Heath in Suffolk.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAHotter, drier conditions could also mean that previously minor ignition sources start more fires. Lightning is one example, birds striking overhead power cables another. “The bird will typically receive a very considerable voltage, catch fire and drop to the ground,” said Elliott. Usually, wet or green vegetation prevents this going any further. “Now we’re seeing conditions where the vegetation is very dry, bird strikes could be contributing to more fires.”The timing of Britain’s wildfires is changing too. Traditionally, they have predominantly occurred in late winter and spring, when dead grasses, bracken and other vegetation left over from winter provide plentiful fuel. By summer, however, most of the landscape has greened up, creating a natural barrier to fire. Prolonged drought can disrupt this, creating the kind of parched, brown summer landscape more familiar in the Mediterranean.A recent study published in the journalEnvironmental Research Lettersfound that the UK’s wildfire season lengthened from between one and four months in 2011-16 to between six and nine months in 2017-21. This year, many of the UK’s most significant fires occurred during summer. “Summer fires are much more difficult to put out, and they’re also much more dangerous in many ways,” Doerr said.One reason is that summer droughts can dry out grasses and crops extending right up to towns and homes. Fires can then become too intense to tackle directly and rapidly escalate. “They’ll cross roads quite happily, and they move into people’s gardens and into their homes,” said Elliott.The environmental consequences can also be more severe. Sarah Baker, the assistant director of the Wildfire Lab at the University of Exeter, who led the study on the UK’s lengthening fire season, has been examining the aftermath of recent summer fires on British moorlands. “We’re seeing a lot more fires that are capable of burning down into the underlying peat layers,” she said. “We’re getting measurements of up to 20 centimetres in some areas, which is quite a chunk of soil gone, consumed by the fire.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHomes damaged by fire in Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesThis could hinder the regeneration of burnt moorland and release additional carbon as peat burns.If preventing ignitions is one part of the challenge, predicting how and where they will spread is another. Until recently, efforts to predict wildfire risk have largely focused on the weather, but the fuel also matters. This is particularly true of the UK, where the condition and flammability of vegetation changes dramatically through the seasons.To capture this complexity, Baker and other researchers have been burning samples of British wildfire fuels inside a laboratory cone calorimeter, measuring how readily they ignite and how much heat and energy they release at different times of year.These experiments have contributed to the development of a UK wildfire-behaviour prediction system known as FireInSite, which firefighters are increasingly using to predict how rapidly a fire may spread through the vegetation in front of them and how large its flames could become, based on the type and quantity of that vegetation, the season and current weather conditions.By looking up to five days ahead, FireInSite can help firefighters and land managers identify “windows of opportunity” for tackling a fire, as well as devising an appropriate strategy. “If, for example, it tells you you’re going to get flame lengths of six to eight metres, then attacking it with a fire beater is just not going to work, because you’re looking at helicopters,” said Elliott. “It also tells you when to step back and let the fire burn.”Useful as FireInSite is, its predictive power is limited. “Our model tells you how a fire will burn. It won’t tell you where the fire will go,” said Doerr. This requires a different kind of modelling, combining information about how individual fuels burn, with terrain, weather and the precise patchwork of vegetation across a landscape.Fire spread models exist in other countries such as Canada, but they are built around local fuel types, rather than British vegetation. The goal is not necessarily to predict the precise path of an individual wildfire in real time, which remains extremely tricky. “There’s a certain element of randomness with fire that no model will ever be able to recreate,” said Prof Tom Smith, of the London School of Economics, who is trying to adapt fire-spread models to UK landscapes.View image in fullscreenFirefighters at the scene of the Dunwich Heath wildfire.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAInstead, researchers could simulate thousands of fires starting at different points and calculate the probability of a fire reaching particular places. This could identify high-risk communities or “pinch points” through which fires repeatedly spread, helping land managers target and test interventions such as removing or changing vegetation in strategic locations.Modelling could also help high-risk communities develop evacuation plans, potentially avoiding tragedies such as the 2017Pedrógão Grande fire in Portugal, where dozens died trying to escape the flames. “The beauty of modelling is you can run hundreds of [simulations], and you don’t destroy any landscape. You don’t kill anybody,” Elliott said. “You just keep running the models, and you learn from them.”A big obstacle is that Britain currently lacks a sufficiently detailed map of its wildfire fuels. FireInSite relies on users selecting the vegetation they see in front of them, but a spread model needs to know what vegetation a fire will encounter as it travels across the landscape, as well as the terrain and weather. Fires generally spread faster uphill, while the direction a slope faces can affect how dry it is.The patchiness of the British landscape makes this fine detail particularly important. Smith said: “In the UK, a lot can happen in 30 metres.”For now, researchers can construct detailed fuel maps for relatively small areas using aerial imagery, but doing this for the whole country is another matter. Even the difference between a 1-metre and 2-metre-wide path could determine whether flames cross from one patch of vegetation to another, said Smith.Yet it is worth persevering. Severe wildfires were once unusual features of Britain’s green, frequently damp summers. Increasingly they look like something we will have to learn to live with. Understanding how they start and where they are likely to go may be our best shot at stopping more of them from becoming disasters.Explore more on these topicsUK newsWildfiresExtreme heatFirefightersDroughtClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones
Content: Oleshky was once home to 24,000 people but only 2,000 or so remain.Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine BrigadeView image in fullscreenOleshky was once home to 24,000 people but only 2,000 or so remain.Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine BrigadeUkraine‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied OleshkyUkrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from dronesPeter BeaumontandArtem MazhulinSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages.“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians.The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted.The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A“Save Oleshky” bannerwas lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.”Russian occupation of UkraineThe Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far.“Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation.“Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.”He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.”View image in fullscreenWar-damaged buildings in Oleshky.Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine BrigadeAccording to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russiablew up the Kakhovka damin 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker. The rest say he is changing this year’s elections | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: The popular Twitch streamer has been vilified by Republicans, but the socialist commentator has a large audience that some Democrats have courted
Author: Rachel Leingang
Headline: The popular Twitch streamer has been vilified by Republicans, but the socialist commentator has a large audience that some Democrats have courted
Content: Piker’s sometimes controversial statements have made him a punching bag for the right.Illustration: Eddie Guy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPiker’s sometimes controversial statements have made him a punching bag for the right.Illustration: Eddie Guy/The GuardianThe election operators 2026US midterm elections 2026Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker. The rest say he is changing this year’s electionsThe popular Twitch streamer has been vilified by Republicans, but the socialist commentator has a large audience that some Democrats have courtedRachel Leingangin Los Angeles, CaliforniaSun 27 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.36 EDTShareIt’s only9am and the latest media shitstorm is well under way. Hasan Piker scrolls through his social media feeds as he comes down the stairs of his home in West Hollywood.An interview with Axios, in which Piker said the US had committed more atrocities than al-Qaida, is blowing up his phone. Requests from reporters arestreaming in. Comments on the interview flood his replies.Just another day, and just another news cycle, for a 35-year-old socialist streamerwho has no elected or appointed power.Never mind thatmany voters don’t knowwho Piker is – and haven’t heard of Twitch, his streaming platform of choice – despite months of concerted efforts by political opponents to elevate his profile, and tie Democratic candidates to his most incendiary comments.Facing an uphill battle to retain control of Congress in November’sUS midterm elections, and struggling to land on a coherent message to rally support,Republicanshave fixated on Piker – and held him up as a representative of their political targets, from socialists and leftists to Muslims.Why do elite Democrats fear Hasan Piker? | Bhaskar SunkaraRead moreVoters, so far, don’t seem to care about Piker – at least not more than the cost of gas, or the war in Iran, or healthcare, or artificial intelligence, or immigration, or corruption. Around the country, many told the Guardian they hadn’t heard of Piker, or they knew who he was and sometimes had opinions, but those opinions didn’t factor into their voting decisions.Still, Piker features in Republican campaign ads. A photo of him nearly nude, inexplicably, appeared on the jumbotron at the party’s midterm convention. AndRepublicanshave tried hard to tie Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in the critical swing state of Michigan, to Piker after El-Sayed campaigned with him in the primary. (The candidate has since distanced himself from Piker.)Fielding questions in quick pockets of time around his hours of streaming, podcasts and media appearances, Piker says he is not overly troubled by such attacks. “Republicans believe this is an incredible narrative, for the record,” he says. “They truly believe that this is successful. I’m willing to bet it’s because they’re fucking brain-poisoned by the internet.”But the spotlight is glaringly bright. He was even called out from the stage of this week’s United Nations general assembly, as the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,singled outone of Piker’s most controversial remarks.ModerateDemocratshave also used Piker as a proxy in their battle against their party’s ascendant left, which notched key upsets in primaries this year, challenging the centrist establishment.And Piker won’t shut up. He streams for seven hours nonstop each day, with hundreds of thousands of followers tuning in each hour. And even then, he’s not done.Depicted on the right as an extremist, Piker is trying to be tame, he says. “For the election season, I have tried to be as serious as possible,” he says in his signature suit and tie.Unlike the Democratic primaries, where he appeared alongside his chosen candidates from El-Sayed in Michigan to Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Pikerisn’t campaigning for anyone in the general election.51:24What is Hasan Piker’s dude bro project really about? – Stateside with Kai and CarterIt has not escaped Piker’s notice that Republicans continue to target Democrats over their ties with him, and his more controversial statements. “It’s not necessarily my affiliation that’s so negative,” he suggests. But more questions about him mean fewer questions about policy and their opponents. It’s a missed opportunity when they constantly have to answer “What about Hasan Piker?” Piker says.News cycles focused on Piker are driven by a push to attack progressive candidates, according to him, while news outlets carry negative stories about him in a bid to chase clicks and protect their own relevance in the media ecosystem.But in the longer term, Piker also sees the focus on him as a wider test, for a potential 2028 presidential run from the left by candidate like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive congresswoman.“Most people on the left are in some way, shape or form connected back to my community,or myself, or organizations that I work with,” he says. “This is an active way to try and eliminate a political opponent before it becomes too big of a problem for them.”Who is this guy?Piker was born in New Jersey and grew up mostly in Turkey; his parents – his father a political scientist and his mother an architectural and art historian – are Turkish immigrants. While a student at Rutgers University in New Jersey, he got his start as an intern at the progressive outlet The Young Turks, which was co-founded by his uncle, Cenk Uygur. He went on to host a show on the network and started streaming onTwitchin 2018, eventually leaving The Young Turks to focus on his own platform.He now has more than 3 million followers on Twitch, nearly 2 million on YouTube and nearly 2 million on X.The media’s Hasan Piker obsession is letting Republican Mike Rogers off the hook | Mehdi HasanRead moreFrom the start, he made controversial comments – comments that now appear in political ads attacking candidates that Piker has supported. Perhaps the most notable, when in 2019 he said “America deserved 9/11,” features prominently in an ad by Mike Rogers, the Republican contender for US Senate in Michigan, to attack El-Sayed. (Piker has since said the comment was “inappropriate”.)A stream in August led to another round of condemnations. Piker, a frequent critic of Israel, said while talking about DemocraticMichigan congressional candidate Jeremy Moss: “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action–not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” His anti-Israel views, in particular, took center stage in the Michigan Senate primary, where El-Sayed faced pro-Israel congresswoman Haley Stevens. El-Sayed has worked since his primary win to bring in Jewish voters in the state.In the Axios interview that sparked the shitstorm earlier this month, Pikerwas askedwhether he thought America was worse than al-Qaida, the terrorist group. “Pound for pound, as far as the number of deaths, yes,” he responded. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.”Earlier this year, the UKwould not allowPiker or Uygur to enter the country to do speaking events, with the Home Office saying their visit “may not be conducive to the public good”. And in Australia in August, a program on the ABC that featured an interview with Pikerled to a round of complaintsto the national broadcaster.Trump this month called Piker a “terrible liability” who has “a power over some of these Democrats”. The Democratic National Committee chair, Ken Martin, said some of Piker’s comments are “absolutely disgusting and deplorable” and that he “does not represent the Democratic party” or its candidates.After13 years on camera, Piker concedes that his sheer volume of talking means he is not always considered in his comments. After some22,000 hours of extemporaneous commentary on hot-button issues, some of his remarks almost inevitably test what people find acceptable. His stream, he notes, is not prepackaged or scripted like the conventional programs of other political commentators.His audience is dedicated, albeit niche. Members of Congress have appeared on his streams, including Ocasio-Cortez in 2020. In 2025, he stepped more into campaigning for democratic socialist and progressive candidates, first with the then future New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani. In the 2026 cycle, he lent his name recognition to El-Sayed, Pennsylvania congressional candidate Rabb, Colorado’s Milat Kiros, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey and others.After Democrats lost the presidential race in 2024, their soul-searching included a quest for a “Joe Rogan of the left” who could counter the influence the right had on podcasts. Rogan, for what it’s worth, has more than 21 million followers on YouTube alone. This elevated Piker’s profile further, but misunderstood the realm of nonstop speaking to camera online. It is inherently not polished, and the potential for controversy exceeds the tolerance of most Democratic politicians.Piker has said that he isn’t the Joe Rogan of the left, that really there could be no such thing. Democrats were looking for someone with a platform like Rogan’s that would be a “lackey for the party”. “I’m not that person,” he says.He could elect to not answer a question posed like the al-Qaida one. He could soft-pedal or redirect or say something he doesn’t really believe. But instead, he takes the opportunity to be in front of larger audiences as a chance to find other people who will resonate with what he’s saying, even if it’s “intentionally provocative”.Candidates reached out to him, he says. It hasn’t brought him more money but has increased viewership on YouTube. If he were truly irrelevant, no candidate would risk associating with him, he says. They’ve made a calculation – and sometimes campaigns are open with him about that, saying they’ve tested him in their districts to see if he will help or hurt, he says.Who is Hasan Piker – and why are some Australian conservatives outraged about his return to the ABC?Read more“This is bad content. It sucks to admit,” he says. “From my perspective, it’s much easier for me to stay the hell away from real campaigns, and I think part of the reason for why I’m getting attacked so much is so that that is what I do, I sit it out next time, or it’s a lesson for even progressive candidates that they shy away from entertaining my platform at all.”Voters don’t careFor voters, Piker is mostly a distraction.“I kind of liken it to following Kim Kardashian,” Phil Verges, a farmer in Spring Valley, Wisconsin, said of Piker. “Now, I don’t – excuse my language – I don’t give a shit.”Verges, who votes mostly for Democrats, said he only started to hear Piker’s name while following El-Sayed’s campaign. The stream is “totally meaningless to me”, he added, “as Joe Rogan is to me”.Two things can be true at once. Piker has sway over a set of dedicated leftwing, often younger, people who can help increase a candidate’s profile in a Democratic primary. But many Americans do not care, or even know, about him.Despite the countless news cycles, aNew York Times/Siena pollfrom mid-September found 62% of likely voters across three US Senate battleground states did not know who Piker was. Even in Michigan, where ads are running about Piker, 54% of voters didn’t know him.Guardian reporters who approached voters across the country encountered the same reality. Some said his name sounded familiar, or that they’d only heard it in recent weeks in the media.Rabb, the Democratic congressional candidate in Pennsylvania’s solidly blue third congressional district, was the oldest candidate, at 56, in a crowded primary this year. He credits Piker with having brought awareness to his campaign among a demographic that would have otherwise been hard, and expensive, to reach.Whether Piker’s support won him the primary is “unknowable”, Rabb said, but it “significantly increased” his capacity to reach more people – and bring on more volunteers to talk about his candidacy. “What he could do in one stream could have taken me months to cultivate,” he said.Piker has all the while become a central focus of Republican attacks. A recent push poll in Georgia attempted to tie Piker to the Democratic US senator Jon Ossoff, a rising star in the party. The pair have not campaigned together once.At this month’s Republican convention, Piker proved an unlikely star, with speakers frequently citing him as the personification of a supposed communist and anti-Israel takeover of the Democratic party. Most of the 15 attenders interviewed by the Guardian had never heard of him.Even seasoned convention-goers were in the dark. Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, Texas, who has attended every Republican convention since 2004, assumed that Piker must be a British political candidate.But after months of pillorying on the right, the name did resonate with some.AJ Louderback, a Texas state legislator, dismissed him in stark ideological terms as “just another radical Muslim”, and remarked: “He doesn’t stand for American values.”Republicans, andrightwing media, are expert at creating a “boogeyman”, Piker notes, from transgender athletes to migrant caravans. But the attack isn’t as salient when it’s a “rabble rouser, Twitch streamer, random entertainer guy”, he says.“There’s just chaos everywhere, and people are just going about their daily lives, trying to make sense of it all and trying to find some kind of peace and stability and prosperity,” adds Piker. “No one is saying it’s because of a Twitch streamer. I’m not top of mind for anybody.”A day in Piker’s worldAt Piker’s house, the day begins with coffee delivery and checking his friend group’s standings in their fantasy football league. Piker grabs a new Zyn before getting on camera to record a pop culture podcast he does with his friends called Fear&. His dog, a fluffy Tibetan mastiff named Kaya, sits outside the podcast recording room.After almost two hours of podcasting, Piker moves over to the room where he streams on Twitch for seven hours. Art from fans, mostly of Piker, lines the walls around him. He scrolls through news stories, tweets and an endless chat window.Today he launches into the interview with Axios, which he calls a “hit job”, and as the circus around the interview spreads, suggests he maybe shouldn’t have done it, or didn’t expect it to become a clip show, or shouldn’t have used the term “pound for pound”, but that it wasn’t the “end of the world”.Piker spends the majority of each day on camera. He even eats on camera, taking breaks to use the bathroom. He works out and streams – that’s basically it – although he does have friends, who are around much of the time.At any given time, about 25,000 to 30,000 people are viewing the stream. Most of those do not watch for the duration, according to Piker, who says between 300,000 and 500,000 unique visitors will tune in each hour.In the chat, viewers lob questions, praise and criticism. “baby wake up, a new hasan bad press tour,” one person writes in the chat. “Rare hasan L shouldn’t have done this interview,” says another. Today’s stream focuses heavily on Piker himself.After a full streaming shift, he’s not done talking. Piker heads from his home studio to a live taping of Lovett or Leave It, a show from Pod Save America co-host Jon Lovett that broadcasts on MS Now. (At arrival, a security guard asks me if I’m Piker’s publicist. A publicist, the streamer reflects later, would tell him not to do any interviews, even with friendlier outlets, at this point – when his whole job, really, is “dealing with the media”.)In his opening remarks, Lovett jokes, “If Democrats lose the midterms, we should not have to wonder if it’s because of missing mail-in ballots,” after talking about Trump’s efforts to derail mail voting. “We should know, without a shadow of a doubt, that it is because of Hasan Piker.”“I denounce you,” Lovett declares to Piker as he walks out on stage, a jocular nod to the string of condemnations of Piker’s statements that have featured during this year’s midterm campaigns. Lovett thinks Piker has said some “very stupid and bad” things, but also that a lot of his words have been taken out of context. But, he asks, how does Piker view his responsibility, given his influence and proximity to candidates who he wants to win?It’s a question Piker seems to wrestle with throughout the day. Still, he tells Lovett at one point, “The idea that a Twitch streamer is supposed to be held to a higher standard than the president is such an insane phenomenon.”“They’re elevating my status as this super-serious political commentator and then campaign consultant, campaign surrogate, when I’ve never wanted to be that,” he adds.Afterward, fans approach Piker for photos. One person, he says later, asks how he puts up with so much hatred coming his way for saying what he believes. He is both “very stubborn” and “very mission-oriented”, he explains.Has he considered talking less?“No,” he replies. “I mean, I talk less, I say the same stuff. Still going to be a problem.”David Smith contributedreporting

title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town
Content: People gather at the store in Lwandle, near Cape Town, where 10 people were killed.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople gather at the store in Lwandle, near Cape Town, where 10 people were killed.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersSouth AfricaAt least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police saySeventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape TownRachel Savagein Johannesburg and agenciesSun 27 Sep 2026 09.46 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 04.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known asshisanyama,in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”View image in fullscreenA man clears the debris in ashisanyamain Lwandle after gunmen stormed the premises.Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty ImagesPolice in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.Illegal miners, known aszama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMembers of South Africa’s forensic pathology service and armed forces personnel inspect the scene of the shooting at the bar in Wedela.Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty ImagesWestern Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered theshinsanyamavenue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.South Africans are already reeling after thediscovery of numerous women’s bodiesnear Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according topolice data.Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsSouth AfricaAfricaGangsGun crimeOrganised crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys | Animal welfare | The Guardian
description: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer
Content: The baboons’ presence has affected house prices on the Cape Peninsula, as they raid bins and kitchens and poo on properties.Photograph: Nic Bothma/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe baboons’ presence has affected house prices on the Cape Peninsula, as they raid bins and kitchens and poo on properties.Photograph: Nic Bothma/ReutersThe age of extinctionAnimal welfare‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeysTwo troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answerThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentGloria DickieSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming intorepeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A2025 censusfound that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.View image in fullscreenA community volunteer reminds drivers to slow down to protect baboons in Cape Town, May 2022.Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”View image in fullscreenA young boy at a protest outside the Urban Wildlife Centre near Simon’s Town on 13 September.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersInitially, the CBP’s2025 management planproposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.View image in fullscreenA baboon tries to open a car door. The animals often enter cars and buildings and take food.Photograph: Gallo Images/ShutterstockAnimal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, andsome scientistssay the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journeyRead moreHowever, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.View image in fullscreenA chacma baboon looking through a windscreen on the Cape of Good Hope.Photograph: Ryogo i Kubo/imageBroker/Shutterstock“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsAnimal welfareThe age of extinctionSouth AfricaAnimalsConservationAfricaUrban wildlifeWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91 | Music | The Guardian
description: Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York
Content: The Calypso singer Mighty Sparrow. The performer, born Slinger Francisco, has died aged 91 after a brief illness.Photograph: Max Burkhalter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Calypso singer Mighty Sparrow.
