The performer, born Slinger Francisco, has died aged 91 after a brief illness.Photograph: Max Burkhalter/The GuardianMusicMighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New YorkAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSlinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.Mighty Sparrow: the king of calypso on freedom, Windrush and oral sexRead moreHis death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.View image in fullscreenMighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.Photograph: Frans Schellekens/RedfernsThe Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso fromTrinidad and Tobagoto the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.Explore more on these topicsMusicTrinidad and TobagoCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo | US news | The Guardian
description: Hurricane Nolo moving away from Hawaiian islands but the threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hurricane Nolo moving away from Hawaiian islands but the threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists
Content: Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday, near Naalehu, Hawaii.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APView image in fullscreenHurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday, near Naalehu, Hawaii.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APUS newsHurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane PoloHurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persistsAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19kph). But theHawaii county civil defense agencysaid a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph (165kph).Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach thePapahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, a national conservation area, early this week.Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center.Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday.Photograph: Gregory Bull/APNear Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, National Guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation.Residents are still recovering fromHurricane Lala, which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.About a dozen people were in the water Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family.Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms are common, but hurricanes are rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact.“We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said.Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo.The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.View image in fullscreenYellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico.Photograph: Raquel Cunha/ReutersMeanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds.Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph (205kph) and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph (19kph) about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph (19kph).Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, orSMN, said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday.Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas.The Mexican navy said in a statement that it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitucion.“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican Army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival.Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65kph) and was located about 300 miles (485km ) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.Explore more on these topicsUS newsHawaiiUS weatherHurricanesFloodingMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two giant pandas arrive in Atlanta from China after Xi-Trump summit | Atlanta | The Guardian
description: Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to live at Atlanta zoo in Georgia as part of loan deal between Chinese and US governments
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to live at Atlanta zoo in Georgia as part of loan deal between Chinese and US governments
Content: The ‘FedEx Panda Express’ Boeing 777 aircraft arrives at Hartsfield-Jackson international airport in Atlanta, Georgia, on 27 September.Photograph: FedEx/APView image in fullscreenThe ‘FedEx Panda Express’ Boeing 777 aircraft arrives at Hartsfield-Jackson international airport in Atlanta, Georgia, on 27 September.Photograph: FedEx/APAtlantaTwo giant pandas arrive in Atlanta from China after Xi-Trump summitPing Ping and Fu Shuang to live at Atlanta zoo in Georgia as part of loan deal between Chinese and US governmentsAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo giant pandas from China arrived inAtlanta, Georgia, on Sunday morning as part of an agreement between the Chinese and American governments.While in Washington DC for athree-daysummitwithDonald Trump, Chinese presidentXi Jinpingannounced that the pandas would arrive in Atlanta in the coming days. The loan of the pandas to the Atlanta zoo was one of thefew concrete outcomesto come out of Xi’s state visit with the US president, which saw expressions of goodwill between the leaders, but no fixes to any of the longstanding differences between the two countries.Atlanta saidfarewellto its last pandas in 2024, leaving the zoo without the bears. The new agreement was announced back in April, but without any dates.View image in fullscreenA farewell ceremony is held on Saturday for giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang at Chengdu research base of giant panda breeding.Photograph: Xu Bingjie/Xinhua/APPing Ping and Fu Shuang are the two adult pandas that will be on loan to ZooAtlantafor 10 years as part of the agreement. They departed Chengdu in south-western China early on Sunday aboard a dedicated “FedEx Panda Express” Boeing 777 aircraft, officials said. A new agreement between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association makes Atlanta one of three zoos in the US to house giant pandas.Ping Ping and Fu Shuang were born in 2020 and were kept at the Chengdu research base of giant panda breeding. The male Ping Ping has dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, a female, has a forehead that protrudes a bit, according to the Xinhua News Agency.China has long used the pandas as part of its diplomacy globally, deploying the bears in loan programs as expressions of goodwill and letting loan agreements lapse when tensions arise.Xi had said the loan program was an example of “friendship between the Chinese and Americans”.Explore more on these topicsAtlantaChinaZoosUS politicsGeorgiaDonald TrumpXi JinpingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shannon felt a ‘sense of doom’ as she sought justice for sexual assault. A new NSW program hopes to alleviate that | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Dedicated service to support sexual assault victim-survivors as they navigate legal system to open in NSW
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: Exclusive: Dedicated service to support sexual assault victim-survivors as they navigate legal system to open in NSW
Content: Shannon Stokes found a lack of appropriate legal assistance as she navigated the justice system, a world she said felt ‘so alien’ to her.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShannon Stokes found a lack of appropriate legal assistance as she navigated the justice system, a world she said felt ‘so alien’ to her.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianNew South WalesShannon felt a ‘sense of doom’ as she sought justice for sexual assault. A new NSW program hopes to alleviate thatExclusive:Dedicated service to support sexual assault victim-survivors as they navigate legal system to open in NSWFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokSun 27 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 17.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt took Shannon Stokes two years and 11 days to successfully prosecute her former boyfriend for sexual assault and domestic violence offences. The lengthy trial left her feeling as though “there wasn’t going to be an end in sight”.Prosecutors secured convictions on nine of the 11 charges, and he was later sentenced to five years in prison.Stokes, 28, fromNew South Wales, said a “sense of doom” throughout the trial was compounded by a lack of appropriate legal assistance as she navigated the justice system, a world she said felt “so alien” to her.Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivorsRead moreShe recalled receiving pamphlets in the lead-up to the trial that she said were “more or less about how to look presentable” in court.“I also had a few pieces of paper handed to me on the day going into that courtroom, and that was what I had to kind of go off … it just makes you feel so isolated and like a number in the system rather than a person who has actually been victimised by violence.”Experts say Stokes’ experience is common among sexual assault victim-survivors pursuing justice. Sarah Rosenberg, the executive director of the victim-led networkWith You We Can and an advocate for justice reform, has long called for greater support for victim-survivors navigating the legal system.“They’re expected to navigate a very isolating, very complex system entirely alone,” she said. “They’d essentially have to become legal experts overnight just to figure out what is going on in a case that supposedly revolves around them.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailRosenberg said an adversarial justice system often further traumatises victim-survivors.“That process of having the victim-survivor be a witness opens them up to a lot of re-traumatising during the process … There is nothing that mimics the dynamics of abuse more than being relegated to just a witness in the accountability process.”This week, the NSW government announced it would establish the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Legal Service, operating through Legal Aid NSW.The $1.74m expansion will provide free legal support for a range of sexual assault matters, including advice about the criminal process, survivors’ rights during police investigations and prosecutions, and assistance with access to victims’ compensation.The pilot program is part of the state government’s $6.2m strengthening sexual violence justice responses package announced last month, which is backed by federal funding.Robyn Gilbert, a senior solicitor at Legal Aid NSW who will lead the service, said: “The point of the service is to bring some autonomy and choice back to survivors, to be better informed and have a clearer idea of their own rights and their role in the system.”She said the service would be “open to all callers” across the state.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Really, the only eligibility criteria is to have experienced a sexual assault,” Gilbert said.View image in fullscreenAssault survivor Shannon Stokes says the drawn-out legal process ‘traumatised me more than my actual assault’.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianThe NSW minister for the prevention of domestic violence and sexual assault, Jodie Harrison, said navigating the legal system could be overwhelming for many victim-survivors.“Accessing the right support at the right time is an important part of ensuring they are treated with dignity and respect throughout the justice process,” she said.Ged Kearney, the federal assistant minister for the prevention of family violence, said: “I have heard from many victim-survivors of sexual violence that their experience seeking legal advice after an assault can be traumatic during what’s already a very traumatic period.”Stokes said she experienced those challenges during her own trial, when questions were dismissed or repeated, and she was required to submit evidence for victims’ compensation more than once.The pilot program was a step towards addressing the trauma of navigating “a really hard legal system”, she said.“Having such a big time pass between my assault and going to court definitely affected me more mentally … I say it light-heartedly, but I think it actually traumatised me more than my actual assault did.”Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesDomestic violenceCrime - AustraliaSexual harassmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation boss called David Farley an ‘asshole’ in lead-up to Farrer byelection, text messages reveal | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteers
Author: Sarah Martin
Headline: Exclusive: Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteers
Content: One Nation general manager Kelvin Morton referred to  David Farley as an ‘asshole’ days before Farley won the Farrer byelection.Composite: Nine News/Guardian designView image in fullscreenOne Nation general manager Kelvin Morton referred to  David Farley as an ‘asshole’ days before Farley won the Farrer byelection.Composite: Nine News/Guardian designOne NationOne Nation boss called David Farley an ‘asshole’ in lead-up to Farrer byelection, text messages revealExclusive:Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteersListen to episode 3 ofThe Populist podcastFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastSarah MartinSun 27 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Nation’s general manager, Kelvin Morton – brought in by the party to improve its vetting processes – referred to David Farley as an “asshole” just days beforeFarley’s historic Farrer byelection winfor the party in May.In a series of text messages seen by Guardian Australia, Morton responds to anews article published in the Sydney Morning Heraldabout infighting among senior party figures over Farley’s previously undeclared support for the Labor party.“Shit stirring,” he writes.“We need to do way better with our candidate selection – we need to stop finding these assholes … or letting them find us.“I guess this might nail David’s colours to us a little more. He’s sworn allegiance in the face of all the concerns being raised – he’d look like a completely untrustworthy snake if he jumped ship after the election – he’d be ruined forever.”AOne Nationparty spokesperson said that Farley was “a dedicated One Nation MP”.“The comments made do not reflect the view of the party.“The only untrustworthy snake is the person who leaked the text messages.”The Populist: Money nation | Episode 3 - podcastRead moreTensions between Farley and other One Nation MPs and staff have reportedly been high since he was elected to parliament, with the party having topublicly criticise himafter he claimed One Nation’s migration policy was not dissimilar to the Labor government’s.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereMorton, who claims on his LinkedIn to be a “strategic business transformation leader” with vast experience with some of the world’s biggest companies, was appointed as general manager in February.At the time, he said the party’s national executive had wanted him to build a “professional, scalable, and legally robust organisation capable of outright victory at the next general election”. He claimed to be introducing a new vetting process and was in his position when Farley was preselected.But while his appointment was heralded as a turning point for the professionalisation of the party, the Guardian can reveal that Morton has since clashed with staff at the party’sBrisbaneheadquarters and officials at one of the party’s most active branches.He was recently appointed to the One Nation national executive, replacing former treasurer Alex Jones.Documents seen by the Guardian show he wrote to the Lilley branch in Brisbane advising it of federal intervention, which included removing the entire committee of volunteers. This came after a dispute about access to promotional materials and a local fundraiser that raised $12,000 for the party.The dispute arose after Morton and the Lilley branch coordinator, Mark McGuire, clashed over access to promotional materials for a different event, which prompted Morton to suspend him.How close is One Nation to Australia’s richest person? – video“Your membership will continue to remain suspended until a formal written apology is received by you,” Morton said, accusing him of removing promotional materials from head office and clashing with a staff member.McGuire told the Guardian he had accessed policy flyers to take to an event being run by the party’s Brisbane branch.Other volunteer branch members and the president, Deb Dalton, complained about McGuire’s treatment, advising head office that the branch committee would cease volunteering in protest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne Nation admits using party funds to build $56,000 shed on James Ashby’s private propertyRead moreThe letter from Morton sent in response stated that he accepted the board’s “resignation”, despite the branch members only advising they would cease volunteering.“The Federal Executive is now intervening in the management of the Lilley branch as its functioning and compliance are in question,” he writes.“All branch decisions and actions are now subject to direct review and management by the Federal Executive, which reserves the right to overturn any local decision which is not in the best interest of the Party.”View image in fullscreenPauline Hanson and David Farley (right) speak to supporters after winning the Farrer by-election in May.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPMorton also accused the branch of not handing over $12,000 raised at a branch fundraising dinner last year and demanded it be transferred to party headquarters where it would be controlled by the party’s national executive.“You are reminded that … branches are strictly prohibited from maintaining independent bank accounts,” Morton said in a letter to the branch president.“All branch funds – including the $12,000 referred to by Mark McGuire in his phone call to me – must be managed centrally.”He said he would revoke the membership of all branch committee members, and that “ongoing membership is contingent upon the full and transparent return of all party property, financial records, and the $12,000 in raised funds”.McGuire told the Guardian that he believed the party’s volunteers had been treated unfairly and the $12,000 had already been paid automatically to central office when people bought tickets.“They were treated with no procedural fairness and total disrespect,” McGuire said. “They all put their own time in, they make a sacrifice for their own family.“The fact is that he’s got it wrong, the question is, where’s the 12 grand? Who’s had their sticky fingers in the pie? He needs to stand up and be accountable to show the whole of the branch where the 12 grand is.”A One Nation spokesperson said the party “does not provide comment on internal disciplinary actions”.“All branch donations are managed through a microsite that tags funds with the corresponding branch. Branch funds are quarantined for localised campaigns.”Explore more on these topicsOne NationAustralian politicsAustralian political donationsQueenslandBrisbanenewsShareReuse this content

title: RBA expected to hike cash rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011  | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Outcome of meetings of Reserve Bank on Monday and Tuesday will affect Australian mortgage rates, household budgets and house prices
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Outcome of meetings of Reserve Bank on Monday and Tuesday will affect Australian mortgage rates, household budgets and house prices
Content: The Reserve Bank board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.Photograph: mikulas1/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe Reserve Bank board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.Photograph: mikulas1/Getty Images/iStockphotoInterest ratesRBA expected to hike cash rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011Outcome of meetings of Reserve Bank on Monday and Tuesday will affect Australian mortgage rates, household budgets and house pricesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniSun 27 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s key interest rate is expected to hit its highest level since 2011, drag down house prices and add more than $100 to typical monthly mortgage repayments.The Reserve Bank board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailFor someone with an average-sized new mortgage of $731,000, now paying a rate of 6.2%, an increase would add about $119 to their $4,477 monthly repayments. That would take the total rise in repayments since January to nearly $480.The share of borrowers behind on their home loan repayments is small but rising, S&P data analysed by Westpac shows.Household budgets have also been strained byrising petrol pricesamid the US war on Iran, now 80c higher since the start of the year, adding $44 to the cost of filling up a vehicle with a 55-litre tank.‘I would be happy if prices came down’: the older Australians wanting house prices to fall for their kids’ sakeRead moreConsumer spending is already slowing, with Commonwealth Bank data showing households cut back on purchases of education, motor vehicles and household goods in August.House prices would fall further after a fourth rate rise. Comparison website Canstar estimated a hike would cut $11,200 from the borrowing capacity of someone earning an average annual full-time wage of $108,650, taking the total lost borrowing power to $47,400.Shrinking borrowing capacities have locked buyers out of markets. Three rate rises and the Albanese government’s investor tax reforms have seen home loan inquiries slump from nearly 15,000 a week at the start of 2026 to just over 12,000 in August and September, Equifax data shows.Home prices around Australia have fallen more than 4% from their peak earlier this year, Cotality data shows.On Friday, the bank predicted prices would fall 7.3% by mid-2027, then begin rising again if the RBA prepared to cut rates.RBA cash rate targetWestpac has predicted falls of 10% in Sydney and 8% in Melbourne, suggesting new buyers in some areas may find housing more affordable even after accounting for higher interest rates.But most capital cities are not expected to see significant price drops, meaning housing affordability would not improve after accounting for higher interest rates and repayments.When the cash rate last rose above 4.35% in 2010, inflation was 3%, housing markets were buoyant and the mining boom was boosting household incomes. Rates stayed above that level until the end of 2011.Nearly 15 years later, the RBA is poised to return interest rates to the same level despite a weak economy and slumping house prices because inflation has persisted above the target range of 3%.Senior RBA staff in recent weeks have highlighted the risk households could be starting to expect high inflation will endure beyond the disruptions to oil prices from the conflict in the Middle East.Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said on Saturday the central bank was at risk of losing financial markets’ confidence if it did not raise rates again.“After more than five years of inflation being above target, threatening RBA credibility, it does not have the luxury of continuing to wait and assess,” Oliver said.Financial markets expect an additional cash rate rise early next year.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesReserve Bank of AustraliaHousingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Serbia’s populist president Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime minister  | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Vučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and election will test his grip on rule after widespread protests
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and election will test his grip on rule after widespread protests
Content: Aleksandar Vučić gestures to supporters in Belgrade after his resignation on Sunday.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersView image in fullscreenAleksandar Vučić gestures to supporters in Belgrade after his resignation on Sunday.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersSerbiaSerbia’s populist president Aleksandar Vučić resigns to run for prime ministerVučić not allowed to seek third presidential term and election will test his grip on rule after widespread protestsAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue an attempt to become prime minister in an early parliamentary election that will test his firm rule in the Balkan country after nearly two years of protests.Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in the 25 October ballot.The governing populists face a major challenge from a youth-backed movement that led protests triggered bya train station canopy collapsein November 2024 that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad.University students demanded accountability for the tragedy.Their struggle for justice and against corruptionhas grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust the SNS after 14 years in power. Vučić has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.“I am resigning the duty of the president of the republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread discontent. His decision to run for prime minister is seen as an attempt to retain a top position and boost his party’s chances against the student movement.View image in fullscreenVučić supporters light flares outside the presidency in Belgrade after his resignation.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersVučić has toured the country in recent weeks with live coverage on pro-government media. He has opened new roads, offered assistance money and cheaper medicines and visited voters in their homes.The prime minister in Serbia is formally more powerful than the president, but Vučić still played a dominant role during his two five-year terms, sometimes presiding over government sessions and routinely announcing all important decisions and plans.Serbia’s independent Bureau for Social Research has filed a complaint alleging that Vučić has abused a public institution as president to promote his party, which he has dismissed. There has been no response from the anti-corruption authorities, which are under government control.The new acting president will be Ana Brnabić, a close Vučić ally and former prime minister who is the outgoing speaker of parliament. Once a new parliament is elected, the new speaker will take over from Brnabić, appoint the prime minister and schedule a presidential vote.Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including critical media. The SNS has gradually taken control of all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight corruption.The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life. Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign urging the rule of law and an end to corruption.Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling closelyin a referendum-like atmosphere. Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions, as Vučić, without offering evidence, has accused his opponents and critical media of intending to destroy the state under unspecified foreign influence.He told Serbia’s state RTS television on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country planned to stir unrest on election night.Serbia’s efforts to join the EU have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in France | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’
Content: Pope Leo waves from a popemobile in Lourdes.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPope Leo waves from a popemobile in Lourdes.Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty ImagesPope Leo XIVPope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in FrancePontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’Jennifer RankinSun 27 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit toFrance.Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday,Pope Leo XIVcalled on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.Leo met seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy privately on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.The survivors said the pope had listened to them, was informed of their cases and said more work was needed to respond to the scandal.Five of the seven held a press conference in Lourdes. Jean-Marie Delbos said he never thought the day would come when he would meet a pope. He asked Leo to bless a photo of his grandmother, which he did. “It was extraordinary,” he said.View image in fullscreenPope Leo celebrates a mass in Lourdes.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersDuring a homily to the faithful, the pope also attacked medically assisted dying as immoral “false compassion” in a staunch articulation of the Catholic church’s teaching that all human life must be defended from conception until natural death.After years of debate, France formally adopted legislation last monthallowing incurably ill adults the right to “aid in dying”, joining a small number of countries with similar laws, including Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Canada.The pope said: “It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral.”The pope was due to take part in six events while in Lourdes, including a meeting with staff and patients at the shrine’s care centre.Lourdes has drawn millions of sick and disabled believers seeking a cure from its spring waters since the Catholic church officially recognised visions of the Virgin Mary reported by a local girl in 1858.Arriving there in a white popemobile on Saturday night, however, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing women over three decades.Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court,accused by more than two dozen womenof having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.View image in fullscreenLeo’s is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty ImagesRupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.Among the survivors who met the pope was a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram. Former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to bethe biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn an interview published last year, the pope spoke of a crisis of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.Thefirst official papal visit to France in 18 yearsfollows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in ParisRead moreFrance’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation aftera landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abusedover seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.View image in fullscreenCarmelite nuns attend mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV in Lourdes, France.Photograph: Valentine Chapuis/AFP/Getty Images“You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération.The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines InternationalExplore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVChild protectionThe papacyChildrenCatholicismChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would have curbed Nato cooperation | Switzerland | The Guardian
description: 70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: 70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia
Content: Give Peace A Chance by John Lennon, used in the campaign for tightening Switzerland’s neutrality rules.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPAView image in fullscreenGive Peace A Chance by John Lennon, used in the campaign for tightening Switzerland’s neutrality rules.Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPASwitzerlandSwiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would have curbed Nato cooperation70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against RussiaJennifer RankinSun 27 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSwiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have requiredSwitzerlandto curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be ⁠written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amidincreasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’sdecision to mirror EU sanctionsagainst Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the UN.The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2m francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign.Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy”, leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate withNato.Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve,leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.Explore more on these topicsSwitzerlandEuropean UnionNatoEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones
Content: Oleshky was once home to 24,000 people but only 2,000 or so remain.Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine BrigadeView image in fullscreenOleshky was once home to 24,000 people but only 2,000 or so remain.Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine BrigadeUkraine‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied OleshkyUkrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from dronesPeter BeaumontandArtem MazhulinSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages.“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians.The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted.The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A“Save Oleshky” bannerwas lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.”Russian occupation of UkraineThe Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far.“Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation.“Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.”He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.”View image in fullscreenWar-damaged buildings in Oleshky.Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine BrigadeAccording to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russiablew up the Kakhovka damin 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.”She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’
Content: Mike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN, speaks during a UN security council meeting on ‘Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine’ at UN headquarters on 23 September 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN, speaks during a UN security council meeting on ‘Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine’ at UN headquarters on 23 September 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesTrump administrationUN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end warWaltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’Edward HelmoreSun 27 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejectedIran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”.Echoing comments byDonald Trumpon Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador Mike Waltz told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz.“They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.”Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said.Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”.Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of HormuzRead moreIncomments to Axioson Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.”Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace.Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”.Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.“Our conditions are clear, ​and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.”Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country is prepared to resume fighting with the US but has not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal.“We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war.“At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.”The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for ​talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not ​accept “bullying or coercion”.“Iran is not seeking war, but will ​defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region.Senate Republicans block Democratic effort to end US war with IranRead moreWaltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China premier Xi Jinping during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz.“I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.”Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.“They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.”Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating.“The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranUS politicsIranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after the midterms
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: US president is said to expect renewed strikes after the midterms
Content: People walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz in Tehran. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day ceasefire.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a billboard about the strait of Hormuz in Tehran. Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s offer of a seven-day ceasefire.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersMiddle East and north AfricaTrump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of HormuzUS president is said to expect renewed strikes after the midtermsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSun 27 Sep 2026 02.34 EDTFirst published on Sat 26 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.“They made a proposal but I reject it,” the US president told reporters at the White House.The president was earlier said to be privately scepticalIranwould meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midtermsRead moreMeanwhile, on Friday evening, hepublisheda post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.During a three-hour meeting at theUN general assemblyin New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would relieve pressure on global energy markets, and restart talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday said “our conditions are clear and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled”.“We will not back down from them,” Araghchi said, state broadcaster IRIB reported. “We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights.”Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.View image in fullscreenIran president Masoud Pezeshkian (left) with UN secretary general António Guterres in New York.Photograph: Caitlin Ochs/ReutersAfter a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”Araghchi said on Sunday that the Iranians “saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators”.“We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them,” the foreign minister added.Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump during his address to the UN general assembly.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersIran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and APExplore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaIranUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpUS foreign policyStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: Failure to protect free speech could cost Labour votes at next election, says Liberty | Freedom of speech | The Guardian
description: Polling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effect
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Polling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effect
Content: Protesters at a ‘united not divided’ rally in London in September 2024.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters at a ‘united not divided’ rally in London in September 2024.Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press/ShutterstockFreedom of speechFailure to protect free speech could cost Labour votes at next election, says LibertyPolling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effectHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 27 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFree speech will be a big concern for voters at the next general election, with the government’s current approach on the issue perceived by many to be bad for Britain, polling suggests.Three in five people said a political party’s position on free speech would affect how they voted at a general election. The human rights organisation Liberty, which commissioned the polling from More in Common, claimed the results showed that Labour’s failure to protect free speech could cost it votes.A significant proportion of those polled felt certain policies and rhetoric by politicians had been detrimental for free speech. For example, two in five said arrests of peoplefor holding signsin support of the banned group Palestine Action had had a negative effect on freedom of speech. That compared with one in five who said it was positive.Only about one in seven thought Andy Burnham cared more about protecting free speech than his predecessor, Keir Starmer.Akiko Hart, the director of Liberty, said:“The ability to express ourselves freely makes us all who we are, and free speech is of vital importance to the British public. These findings should serve as a stark wake-up call for the government, which has lost the public’s confidence on protecting this fundamental human right.“We’re fortunate to live in a nation shaped by many identities and perspectives, which means differences of opinion and sometimes uncomfortable views that could upset or offend others. This requires the government to adopt a consistent, non-partisan approach to safeguard everyone’s right to speak freely while protecting people from discrimination.”Graph on voter opinions on free speechThe polling, released ahead of a joint Liberty and More in Common panel event at the Labour party conference on Monday, also found that more than a third of people believe politicians calling for phrases to be banned at protests is bad for free speech, compared with just over a quarter who think it is positive.When asked about police getting greater powers to restrict protests or marches, a similar proportion – a third – believed it was good as thought it was bad. More than half of people polled said calling protests “hate marches” or “thuggery” had been bad.Starmercalled for “tougher action”against people who used phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – intifada is an Arabic word that translates as uprising or “shaking off” – at pro-Palestinian demonstrations, and therehave been arrests.Graph showing what voters think have been good or bad for freedom of speechThe Crime and Policing Act, which received royal assent in April under Starmer, gave police increased powers to restrict protests, including requiring them toconsider the “cumulative impact”of repeated demonstrations in the same area when imposing conditions. Many civil society groups were critical of the measure.Since Palestine Action became the first direct action protest group to be proscribed,in July last year, more than 3,600 people are believed to have been arrested for showing support for the organisation, most for holding placards saying “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”. Arrests have continued since Burnham entered office.The UK supreme courtwill hear an appeal against the ban in November, having decided it is arguable that proscription represents a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively.Both left and right have complained about so-called “cancel culture” in recent years, with each side portraying the other as the chief culprit.Hart said: “The prime minister must show urgent leadership on an issue that is dividing the country, and change course away from heavier restrictions and towards a principled defence of free speech.”A Home Office spokesperson said:“Freedom of speech and peaceful protest are fundamental rights that this government will always protect. But there is a clear difference between expressing a view and engaging in unlawful behaviour – such as inciting hatred and violence or supporting proscribed organisations. It is right that as a society and a government, we draw that line clearly.”The Labour party was also approached for comment.More in Common polled a nationally representative sample of 2,017 people in Great Britain between 11 and 15 September.Explore more on these topicsFreedom of speechOpinion pollsLabourProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Late-night drive and a 999 call: farmer’s chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF base | UK news | The Guardian
description: Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight
Content: An officer at a roadblock outside RAF Fairford on Sunday.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenAn officer at a roadblock outside RAF Fairford on Sunday.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyUK newsLate-night drive and a 999 call: farmer’s chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF baseLocal people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnightJamie GriersonandHelena HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called 999 and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later.The resident, who asked not to be named but reportedly is a local farmer, told the Press Association: “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they [the men] were planning. A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the airbase is on high alert. I think it’s absolutely astonishing.”If there had been no 999 call, it appears the authorities would have been unaware of the vans and the potential threat they posed to nearby RAF Fairford.People living in the area have been used to disturbance from protesters and a heavy police presence ever since the decision to allow the US air force to use Fairford as a base for attacks on Iran.But in recent weeks they have noticed dramatically increased security measures, with the gates of the base newly barricaded.Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air base“In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy vehicles across all gates,” another resident said. She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously.”The resident said “great big concrete walls” had also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road.If local people had questioned the necessity of those steps, they may have been persuaded this weekend. In the early hours of Sunday morning, others in Whelford became aware of suspicious activity as the local WhatsApp group lit up with messages.Map showing location of RAF Fairford and Whelford in the wider areaOne resident of Whelford, named Jason, who declined to give his surname, said they were first alerted that something was happening at about 1.30am when people in the chat group started discussing the vans.Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said the 999 call had only come after an attempt to contact the airbase itself. “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.”A photograph published by the Daily Mail showed police arresting five shirtless men at night. Police later confirmed that five men had been taken into custody on suspicion of explosives and terror-related offences.Residents were then woken at 6am by police banging on their doors and telling them to leave immediately. People from 85 households were taken to a nearby leisure centre.Tudsbery said: “[The police] were banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown. There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.”View image in fullscreenUS air force military personnel tend to a Jdam precision-guided munition and a Rockwell B-1 Lancer heavy bomber on the tarmac at RAF Fairford in April.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAThirty emergency vehicles were seen in the village, with the army, a bomb squad and counter-terrorism police all investigating at the scene. Explosives experts were seen examining three vans.The RAF base has come to prominence since March and the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran. From the perimeter of the RAF base it has been possible to see heavy bombs being loaded on to American aircraft.Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.Jason, 50, was evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre at 6am on Sunday with his family and 11-week-old puppy, Poppy, and friends who were visiting from London.“We went to bed [the previous night],” he said. “It was early the next morning when the doorbell rang. It was the police asking residents to evacuate as there had been a major incident.”Jason, who works in consulting, said there were about 40 to 50 people in the leisure centre, ranging from toddlers to elderly villagers, as well as a number of dogs. He said they had been given no more details than those that had been released publicly by police.View image in fullscreenA Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is stopped at a roadblock in Fairford.Photograph: Getty ImagesThe Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives.
