Those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.By Sunday afternoon, the cordon around the village had expanded so no one could get anywhere near it. Access to the village of Whelford remained closed. With RAF Fairford located along one side of the road, a single police vehicle acted as a blockade against further passage into the village.Tudsbery said he hoped he could get home soon. He had left his cat, Misty, behind.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care service | Labour conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’
Content: ‘I realise it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me],’ Andy Burnham said of his social care plan.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I realise it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me],’ Andy Burnham said of his social care plan.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianLabour conference 2026Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care servicePM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’Analysis: can Labour hang on to Burnham bounce?Pippa Crerar,Alexandra ToppingandKiran StaceySun 27 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will fight the next election with a pledge to finally fix the broken social care system, acknowledging he is willing to expend political capital by asking taxpayers to cover the cost.As Labour’s party conference began in Liverpool, he pledged to “rip the plaster off” to radically transform care, setting out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everyone in England.The prime minister said the new NHS-style service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details on how his long-term plan would be paid for, indicating that a tax rise may be on the cards.One option could be to link reform of social care with looking again at the pensions triple lock, with government insiders not ruling it out in the future.He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks over “death taxes” would sink the policy.Burnham acknowledged there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement, although he rejected suggestions it could cost £18bn a year. “It’s not that high,” he told the BBC.“Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said. “I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].”But he said he would take his time to work out how it could be fairly funded. “The challenge in the public finances is real. So it has to be done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse. But I will bring forward proposals.”Labour’s annual gathering is intended to be an upbeat affair, with the prime minister wanting to restore hope that some of the country’s most intractable political problems can be solved despite severe economic headwinds.With political courage a theme of the conference, he said in aninterview with the Guardianat the weekend: “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”Burnham acknowledged the public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but he said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems.A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government with limited room for manoeuvre.On Sunday, Burnham said he did not want to focus on a “narrative of doom” about the UK’s economy but that he would show in his leader’s speech that he was prepared to take tough decisions.He acknowledged there was “real concern” in the financial markets about the state of the British economy, pointing to the “febrile” global backdrop. He said he was willing to cut government spending to balance the books, and he believed money could be saved by taking a more “productive” long-term approach to issues such as rough sleeping and youth unemployment.Amid concerns that the government could be hemmed in at the budget by the parlous state of the public finances, he said the chancellor, John Healey, would be “highly prudent” in running the economy. “I won’t do what the previous Tory government did and take risks with the economy that are actually still hurting us right now,” he said.Burnham suggested to the Guardian that a significant fiscal buffer would be necessary, with speculation that the Treasury could now consider £15bn acceptable.“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things,” he said. “But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances.”Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show | John CraceRead moreLouise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, and Healey are using the conference to stress the government’s commitment to boosting British manufacturing through procurement.Healey will tell the conference on Monday he plans to commission three new floating docks to service navy submarines, with the tendering process only open to British companies. The chancellor will promise “a new age of industrialisation”.Meanwhile, Haigh is using her speech to announce a £115m marine research vessel for assessing fish stocks, mapping the seabed, monitoring pollution and responding to marine incidents.Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said the “heavy lifting” on making the case for rejoining the EU needed to be done by the government now, after Burnham signalled that the move could be in the next manifesto.“The pitch rolling must be done now, explaining to the country the dis-benefits of being outside the European Union and the benefits of being part of this family,” Khan said.However, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, appeared to criticise Khan – and Burnham – telling Politico that the speculation “frankly cause[s] a lot of uncertainty for business”.Meanwhile, plans for a third runway at Heathrow are once again up in the air after Burnhamrefused to saywhether he backed the “contested” project, which is delayed by up to four years, saying it was “principally” a matter for London.Explore more on these topicsLabour conference 2026Andy BurnhamLabourLabour conferenceSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Five arrested on terrorism charges after explosives found near RAF base used by US  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Counter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehicles
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Counter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehicles
Content: Five men have been arrested and three vans are being examined by army bomb disposal experts.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenFive men have been arrested and three vans are being examined by army bomb disposal experts.Photograph: BBCUK newsFive arrested on terrorism charges after explosives found near RAF base used by USCounter-terrorism police investigate whether Iran is behind suspected bomb plot after member of public calls 999 over suspicious vehiclesJamie Grierson,Vikram DoddandHelena HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 14.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCounter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military.The Guardian understands that after five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans, with an initial view being they were consistent with improvised explosive devices.Images circulating on Sunday showed shirtless men being handcuffed in a dark country lane in the early hours of Sunday after police were called to reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which hosts US air force missions against Iran.The suspected plot appears to have been foiled by chance when a member of the public spotted unusual behaviour late at night in the countryside from a group of men and called 999.Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air baseDuring the major incident the residents of 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were rapidly evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre and a 400m cordon was placed around the white vans as robots from the army’s bomb squad examined them.Tests were ongoing to find out whether the suspected explosive devices were viable, with bomb robots deployed in the Gloucestershire countryside as investigations continued.View image in fullscreenArmed police maintain a roadblock close to RAF Fairford on Sunday evening.Photograph: Marcin Nowak/Anadolu/Getty ImagesAfter their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act. The pictures of the men with their shirts off could point to a precautionary measure against the risk of suicide vests or concealed weapons.At least one van carried the logo of a fuel company and a phone number missing a digit. A real fuel company of the same name firmly rejected any connection to the incident and said: “We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission.” It said it was cooperating with the authorities.In a statement, counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am today (Sunday 27 September), police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase.View image in fullscreenPolice moved on the three vans after a 999 call from a resident who spotted them as she drove home.Photograph: BBC news“Armed officers responded and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.”The arrests come as the war between the US and Iran limps on. In July Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.Counter-terror police and the security services are searching for the motive. The circumstances of the arrest near the base and prior warnings from Tehran leave an Iranian motive high in the investigators’ and government’s thinking. But sources warn nothing is being ruled out, including a jihadist or other motive, and the UK threat level remains at severe, the second highest, meaning an attack is highly likely.location mapWhether there was any foreign involvement forms part of the investigation, and Iran’s ministry of intelligence and security has orchestrated attacks overseas before.Any proven link with Iran would be a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the UK and Tehran. While several recent incidents in the UK have been linked to the Middle-Eastern country, including theantisemitic arson attack on four Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, the alleged plot at RAF Fairford appears to be significantly more serious.And it raises urgent questions for the UK security services after it appeared the authorities had been unaware of the alleged plot, with police only moving on the three vans after a 999 call from a resident who spotted them as she drove home.View image in fullscreenRAF Fairford is a military base that hosts US air force bombers involved in the Iran conflict.Photograph: Getty ImagesThe US president, Donald Trump, claimed to have had the suspects under view for a “long time” and alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” – although the Guardian understands the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.“It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job,” Trump said.The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the incident.He said it was “deeply concerning” and the government will “always take every step necessary” to protect people.View image in fullscreenA B‑1B Lancer bomber parked at the RAF Fairford airbase, which hosts US air force personnel, in Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersFairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.In March this year, after then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases, four American bombers landed at RAF Fairford and the US started using British bases for “specific defensive operations”.There have been protests in recent months over the UK government’s decision to allow the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.At the time of Iran’s warning in July, a government spokesperson said: “Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.”Evacuated residents of Whelford spoke of “heightened tensions” in recent weeks around the base with more frequent, visible police patrols.Outside Cirencester leisure centre, Jason, a resident of Whelford who declined to give his surname, said: “There have been heightened tensions recently around the base, we are aware it is used by the USAF … It always feels pretty safe. Some residents have seen increased police patrols.”View image in fullscreenResidents of the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre.Photograph: Getty ImagesIt was unclear when people would be able to return to their normal lives; those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles (2.4km) north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.View image in fullscreenFairford youth football club.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersRichard Ocone, the assistant chief constable with Gloucestershire constabulary, said: “We appreciate the disruption this will have caused and would like to reassure them we are working as quickly as we can to get them back in their properties.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads | US politics | The Guardian
description: John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms
Content: A screenshot from a pro-Trump ad the US government paid to broadcast in 2026.Photograph: White HouseView image in fullscreenA screenshot from a pro-Trump ad the US government paid to broadcast in 2026.Photograph: White HouseUS politicsRepublican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump adsJohn Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midtermsRobert MackeySun 27 Sep 2026 19.40 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promoteDonald Trump’s political agenda before theNovember midterm elections, US senator John Kennedytold CBS Newson Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal.Kennedy, the US president’s fellowRepublican, was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multipleads featuring Trump– including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign.Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he hadrebukedKristi Noem, then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a$220mseries of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”.“Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?”White House claims pro-Trump ad it paid Fox to air was ‘public service announcement’Read moreKennedy replied: “Well, first, as to secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.”“This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to thefirst ad in the series, a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists.“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump orKristi Noemor John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.”Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging theargumentmade by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of theHatch act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities.According to Medium Buying, a company thatbuys airtime for Republican candidates, the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcastanother partisan adfeaturing the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday.That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays theclosing riff of a campaign speechhe gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024.“This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start awar with Iranthat has left some supporters feeling betrayed.“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem.The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it waspostedon his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe rhetoric was written in to Trump’s standard campaign speechas early as July 2023, and then repeated by himagainandagainat dozens of rallies and appeals for donations.View image in fullscreenA screenshot from a Trump campaign ad played at the Republican national convention on 18 July 2024.Photograph: CSPANThe ad was evenplayed on giant screensduring the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-SPAN on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”.At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive toputhisownnameon public buildings.“I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there is such astatutein his home state.“Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS SenateUS CongressRepublicansUS political financingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nor’easter storm batters US east coast with heavy winds and power outages | US weather | The Guardian
description: At least one person killed and about 110,500 households still without power from North Carolina to New England
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: At least one person killed and about 110,500 households still without power from North Carolina to New England
Content: Cars drive through a flooded road during a nor'easter storm where a voluntary evacuation has been issued in the community on 26 September 2026 in Point Pleasant, New Jersey.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCars drive through a flooded road during a nor'easter storm where a voluntary evacuation has been issued in the community on 26 September 2026 in Point Pleasant, New Jersey.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesUS weatherNor’easter storm batters US east coast with heavy winds and power outagesAt least one person killed and about 110,500 households still without power from North Carolina to New EnglandMarina DunbarSun 27 Sep 2026 17.52 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA strong, deadly storm known as anor’easterbattered the US’s east coast over the weekend,bringingpower outages, flooding, damaging winds and hazardous ocean conditions.Trees and power lines were knocked down across the region, at least one person was killed and hundreds of thousands were left without electricity.There was significant coastal flooding, rough surf, powerful winds, rain and dangerous rip currents from North Carolina through New England. Boston and theNew York Citytri-state area were among the regions affected.View image in fullscreenWaves crash over homes on Rebecca Road during a nor’easter on 26 September in Scituate, Massachusetts.Photograph: Scott Eisen/Getty ImagesPower was slowly being restored by Sunday afternoon , with about 110,500 households still without electricity, according to the websitePoweroutage.US. In New York, more than 21,000 customers remained without electricity, while the power was out for about 11,940 customers in New Jersey.The National Weather Servicesaidthe nor’easter was expected to weaken on Sunday night, with heavy rainfall persisting into Monday in several regions of the mMid-Atlantic and New England. Coastal flood warnings were canceled several regions of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)advisedtravelers to check with their airlines for updated flight information.FlightAwarereported more than 5,000US delays and nearly 550 cancellations. In Massachusetts, a temporary ground delay was issued at the Boston Logan international airport amid the weather.Major storm in US north-east knocks out power for 100,000 and floods roadsRead moreAs a result of the storm, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul,declareda state of emergency covering the Bronx, Kings, Nassau, New York, Queens, Richmond, Suffolk and Westchester counties.A fallen tree in the east New York City borough of Brooklyn resulted in adeathon Saturday during the nor’easter. A 56-year-old New York City housing authority employee was killed when a tree came down on him in a parking lot.Police said he was pronounced dead at Brookdale University hospital. Authorities had not immediately determined whether wind caused the tree to fall.In Queens, high winds caused widespread disruption after a tree fell at about 5.40pm in the Glendale area, with downed power lines forcing authorities to close the roadway. As a precaution, theNew YorkCity fire department evacuated a nearby building. No injuries were reported in that incident.View image in fullscreenCrews work to clear fallen trees from the property of Burnet Hill’s Haunted Ridge after a nor’easter storm in Livingston, New Jersey, on Saturday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/Getty ImagesAlong the Jersey Shore, residents spent Saturday removing debris and cleaning up between periods of high tide after thenor’easterforced flood water into streets and homes near theNew Jerseycoast. Eight counties in New Jerseyremain under a state of emergencyissued before the coastal storm arrived.The storm struck the mid-Atlantic and New England over the weekend and was forecast to continue into the early part of this week. As the week continues, flooding was expected to rise and recede along with the tides.TheNational Weather Service(NWS) expected coastal flooding to bring significant flooding from the Jersey Shore south to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, with more moderate flooding forecast along theMassachusettscoast.Explore more on these topicsUS weatherNew YorkBostonNew JerseyNorth CarolinaMassachusettsFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’ | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: US attorney general argues that president was ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: US attorney general argues that president was ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico
Content: US attorney general Todd Blanche holds a press conference at the White House on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersView image in fullscreenUS attorney general Todd Blanche holds a press conference at the White House on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersTrump administrationBlanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’US attorney general argues that president was ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and PoliticoEdward HelmoreSun 27 Sep 2026 17.42 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 16.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s attorney general Todd Blanche argued on Sunday that the administration was permitted toban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”.Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN,MS Nowand Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting.Blanche offered no evidence for his claim that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate, rather than simply unflattering to the president. Pressed by the interviewer, Martha Raddatz, to point to a report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate.“Wait, give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that,”Blanche replied. “There’s not even a real dispute that the information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100 percent negative toward the president.”On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex.But on Saturday,CNNsaid its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One.“The president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told ABC. “That’s not the right way to describe it.”The continuing dispute between the administration and the White House press corps had appeared to be resolving before CNN was again blocked from providing pool TV coverage of Trump on Saturday. That was after outlets stood in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico by briefly refusing to provide any pool TV feeds of the president.On ABC, Blanche said it wasn’t unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed on to the president’s plane.“The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One,” Blanche said. “This wasn’t a one-time denial of CNN. There’s all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying.“It’s not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it’s common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president.”What Blanche did not explain is that, before Trump’s second term, the choice of which correspondents were part of the pool covering presidential travel was left to the White House Correspondents’ Association and the broadcast networks that take turns providing camera crews. After Trump returned to office last year, the White House took control of which outlets would be permitted in the Oval Office, or on Air Force One, leading to increased access for partisan, pro-Trump journalists.Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”.Raddatz reminded Blanche that Trump himself said ha had banned CNN, MS Now and Politico, because, he said, “they purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration”.In the ruling to temporarily restore the three banned outlets’ White House access for 14 days, US district judge Timothy Kelly said there was nothing in the record suggesting that revocation of the press passes was motivated by national security concerns.“Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote in his ruling.Trump was faced with a gloomy political landscape with just over a month before the federal midterm elections in November. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low.But confidence in the news media polls lower, with just 28% expressing a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in newspapers, television channels and radio outlets to report the news fully, accurately and fairly,according to a 2025 Gallup survey.Bill Clinton recently commented on the battle between what the news media see as a crude effort at censorship and a denial of constitutional rights – and what the White House views as unfairly negative reporting.“There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said at theClinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution – because none of us are immune from being pissed off.“But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is.”Blanche was asked what the US constitution’s first amendment – which guarantees the right to a free press – meant to him.“The law says – what the free press can do is they are free to report whatever they want,” Blanche remarked. “Of course, they can. But when it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house. It is a privilege and not a right to be there.”He added that “it is absolutely the president’s duty to make sure that the American people are hearing accurate news.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpTodd BlancheUS politicsUS press and publishingPress freedomUS constitution and civil libertiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’ | Republicans | The Guardian
description: Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for Republicans
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for Republicans
Content: Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, is is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreenSenator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, is is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APRepublicansRepublican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton over John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for RepublicansMarina DunbarSun 27 Sep 2026 14.19 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticizedDonald Trump, his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary.“He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary.Trump-backed Ken Paxton ousts John Cornyn in heated Texas primary after scandal-plagued campaignRead more“John Cornyn’s a great member of the US Senate. Paxton has his challenges,” the retiring Tillis added. “We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars inTexasif Cornyn had won.”Tillis pointed to the president’s involvement in the contest and described Trump’s decision to backPaxtoninstead of Cornyn as an “unforced error” that has put the Senate seat at risk for the GOP.Trump endorsed Paxton just days before the Texas attorney general defeated Cornyn, a four-term senator, and advanced to face Democratic candidate James Talarico, a in the general election on 3 November.The race had wide implications for Trump’s strength heading into November’s midterm federal elections. Paxton will now face Talarico, a Democratic pastor and state legislator whose message of peace and populism has attracted much attention. If he wins, Talarico would become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide office in Texas.When he chose to support Paxton over Cornyn, Trump highlighted the Texas attorney general’s record as a steadfast supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.Cornyn had previously said during the 2024 presidential campaign thatRepublicansshould move on from Trump.In a social media post shortly before the election day, Trump said Cornyn had been “VERY disloyal” to him and implored voters in Texas to “REMEMBER!”Paxton, meanwhile, is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption andlater acquittedin a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud, but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement.In July 2025, his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery.Tillis is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions. In April, he spoke out indefense of the Nato military allianceafter Trump said he was “absolutely” considering withdrawing the US from it.“Any president that contemplates attempting to withdraw from Nato is not only fulfilling [Russian leader] Vladimir Putin and [Chinese premier] Xi Jinping’s greatest dreams but would be undermining America’s own national security interests,” Tillis said at the time.He also called for then secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem’s resignation after immigration agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis in January, calling her leadership “a disaster” during the last Senate hearing before her firing.Tillis was one of a small number of Republicans on Thursday to vote in favor of a Democrat-ledwar powers resolutionthat aimed to end the US war with Iran. Despite gaining some Republican support, the proposal failed to pass in the Senate by a 49-50 vote.Explore more on these topicsRepublicansDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsTexasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Datacenter developers accused of skirting key US pollution rules | Datacenters – US | The Guardian
description: Firms manipulating process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental groups warn
Author: Tom Perkins
Headline: Firms manipulating process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental groups warn
Content: Protesters gather outside the New Mexico environment department in Santa Fe to voice opposition to the Project Jupiter datacenter.Photograph: Susan Montoya Bryan/APView image in fullscreenProtesters gather outside the New Mexico environment department in Santa Fe to voice opposition to the Project Jupiter datacenter.Photograph: Susan Montoya Bryan/APDatacenters – USDatacenter developers accused of skirting key US pollution rulesFirms manipulating process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental groups warnTom PerkinsSun 27 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDatacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege.Companies need federal permits to emit a range of pollutants. In their permit applications, some in big tech are avoiding “major” reviews by dividing their emissions sources into separate, multiple “minor” sources that require less regulatory oversight, the advocates say.New Jersey datacenter fined $1.1m after visual investigation showed dozens of unpermitted generatorsRead moreThis helps datacenters avoid public scrutiny, and permit applications are typically approved much faster. It also likely saves tech companies money, and avoids the hassle and cost of potential pollution controls, advocates say. Datacenters can be significant sources of nitrogen oxide, ozone, heavy metals, particulate matter, greenhouse gas and other dangerous air pollutants.In North Carolina, Amazon and utility giant Duke Energy are installing 649 diesel generators to back up a new hyperscale center. They submitted twopermits,and avoided a major review despite being in a low income area that already suffers from high levels of air pollution.In New Mexico, the Project Jupiter datacenter developers attempted to circumvent a major review byproposingtwo natural gas “microgrids” for either side of the facility andsubmittingtwo “minor” permits. The overall project would have released enough pollution to trigger a major review.In Frederick, Maryland, four datacenters with separate minor permits, including one by Amazon, operate on a single campus with a master developer,regulatory documentsshow. In other instances, data center developers have staggered minor permit requests over months that cumulatively emit as much pollution as a major source, advocates say.These regulatory maneuvers make it less clear how much pollution residents living near the facilities are exposed to, and the move amounts to “lego permitting”, said Michael Koerber, a retired deputy director of the EPA’s Office of Air Quality Planning and Standards, which worked on permitting.“They want to fly under the radar,” said Koerber, who now volunteers with the Environmental Protection Network nonprofit. “The more attention they have, the more difficult it gets to get the permit. They have consultants who are very good and know where the shortcuts are.”Koerber noted that the situation is not unique to the data center industry. Cheryl Vetter, a former EPA employee who worked with Koeber and left the agency last year, said it was not common for data centers to use this tactic until after she left.In a statement, an Amazon spokesperson said the company “appropriately applied for and obtained an air permit for our datacenter project”.Under the Clean Air Act, companies building a project that will be a “major” source of air pollution, like some hyperscale data centers, are typically supposed to undergo a more stringent air emissions review. Among other protections, it is supposed to ensure that the pollution the facility would add to the local airshed would not violate air quality limits when combined with the air pollution already in the region.This process can be lengthy, may require pre-construction monitoring, and, if the proposed data center is found to violate limits, may require companies to take steps to limit their pollution, like adding scrubbers to their smokestacks.The Project Jupiter datacenter plans to divide its natural turbines into minor permits was “nothing short of preposterous”, attorneys with the New Mexico Environmental Law Centerwrotein March comments submitted to state regulators. The firm is representing community members who would be impacted by the proposed plans’ pollution.It in effect created a scenario in which one natural gas power plant would have operated with two minor permits, attorneys wrote. The permit application points to why the data center’s developers, Austin-based BorderPlex, attempted to do two permits.The federal limit for a minor permit for hazardous air pollution is 25 tons per year. The project’s developers proposed releasing between 20.2 and 24.2 tons of hazardous air pollution from each of the grids, meaning that together they would have released as much as 44 tons of hazardous air pollution.In regulatory documents, Maslyn Locke, an attorney working on the case, wrote that the “audacious attempt to arbitrarily distinguish two halves of the same source is insulting to both [regulators] and community members, as it is so clearly an attempt to avoid air pollution control requirements.”The developer withdrew the application in April amid fierce community pushback, Locke said. The New Mexico environment department also opposed the proposal, a spokesperson told the Guardian. However, Locke told the Guardian there was no public evidence that regulators opposed it until now. New plans for the data center have been held up by the state supreme court over procedural problems, Locke said.Vetter said the law allows for divided permits in some instances. Permits can be divided if two companies are polluting at the same location, but not if all the polluting activities are under common control. The sources must also be adjacent, though the definition of “adjacent” can include those that do not share a border, but operate as part of the same facility.Amazon and Duke’s North Carolinaplanscall for nearly 250 tons per year of nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and volatile organic compounds. Amazon is proposing to emit about 98 tons of particulate matter annually, and 6.4 tons per year of hazardous air pollutants, including benzene and formaldehyde.The heavily industrial region is already burdened by pollution from a Duke power plant and other plastic pellet factory, the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC) wrote in comments to North Carolina state regulators.Heart disease, cancer, and respiratory disease are among the leading causes of death in the region, and the datacenter’s diesel generators’ particulate matter and hazardous pollutants will almost certainly increase those problems, advocates warn.It appears the companies split the permits to avoid a major review, Kathleen Sullivan, a SELC attorney, told the Guardian. North Carolina regulators wrote that Duke’s generators are providing temporary power for about a year, and that Duke is operating them separately from Amazon’s generators. But the companies did not provide to regulators lease agreements and contracts, and some documents suggest Amazon controls all the generators, Sullivan alleged.In its statement, Amazon said: “The separate permitting of Amazon’s and Duke’s respective projects reflects the actual ownership and operational structure.”“They should be – and are – permitted under separate air permits,” the spokesperson said.Even if some of the generators are only temporary, high levels of exposure to the dangerous pollutants for even an hour can cause health problems, and the plans should undergo more meaningful scrutiny, Sullivan added.She said state regulators are “simply trusting two extremely wealthy and politically powerful companies without any verification”.“North Carolina regulators failed to protect people’s health and the air we all breathe by blindly accepting the companies’ self-interested statements instead of doing their job to investigate the key facts,” Sullivan said.Explore more on these topicsDatacenters – USnewsShareReuse this content

title: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’
Content: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’Eduardo PorterSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTShareThe Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by aSilicon Valleymogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world withartificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their projectin the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do.Everyday Americans are up in arms against theAI datacenters sproutingacross their communities. Villages, counties, citiesand statesareimposing moratoriaand bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development.Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits,according to a surveyby the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society.Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastlymore concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generallymore mistrustfulof the technology than people in other countries.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators rally during a protest calling for a citywide datacenter moratorium outside city hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on 14 September 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThis surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could causehuman extinctionhas, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net.The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch ofweird, sci-fi addled plutocratsto pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.”People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhurypoints out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whateverharm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law.The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters.Donald Trumpremains steadfastlyon the sideof the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which couldkeep locals in the darkuntil construction starts.The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.”Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology.And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule.This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum.But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead,has flushed workerswithout a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI.One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them.Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach.The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest ratesfree from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest.But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.”The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.”View image in fullscreenSam Altman, chief executive officer of OpenAI Inc, during a Senate commerce, science, and transportation Committee hearing in Washington DC on 8 May 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPeter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued thatdemocracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altmansalivates about an “awesome” futurein which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.”The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about asuperintelligent Golem.Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to beanswerable to no oneand will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,”he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way.There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of theEnd of Historyin Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word.Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass:section 230of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it.Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage.Reports of teen suicidesandonline bullyingbred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed tohook users to their screens.When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny.By the time Covid hit in 2020, the former paragons of liberal democracy had found a new role as magnifiers of conspiracy theories, enemies of “woke”, partisans in a libertarian revolt against “government control”. Joe Biden’s attempts touse antitrust lawand other regulations against the techno-plutocrats’ empires pushed them to the dark side, where Trump and his angry Maga movement awaited their embrace.How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising topunish European countrieswho dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which isproving so lucrativefor him and his family.View image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed, a US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of ‘The Barn’  datacenter, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, in Saline Township, Michigan, on 30 July 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesStill, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck.Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in aconversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.”Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.”Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletterBeing Thereon Substack

title: Snedeker says Trump ‘gets all the credit’ after US complete huge Presidents Cup comeback | Golf | The Guardian
description: The United States made a stunning rally to capture an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup title on Sunday, completing a 17-13 victory over the Internationals
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The United States made a stunning rally to capture an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup title on Sunday, completing a 17-13 victory over the Internationals
Content: Team USA celebrate their win on Sunday.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTeam USA celebrate their win on Sunday.Photograph: Sarah Stier/Getty ImagesGolfSnedeker says Trump ‘gets all the credit’ after US complete huge Presidents Cup comebackAmericans dominate final day singles contestsUS president gives speech before final dayAgence France-PresseSun 27 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States made a stunning rally to capture an 11th consecutive Presidents Cup title on Sunday, completing a 17-13 victory over the Internationals withDonald Trumpin attendance.Jacob Bridgeman secured the clinching point at Medinah by sinking a four-foot par putt at the 18th hole to defeat Australian Min Woo Lee 1-up.An embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as prop | Leander SchaerlaeckensRead moreThe Americans improved to 14-1-1 in the biennial rivalry after trailing 10.5-7.5 entering Sunday’s 12 concluding singles matches. The Internationals were poised to end a 28-year win drought but fell short once again.The Americans, boasting eight of the world’s 11 top-ranked golfers, won on the same suburban Chicago layout where Europe took the 2012 Ryder Cup with the famedMiracle at Medinah fightback.“These guys never lost faith,” US captain Brandt Snedeker said. “I told the guys last night that funny stuff happens here. Medinah’s got a history of funny things happening, and sure enough, they went out there and played their asses off. I’m so damn proud of those guys.”Trump, who attendedlast year’s US Ryder Cuploss, added tohis 2026 live sports viewing listthat has included the World Cup final, the NBA finals, college football, UFC and IndyCar events plus various golf events.“[Trump] told me I was going to bring some energy today for you guys. You guys need it,” Snedeker said. “And I told him if we did this, he gets all the credit. So thank you, President Trump.”Explore more on these topicsGolfUS sportsAustralia sportDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: USC suspend Stephens for ‘disgusting’ late hit that sent Oregon QB Dante Moore to hospital | College football | The Guardian
description: Oregon head coach Dan Lanning has decried a ‘disgusting play’ that left his starting quarterback, Dante Moore, in hospital
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Oregon head coach Dan Lanning has decried a ‘disgusting play’ that left his starting quarterback, Dante Moore, in hospital
Content: Dante Moore takes a late hit during Oregon’s win over USC.Photograph: Javier Rojas/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDante Moore takes a late hit during Oregon’s win over USC.Photograph: Javier Rojas/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockCollege footballUSC suspend Stephens for ‘disgusting’ late hit that sent Oregon QB Dante Moore to hospitalSenior able to move limbs but taken to hospitalUSC describe linebacker’s play as ‘unacceptable’Guardian sportand agenciesSun 27 Sep 2026 15.37 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USC Trojans have suspended their linebacker ⁠Desman Stephens II after what was described asa “disgusting play”that left Oregon quarterback Dante Moore in hospital.Moore was carted off the field after a late hit by Stephens in the first half of Oregon’s 41-27 win over USC on Saturday. During the play, Moore took off on a scramble. As he attempted to slide, he was hit in the head by Stephens, who was called for targeting and disqualified ‌from the game. Moore was taken to hospital, and was later diagnosed with a concussion.“Fortunately, his MRI and CT scans came back clean and he did not suffer any additional injuries,” Oregon head coach Dan Lanning said on Sunday.USC coach Lincoln Riley did not condone his player’s conduct. “Desman’s actions in last night’s game are unacceptable and are not reflective of USC Football nor of his personal character,” Riley said in a statement on Sunday. “He understands his mistake, accepts the consequences of his actions and will learn from this. The entire Trojan family wishes Dante a full recovery.”ICE has abducted a college athlete. What are the NCAA and universities going to do about it?Read moreView image in fullscreenOregon Ducks head coach Dan Lanning is held back by staff after the late hit on Dante Moore.Photograph: Javier Rojas/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockLanning was incensed by the hit. “It was a disgusting play,” Lanning said after the game. “The energy changed. A lot of guys on the sideline, they were emotional in ​that moment, including myself.”Fights broke out between players after the hit as Moore lay on the ground, and both teams were penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct.“Seeing him like that shook the whole team,” said Oregon backup quarterback Dylan Raiola, who replaced Moore for the rest of the game. “But at the same time, we knew that it was our brother, and we were gonna fight for him.”Stephens drew the ire of his opponents for appearing to celebrate his hit on Moore. On Sunday, he admitted his actions were unacceptable.“Seeing a player injured like that is incredibly serious, and my reaction in the moments afterward was completely inappropriate and inexcusable. Regardless of what was going through my mind at the time, there is no justification for smiling or celebrating while another player receives medical attention,” Stephens said in the statement. “I take full responsibility for my actions. That is not the person or teammate I want to be, and I will learn from this. I am deeply sorry to Dante, his family and everyone who saw my reaction. It is not representative of USC or our program. I hope he makes a full and speedy recovery.”Moore was an All-Big ​Ten third-team selection last season, throwing for 3,565 yards, 30 ​touchdowns and 10 ‌interceptions as the ​team went ​13-2. This season, he was off to a strong start with 849 passing yards and nine passing touchdowns in three games. He had been predicted to be a top pick in this year’s NFL draft but chose to return to college.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsWest CoastUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Liberty win Game 1 to put top-seeded Lynx on brink of WNBA playoff exit | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Breanna Stewart produced yet another clutch performance in the WNBA playoffs in the Liberty’s win over the Lynx.
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Breanna Stewart produced yet another clutch performance in the WNBA playoffs in the Liberty’s win over the Lynx.
Content: Breanna Stewart put forth another clutch playoffs performance.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/APView image in fullscreenBreanna Stewart put forth another clutch playoffs performance.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/APWNBALiberty win Game 1 to put top-seeded Lynx on brink of WNBA playoff exitBreanna Stewart scored 34 points with 12 reboundsLynx face must-win Game 2 in New York on TuesdayAssociated PressSun 27 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBreanna Stewart produced yet another clutch performance in the WNBA playoffs with 34 points and 12 rebounds for theNew York Libertyin a 91-75 victory over the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx to open their best-of-three first-round series on Sunday.Stewart, the two-time league MVP, added six assists, two steals and two blocks. She shot 11 for 18 from the floor with her friend and former college teammate Napheesa Collier, the 2024WNBAdefensive player of the year, guarding her most of the afternoon.Lynx’s Olivia Miles breaks Caitlin Clark’s WNBA rookie scoring recordRead moreStewart, who recently helped the US national teamwin a fifth consecutive World Cup, has the second-highest postseason scoring average by any player in league history. She was two short of the Liberty franchise record for points in a playoff game.Nia Brodie led the Lynx with 16 points in 19 minutes off the bench and Kayla McBride had 14 points after missing her first five 3-point attempts.
