title: USA’s McNulty transcends chaos of Montreal road race to claim ‘miracle’ world title | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Brandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded him as world road race champion with an unexpected solo win in Montreal
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Brandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded him as world road race champion with an unexpected solo win in Montreal
Content: ‘Until the last 100m, I didn’t believe it’: Brandon McNulty celebrates as he approaches the finish line in Montreal.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Until the last 100m, I didn’t believe it’: Brandon McNulty celebrates as he approaches the finish line in Montreal.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesCyclingUSA’s McNulty transcends chaos of Montreal road race to claim ‘miracle’ world titleArizona rider first US champion since Lance ArmstrongPre-race favourite Evenpoel fails to add second goldJeremy WhittleSun 27 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded the Slovene as world champion with an unexpected solo win in the men’s UCI road race in Montreal.In the biggest triumph of his career, the 28-year-old American took his country’s first win in the UCI’s blue riband event since Lance Armstrong’s lone victory in Oslo in 1993.Vollering pips Niewiadoma to seal dramatic road race world titleRead more“I’m really at a loss,” McNulty said. “Until the last hundred metres, I didn’t believe it, I was so tired. I was just dying, but I kept pushing. We have said for weeks now that we had a super strong team. We talked about it, but I knew it would take a miracle. I guess miracles happen.”McNulty’s 50-second lead at the start of the closing lap of the hilly Montreal circuit was enough to hold on to the finish line, despite a last‑ditch attempt by Tom Pidcock to chase down the American that, at one point, reduced his advantage to only a handful of seconds.Australian Michael Matthews claimed silver while former world champion Mathieu van der Poel of the Netherlands finished third.Pidcock was one of the animators of the final hour of racing, which followed the same volatile and unpredictable pattern as the women’s road race on Saturday, which was won by Demi Vollering of the Netherlands. A gruelling race, ridden without the benefit of race radios, was at times chaotic, particularly within the Belgium team’s confused tactics, with the Olympic road race champion, Remco Evenepoel, left once again to ponder what might have been.With 90 kilometres to go, a select group of a dozen riders, including Pidcock’s British teammate Oscar Onley, went clear on the pivotal climb of the Voie Camillien-Houde. That group reduced to an elite six, including Van der Poel, and this year’s Paris-Roubaix winner, Wout van Aert.In the constant ebb and flow, the biggest loser, seemingly hamstrung by team tactics, was Van Aert’s fellow Belgian and pre-race favourite Evenepoel, who was seeking to add the road race title to the time trial gold medal he won seven days ago. With the leading group increasing their lead, Paul Seixas’s France team combined with Isaac del Toro of Mexico to lead a nine-man group in pursuit. But Van der Poel, recently the author of a successful 172km lone break in the Tour of Luxembourg, pressed on with Onley, the Slovene Primoz Roglic and Quinn Simmons of the US.View image in fullscreenBrandon McNulty (centre) flanked by the Australian silver-medalist Michael Matthews (left) and third-placed Mathieu van der Poel.Photograph: Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press/APRenewed accelerations from Van der Poel finally distanced Onley and split the peloton to an even greater extent. In a succession of regroupings the lead changed multiple times, until McNulty finally and definitively seized the initiative with just over 30km to race.Matthews won the sprint duel for second place, 13 seconds behind McNulty. The Canberra-raised rider previously won silver in 2015 and bronze in 2017 and 2022.“It’s not only the way I raced the race today, it’s after what I’ve been through the last two years with the embolism in my lungs thinking my career was done, to breaking both my arms at the start of this year and thinking my career was done,” the Australian said after the race.“Now bouncing back to being second in the world’s road race, I’m just speechless honestly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I said to my wife at the start today, ‘Let’s just leave it all out there and be proud of the ride and at the end of the day make sure I finish with nothing left’, and that’s exactly what happened today.”Matthewsbroke both wrists in a training crashin March that sidelined him earlier in the season.Twenty-four hours after Vollering’s last-gasp win in a brutal women’s road race, McNulty’s victory was equally enthralling. Vollering’s joy at her success was dampened by the UCI’s decision to fine her 1,000 Swiss francs and give her a points deduction and a yellow card for a “non-compliant” racing position. However, the results were not affected by the post-race ruling.Katarzyna Niewiadoma, second to Vollering in the Tour de France Femmes this year, claimed another silver medal, but the Dutch rider paid tribute to her rival’s efforts. “In the end, your greatest competitors are also your greatest motivation,” Vollering said.As the week of competition ended, the Spanish media revealed that one of the stars of the championships, the Spanish teenager Benjamín Noval, winner of the world junior road and time trial titles in Montreal, had escaped being sanctioned by the country’s anti-doping body Celad.El País reported that in 2024 Noval, who will race for Netcompany Ineos in 2027, had been found working with José “Pepe” Martí, banned for 15 years in the aftermath of the Armstrong doping scandal and prohibited from associating with athletes in any sport. Martí, who remains banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency until June, met Noval for physiological testing while under Celad surveillance, but Noval, who was only 15 at the time of the incident, was not subjected to any sanction.Explore more on these topicsCyclingUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Republic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over Israel | Nations League | The Guardian
description: First-half goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan gave Ireland a 3-0 win against Israel in a near-empty stadium in Debrecen
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: First-half goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan gave Ireland a 3-0 win against Israel in a near-empty stadium in Debrecen
Content: Troy Parrott gestures after opening the scoring for Republic of Ireland against Israel.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTroy Parrott gestures after opening the scoring for Republic of Ireland against Israel.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesNations LeagueRepublic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over IsraelPaul MacInnesat Nagyerdei Stadion, DebrecenSun 27 Sep 2026 17.24 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFootball and politics are inseparable in the modern world, no matter how many people wish they were not. But whether the beautiful game can ease the ills of our age is another matter. After a week in which the issue of Irish support for the people of Gaza had turned this fixture into a battle of conscience, the outcome of this underwhelming match ultimately felt inconsequential.In the end the result was indeed a walkover, just not because of a boycott. On Saturday night the question had been whether Heimir Hallgrimsson’s side would take to the field in Hungary at all. If they did, would their heads be in the game? It turned out that a week of internal angst had been enough to produce collective resolve among the Irish squad, or at least those selected to play. Strong and assertive from the off, their forwards each scored in the first half to settle the contest, with plenty of symbolic action to assure those back home of their feelings.Israel v Republic of Ireland, Norway v Portugal, Germany v Greece: Nations League – liveRead more“It’s probably been the toughest days of my coaching career,” Hallgrimsson said after the match. “But it’s not about me. It’s about the players and they’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them. They represented themselves on the pitch with dignity but also with the power of proud Irishmen. They’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them and hopefully they will have the support of the Irish people.”In a way the atmosphere in Debrecen was reminiscent of a match played during Covid. Every word uttered in the ground was audible and the nigh-on empty stands carried their own oppressive weight. As the nominal home side,Israelhad been allowed a small delegation of fans, about 150, who were doing their best to be excitable. Meanwhile, two blocks away were the Irish contingent, around a dozen people who had got into the ground despite the Football Association of Ireland’s decision not to bring an away allocation. They were all stood hands in pockets in a stairway.This odd, almost haunted mood was heightened further by Ireland’s mannered approach to the pre-match rituals. Irish staff faced away from the pitch when their national anthem was played. Ireland’s players, all wearing black armbands, stared at the ground during Israel’s. There was no exchanging of pennants and no shaking of hands, with both squads hurried away from the centre circle into their own huddles.The game had come close to being abandoned on Saturday, when the goalkeeper Gavin Bazunumade himself unavailable for selection, his decision prompting emotional exchanges among players and management. Hallgrimsson therefore picked a team with defender Jimmy Dunne nominally a third goalkeeper and also dropped the key forward Finn Azaz to the bench in one of five changes to the team that lost meekly to Kosovo. Azaz’s mother has Israeli citizenship and the Southampton forward was reported to have made an impassioned contribution to Saturday’s discussion. “Today we thought others would fit this game better than him,” Halgrimsson said.View image in fullscreenThe Republic of Ireland team bow their heads during the Israeli national anthem.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesAfter all the soul-searching, Ireland decided the contest in only 11 first-half minutes. Troy Parrott opened the scoring in the 14th minute, turning home a low shot through the body of Daniel Peretz after impressive work on the right by wingback James Abankwah. Two minutes later the lead was doubled when, running on the shoulder of the last defender, Adam Idah collected a smart through ball from Jack Moylan and wrapped a calm finish inside Peretz’s left-hand post.In the 25th minute Moylan got a goal of his own, his fourth in as many caps to continue a stellar start to his international career, driving 25 yards into the box before shooting low into the net. Moylan wheeled away to the corner flag, took off his black armband and kissed it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael raised their levels momentarily in the second half, with the substitute Dor Peretz drawing one excellent save from Caoimhín Kelleher. But ultimately the game deteriorated into just a series of scuffles, cheered on deliriously by the Israeli support who appeared to be chanting for the IDF as the final whistle blew.Their manager, Ran Ben-Shimon, was asked by Israeli media after the match if he would resign following the defeat, to which he answered no. “We didn’t handle the pressure well that is obvious, we failed mentally, we failed tactically,” Ben-Shimon said. “But in a few days there is another game we will have to find the energy to rise again.”Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueIsraelRepublic of Irelandmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: In playful moments, the USMNT’s new youth movement is already paying off | USA | The Guardian
description: After a crushing World Cup exit, 11 debutants and two teenage scorers are giving the program renewed verve
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: After a crushing World Cup exit, 11 debutants and two teenage scorers are giving the program renewed verve
Content: Justin Ellis and Alex Freeman celebrated in front of Orlando fans, with both having come up through the club’s youth system.Photograph: Mark Thorstenson/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJustin Ellis and Alex Freeman celebrated in front of Orlando fans, with both having come up through the club’s youth system.Photograph: Mark Thorstenson/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesUSAIn playful moments, the USMNT’s new youth movement is already paying offAfter a crushing World Cup exit, 11 debutants and two teenage scorers are giving the program renewed verveSubscribe to our free newsletter for US soccer fansFollow Guardian Soccer onInstagramandTikTokPablo Iglesias Maurerat Inter&Co StadiumSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fans who witnessed the United States’ 4-1 thrashing ofPeruin Orlando on Saturday did not have to wait long to get their flashbulb moment. It came just four minutes into the match, only moments after 19-year-old Orlando City attacker Justin Ellis headed home the US opener.Ellis, making his first appearance for the US, sprinted toward the near corner to celebrate, then turned and faced the US supporters in the north end ofInter.coStadium – a supporters’ section nicknamed “the wall”. Quickly, he was joined by Villarreal defender Alex Freeman, himself an Orlando City product. For a moment, the two former teammates posed arm in arm, gazing up at the home crowd. Then they embraced, laughed, and attempted to run back to the center circle. Gio Reyna, who’d assisted on the goal, shoved him back toward the fans.“Celebrating that goal with Alex – it was ridiculous,” Ellis told reporters after the match. “He’s like family to me. It was unbelievable … I think Gio also just understood the moment, being back home in front of the wall, it was just super special.”USA thrash Peru as teenage newcomers shine in first step toward 2030Read moreYouthful, playful moments like this resonated on Saturday, not entirely unexpected given the fact that the US rolled out eleven newcomers, just one player shy of the program’s all-time record. The game pulsed with a carefree, free-spirited energy; an ideal palate-cleanser to US fans still reeling from the team’s stiff crashout against Belgium in the World Cup.That last-16 match was arguably the most important game the US has played in years. This one had zero stakes whatsoever, more a fact-finding mission than anything else. Which is precisely what made it so lovely to watch.On Saturday, the US kids played with an uncommon familiarity, particularly for their age. Ellis and Reyna were far from the only two who connected. Sixteen-year-old Cavan Sullivan – American soccer’s latest “next big thing” – threatened throughout the entirety of his 60-minute shift. Julian Hall scored the United States’ third on his debut, crashing the back post on a Sebastian Berhalter cross as if they had been club teammates for years.“In the language of football, good players do not need much time together,” Pochettino said after the match. “They only need a few training sessions. It’s the same if they don’t have quality – you can train them for a year and that natural, organic connection never happens … I feel really proud [for Cavan.] 16 years old? Performing and fighting and playing with personality and character? I am so happy with him …. There’s no doubt that he’s very smart, he’s so great, he just needs time. Like [any of the other newcomers.]”View image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan more than held his own in his senior US debut.Photograph: Rich Storry/Getty ImagesSullivan has been under the microscope for years, the subject of rampant speculation and an uncommonly high level of media attention in the sometimes dim spotlight of American club soccer.“It was a really special day,” Sullivan told reporters after the match. “For me, my family, it’s crazy. It is crazy that I represent my country at the highest level, with the men’s national team. I am just really happy to have done this – it was a really amazing night.”Pochettino spoke at length in the run-up to this match about the “contagious” nature of having so many young players in camp, and how it’s rubbed off on his entire staff. In the moments after Saturday’s dismantling of Peru, that much felt very apparent. The Argentine said that the postgame sight of players embracing, wandering around to find family members and soaking in the moment gave him goosebumps.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion"It was amazing,” said Pochettino. “We know what it means for these young players that they made their debut. That means a lot for them, but it also means a lot for us … We really are enjoying that fresh energy a lot – how they listen, how they want to improve, how they want to train, we were talking about energy, it’s very contagious. We can win or lose, we can perform OK or we can’t. But we really enjoy the journey together.”But while the US team’s last generational turnover took place without many established veterans sticking around, this time around those young players have latched on to those who came before – even if the “vets,” this this case, are sometimes still in their early 20s. In his remarks to media pregame, Ellis praised his connection with Gio Reyna, and the rest of the US debutants have mentioned emulating other more senior players on the roster.“Players like Tyler Adams,” said Pochettino, “and how he was out there on the field mixed with [Red Bull New York midfielder] Adri [Mehmeti], who is 17 … the senior players deserve massive credit in the way that they treat and guide and support and welcome, in the way that they create an environment that’s very comfortable, to feel like home. That is I think massive, massive value for us to have these senior players helping in this way.”It was a feeling mirrored by Hall, a player who finds himself at the center of a tug-of-war between the United States and Poland over his services. He had little to say about that on Saturday, choosing instead to savor the moment.“I grew up with a lot of these guys, playing against them,” said Hall. “I know how hard they’ve worked, as well as I have, to get to a stage like this. I think we’re just really, really happy to make our debuts and make an impact.”Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsPerufeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tony Pulis says he and Stoke were ‘cheated’ in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdict | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Tony Pulis says ‘we won’t ever get that day back’ after Manchester City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Tony Pulis says ‘we won’t ever get that day back’ after Manchester City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules
Content: Ryan Shawcross (centre) of Stoke City is consoled by teammates after his side’s defeat in the 2011 FA Cup final.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRyan Shawcross (centre) of Stoke City is consoled by teammates after his side’s defeat in the 2011 FA Cup final.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty ImagesManchester CityTony Pulis says he and Stoke were ‘cheated’ in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdictManchester City won match 1-0 after goal by Yaya TouréClub deny wrongdoing and say ‘process is ongoing’Jamie JacksonSun 27 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Pulis has said his Stoke City team were “cheated” out of the 2011 FA Cup after Manchester Citywere found guilty on virtually all countsof breaching Premier League financial rules.Pulis’s Stokelost the 2011 Cup final 1-0after Yaya Touré’s goal. Yet following Friday’s news that City are guilty on all but one of the more than 100 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, Pulis feels serious discontent. City are expected to appeal and they deny any wrongdoing.Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict | Jonathan WilsonRead more“When do we get our FA Cup?” the 68-year-old wrotein his BBC Sport column. “That is what all Stoke fans have been asking me since the news broke on Friday. I thought exactly the same.“I don’t expectManchester Cityto offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners’ medals their players received. I don’t seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely.“But I still feel cheated. We won’t ever get that day back and the chance to celebrate around Stoke-on-Trent with the cup and medals we so honestly fought for. After breaking the rules, Manchester City got to do that instead. While the process is far from over because City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth.”Pulis pointed to City’s outlay on Touré, who was signed from Barcelona for £24m and earned about £180,000-a-week. He said: “Yaya Touré, who scored the winning goal, was reportedly earning 10 times what we were paying any of our players and, on his own, had cost more than our entire starting 11 when they had signed him from Barcelona in 2010.”View image in fullscreenManchester City’s Yaya Touré (left) scores during the 2011 FA Cup final.Photograph: Andrew Yates/AFP/Getty ImagesPulis underlined how his emotion has been changed by the verdict. “My disappointment was buried in the fact we had played a team full of superstars, and faced an elite coach in Roberto Mancini, and had just fallen short. Today, I feel very differently, as I am sure people connected with the other clubs affected by City’s successes in the same period, between 2009 and 2018 [will feel].“We lost, but to a team that have been found guilty of breaking the financial rules set out by the Premier League. In doing so, they did not just beat Stoke in an FA Cup final, they collected a stack of titles and went on to completely dominate English football for more than a decade. So, with those rules having been broken, what will the punishment be?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTony Pulis of Stoke City reacts in defeat.Photograph: Laurence Griffiths/The FA/Getty ImagesPulis believes action may be widespread. “I know all Stoke supporters will be demanding that City pass the trophy over and every club that has been affected by their actions will be considering their legal options,” he said.On Saturday, Khaldoon al-Mubarak,reiterated the club’s position. “There is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity,” said City’s chair.On Friday a City spokesperson had said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023. The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityTony PulisStoke CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Thomas Tuchel resists ‘madness’ of calls to rest England players despite longer window | England | The Guardian
description: England head coach says it would not be right to allow his players or the clubs to pick and choose their matches during the elongated Nations League window
Author: David Hytner
Headline: England head coach says it would not be right to allow his players or the clubs to pick and choose their matches during the elongated Nations League window
Content: Thomas Tuchel said he was pleased with England’s performance against Spain.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said he was pleased with England’s performance against Spain.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianEnglandThomas Tuchel resists ‘madness’ of calls to rest England players despite longer windowI don’t take calls from Premier League managers, he saysEngland play Czechia in Prague on TuesdayDavid HytnerSun 27 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel says it would be “madness” to allow his England players or the clubs to pick and choose their matches during the elongatedNations Leaguewindow as he promised to go full throttle for victory against Czechia in Prague on Tuesday.The manager did accept that Declan Rice needed to rest and could not be part of the squad in light of the Arsenal midfielder’s heavy workload across a number of seasons and well-documented fitness issues. Rice was at Wembley on Saturday to watchEngland lose 3-2 against Spainin their opening Nations League game.James Trafford’s England dream burns with No 1 spot finally up for grabs againRead moreBut now that Tuchel has his group, he says there is no room for compromise and certainly not to speak to club managers who might want to make deals over their players’ minutes. Tuchel does not want to rotate his starting personnel, although he does accept it could be impractical. After Prague,Englandgo to Rijeka to play Croatia on Saturday before returning to Wembley to face Czechia next Tuesday.“I don’t take calls from Premier League managers,” Tuchel said. “I never called any national team coach [when he was in club football]. I cannot manage [the minutes of] the players. It’s just impossible. I knew as a club coach … if I would call a coach in Brazil or Argentina, they would not know what I am talking about. The players would not know what I am talking about.“Why would I do this and start giving the players the impression that it’s OK to take a step back or share a half or to rest one match? I would never. It’s madness. We want to win the next match. I would love not to rotate but I am not sure if it’s possible. An ideal scenario would be to go again and go again and go again. With six or seven players minimum that start again – to put the responsibility on them and for them to feel the trust.”Tuchel accepted the Spain defeat had increased the pressure for the trip to Prague but he was unconcerned. “It’s nothing we can’t handle,” he said. “We need to be proactive and go for it. There is no room for managing [the players] or an economic style. It’s how the team want to play, how we want to play so let’s go.”Tuchel was asked whether Jude Bellingham, who was at his rampaging best against Spain, could sustain his all-or-nothing style for another three England games in quick succession. “It’s the only style he can play,” Tuchel said.“That’s just his game. It’s not an economic game. Let’s see. I would love to have him four times on the pitch. The concern is that he hasn’t done it this season in this tight period. We will need to check with the physios. We will not put Jude at any risk.”Bellingham created a game-high five chances against Spain, including the assist for Anthony Gordon’s equaliser for 1-1. He won the penalty thatHarry Kanemissed that would have given England a 3-1 lead. His running with the ball repeatedly stretched the world champions. There was also the moment on 35 minutes when he clashed with his Real Madrid teammate Marc Cucurella.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHarry Kane’s penalty miss was costly for England.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“Jude likes that, he gets better if that happens,” Tuchel said. “It’s better if he plays with a bit of rage. It’s what he does. I think sometimes he is looking for these moments to get his fire going. He doesn’t know any [Madrid] teammates [during an international game]. He is still friends with them but not for the 90 minutes.”It was a wild game against Spain. England conceded early and could have been four or five down by the 35th minute. Their defending was loose. They rallied to lead 2-1 at half-time and the match turned after Kane’s penalty miss in the 54th minute when he felt his standing foot give way. Tuchel insisted his team was not far away from beating the very best.“If Harry doesn’t slip we win the game,” Tuchel said. “If Harry doesn’t slip we go two goals up. We were clearly the better team until that moment. Of course, Spain never panic. How far away are we from that? One small slip from Harry.“If we had won, we would have deserved it but it wouldn’t have made us favourites for the Euros. We need to go step by step. They came with their strongest team. We had some key players missing. I am fine with this performance. We could have won the game and didn’t.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelHarry KaneNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League: Greece stun Klopp’s Germany, Netherlands sink Serbia but Gakpo hurt | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Dimitris Kourbelis’s winner spoiled Jürgen Klopp’s home debut, while the Netherlands’ victory in Serbia was marred by Cody Gakpo’s injury
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dimitris Kourbelis’s winner spoiled Jürgen Klopp’s home debut, while the Netherlands’ victory in Serbia was marred by Cody Gakpo’s injury
Content: Dimitrios Kourbelis celebrates after scoring a historic winner for Greece in Augsburg.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersView image in fullscreenDimitrios Kourbelis celebrates after scoring a historic winner for Greece in Augsburg.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersNations LeagueNations League: Greece stun Klopp’s Germany, Netherlands sink Serbia but Gakpo hurtJürgen Klopp ‘unbothered’ despite 1-0 home defeatGakpo goes off in 2-1 win, Portugal edge past NorwayReuters and AFPSun 27 Sep 2026 18.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreecestunnedGermany1-0 in Augsburg to go top of theirNations Leaguegroup and spoil Jürgen Klopp’s debut in the home dugout.Dimitrios Kourbelis scored the only goal in the 74th minute, earning Greece their first-ever victory in 11 matches against Germany. Ivan Jovanovic’s side now lead ⁠Group A2 with six points ⁠from two matches; Klopp’s side are third with one point from two games after a 1-1 draw against theNetherlandson Thursday.Ireland’s comfortable win over Israel cannot dispel controversyRead moreThe hosts were in control for most of the game and had close to 80% possession in the first half alone.Germanywere ultimately punished ⁠for sloppy defending, especially in the second half, which gave the visitors space to attack.Felix Nmecha fired wide in the 54th minute, moments after theGreecekeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis ‌had palmed a Joshua Kimmich free-kick over the bar. The Greeks then almost scored in the 66th after Kimmich lost possession in his own half, but the substitute Fotis Ioannidis fired just wide of the post.View image in fullscreenIt was a frustrating first home game in charge of the Germany side for Jürgen Klopp.Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/ReutersThey did better eight minutes later, with Kourbelis’s deflected low drive earning their second victory in a row after their last-gasp 2-1 win overSerbiaon Thursday. Greece will now host the Dutch on Thursday, while Germany are at home to Serbia.Klopp shrugged off the defeat after the final whistle. “Personally, I’m completely unbothered by it,” he told ARD. “I’ve lost far more matches in my life than I would have liked … but as long as you draw the right conclusions, a loss is ultimately just a piece of information – no different from a win.”“We absolutely need these kinds of matches – they are exactly the games we wanted to have,” Klopp added, while Kimmich said his new coach “has been very clear about what he wants – as players, we need to implement it”.Earlier, theNetherlandsearned a 2-1 victory inSerbiathanks to Mexx ‌Meerdink’s double on his second appearance for his country. It was their first win under their new coach, Xavi Hernández, following Thursday’s draw with Germany.Meerdink, who plays for the Eredivisie leaders, AZ, opened the scoring with a confidently taken penalty in the 30th minute. Luka Jovic equalised for the hosts but Meerdink struck again in the 69th minute to earn three points.“It’s a boyhood dream,” Meerdink said. “Everything is happening so quickly. You just don’t realise what can happen in the space of a week. It’s also great that we managed to win here. I did feel a little pressure, but you play that out of your system. And then to score two ​is fantastic.”Cody Gakpo is an injury concern after going off in the 17th minute and will undergo a scan on Monday. “It’s his ankle, that’s all I know,” Xavi said on the Liverpool winger’s injury. “Tomorrow we will know, but hopefully it’s not too important.”View image in fullscreenMexx Meerdink scores his second goal in the Netherlands’ 2-1 victory in Belgrade.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersJoão Félix scored for the second ​consecutivePortugalmatch as the defending champions edged pastNorway2-1 in Oslo to top Group A4 with two wins from two games. Erling Haaland cancelled out João Félix’s 17th-minute opener in the 54th minute, but Gonçalo ​Ramos’s chip three minutes later secured victory for Jorge Jesus’s side in Oslo.Bruno Fernandes was left out of the Portugal squad on Sunday, with Jesus revealing beforehand that the Manchester United captain had “played through the pain” in Thursday’s 1-0 win over Wales.“He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United,” the Portugal head coach said. “He wasn’t his usual self … [but] he really wanted to play against Wales.”Portugal stay in Scandinavia for their next game, away to Denmark on Thursday. Norway visit Cardiff to take on Wales, who earlierlost 2-0 to the Danesin Copenhagen.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueGermanyGreeceNetherlandsNorwayPortugalSerbianewsShareReuse this content

title: McTominay’s role a poser for Pocognoli as Scotland offer positives in Slovenia | Scotland | The Guardian
description: New coach still learning about his squad as they prepare to face Switzerland with the Napoli midfielder expected to return in November
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: New coach still learning about his squad as they prepare to face Switzerland with the Napoli midfielder expected to return in November
Content: Scott McTominay has been absent from Scotland’s opening Nations League games after undergoing surgery for a minor heart issue.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenScott McTominay has been absent from Scotland’s opening Nations League games after undergoing surgery for a minor heart issue.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScotlandMcTominay’s role a poser for Pocognoli as Scotland offer positives in SloveniaNew coach still learning about his squad as they prepare to face Switzerland with the Napoli midfielder expected to return in NovemberEwan MurraySun 27 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn elongated international window does not prevent Sébastien Pocognoli from glancing towards the next one. Scott McTominay’s absence from Scotland’s opening set ofNations Leaguegames is understandable as the Napoli midfielder recovers from a heart procedure.Thescoreless draw in Sloveniaon Saturday raised the question of where McTominay will fit in when he returns. “He can play in many positions,” Pocognoli said. “He is a top player so he can read the game. We will see.”Pocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in SloveniaRead moreIndeed we will. The answer is not immediately obvious. Pocognoli deployed Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson as central midfielders in Ljubljana with John McGinn placed ahead of them to support a two-man strike force. Gilmour was heavily influential during Scotland’s impressive second half. Ferguson’s combative and defensive skills are valuable. McGinn, like McTominay, is a mainstay of the team. It is therefore legitimate to ask how Pocognoli handles McTominay, who is expected to return to theScotlandscene in November.“For now we just need to put the structure in place,” Pocognoli said. “I hope Scott watched the game and thought ‘OK, I see myself in that shape in the second half’, and that with good discipline he can enjoy it. I hope he can look and think: ‘Yeah, I want to play.’“Andy Robertson was really positive after the game and said that he really enjoyed it. It is really good to hear that from top players.”That Scotland improved markedly after half-time messaging from Pocognoli, in hismaiden match as the country’s manager, reflected well on the 39‑year‑old Belgian. Pocognoli seems determined to emphasise that he is not tactically inflexible, despite Scotland’s shape being typical of what he deployed at Union Saint‑Gilloise and Monaco. Pocognoli also insisted there will be consistent involvement for Ben Gannon-Doak, a winger who does not automatically seem to fit into a 3-4-1-2 setup. Gannon‑Doak, whose game time has been restricted at Bournemouth, appeared as a second-half substitute in Slovenia.“It will not be difficult to find a place for him,” Pocognoli said. “It is a process. At his club he also needs to settle. He is young and he needs to play more for his club.“He is a top, top kid first of all and a top player and a gamechanger and we don’t have a lot of those. That is why Josh McPake is also with us because I want more of that. Maybe in the future if those two make the step we can be open to exploring many shapes.“I think in that wide position in the shape we had in Slovenia it is risky to start him, because we have to know that sometimes you can be beaten in transition. The pattern on the ball can sometimes be bad and then it is not the game for Ben. But when we have good control on the pitch, like in the second half, that becomes his game.”View image in fullscreenSébastien Pocognoli is in a tricky position of trying to learn about his team while facing credible opposition.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAA sterner test surely awaits for Scotland on Tuesday. Switzerland may be without Granit Xhaka but they still swatted aside North Macedonia 3-0 on Saturday evening. Pocognoli is in that tricky position of trying to learn about his squad while facing credible opposition. He was aware of the frustrations of the Scotland support during the first half in Slovenia, with those fans roused by the creation of numerous second‑half chances.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“As long as we continue to create chances, you bring the fans alive,” Pocognoli said. “If we can produce the second-half performance at home I think it will be OK. But we cannot play 90 minutes like this. When we are resilient like we were in defending the box in the first half that is something we have to enjoy because it is not easy to defend like they did.“I think the crowd was positive at the end because we produced something that they wanted to see. At least we attacked and they did not have the feeling that they travelled for nothing.”Oli McBurnie is likely to retain his place in attack despite his run without scoring in Scotland colours stretching to 17 games. Pocognoli has been delighted with the application and attitude of McBurnie, who had been shunned by the previous manager, Steve Clarke. Scotland need potency; they have found the net only once in four games.“He played a good game,” Pocognoli said of McBurnie. “In the first half when it was difficult … but in that moment you give up or you stick together to fight for the team. Oli never gave up. He showed that he is proud and hungry to be here.”Explore more on these topicsScotlandNations LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derby | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Alyssa Thompson’s goal before half-time at Stamford Bridge proved enough to earn a precious win for the hosts against blunt opponents
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Alyssa Thompson’s goal before half-time at Stamford Bridge proved enough to earn a precious win for the hosts against blunt opponents
Content: Alyssa Thompson (left) slotted home a rebound to put Chelsea ahead of Arsenal at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Getty Images/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenAlyssa Thompson (left) slotted home a rebound to put Chelsea ahead of Arsenal at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Getty Images/Sportsphoto/AllstarWomen's Super LeagueChelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derbySophie Downeyat Stamford BridgeSun 27 Sep 2026 16.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal’s title chances were dealt a significant blow after a narrow defeat at the hands of Chelsea. Alyssa Thompson’s first-half finish was the difference on a competitive afternoon at Stamford Bridge but one that ultimately left Renée Slegers with more questions than answers about how to save their season.“Worried? No,” Slegers said. “Confidence is something that fluctuates. They know who they are and they know what they can bring. What’s important is that there’s always phases in the season and there’s different things you need to work on or focus on.Liverpool sink Everton and end derby drought after Olsson and Kapocs strikeRead more“It’s important that we keep any pressure and any complexity away from the players because we believe in them. It’s just really important that we keep that simplicity and clear minds for the players.”There is no game quite as eagerly anticipated in the Women’s Super League as the meeting between Chelsea and Arsenal. While other derbies and duels are in their early development, the London derby is the one year after year that brings the pressure, the drama and, of course, the eyeballs. While both sides clearly respect each other off the pitch, there is a distinct sense that once they cross the white line there is true competitive animosity there, one that lifts the levels of everyone in the vicinity.This edition was no different with expectation and apprehension buzzing around Stamford Bridge before kick-off and no shortage of new narratives. This was the first time Katie McCabe, 11 years a Gunner, would face her old team having moved in the summer. Would she help Chelsea to inflict more pain on Arsenal’s stuttering start, or could Slegers’s side put a pin in the pressure balloon and breathe new life into their search for a first title in eight years?Both teams came into this encounter having not yet hit form. Arsenal have created opportunities but have looked predictable in their buildup and lacked a finishing touch. In contrast, Chelsea have looked energetic and full of ideas but, excluding their win against Manchester United, have also struggled with ruthlessness in front of goal.View image in fullscreenChelsea’s Katie McCabe took on her former Arsenal teammates for the first time since her summer move.Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesSonia Bompastor was handed a significant boost before kick-off with the news that both Keira Walsh and Lauren James were available to start. Lexi Potter was given the nod alongside Walsh in midfield, a sign of how much trust the head coach has in the 20-year-old, while Melvine Malard was fit enough to begin up front.Slegers, meanwhile, rang the changes from Arsenal’s hard-fought victory against HB Køge during the week. Two who remained were Kyra Cooney-Cross and the goalkeeper Anneke Borbe, who kept out Misa Rodríguez.The visitors came out full of energy and looking to make an early statement. They dominated early on with 44.2% of the action happening in Chelsea’s defensive third in the first quarter and Arsenal looking to reap the rewards of their high press.Their biggest threat early on came from Lisa Baum. The 19-year-old has been one of the more positive aspects of their season to date and was given space down the right by Chelsea.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all of their control, however, it was much of the same old story for Slegers’s side, haunted by their inability to take their chances. Of the eight shots they created, they failed to register one on target and hit the woodwork twice through Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey.With every rattle of a post that reverberated around Stamford Bridge, Arsenal’s early confidence dwindled and Bompastor’s side started to find more joy. In direct contrast to their opponents, the Blues took their chance when it came when Malard pounced on Steph Catley as she played out from the back. Borbe made a good save to deny Walsh initially but the rebound fell perfectly for Thompson to hammer home.It was the ideal time to score and Chelsea went in ahead at the break with the momentum of the game having shifted significantly. They went on to create big opportunities of their own with Malard dragging a shot narrowly wide on two occasions.While Arsenal were able to create opportunities, the hosts looked comfortable in the circumstances and defended resolutely to see out the game and take home a valuable three points.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueChelsea WomenArsenal WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Denmark dominate Wales in Nations League to leave Bellamy ‘really hurting’ | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Wales wilted in Copenhagen as a Ben Davies own goal and Gustav Isaksen’s instinctive strike left Craig Bellamy’s side bottom of their group
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Wales wilted in Copenhagen as a Ben Davies own goal and Gustav Isaksen’s instinctive strike left Craig Bellamy’s side bottom of their group
Content: Gustav Isaksen (second left, No 8) celebrates his goal with Denmark teammates at Parken Stadium.Photograph: Ritzau Scanpix Denmark/ReutersView image in fullscreenGustav Isaksen (second left, No 8) celebrates his goal with Denmark teammates at Parken Stadium.Photograph: Ritzau Scanpix Denmark/ReutersNations LeagueDenmark dominate Wales in Nations League to leave Bellamy ‘really hurting’Press AssociationSun 27 Sep 2026 17.14 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWales wilted in Copenhagen as a 2-0 defeat to Denmark left them bottom of theirNations Leaguegroup with no points or goals from their first two games.After a first half in which Wales were very much second-best and fortunate to reach the break level, Denmark’s domination was rewarded by a Ben Davies own goal and a Gustav Isaksen strike in the second period.Israel v Republic of Ireland, Norway v Portugal, Germany v Greece: Nations League – liveRead moreWaleslost Thursday’s opener to Portugal 1-0and Sunday’s result leaves them already facing an uphill battle to avoid relegation from Group A4. Denmark were under similar pressure after being beaten 3-2 by Norway on Thursday, but rose to the occasion and should have won more comfortably.“I’m really hurting. When you see an athletic team run over you a little bit … but then, will we improve? I think we will,” said theWalesmanager, Craig Bellamy. “This team will get better, these players will keep improving. For me now it’s just focus, two more games to go.”Bellamy had happy memories of the Parken Stadium when as a 19-year-old he had scored the Wales winner in a Euro 2000 qualifier. Bellamy had promised to make changes given the short turnaround of fixtures and, in the event, made six with Charlie Savage’s surprise promotion the most notable switch.The son of former Wales international Robbie Savage, Charlie joined the squad after several withdrawals, with his previous two caps having both come against Gibraltar. Daniel James, Kieffer Moore and Sorba Thomas formed a reshaped frontline, while Chris Mepham and Connor Roberts were drafted into defence.View image in fullscreenCraig Bellamy made a number of changes to the team that lost 1-0 in Portugal, but could not deliver a different result.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockDenmark were soon playing their way through a porous Wales midfield though, and chances came their way. Neco Williams was caught out by Joachim Andersen’s pass from the back and Isaksen flashed his shot wide. Isaksen then sent over a cross that Patrick Dorgu headed off target.The hosts thought they had taken the lead after 24 minutes. Wales were exposed by a counterattack led by Mikkel Damsgaard and Isaksen met Rasmus Højlund’s cross with a thumping volley, only for VAR to rule offside in the buildup.Damsgaard struck a post seconds later and it looked a matter of time before Denmark would score. But Dorgu headed off straight down the tunnel in a potential injury blow for Manchester United, and Wales began to create chances of their own.Thomas was just off target from 20 yards after an Andersen error and Wales went even closer two minutes before the interval. Brennan Johnson got to the byline after working a one-two with Thomas and pulled the ball back to Roberts, whose shot under pressure was tipped away by Filip Jörgensen from close range.Williams fired straight at Jörgensen at the start of the second half, but Wales were behind after 53 minutes from a free-kick. Damsgaard delivered a delicious ball and, while Højlund wheeled away celebrating the final touch, it ultimately went in off the unfortunate Davies for an own goal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsaksen put the contest beyond Wales after 66 minutes. Moore headed off the Wales goalline, but the Lazio winger was quickest on to the loose ball and his deflected strike went in off the underside of the bar.Mohamed Daramy spurned a great chance to add further Danish gloss and both sides had late efforts ruled out, with Williams’s header disallowed for a push by Ethan Ampadu.It does not get any easier for Wales with a visit from Erling Haaland’s Norway on Thursday, before a return date against Denmark in Cardiff.“I said to the players before the game, ‘this is going to be tougher than Portugal’,” Bellamy added. “It was a different challenge, but a very difficult one. The best team won overall.“As disappointed as I am with that, the result I probably think was fair. We move on. It will be a tough watch back. How the players put their bodies on the line was brilliant. They are really special for that. I really admire that, but I want more.”Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueDenmarkWalesmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool sink Everton and end derby drought after Olsson and Kapocs strike | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: After six wins in six Anfield visits during the WSL era, the Reds finally saw off their rivals with a well-deserved 2-0 win
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: After six wins in six Anfield visits during the WSL era, the Reds finally saw off their rivals with a well-deserved 2-0 win
Content: Cornelia Kapocs wheels away after scoring Liverpool’s second goal to secure victory against Everton.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenCornelia Kapocs wheels away after scoring Liverpool’s second goal to secure victory against Everton.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAWomen's Super LeagueLiverpool sink Everton and end derby drought after Olsson and Kapocs strikeTom Garryat AnfieldSun 27 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt last, their wait is over. Liverpool’s players could gather in front of the Kop for a celebratory team photograph after the final whistle and rejoice in a new feeling, after beating Everton at Anfield in a Women’s Super League fixture for the first time and finally ending their long run of derby pain.After six wins from six visits to Anfield for Everton in the WSL era and even quips from their former manager Brian Sørensen in previous campaigns about making Anfield their “training pitch” during their persistent run of victories in this showpiece fixture, Beata Olsson’s early header and Cornelia Kapocs’s late finish were enough to give them a deserved 2-0 victory.WSL roundup: Putellas scores first London City goal, Manchester City maintain perfect startRead more“It’s nice to break that duck, definitely,” the Liverpool head coach, Gareth Taylor, said. “We just downplayed the game, if that makes sense, because it becomes something that’s so big that players start to worry. We want players to go out and feel natural, like they’re playing like they were when they were growing up.“It is nice because it’s a stat that can just grow and grow. I felt we were hard done by [at Anfield] last season – if you look at their xG in that game, they scored four goals but they were absolute worldies, whereas today we’ve scored two [but] we probably could have had six.”Taylor was not wrong; the hosts were undeniably the better side and should have scored more goals. Indeed, they would have done had it not been for the heroics of the Everton midfielder Ruby Mace.When Olsson got in front of her marker, Hannah Blundell, to meet Natalia Ramos’s right-sided corner and angle her header perfectly, diagonally across goal and into the far corner inside the first four minutes you could have been forgiven for thinking Liverpool were set for an easy afternoon such was the simplicity of the goal. Instead, what followed was something of a slog at times with Liverpool trying to break down an Everton backline that initially proved difficult to open up.After the break, another set piece almost did the job for Liverpool but Vivien Endemann’s volley smacked against the crossbar. By now the pressure was almost relentless and, with just over 20 minutes remaining, Ramos looked certain to score, with time to shoot less than 10 yards out. But the effort was blocked by Mace, who threw her body in front of the ball to keep her side in the contest.Five minutes later, Mace again came to Everton’s rescue and hooked Kapocs’s effort off the line. The Liverpool forward’s attempted header had come off the top of her shoulder and bounced goalwards, but Mace intervened just in time.View image in fullscreenCornelia Kapocs fires in Liverpool’s second goal against Everton.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAEventually, Kapocs found room inside the area to turn and fire home in the closing stages, much to the relief of Liverpool’s supporters. The result continued the side’s encouraging start to the campaign as they moved on to seven points from their opening four games, their only defeat having come away against the defending champions, Manchester City.It took Taylor’s side until 25 January to accumulate seven points last season but they look significantly improved and have built on the progress they made during the second half of 2025-26.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe visitors had spurned a couple of decent chances on the counterattack before the break, including Hannah Cain scuffing over from a promising position. Overall, however, Everton, whose only two league goals this season have been own goals, will be concerned about their comparative lack of creativity.Quick GuideWSL roundup: Spurs go second, Man Utd earn first winShowVictoria Pelova scored twice asTottenhammoved up to second in the WSL table with a 4-0 win overAston Villa, whileManchester Unitedearned their first win of the season, edgingWest Ham2-1.Dutch midfielder Pelova [pictured] broke the deadlock in the 54th minute at Brisbane Road, and then fired in a second off the underside of the crossbar, taking her tally to four goals in two WSL games. Spurs sealed victory as Caitlin Dijkstra headed in, and Cathinka Tandberg added a fourth with two minutes left.Manchester United secured their first WSL victory under new manager Eva Olid, defeating West Ham in Leigh. Elisabeth Terland’s header set United on their way after nine minutes, with summer signing Andrea Medina doubling the lead late in the second half. Viviane Asseyi scored a late penalty for the visitors.Océane Hurtré firedBirmingham Cityahead after 40 seconds againstCrystal Palace, scoring the quickest goal of the season so far.  Shanade Hopcroft’s long-range free-kick had Palace level on the half-hour, before Hurtré restored Birmingham’s lead with an angled strike.Palace fought back to lead at St Andrew's, their goals coming from Bethany England and Lexi Lloyd-Smith, but Suzu Amano struck with three minutes left to secure Birmingham a point in a thrilling 3-3 draw.Press AssocationPhotograph: Richard Pelham/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Asked about that wait for one of his own players to score a league goal, the Everton head coach, Scott Phelan, spoke calmly, saying: “We know we need to be more decisive in those actions, 100%. We have won two games as well and three on the bounce, so we don’t forget that. [But] yes, we want to start contributing more in the final third and that’ll be a challenge for all of us.“We’ve played four games, so it’s definitely not panic stations. We’ve got good players in those areas of the pitch, we’re convinced they will contribute more – we’ve just got to wait for that moment to appear and hopefully it’s sooner rather than later.”Phelan’s team still sit comfortably in the middle of the table with two wins from four games. Perhaps the most disappointing aspect for Everton fans will be that they can no longer rely on their annual collection of three points from Anfield.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueLiverpool FC WomenEverton WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Gateshead’s fruitless trip south offers hint of Manchester City’s doomsday future | Gateshead | The Guardian
description: His team bottom of the National League, Lee Cattermole’s ‘bomb squad’ approach could well end with him departing
Author: John Brewin
Headline: His team bottom of the National League, Lee Cattermole’s ‘bomb squad’ approach could well end with him departing
Content: Lee Cattermole’s first managerial job may not last much longer, with his Gateshead team shipping 15 goals in their last four games.Photograph: Wayne Tuckwell/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLee Cattermole’s first managerial job may not last much longer, with his Gateshead team shipping 15 goals in their last four games.Photograph: Wayne Tuckwell/ProSports/ShutterstockGatesheadGateshead’s fruitless trip south offers hint of Manchester City’s doomsday futureHis team bottom of the National League, Lee Cattermole’s ‘bomb squad’ approach could well end with him departingJohn Brewinat Grosvenor ValeSun 27 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmongmany doomsday scenariosfacing Manchester City is plunging down the football pyramid. Would that be so bad? Instead of yawning at the prospect of yet another meeting with Real Madrid or repeated Avanti train-hampered journeys to Wembley, how about the exoticism of away travel to Wealdstone? In the National League, City’s ownership may wish to know, there are no formal financial fair play or strict salary cap regulations.Wrexham, Notts County and Chesterfield have taken advantage of such lax constraints to regenerate. For City fans, Ruislip’s buzzy high street, full of nail bars, estate agents and a couple of homely pubs, would represent a welcome world away from Milan’s Via Monte Napoleone, as would the suburbia of Grosvenor Vale, Wealdstone’s home in the middle of a housing estate, which may jog memories of late-90s visits to Macclesfield and Lincoln. Simpler, happier times, perhaps.Kieron Dyer making waves at Southend after leaving ‘hooligan’ days and ‘deathbed’ behindRead moreOn the fringes of west London, with rich, non-league history, last season’s FA Trophy finalists, managed by the 1980s QPR hero Gary Waddock, Wealdstone is the club from where Stuart Pearce, Vinny Jones and Jermaine Beckford began their journey.In the digital age, the club became famous for the meme pioneer Gordon Parmar Hill, AKA the Wealdstone Raider, whose “you’ve got no fans” war cry went viral on a pandemic scale in 2014, the same year his assault on the UK Christmas No 1 with, naturally, “Got No Fans”, reached No 5. The Raider even made himself available for hire on stag weekends, though despite a recent social media comeback that revenue stream has been shuttered, a quieter life now observed.Kicking off fifth from bottom in the National League, if this season’s outlook could be brighter for the Stones, then Saturday confirmed there is always someone worse off. Gateshead hosted a Football League club on the southern bank of the Tyne from 1930 to 1960, the last teamthe legendary Hughie Gallacherturned out for, though extinction came in 1973. The re-founded Gateshead that has been knocking around the non-league pyramid since 1977 has little hope of reaching the Football League anytime soon.Before kick-off, the Vale club bar outside the stadium was doing brisk business. At a fifth-tier club, drinking in view of the pitch isverboten. A revocation ofthe 1985 alcohol statutethe prime ministerthis week floatedwould prove a significant revenue driver for clubs of Wealdstone’s size; clubs in the divisions below make considerable cash from in-game hospitality.In the Gateshead dugout, the familiar face of Lee Cattermole. For the time being, at least – his first senior management role is not going at all well. The former hard-tackling Middlesbrough, Wigan and Sunderland midfielder, collector of 88 yellow cards and seven reds in 271 Premier League games, has approached management in a characteristically uncompromising fashion. His team bottom of the National League, one win from 10 matches, Cattermole has employed the “bomb squad” approach favoured byEnzo Maresca at ChelseaandRuben Amorim at Manchester United.Eight players are reported to be training at alternative times to the first team, having also been removed from WhatsApp group chats. Neither Maresca nor Amorim’s shunning of players was particularly successful at an elite level, and being six goals down by half-time at home to Southend the previous week hardly heralded the success of Cattermole’s tough-love strategy either.Alfie McCalmont, a Northern Ireland international lately of Central Coast Mariners in Australia, joined the Heed in midweek. Anchoring midfield, after what were bright beginnings for the team that had travelled 278 miles, about 100 away fans willing them on, the new arrival soon found himself dragged into the torpor of his new teammates.Gateshead’s manager visibly sagged once Olufela Olomola scored the first of two unanswered goals before half-time. Not half as bad as Southend, but bad enough. “Make them work,” bellowed Cattermole while his team were still level, among other, more colourful, language.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOnce Wealdstone’s second goal came, Luke Norris converting a softly conceded penalty, Cattermole sat himself down, distractedly fiddling with notebook and pen before a half-time team talk delayed by his slow return to the away dressing room.Whatever was said, a third Wealdstone goal came within two minutes of the resumption, and a fourth just before the end. Waddock, who as a player was not dissimilar to Cattermole – combative, lover of a tackle – could keep quiet counsel, relaxedly leaning on a handy gatepost. Such serenity in a difficult season for Wealdstone came by contrast to the portentous chants of “sacked in the morning” from the away end, followed by “time to go”.It was Ben Clark, Cattermole’s assistant, sent out to deliver a post-match verdict. “We conceded a soft goal, and struggled from there on in,” he said. “The lads are struggling a bit with their confidence.”The possibility of Cattermole being bombed out had heightened, such news likely to be accompanied by a corner-flag image on the club website. Should City drop down the divisions to alight on suburban outposts such as Wealdstone, it is already unlikely Cattermole would get the chance to face them, let alone manage them.Explore more on these topicsGatesheadEnterprise National LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Abell’s 307 offers solace for Somerset as season slips into sepia – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: As Warwickshire celebrated the title, Tom Abell gave fans of the repeat runners-up something to cheer at Taunton
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: As Warwickshire celebrated the title, Tom Abell gave fans of the repeat runners-up something to cheer at Taunton
Content: 5h ago16.03 EDTLate solace for Somerset after Warwickshire win titleTanya AldredWith the champions already crowned at Edgbaston, there was a spoonful of solace for thoseSomersetfans who had hoped the season’s final day would bring a title to Taunton at last.At a warm County Ground withSurreyfielding in sunhats, Tom Abell completed his first triple hundred, an epic of 30 fours, eight sixes, 402 balls and nearly nine hours of batting. He became the eighth Somerset cricketer to tuck one under his arm. When Abell was finally out for 307, aiming for the rope, he was the second highest scorer in the 2026 summer with 1,287 runs – just one short of Nottinghamshire’s Joe Clarke.With a monster total of 731 under their belts, and a lead of 309, there was hope of a last-day win. And when Surrey lost four quick wickets, including Dom Sibley nudging to slip, it seemed possible, but Ben Foakes and Mahipal Lomror calmed the waters. Wicketkeeper James Rew took off his gloves to send down the final over of the season, some lollipop slow left-arm. Handshakes and wistful smiles followed, Somerset bridesmaids for the seventh time this century.“I don’t think there’s a reason why we can’t get over the line other than it is a bloody difficult competition to win,” said the Somerset, captain Lewis Gregory. “We can look forward to next season with great confidence. The support we get is fantastic and this is a wonderful place to play cricket.”At Old Trafford, bad light kept the ground staff busy.Lancashirepassed 300 for the first time since April and Josh Bohannon’s 190 not out was the club’s highest score of the season.Durham, runaway winners of Division Two, jumped in the coach home to prepare for a summer back with the big boys. ForLancashire, who finish 17th for the first time in their history, the winter’s aim is more prosaic: to rediscover their mojo.Only 21 balls were possible at Sophia Gardens, strugglingEssexsafe barring a successful appeal by Leicestershire over their points deduction. And with that, the season slipped into sepia.Share

title: England thrash Sri Lanka by 223 runs to win the deciding men’s ODI – as it happened | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Over-by-over report: How our writers saw the final match of the English international summer, which ended in a resounding win for England
Author: Tim de Lisle
Headline: Over-by-over report: How our writers saw the final match of the English international summer, which ended in a resounding win for England
Content: 9h ago13.02 EDTAnd so we reach the end of a long, hot summer.England won every series they played in except one, the three-Test tussle with New Zealand, which went so badly wrong that Ben Stokes resigned as the Test captain and Brendon McCullum was sacked as the Test coach.Joe Root went from being a great ex-captain, reeling off hundreds, to an unexpected Test captain again, winning every game but unable to reach three figures. Stephen Fleming was appointed Test coach but didn’t actually start, flying over just to say hello and make the right noises.Jofra Archer went from being kept in cotton wool to playing almost every game and once again bowling so fast that it was thrilling to watch. Ollie Robinson returned and took so many wickets so cheaply that, as Andy Bull memorably said, he could have been wearing a top hat. Throw in Josh Tongue’s ability to blow away the tail and Gus Atkinson’s steep bounce, and England just may have another fab four to rival the one from 2005.Jordan Cox announced himself as a rising star, whatever the colour of the ball, whether batting or standing in as a keeper for Jamie Smith or Jos Buttler. Harry Brook continued to bat like a dream and also began to look like a proper captain, showing just the right amount of bravery. And, today, Tom Banton made his big breakthrough.For all the embarrassment of their after-hours escapades, England also have another kind of embarrassment – of riches. They have a generation of young cricketers who are talented and likeable and seem comfortable on the big stage. It should be a lot of fun seeing how far they can go.England are going all over the place this winter, starting with some ODIs in Pakistan in about three weeks’ time – also involving Sri Lanka. We will of course be back to bring you those. For now, thanks for your company and correspondence, all summer long. The OBO community is a wonderful thing.England demolish Sri Lanka in ODI series decider as Banton bashes maiden tonRead moreShareUpdated at13.40 EDT

title: Saracens overcome adversity to battle back and edge Leicester in 12-try thriller | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Despite Nick Isiekwe’s 20-minute red card, Saracens held on to earn a hard-fought 40-38 victory at Leicester
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Despite Nick Isiekwe’s 20-minute red card, Saracens held on to earn a hard-fought 40-38 victory at Leicester
Content: Juan Martín González goes over for Saracens in the second minute to ignite an electrifying encounter.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenJuan Martín González goes over for Saracens in the second minute to ignite an electrifying encounter.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAPrem RugbySaracens overcome adversity to battle back and edge Leicester in 12-try thrillerLeicester 38-40 SaracensVisitors hold on despite Isiekwe’s 20-minute red cardGerard Meagherat Mattioli Woods Welford RoadSun 27 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the full-time whistle, Brendan Venter let out a roar of delight. Until then the South African had been on his best behaviour, but after beginning his return to the Saracens hotseat with a nail-biting victory againstLeicester, Venter could no longer hold it in.It no doubt felt all the sweeter at Welford Road, having 16 years ago been slapped with a lengthy ban for making inappropriate and provocative gestures at the Tigers faithful. A celebratory swagger had been a long time coming and who could deny the director of rugby afterSaracensovercame Nick Isiekwe’s 20-minute red card to edge this 12-try thriller.Leicester will be desperately disappointed by how often they conceded the momentum to Saracens and it is not often Gabriel Hamer-Webb will score a hat‑trick and end up on the losing side. Freddie Steward has rarely been in such fine counterattacking form and Aaron Wainwright’s debut suggests he will soon be a fan favourite.Gloucester’s Dewi Lake in full flow with two tries in emphatic win at ExeterRead moreBut to the visitors, the spoils. Ben Earl was inspired off the bench and Tomos Williams imperious on debut. Saracens’ ability to overcome adversity, losing Olly Hartley to a nasty-looking arm injury early on and having to briefly deploy Earl at centre, is testament to the spirit engendered by Venter after retaking the reins from Mark McCall. Maro Itoje looks refreshed after his summer break while Elliot Daly, who cropped up in four different positions, is clearly hitting his straps again, too.In a match that pitted fourth against fifth from last season it appeared likely these two would deliver the pick of the opening weekend’s fixtures and so it proved. It was the kind of afternoon that will delight attack coaches, infuriate their defensive counterparts and it rounded off a record-breaking first weekend with 52 tries. Rotimi Segun’s second proved decisive here but credit goes to Fergus Burke, too, with five conversions to Billy Searle’s four and that ultimately proved decisive.View image in fullscreenLeicester’s Jack van Poortvliet charges past Maro Itoje.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesVenter has largely kept his powder dry since his return, provoking Prem Rugby’s ire by dodging media duties at the season’s launch and doing so again before and after this victory. In his place, the head coach, Joe Shaw, said: “You get hit with the 20-minute red at a place like this, if you want to be in the top four you have got to be able to keep your cool. We came for the win, to put a marker down on what our forward pack have been trying to do in the pre-season.”Saracens began in emphatic fashion and were a try to the good inside two minutes when Juan Martín González powered over. The Argentinean’s robust finish came on the back of a probing passage of play, new signings Williams and Alfie Barbeary heavily involved before González seized Searle’s failed interception to score. Inside 10 minutes they doubled their lead. Turning down a kick at goal, Saracens went to the corner on the left before fine passes from Williams and Burke put Tobias Elliott away on the right.Before the half-hour, Leicester had two tries of their own, however, hitting back in fine fashion. Solomone Kata struck with the first, picking up a loose ball and shrugging off Elliott far too easily. Leicester’s second was finished by the always dangerous Hamer-Webb. Sharp hands from Steward put him away but the try owed everything to Jack van Poortvliet’s dart up the middle.Elliott’s temporary withdrawal meant an Earl cameo at centre just after the half-hour mark and minutes later Saracens had their third try. Earl’s versatility is a considerable string to his bow but there is no substitute for footballing talent and the manner in which Burke, Max Malins and Daly combined for the latter to go over on the left was a sight to behold.Elliott returned to the field after half-time – Earl shifting to the pack with Barbeary making way – and it was down his wing that Leicester had their third try, and Hamer-Webb his second, after good work from Wainwright.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBack at home at No 8, Earl’s powerful finish from close range re-established Saracens’ breathing space on the scoreboard but in keeping with the topsy-turvy nature of this contest, Hamer-Webb had his hat-trick – and the pick of his tries – after a fine break from deep by Steward and another sharp pass from Wainwright.View image in fullscreenRotimi Segun dives over the line to claim Saracens’ sixth – and decisive – try against Leicester.Photograph: Colorsport/Ashley Western/ShutterstockLeicester had the bit between their teeth and took the lead for the first time in the match with Adam Radwan’s 54th-minute score. Kata, always a handful, made the initial break before Van Poortvliet’s delightful dink put the ball on a plate for the ex-Newcastle winger. To make matters worse for Saracens, Isiekwe was then handed a 20-minute red card for a high tackle on Steward in the buildup.Segun’s first try came after Daly’s perfect crossfield kick. Leicester nosed ahead again through James Thompson’s close-range effort but the Tigers were soon down to 14 when Tarek Haffar was sent to the sin-bin. Segun finished on the left with seven minutes to go after slick hands through the backs and Saracens, back to 15 men, clung on with the kind of determination that suggests they will be in the mix this season.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyLeicesterSaracensRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content
