title: NFL today: How to watch Rams v Broncos, TV channels & live stream Sunday 27 September | NFL | The Guardian
description: How will the Rams and Broncos fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will the Rams and Broncos fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Matthew Stafford will lead the Rams against the Broncos on Sunday.Photograph: Ariana Ruiz/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMatthew Stafford will lead the Rams against the Broncos on Sunday.Photograph: Ariana Ruiz/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockNFLNFL today: How to watch Rams v Broncos, TV channels & live stream Sunday 27 SeptemberHow will the Rams and Broncos fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerSun 27 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rams may have just needed a change in continent.The preseason Super Bowl favorites briefly surrendered that status after going to Australia in Week 1 and falling flat against their NFC West rivals, the 49ers. Playing in Melbourne, the Rams lost the time of possession battle 36 minutes to 24, gained fewer than 300 yards of offense, and lost a 27-7 decision.“Sometimes you win, sometimes you learn, and you know, sometimes you have a dumbass coach that makes travel plans that put you in a bad spot,” coach Sean McVay cracked last week. He could afford to be lighthearted because the Rams had just righted the ship on Monday Night Football, shellacking the visiting Giants by a nearly equivalent score of 28-6. MVP Matthew Stafford looked like himself, legendary defensive tackle Aaron Donald rejoined the lineup, and all was well again in Los Angeles.Another challenge awaits in Denver, where the Broncos rebounded from their own Week 1 disaster (a 31-10 loss to the Chiefs) to beat a solid Jaguars team last Sunday. Last year’s top seed in the AFC playoffs, the Broncos have QB Bo Nix back from a right ankle fracture suffered during that run. The two teams will get together at Mile High for their first meeting since a 51-14 Rams rout in December 2022.Rams at BroncosTime:8.20pm ET/1.20am BSTStadium:Empower Field at Mile High (Denver, Colorado)How to watchUnited States:Watch onNBC or Peacock;Stream on FuboCanada:Watch on TSN1/3/4/5 & CTV;Stream on FuboUnited Kingdom:Watch on Sky Sports Main EventWhat to watch forNix is back, but the Broncos need him to find his sea legs. Through two weeks, a tiny sample, Nix is 26th in theNFLin passer rating and 24th in adjusted net yards per attempt. He’s thrown an interception in both of his games. But his stats are mainly weighed down by a horrendous Week 1, and Nix may have found something (or someone) important in Week 2: Newly acquired wideout Jaylen Waddle took off like a missile and caught eight balls on 10 targets for 138 yards. Waddle appears to be ready to take the No 1 receiver role from one of the team’s longtime stars, the consistent Courtland Sutton.The Rams will expect the usual excellence from Stafford and the offense. A fascinating subplot will be Donald, the future first-ball Hall of Famer who returned on the defensive line last week after being retired during the 2024 and 2025 seasons. Donald played 33 snaps as he worked his way back into game condition, and now he gets to play a game in Denver’s thin air. He made one solo tackle (and one tackle for loss) in his return game. One would expect it to only be up from here for the 35-year-old.Explore more on these topicsNFLDenver BroncosLos Angeles RamsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation | Bill Gates | The Guardian
description: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
Content: Bill Gates in New York City on 8 May 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenBill Gates in New York City on 8 May 2025.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersBill GatesBill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulationMicrosoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on SundayRamon Antonio VargasSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Gateshas called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropistsaidto Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”Another portion of the interview –excerptsof which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AIRead more“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similarwarningsby a wide array of tech and political figures.Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.His fellow tech moguls includingSam AltmanandElon Muskhave joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some expertstheorizecould precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.Meanwhile,Microsoftitself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to aGuardian essaypublished on Friday.The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure tomonitor, arrest and deport immigrantsen masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.Bill Gates calls for ‘human-reserved’ jobs in face of AI takeoverRead moreAn external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in Julydeterminedthat he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the hostaskedhim: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”Explore more on these topicsBill GatesAI (artificial intelligence)MicrosoftUS politicsComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Decision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected ways
Content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The company said it would resume training its latest models ‘only when we are confident that we have addition safeguards’.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyView image in fullscreenOpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The company said it would resume training its latest models ‘only when we are confident that we have addition safeguards’.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyOpenAIOpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogueDecision follows disclosures that OpenAI agents searching government websites had acted in unexpected waysAssociated PressSat 26 Sep 2026 21.10 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount.The decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in whichOpenAIagents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.OpenAI said in a statement that it will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expects it will have to “hit pause” again as AI develops and other issues emerge.Last week Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese,revealedan OpenAI agent had breached the government’s national healthcare system – but saidno sensitive informationhad been compromised.AI labs are facing pressure from lawmakers and tech experts to slow development so they can build guardrails to stop agents from acting on their own, hacking websites and disclosing nonpublic information. The heads of both OpenAI and rival Anthropichave called for a slowdowntoo.OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemmaRead moreIt is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first came in July after disclosure of a cyber-attacktargeting AI startup Hugging Face, a now notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.In a meetingwith Chinese president Xi Jinping this week, Donald Trump agreed to share information on AI dangers and coordinate efforts to keep it safe. Trump believes AI fears are overblown, though, and later suggested that he plans no crackdown of his own.The US is not going to be “putting on brakes”, Trump told reporters outside the White House. “They want to stop our progress because we’re leading China by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”The latest OpenAI incidents did not appear to involve the disclosure of any nonpublic information but were concerning enough for the company to warn the federal agencies involved.In the education department incident, OpenAI agents found API “developer keys” to access government data, though ultimately only publicly available information was gathered.In another case involving the securities and exchange commission, agents found information freely available to all but then posted it elsewhere on the internet, an act that went beyond what they were instructed to do.US Securities and Exchange Commission spokesperson Kurt Hopfenspirger said on Saturday that “no nonpublic information was accessed”.The Department of Education said earlier that it found “no evidence of any impact to our website or databases”.Several other AI companies have disclosed incidents of their models going rogue and even hacking websites.OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, said in a social media post on Friday that the Hugging Face incident “is still the most severe event we’ve seen”.OpenAI previously shared six other reports of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingCybercrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children | Roblox | The Guardian
description: Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data
Content: Roblox says that to avoid scams, users should always go through the official app or website, and ‘never click through links or download anything from unknown senders or websites’.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoblox says that to avoid scams, users should always go through the official app or website, and ‘never click through links or download anything from unknown senders or websites’.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersScam watchRoblox‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting childrenCriminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal dataShane HickeySun 27 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 02.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour 10-year-old son has started playingRoblox, when he realises all of his in-game currency, Robux, is gone.When you try to find out what happened, he says he was recently promised extra Robux if he followed a link on YouTube. When he signed on at the site link, he was taken to the Roblox site as usual but there was no sign of the extra currency.He has fallen victim to a fraud where Roblox users – many of whom are children – are being targeted for their login details. With those details criminals can steal the virtual currency and players’ personal data.Within Roblox, players use Robux to buy virtual items, such as skins or animations for their avatar. You can earn the currency within the game, but it can also be bought. At Roblox’s online store you can buypackages costing up to £199.99.Using ready-made kits bought on the dark web, fraudsters create a fake login page that is identical in appearance to the legitimate Roblox site.View image in fullscreenA screengrab of a scam webpage targeting young Roblox usersPhotograph: Screengrab“The kid will enter their details and the fake website will actually redirect them to a legitimate Roblox page,” says Gerald Kasulis, the vice-president of global affairs at the cybersecurity company NordVPN. “So ultimately, the kid will get to where they want to go.”By that stage, however, the criminals will have the details they need for defrauding.Researchers from NordVPN say that over a seven-day period they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages that provided the tools to defraud Roblox users.What it looks likeOften the links to the phishing sites are in comments on YouTube or TikTok videos or in chats on Discord, the chat app for gamers.The message might say there are free Robux available if a player clicks on the link provided. Like many scams, there will often be an element of urgency attached, such as the offer apparently only being valid for a few hours, to encourage the victim to act without fully thinking through the consequences.From that link, the child will be taken to a fake sign-in page that will probably be identical to a legitimate Roblox site in appearance. The address will usually contain the name Roblox, for example “Roblox-verify” or “login-Roblox”.View image in fullscreenA screengrab of a scam webpage targeting young Roblox usersPhotograph: ScreengrabWhen they are on the scam site, the child will be asked for their username and password but may also be told to put in two-factor identification codes, says NordVPN. But then the child is taken to the legitimate Roblox site so they can play their games as normal, leaving little indication that anything is amiss.Once they have the login details, the fraudster may sell them on or use them to transfer Robux to another account.What to doTalk to children about scams.“One of the simplest habits is to encourage children to open Roblox directly through the official app or website rather than logging in through links they are sent,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN.“Two-factor authentication remains an important protection, but authentication codes and backup codes should be treated just like passwords and never handed over to somebody else.”If your player has lost their Robux to a hacker, it seems unlikely that they will get it back. Roblox says that it is under “no obligation” to assist people whose accounts have been compromised, unless it is required to do so by law.“Roblox does not guarantee that an individual’s account will be restored to its previous state, or that Roblox will be able to recover lost virtual items or virtual currency,” it says.In “very limited circumstances”, Roblox says it may recover lost items or the value of them.A spokesperson for Roblox says there are security measures in place to prevent phishing, such as two-factor authentication and a feature that stops criminals logging into your account from elsewhere.“We continue to work on new ways to minimise the risk of account theft and actively encourage Roblox users to follow security best practices, including not clicking on links or downloading anything from unknown senders or websites,” the spokesperson adds.Explore more on these topicsRobloxScam watchScamsConsumer affairsGamesInternet safetyCybercrimeChildren's techfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’
Content: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’Eduardo PorterSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTShareThe Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by aSilicon Valleymogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world withartificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their projectin the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do.Everyday Americans are up in arms against theAI datacenters sproutingacross their communities. Villages, counties, citiesand statesareimposing moratoriaand bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development.Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits,according to a surveyby the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society.Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastlymore concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generallymore mistrustfulof the technology than people in other countries.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators rally during a protest calling for a citywide datacenter moratorium outside city hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on 14 September 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThis surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could causehuman extinctionhas, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net.The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch ofweird, sci-fi addled plutocratsto pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.”People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhurypoints out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whateverharm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law.The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters.Donald Trumpremains steadfastlyon the sideof the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which couldkeep locals in the darkuntil construction starts.The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.”Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology.And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule.This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum.But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead,has flushed workerswithout a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI.One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them.Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach.The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest ratesfree from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest.But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.”The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.”View image in fullscreenSam Altman, chief executive officer of OpenAI Inc, during a Senate commerce, science, and transportation Committee hearing in Washington DC on 8 May 2025.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesPeter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued thatdemocracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altmansalivates about an “awesome” futurein which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.”The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about asuperintelligent Golem.Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to beanswerable to no oneand will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,”he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way.There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of theEnd of Historyin Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word.Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass:section 230of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it.Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage.Reports of teen suicidesandonline bullyingbred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed tohook users to their screens.When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny.By the time Covid hit in 2020, the former paragons of liberal democracy had found a new role as magnifiers of conspiracy theories, enemies of “woke”, partisans in a libertarian revolt against “government control”. Joe Biden’s attempts touse antitrust lawand other regulations against the techno-plutocrats’ empires pushed them to the dark side, where Trump and his angry Maga movement awaited their embrace.How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising topunish European countrieswho dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which isproving so lucrativefor him and his family.View image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed, a US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of ‘The Barn’  datacenter, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, in Saline Township, Michigan, on 30 July 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesStill, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck.Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in aconversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.”Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.”Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletterBeing Thereon Substack

title: I spent a full hour watching Trump TV. It’s a digital pathway to hell | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull
Content: ‘Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionDonald TrumpI spent a full hour watching Trump TV. It’s a digital pathway to hellDave SchillingThe streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dullSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareAre you currently at an airport? Strapped to a hospital bed, with various tubes protruding from your body? Maybe you’re on a treadmill or visiting an elder care facility? Chained to a radiator in the basement from the Saw movies?If you said yes to any of these questions, you might be watching cable news while reading this column. Or maybe you’re one of the hundreds of people currently watching Donald Trump’s answer to cable news, Trump TV – a YouTube streaming channel that airs nothing but White House-sanctioned content 24 hours a day, seven days a week.Kudos to you for multitasking, and thank you for the click. I know Jacob Soboroff is hard to look away from, but at least finish this.I don’t typically watch cable news. Or broadcast news. I feel like the best way to consume vital information is through the glorious written word, full of context and detail, rather than various “experts” yelling at each other about which one is the harbinger of the antichrist. Instead, I can yell all I want at a newspaper or an internet article and no one can tell me not to. Except the people in the dentist waiting room with me.Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching. I gave myself the challenge of watching this neverending digital pathway to hell for one single hour, hoping I could capture whatever joy is being derived from this American horror story.When I first logged onto the stream, I was “treated” to a 11 March 2016 speech Donald Trump gave in Hebron, Kentucky – which Trump on more than one occasion pronounced “Keentucky”, presumably to mimic local speech patterns. That Donald Trump is just a good ol’ country boy, after all.I came in right smack-dab in the middle of the remarks, which very clearly were not prepared. As someone hyper-allergic to cable news, I don’t often witness the president’s speeches in full. I immediately felt as though I were succumbing to a form of intense psychosis, where reality had begun to melt before my eyes, like an ice cream cone that’s sat out in the sun too long.Trump was describing the stairs at the event, stairs he had to walk up and down. Stairs that he traversed despite his own natural sense of self-preservation. “I might slip, it’s soaking wet,” he said of the stairs. “They’re steel stairs. Four sets of stairs.” I immediately begin to imagine him counting the stairs. Slowly.From there, he played his greatest hits and mocked Joe Biden for falling down. But the big swerve was a backhanded compliment to Barack Obama for not falling down. “The only thing is how he bobbed down. He bobbed. I couldn’t believe that he made it without a major, noticeable fall.” The shock on his face that a healthy adult man would not trip on his descent from an airplane certainly made me wonder. You can tell this man has thought a lot about the best ways to not fall down stairs. Eventually, Dr Oz showed up, and I needed to mute my computer. My Uber Eats order had just arrived, and I didn’t want my neighbors getting the wrong idea when I opened the front door.We got a brief respite from Trump up next, with a re-airing of Melania’s ad … excuse me,speechabout how great artificial intelligence is, from 16 January. “The most powerful skill is knowing what to ask,” she declares. I realized the thing I should be asking right then was: “Why am I watching this?”I hung in a little longer for one more event: the National Prayer Breakfast from 6 February. Paula White-Cain, senior adviser to the White House Faith Office, opened the proceedings by saying: “No president in modern history or perhaps all of history has done more to elevate and protect religious liberty” than Donald Trump has. Except maybe George Washington, who presided over the ratification of the first amendment to the US constitution. The first amendment enshrined freedom of religion into the country’s laws. Also, awkwardly, freedom of speech and freedom of the press. You know, the press Donald Trump kicked out of the White House.Trump TV seems like the next escalation of the president’s obsession with and animosity toward cable news. I remain flabbergasted that someone could care about anything on television that much.At last census count, 342 million people live in the United States. Of that population, between 2 and 3 millionwatch cable news in a given day. The vast majority of those people watch Fox News. And the majority of that majority isover the age of 54.When I say “no one watches cable news,” I am only being mildly hyperbolic. To coin a term, I’m being “semibolic”. Just a “hint of bolic”.Yes, there are people who can’t seem to just turn their TV off out there, but MSNOW, CNN, and Fox News aren’t capturing the same level of enthusiasm as the latest episode of HBO’s Lanterns or your local bird-watching club. That cable news retains any significance in our daily discourse is a testament to how fiercely committed our nation’s leaders are to using it as a battlefield for their ideological warfare. And as aretirement community for ex-politicians.When Trump tried toban CNN, MS Now and the website Politicofor allegations of unfair, dishonest coverage of his administration, journalists had a reasonable fear for the state of freedom of the press in this country. Covering the goings-on at the White House is not, as Trump says, a “privilege”. It is a solemn duty. One that defines what’s left of our democracy. Maybe now, I’m being fully hyperbolic, but I’m a journalist. I should declare my own bias on this topic.Trump’s media blackout gambit backfired, as Fox News joined with their cable cousins to abandon coverage of the president’s activities, thereby ending the press pool that provided audio and video for news outlets. Without the press pool,no one can hear what Trump saysduring his speeches. Thankfully for those who use Trump speeches to calm their nerves before a midday nap, they can count on Trump TV to help them off to slumberland.Back to the Trump TV live stream. He was wearing the same purple tie at the prayer breakfast that he’d worn in Kentucky. If you were not an attentive viewer of Trump TV, you might think you were watching the same speech. I realized that just about everything on this stream is from this year, that we’ll probably never see anything from, say, 2020. But I couldn’t stick around long enough to find out, and Trump TV doesn’t seem to list its programming lineup anywhere.‘Literally state-run TV’: Trump launches YouTube channel amid boycott by US networksRead moreI left the house during the National Prayer Breakfast, just as Trump was getting going, declaring “something is wrong” with the Republican congressman Thomas Massie from … Kentucky. You know, the state Trump loves so much. I started to wonder if today’s Trump TV schedule was merely a troll directed at Massie, who lost his re-election bid in the Republican primary, to the former Navy Seal Ed Gallrein, whomm Trump endorsed. The absurdity of using a 24/7 YouTube stream to subtly mock a political rival for an audience of 800 people seems far more possible when you remember the person behind this project is Donald Trump.I took a 30-minute walk with my dog, and when I got back to my desk, I was shocked to learn that Trump wasstill talkingat the National Prayer Breakfast. Specifically about the size of our military budget, which I believe was a direct quote from 1 Corinthians 13:4–8. As Trump droned on (pun intended), the view counter kept going down. Even the die-hards were getting bored.The launch of Trump TV has been a fairly obvious disaster. Unlike cable news, YouTube has real-time data to tell you how many people are watching something.Multiple media outletstook aswipe at Trump for this folly, though in his defense, most YouTube streams get pitiful concurrent viewership unless it’s MrBeast or live footage of a police chase on an LA freeway. Trump TV was obviously never meant to be anything significant. No one in charge of this stream is trying, unless you count trolling Thomas Massie as “trying”. There are no graphics or lower thirds other than a number to text for “updates” from the White House. There’s no slick editing or editorial perspective outside of the purple tie/Massie element.But is this any worse than the ideologically minded focus of cable news – with the three major channels pointing their rhetorical ICBMs at each other all day long? Maybe Trump TV is actually the best way to consume our sitting president. Nothing else presents him in all of his repugnant glory: vain, myopic and worst of all, deeply, deeply dull. This holiday season, turn on Trump TV for your conservative family members. There’s always a chance that the uncut, unfiltered lethal dose of nonsense will break the spell for good.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsUS televisionUS television industryTV newsTelevisioncommentShareReuse this content

title: When a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships? | Bianca Denny | The Guardian
description: These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress
Author: Bianca Denny
Headline: These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress
Content: When a famous singer died, Jodie* experienced grief so strong that for weeks she struggled to attend work and was sleeping poorly, Bianca Denny writes.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhen a famous singer died, Jodie* experienced grief so strong that for weeks she struggled to attend work and was sleeping poorly, Bianca Denny writes.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty ImagesThe modern mindMental healthWhen a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships?Bianca DennyThese one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distressThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 27 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 19.13 EDTShare“It came as such a shock. I just can’t believe he’s gone.”Psychologists are accustomed to seeing bereaved individuals. But working with Jodie* presented a unique challenge – she’d never met the person she was grieving. Jodie was reeling after the recent death of a well known singer. Despite not knowing the singer personally, Jodie’s grief and loss seemed as palpable as other patients speaking about the deaths of family members or loved ones. Jodie reported that weeks after the singer’s death, she was struggling to attend work and was sleeping poorly, describing herself as consumed with thoughts of the singer.Jodie was experiencing grief related to aparasocial relationship. This is a social phenomenon in which a person experiences a one-sided psychological connection with a public figure or famous person. While an intimate and intense sense of friendship or connection is felt, the object of attention is oblivious to their admirer’s existence.Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI | Gaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughRead moreParasocial relationships are a normal part of modern life. Many of us are engaged in some sort of parasocial relationship – perhaps with a famous actor, sportsperson, musician or even a fictional character from a novel or television show. We feel we know these people and become invested in their lives. It’s an uncomfortable truth for some that the people we are focused on are, in fact, strangers. They have no reciprocal care for us, nor investment in our lives the way a friend or family members might have.At best, parasocial relationships allow us to tap into a brief fantasy of a life beyond our own, usually one of wealth and privilege. This daydreaming provides a break from the mundane and opens up space for creativity and lateral thinking for some people. But for others, such as Jodie, parasocial relationships can lead to emotional over-involvement and boundary-crossing behaviour. This can fuel psychological distress, especially when a celebrity dies or experiences a controversial or adverse life event.Despite my own general indifference about the singer’s death, I was mindful to not dismiss Jodie’s feelings. The loss was significant to Jodie; pointing out the crude fact that they were strangers would likely damage our therapeutic rapport and may have led to Jodie becoming further entrenched in the parasocial relationship.I attempted to relate to Jodie’s grief by tapping into my own experiences and observations of parasocial relationships: the anguish of many of my peers after Kurt Cobain’s death, the shock at Michael Jackson’s passing (and the complicated grief that followed), and the unprecedented public outpouring of sorrow following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. More recent examples of parasocial relationships also came to mind: fans’ unashamed obsession with Taylor Swift’swedding, and, on a different note, fierce debate about Ariana Grande’shealth and wellbeing.It was important to manage Jodie’s acute distress before we sought to understand why the singer’s death had been so impactful. We devised a plan to reduce exposure to information about the singer and his death, using a blocking app to taper social media scrolling and news consumption to 20 minutes per day. Together with encouraging a walk twice a day, limiting time online went some way to reducing Jodie’s rumination and improving her sleeping patterns.Jodie felt a strong connection to the singer. She listened to his music heavily during a difficult time in her own life, crediting the lyrics as “saving her”. She came to rely on his songs to lift her mood, providing a sense of company and comfort in an otherwise desolate period. These feelings had resurfaced upon hearing of his death. Allowing Jodie time and space to talk about her experience – of both her connection to the singer and the difficult time she had endured – helped alleviate her grief.double quotation markHer focus on other people’s lives had been to the detriment of her own.While our therapeutic work was prompted by the singer’s death, Jodie also detailed other parasocial relationships. She spoke about famous people as if they were in her own social circle, and expressed genuine delight at their personal and professional achievements.It seemed apparent that Jodie was lacking vitality in her own life and had attempted to fill this gap by investing in parasocial relationships. But her focus on other people’s lives had been to the detriment of her own. We set about bolstering Jodie’s real-life relationships and enriching social interactions, included reconnecting with old friends, trying a range of hobbies where she might meet like-minded people, and making new connections through meet-up groups and local community events.Why are we so obsessed with Taylor Swift’s wedding? | Dave SchillingRead moreFor Jodie, parasocial relationships felt safe. There’s little chance of rejection from someone viewed only from afar, and no need to navigate the usual difficulties and disagreements typical of real-life relationships. While parasocial relationships went some way to meeting Jodie’s fundamental need for affiliation and human connection, establishing genuine friendships brought reciprocity that parasocial relationships never could – people who Jodie cared about, who also cared about her.*All clients are fictional amalgamsIn Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.Dr Bianca Denny is a clinical psychologist based in Melbourne. She is the author of Talk to Me: Lessons from Patients and Their TherapistExplore more on these topicsMental healthThe modern mindHealth (Society)CelebrityHealth (Australia news)commentShareReuse this content

title: What’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?  | Brian Logan | The Guardian
description: The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed, says the Guardian’s comedy critic Brian Logan
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed, says the Guardian’s comedy critic Brian Logan
Content: David Mitchell and Robert Webb on stage during Amnesty International’s Secret Policeman’s Ball at the Royal Albert Hall, London, October 2008.Photograph: Ian West/PA Wire/PA PhotosView image in fullscreenDavid Mitchell and Robert Webb on stage during Amnesty International’s Secret Policeman’s Ball at the Royal Albert Hall, London, October 2008.Photograph: Ian West/PA Wire/PA PhotosOpinionTV comedyWhat’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?Brian LoganThe deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changedSun 27 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTShare“Are we the baddies?”, asked the comedy double actMitchell and Webbin theirmost famous sketch, in which two uniformed SS officers look one another up and down and arrive at that inescapable conclusion. And lo, it turns out they are, if this week’s news about the supposed offensiveness of the duo’s back catalogue is to be believed.Their newfound unpalatability made headlines last Monday,when 11 of the pair’s sketcheswere pulledfrom the rerelease of That Mitchell and Webb Look on iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary – a move that led to loud condemnation from the keyboard cavalry in Britain’s never-ending, and never much fun, culture war.Was the BBC right to expunge the skits? There’s an argument that in this instance, a warning or disclaimer might have been sufficient. The sketches in question variously involve jokes about Jimmy Savile,Robert Webbplaying a rude Gandhi (seemingly wearing skin-darkening makeup) and two further scenes in which the comedians wear blackface. In neither sketch are they doing so to depict people of colour, but instead to depict white people (in one scene, re-enactors of historic battles having a go at an African skirmish) who themselves wear blackface. In both, they are alert to their own indelicacy: “Are you sure,” asks Webb repeatedly throughout one, “that this isn’t racist?”Some have argued that sketches such as these – satires on chauvinism, not examples of it – should therefore be spared the editor’s scissors. But that’s missing the point, which is that blackface (and indeed the N-word, which caused the standup comic Alfie Brownso much troublerecently when he used it in his own anti-racist routine) is considered beyond the pale, irreducibly hurtful to a portion of the BBC’s audience, regardless of context.Is it right that it is so considered? There’s no question these terms and behaviours are associated with very real harms. Perhaps the corporation focus-grouped that question – or perhaps it is pre-empting criticism, erring on the side of caution and care. Is it so outrageous that they should do so? The BBC is, as the comedy producer Jimmy Mulville statedthis weekin the most sensible comment yet made on the controversy, “in an impossible position”.For my part, I can’t get too exercised by the removal of a handful of sketches – one of them, which jokes about therecently deceased Bill Oddie, for reasons of common decency, and others on the same basis that 70s sitcomIt Ain’t Half Hot Mumhas long been withheld, without great controversy, from our screens. It feels important, mind you, that the episodes in question should be prominently marked as abridged, much as those Roald Dahl books adjusted for modern sensitivities were marketed as “updated texts”, in a move even more contested than this one. (Interestingly, David Mitchellresponded very cynicallyto Dahl’s “updating”.)View image in fullscreenStill from Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping, with Stevie Martin and David Mitchell.Photograph: Channel 4That act of bowdlerism felt more extreme because it affected (some would say diluted) the entire text, leaving readers uncertain what was Dahl and what was edited Dahl. (On the other hand, unlike in the case of Mitchell and Webb, the unexpurgated versions remained freely available.) In sketch comedy, by contrast, individual sketches can be removed wholesale, leaving the others unmolested. And yet in both cases, there’s a risk the public will be misled into thinking the past was just like the present, and a chance missed to consider that values – and the boundaries of the acceptable – are perpetually shifting and up for grabs.Do measures such as these give comedians the collywobbles? Mitchell and Webb themselves have apparently sanctioned the sketches’ withdrawal. In 2017,Matt Lucas disavowedhis sketch series Little Britain (“I wouldn’t make that show now. It would upset people”) and didn’t sound as if he were doing so just to stay employable; three years later, the show wasremoved from iPlayer and Netflixfor its egregious use of blackface. In my experience, comics don’t tend to consider anything sacrosanct, least of all old episodes of comedy shows. No one is more aware than a comedian of the shifting of social attitudes over time.But equally, comics are – or should be – constitutionally averse to piety. None would wish to see abridgements to vintage comedy become commonplace, nor for what is sayable to be any more strictly policed. All would defend the space for comedy to be uncomfortable, to tease at cultural faultlines, probing what we think and feel about ourselves, one another and the world.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI doubt many comics will expend outrage on this isolated instance of pruning that renders a well-loved series palatable on a mainstream, licence fee-funded platform in 2026. What they will, and what we should, care more about is that the BBC invests in new comedy. And empower it to explore and address the issues that define and discomfit our times as irreverently as Mitchell and Webb did theirs.Brian Logan is the Guardian’s comedy critic, and the artistic director of A Play, a Pie and a PintDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyOpinionComedyTelevisionDavid MitchellRobert WebbcommentShareReuse this content

title: Labour is nostalgic for two-party politics. That cosy, simple time is over – let it go | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Our fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is key, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Our fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is key, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Andy Burnham travels on the new Royal Daffodil Mersey ferry on Saturday as the Labour party gathers in Liverpool for its annual conference.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham travels on the new Royal Daffodil Mersey ferry on Saturday as the Labour party gathers in Liverpool for its annual conference.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionLabourLabour is nostalgic for two-party politics. That cosy, simple time is over – let it goJohn HarrisOur fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is keySun 27 Sep 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTShareAsI wrote last week, whatever its current troubles, Reform UK has hardly disappeared. Meanwhile, those black-clad quasi-paramilitaries may well be another augury of a frightening immediate future. One more English settlement – the town of Barnham, in Norfolk – is seemingly poised to stage a pretend independence referendum in protest at plans to locally accommodate asylum seekers. Oh, and our new Labour prime minister has just held cordial talks with a US president who has not only brought a modern de facto fascism to his homeland, butwants to export it to Europe.But hold all those cheerful thoughts for a moment, and let us have a look at the Labour party as it gathers in Liverpool. The slogan plastered all over its conference is “Hope Again” – which, unlike last year’s dreadful “Renew Britain”, suggests that a few people at the top might have belatedly learned the basics of pithy political storytelling.The influence of the two slogans that are accepted modern classics – “Take back control” and “Make America Great Again” – is obvious. In Labour’s case, “again” not only implies how badly Starmer’s reign went, but looks back to a better past and implies that something comparable is eminently possible. You might take it as a reference to the best aspects of the NewLabourperiod, Harold Wilson in his pomp or the magical glories of the Attlee years.The slogan also echoessome of the pronouncements made by Andy Burnhamwhen he became leader, about the positive response of the voters of Makerfield to “the promised return of the Labour they once knew”. And it has to be said: those words and the conference tagline tap into his party’s ingrained nostalgia, and the idea that with enough effort, Labour might return to winning a commanding share of the vote, as it did back in the days when footballers chain-smoked and bowler hats were still a common sight (in 1951, although it lost to the Tories, Labour won a record 48.8%, and Wilson came very close to the same figurein 1966).Numbers aside, Labour still largely believes that by rights it should monopolise the progressive half of politics. The Tories have the same idea about the right of the spectrum, which has recently fed into a seductive notion held by both “main” partiesand many pundits: that withZack Polanski’s PR slip-upsand the trouble that has engulfed Nigel Farage, we may be witnessing the rebirth of comfy, cosy, simple two-party politics.What utter rot that is. The UK’s passage into a multiparty system is deeply rooted in a society and economy whose complexity can no longer be smothered by our ludicrous voting system. Look at what has happened where the electoral machinery is different. Labour recentlylost control of Walesto Plaid Cymru, attracting a mere 11% of the vote. The SNP’s dominance in Scotland may have weakened, but it is more than intact. Meanwhile, even with first past the post still creakingly in place, whole swathes of what used to be considered middle England – particularly in the home counties – haveswitched from the Tories to the Lib Dems.At the time of writing,the latest YouGov pollputs Labour on 23% (if that’s accurate, the “Burnham bounce” looks more like a modest bunny-hop), the Tories level with Reform at 21%, and the Greens and Lib Dems on 14% and 12% respectively. The same polling group has also done a multi-level regression and post-stratification – orMRP– that offers a picture of the House of Commons that would be elected if a contest were held today. It forecasts a hung parliament, with Labour dropping to 241 seats, and facing the inevitability of cross-party cooperation. Here, clearly, is further evidence of a fragmented model of politics that will endure for the foreseeable future. And in Liverpool, mostly at fringe meetings, it will be talked about, but not nearly enough.Before he became leader, Burnham seemed to be the only senior Labour politician positively responding to these shifts. He hasrepeatedly backed proportional representation(which he insists he still supports), and said that embracing it would pave the way “foragreement with other partieson wider reforms”. With that, he said, would come “amore honest and collaborativeway of doing politics”, a phrase that chimes withhis promisesof a lot less “finger-pointing” and “point-scoring”. Aside from his talks with the Tories and Lib Dems about social care, what this might look like is unclear; all we know is that Burnham’s drive for English devolution will definitely mean ceding power to other parties, and probably substantially change politics at a national level.And so to the really important bit. Eleven days after the start of Labour conference comes the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Publicly at least, Labour seems to be running a content-lite campaign, though it hasattacked the Greens’alleged fiscal impossibilism and sent members a communique framing the contest as a chance to “get our revenge” for Green triumphs in May’s local elections. The Green leader and candidate, Polanski, is aggressively accusing Labour of a miserable lack of solidarity with Palestine, while an ally also charged Burnham’s party with choosing its contender – the former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali – on the basis of opportunistic “identity politics”. It all looks like politics as usual – and as the far right gains more and more traction here and abroad, what is happening in this corner of London should make us feel very nervous about the next UK general election.The left-leaning cross-party pressure group Compass is about to convene the first meeting of a “council for the progressive majority”, which will bring together leading figures from each of the UK’s progressive parties – including Plaid and the SNP – to firm up how they might collectively defeat Reform. To quote froma recent Compass statement: “There is a progressive majority in this country … yet our outdated political system divides us … splitting the vote and clearing a path for extremist voices to win with little public backing.” This is the kind of urgent warning that will become very vivid in the buildup to the next election, amid campaigning – whatever the efforts of Burnham’s newNational Centre For Information Defence– festooned with lies, deepfakes and worse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA lot of us remain unsure of the exact solutions to a split left taking on a confident, tech-savvy and possibly united right. Electoral pacts tend to look like stitch-ups; parties agreeing to limit their campaigning in certain marginal seats can work much better. Whatever, millions of us – including, it seems, the new PM – increasingly feel that a cultural change is overdue, not least to stop the most basic civilisational values buckling before our eyes.Talking of which, it’s grimly ironic that the man still benefiting most from the fractured politics of the 21st century is Farage, a self-styled throwback permanently surrounded by a cloud of Rothmans smoke. Here, then, is a question for everyone gathered by the old Liverpudlian docks: how can he be comprehensively beaten, possibly when he may end up healing divisions on the right by striking a deal (pre- or post-election) with the Tories, and even Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain? By ludicrously insisting that people must vote Labour whatever their political circumstances? Or somehow cooperating with other parties to ensure his defeat? Those parties also need to change, of course. But the age of monopolistic Labour hegemony is over. Let it go. We need to fight today’s most important battles together, so the prospect of hope might actually start to feel real. Again.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabourOpinionAndy BurnhamReform UKLabour conferenceLocal politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Tony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he? | Tom Baldwin | The Guardian
description: The former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for all, says former Labour party adviser Tom Baldwin
Author: Tom Baldwin
Headline: The former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for all, says former Labour party adviser Tom Baldwin
Content: Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York this week.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York this week.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamTony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he?Tom BaldwinThe former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for allSun 27 Sep 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTShareTony Blair can, apparently, sound slightly wistful when he describes how he once had a cloak-and-dagger meeting withAndy Burnham, who wanted to talk to him about standing for the party leadership. Before anyone gets too excited, however, this wasn’t in the past few months, during which Burnham succeeded in landing the job. The story dates back to 2010. That was when he was a callow member of Gordon Brown’s cabinet and understandably wary of his boss discovering not only his ambition to take over if Labour lost the looming general election, but also from whom he wanted advice.Much has changed since then, not least Burnham himself.His journeyout of Westminster and back again – which in his telling has become an almost spiritual pilgrimage of personal redemption – enabled him to shed the New Labour baggage that proved so cumbersome during his previous, and unsuccessful, runs for the leadership. In common with Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer – all of whom tried with varying degrees of success to distance themselves from Blair – Labour’s latest leader now also wants to keep Blair at arm’s length, and certainly far away from his party conference in Liverpool this week.Their secret meeting long ago nonetheless underlines how often, since he left Downing Street in 2007, Blair has had a residual and sometimes illicit allure for those aspiring to fill his shoes. Part of that is because – with the exception of Starmer – those who came after him failed to win a single general election, let alone three. But it is also that this leader from the past still has a possibly unmatched ability to raise our sights, away from whatever the media tells us is most urgent, towards the colossal compound crisis now casting its shadow across the world and over Britain’s future.Blair does not, of course, always make it easy to agree with him. There was an awful lot to dislike about his5,700 word essayearlier this year, which said Britain had no power to stop either the AI revolution or Donald Trump. It led some to question once more the motives of a former PM whose proximity both to big tech firms and successive US presidents has so tainted his reputation. Burnhamswiftly respondedto the essay by saying Blair just didn’t get “what’s going on” with the impact of “40 years of neoliberalism” on working-class communities. He later promised that the interests of voters in Makerfield, where he was standing in a byelection, would be his test of what made good policy.View image in fullscreenTony Blair with his health minister Andy Burnham at a No 10 summit on reducing NHS waiting times, July 2006.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyIt was, however, a bit disingenuous for himto claimthat Blair agreed “our relentless focus now should be on domestic issues, and fixing our own underlying problems, rather than on re-running divisive arguments about rejoining the European Union”. Indeed, the bulk of the former PM’s essay was about the inability of this country’s politics to navigate an international landscape being churned at terrifying speed by forces far beyond Britain’s control.Conflicts in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have since put further pressure on government borrowing costs and household fuel bills. It is increasingly difficult to see how the inward-looking vision Burnham has painted so far, largely consisting of new powers for mayors and more regulation of privatised utilities, will deliver his promised “good growth in every postcode” any time soon. This week, his determinedly domestic focus relented and he acknowledged the government mustalso offer “resilience”in the face of global storms, before delivering aspeech to the United Nationsin New York on Tuesday night. The speech veered wildly from No 10 North in Manchester to Ukraine, Israel, Iran and China, briefly taking in the climate crisis, before setting out the need to create international safety standards on frontier AI and protect democracy from all kinds of Russian threats, including disinformation on social media.It didn’t go nearly far enough for Blair. On Thursday, his policy institute published a paper calling for Britain to set a course for re-entry into a “reformed European Union” over the next decade. Rather than re-run old arguments about Brexit, he would prefer to start a new one, saying the need for the UK and the EU to build capability in defence and capacity on AI is more pressing than it ever was in the past.Although Blair can point to polls showing a majority of the public and an even bigger slice of Labour voters would support rejoining, there is plenty of evidence to suggest relations with Europe have gone backwards under Burnham’s government. The prospect of Britain drifting alone on the tide of history felt closer to becoming reality last week when the annualstate of the unionspeech from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, made repeated references to Canada, a country about 3,500 miles away to which she offered an associate EU membership, while barely mentioning the UK at all.An EU-UK summit, originally scheduled to have taken place under Starmer’s premiership in May, was delayed until July and then to a yet-to-be confirmed date at the end of the year. What had been talked up as a “done deal” for a youth mobility scheme – by which young people from the EU and the UK could live, work and study in each other’s countries – risks being unstitched by new objections from some of Burnham’s newly appointed minsters that it fails his “Makerfield test”. There are similar claims that the EU’s “made in Europe” policy on supply chains will disadvantage British industry and bea further obstacle to an agreement, while progress that began in February to resolve the issue is said to have stalled.There are a lot of mixed messages on all this just now.Recent commentsthat it must be possible to get a deal agreed with Europe in “an amicable way that will add percentage points to our growth” perhaps made him sound too much like a regional mayor who had missed the past decade of Brexit mayhem in Westminster. But others believe Burnham is considering a big leap beyond the “red line” election pledges that prevented Starmer from rejoining a customs union, the single market or allowing freedom of movement. Over recent days some of those around him have dangled out questions about how, “purely hypothetically”, a case for re-entry could be included in his speech to conference this Tuesday, the 10-year plan later this year or, as Burnham himselfnotably failed to rule out this week, Labour’s manifesto at the next election (whenever that might be).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEither way, the freshly minted new PM will not want to be seen taking inspiration from a sometimes toxic old one. There has been no contact between them since Burnham entered Downing Street and a meeting – clandestine or otherwise – is not scheduled. That seems a shame because, on the issue of Europe at least, Blair really isn’t the worst person from whom Burnham could take advice.Tom Baldwin is a former assistant editor of the Times and a former senior adviser to theLabourparty. He is the author of Keir Starmer: The BiographyExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourTony BlairBrexitEuropean UnionForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: My Instagram reels addiction has ruined my ability to have a conversation. But can I get it back? | Hannah Ewens | The Guardian
description: As a journalist, I’m endlessly curious about people – or I was until short-form video made real-life interactions feel like a drag, says freelance editor and writer Hannah Ewens
Author: Hannah Ewens
Headline: As a journalist, I’m endlessly curious about people – or I was until short-form video made real-life interactions feel like a drag, says freelance editor and writer Hannah Ewens
Content: ‘Subconsciously, I had begun to expect conversations to provide speed, relevance and the ability for me to skip through at will.’Photograph: Xavier Lorenzo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Subconsciously, I had begun to expect conversations to provide speed, relevance and the ability for me to skip through at will.’Photograph: Xavier Lorenzo/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial mediaMy Instagram reels addiction has ruined my ability to have a conversation. But can I get it back?Hannah EwensAs a journalist, I’m endlessly curious about people – or I was until short-form video made real-life interactions feel like a dragSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 05.52 EDTShareIt’s never pleasant to confront something unflattering about yourself, particularly when you catch yourself in the act. Recently I was mid-conversation with a stranger at a party, when I suddenly became conscious of my internal monologue: yes, hurry up, get to the point, you’re going to saythis, thenthat, and what is the takeaway here?This wasn’t the first time I had noticed a shift in my real-life interactions. Over the preceding months, I had felt tired, even irritated, when loved ones so much as veered close to an anecdote or detail about their lives that I thought I had already heard. During interviews I conducted as a journalist, it sometimes took a heroic effort to concentrate on conversations once they failed to be truly stimulating. Ordinarily I am endlessly curious about people, but I couldn’t ignore a creeping feeling that my attention was waning.The source of the problem was clear to me.
