At the beginning of the year, I became freelance and started working from home full-time, and I found myself constantly scrolling social media. I hadn’t noticed before how muchInstagramaggressively forces short-form video into our feeds in the form of “reels”, but now they were the majority of what I was seeing. Hours of my “working day” were spent watching them. It seemed obvious that this content, algorithmically fed to cater to my interests and concerns, had started competing with real-life interactions. Subconsciously, I had begun to expect conversations to provide speed, relevance and the ability for me to skip through at will.It would be highly unusual if this was only happening to me.TikTokand Instagram have boomed in popularity since the pandemic. My very offline boyfriend, who doesn’t use social media, thought what I was saying was horrific – as disgusting as me watching videos on 2x speed, as I am wont to do.It has long been argued that “digital dualism” is a false construct – there is no real separation between offline and online spheres. So of course an increase in digesting short-form content could affect how we relate to people in real life. It was a relief when a friend told me she got addicted to reels and now can’t bear irrelevant information in conversation. And it was even better when another said it would be nice to be able to skip through and speed up interactions in the way you do reel to reel.Short-form video weakens our ability tohold an intention after an interruption, according to one 2023 study, which is troubling when you consider that to have a conversation you must remember information and hold your intentions to reply. One of its authors, user experience researcher Francesco Chiossi, said that my experience is a perfect example of the impatience that watching too much short-form content engenders. “The deeper we try to go, the more information we have to retain and the more impatient we become,” he says. To compensate, he adds, we switch topics, interrupt, drift off or pick up the pace because we (perhaps falsely) believe we’ve already processed what is being said.With the threat of losing my real-life friends in mind, I emailed Marissa Fond, sociolinguistics professor at Georgetown University, for advice on what someone should do if they find their attention waning during everyday conversations. “They could take a deep breath, notice that they’re participating in a practice they don’t like, slow down and try to engage their curiosity about the content or person involved,” she replied. In other words, retrain yourself for the friction and pace of life, dummy.I’ve tried mentally berating myself when I clock I’m getting irritated or distracted. I remind myself that this is exactly (probably) why some tech overlords don’t let their own kids have social media. My next step will be deleting the apps on days off. After all, it’s true that the best conversations are nothing like content. They aren’t all sparky like electricity but take on the form of water. They allow me and another person to meander, to seep into places we have no business being, to become emotional. We push and pull and create a unique tide between us. There is no “hook”. No frenetic pace. Any clear takeaway is often submerged by more questions. Sometimes it’s boring but often it can be quite beautiful – if you have the patience for it.Hannah Ewens is a freelance editor and writer, and the author of Fangirls: Scenes From Modern Music Cultureskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionPsychologyDigital mediaInstagramTikTokcommentShareReuse this content

title: I have seen with pride how British overseas aid saves children’s lives. That is why I say cuts should be reversed | David Harewood | The Guardian
description: I understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground, says actor and Unicef UK ambassador David Harewood
Author: David Harewood
Headline: I understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground, says actor and Unicef UK ambassador David Harewood
Content: ‘UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end in December 2026, two years earlier than planned.’Photograph: Jonathan Porter/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end in December 2026, two years earlier than planned.’Photograph: Jonathan Porter/AlamyOpinionAidI have seen with pride how British overseas aid saves children’s lives. That is why I say cuts should be reversedDavid HarewoodI understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground. Our choices can do so much goodDavid Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassadorSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 03.33 EDTShareAs Labour party conference approaches, politicians will debate spending priorities, fiscal pressures and the UK’s place in the world. Before those discussions begin, I want ministers to picture a hospital ward I visited in Sierra Leone with Unicef (United Nations Children’s Fund).Inside the special-care baby unit at Makeni regional hospital were rows of tiny premature babies, some no bigger than my hand. Around them stood dedicated nurses and anxious parents, all willing these newborns to survive.Then I saw something that stopped me in my tracks. It was 2019, and I noticed a UK aid sticker fixed above a tiny incubator. Inside was a premature baby fighting for breath. Nearby stood oxygen equipment that staff explained had been funded through UK support. I learned that when power outages struck the hospital, as they often did, that equipment helped keep vulnerable newborns alive.Being in the presence of these sometimes inconceivably small children, seeing the UK aid sticker labelled across the incubators that were keeping them alive, emotion completely overcame me. It was not only sadness. It was pride. Pride that people in Britain, most of whom would never meet that baby or their family, had helped make survival possible. Seven years later, that moment remains one of the most impactful of my life.When you are standing beside a newborn fighting for every breath, politics feels very far away. But the truth is that babies live or die because of political choices.Since 2017, Unicef has supported Sierra Leone’s government to establish special-care baby units, providing sick and premature newborns with specialised treatment that was previously unavailable to many in the country.I met doctors and nurses doing extraordinary work despite limited resources. I saw community health workers connecting families with health facilities, and mothers receiving advice and support.One of them was Josephine, whose one-month-old daughter, also called Josephine, had been born dangerously premature at seven months. She told me she believed that without the special-care baby unit, both she and her daughter might have died during or after labour.That is what aid means. It is not charity, and it is not an abstract number on a government spreadsheet.The results in Sierra Leone show what that investment can achieve. Since the expansion of the special-care baby units began, annual admissions have risen from around 1,000 to 14,000, while survival rates had improved from 78% to 90% by the end of 2025.View image in fullscreenDavid Harewood visits Makeni regional hospital’s special-care baby unit in Sierra Leone, April 2019.Photograph: Unicef/Tom DymondBut those gains are now under threat. Since the start of 2025, global aid funding has fallen sharply as major donors have scaled back support. The UK has already reduced spending on overseas developmentfrom 0.7% of national income to 0.3%. Around the world, programmes that help keep children healthy, safe and in school are facing growing uncertainty. In Sierra Leone, those cuts are no longer a future concern. They are already being felt.I learned last week that the UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end this December, two years earlier than planned.I’m already hearing about the consequences. International paediatric support and specialist neonatal nurse training has ended. Reductions affecting the free healthcare programmes have also damaged the availability of lifesaving medicines for newborns, children and pregnant women.The danger is not just that units such as Makeni might suddenly close. It is that the foundations supporting them are gradually eroded. Medical equipment needs spare parts and trained technicians. Oxygen must remain available. Nurses need continuing training and clinical mentorship. Medicines must reach hospitals. Infection prevention, referrals, outreach and follow-up for small and sick babies all require sustained investment.Without that support, the progress I witnessed will be lost.Sierra Leone is building national capacity. But transferring skills and building resilient health systems takes time. Ending support prematurely risks pulling away the scaffolding before the structure is strong enough to stand alone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe scale of the unmet need makes that risk even more alarming. About 45,000 newborns in Sierra Leone require specialised care each year, but existing services reach only about 31%. Approximately 31,000 small and sick babies are still left without access to the essential care they need.This is not a programme that has finished its job. It is a programme that is working, but still reaches only a fraction of the children who need it. That is why I support Unicef UK’s No Choice But Childhood campaign.The Guardian’srecent reportsuggests that ministers are looking for ways to make a smaller aid budget work harder. That is an important discussion. But the question should not only be how aid is spent: it should also be who it is spent for. If children bear the greatest consequences of poverty, conflict and climate shocks, they should be a clear priority in how aid is allocated.The UK government should ringfence at least 25% of its overseas development spending for programmes that directly support children. The government must also set out a credible route back to spending 0.7% of national income on overseas development. Restoring that commitment will not happen overnight, but without a clear path, temporary reductions risk becoming a permanent retreat, with tragic consequences.I understand the pressures on public finances: governments must make difficult choices. But we should be honest about what those choices mean.In Makeni, they can mean whether oxygen is available when a premature baby cannot breathe. Whether a nurse has the training and equipment to act. Whether a mother goes home carrying her child.The special-care baby unit I visited remains open, for now, but declining support is making it harder to sustain its quality, while extending the same care to thousands of newborns who are still not being reached.No child chooses where they are born, and asLabourconference gets under way, I hope ministers think of children – like the tiny baby I saw in the incubator. That is what our choices can do.David Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassadorExplore more on these topicsAidOpinionUnited NationsSierra LeoneLabourAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Korea review – a nirvana of wild beauty shattered by the 20th century | Art | The Guardian
description: The staggering resourcefulness and fantastic originality of bygone artisans is showcased in earthenware so exquisite it will soothe your soul. But a lurch into the modern breaks the spell
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The staggering resourcefulness and fantastic originality of bygone artisans is showcased in earthenware so exquisite it will soothe your soul. But a lurch into the modern breaks the spell
Content: A glorious responce to Korea’s landscape … Jeong Seon, Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang, 1751.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaView image in fullscreenA glorious responce to Korea’s landscape … Jeong Seon, Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang, 1751.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaArtReviewKorea review – a nirvana of wild beauty shattered by the 20th centuryBritish Museum, LondonThe staggering resourcefulness and fantastic originality of bygone artisans is showcased in earthenware so exquisite it will soothe your soul. But a lurch into the modern breaks the spellJonathan JonesSun 27 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan they do it again? The runaway success of theBayeux tapestryhas put the British Museum in a league of its own, perhaps making it, at this moment, the leading museum on earth – and it’s rapidly following up with Korea, a survey of “2,000 years of creativity” in a land that, before its sufferings in the 20th century, enjoyed millennia of calm, at least to judge from its art. But it’s a blockbuster with a tragic flaw, a lovely broken vase badly stuck together.You are lured at first into a nirvana of beauty. A giant bronze bell from a Buddhist monastery, cast in the eighth century AD and bulging with dragons, flames and flowery embossments, strikes the tone. It calls you to meditation. A gong adds to the harmony (and if you need that underlining, there are bells and gongs on the now obligatory exhibition soundtrack). I was held rapt by this Buddhist period in Korea’s history, when the contemplative religion from India interacted with the artistic influence of China to inspire ecstatic hand-copied sutras (spiritual scriptures) and slender little statuettes of bodhisattvas (Buddhist saints who have achieved enlightened holiness).View image in fullscreen‘I was held rapt by this period in Korea’s history’ … Avatamsaka Sutra (The Flower Garland Sutra),  The Practices and Vows of Samantabhadra, 1341-67.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaYet even before Buddhism brought its ethereal aesthetic, the resourcefulness of artisans in the Korean peninsula was staggering. Intricate stoneware objects from as early as the fifth century include a horse standing on a circular plinth with a drinking horn balanced on its back – a practical object of wild beauty.Ceramicscame to Korea from China but took root in creations of fantastic originality. The kingdom of Goryeo, which unified the peninsula from 918 to 1392 and made Buddhism the state religion, sponsored superb courtly ceramics. Potters adopted the green glazed stoneware, celadon, from China’s Zhejiang province and perfected it in smooth pale green bowls and vases that soothe your soul.View image in fullscreenSuperb ceramics … Gourd-shaped ewer with chrysanthemum design, 1200-1300.Photograph: National Museum of KoreaA flair for exquisite earthenware continued under the neo-Confucian Joseon dynasty, which ruled from 1392 until, astonishingly, 1897. The most captivating pot from this era is a huge, white, near-spherical moon jar made in the 18th century. It’s an intoxicating blend of scale and geometry created by throwing two semi-circular bowls and joining them together. You can see the imperfect, dimpled join, cherished in Korean culture, which adds to its uniqueness, its personality.And then the spell is broken. The show shifts forward suddenly, brutally, into some so-so early 20th-century Korean art. Modern pastiches of traditional art mix awkwardly with European and American-style modernism from the 1900s to 1950s. Why this lurch, just as you were starting to grasp the subtle shift from Buddhism to neo-Confucianism and how their aesthetics differ? The blockbuster cultural history of Korea falls apart. It’s just a collection of things, after all.In fact, this is, with a few additions, the collection of Lee Kun-hee, who was the chair of Samsung – the exhibition’s “corporate partner” – until his death in 2020. It’s a fine collection. Several works here, now owned by South Korea’s leading museums, are national treasures of unique significance. But a collection comes with its owner’s idiosyncrasies, and cannot be taken as an objective history of a people’s art and beliefs. It is not very insightful about the modern history of Korea: where are the photographs, news stories, popular imagery, if you want to tell that story? Instead the show shrinks into a display of elite art. Fair enough if it was simply presented as one collector’s taste.The 20th century was a brutal period for Korea: from 1910 to 1945 it was colonised by the Japanese empire but the cosy modern paintings here say nothing about that. More mention is made of theKorean warthat killed three million people. A desperate, cartoon-like pastel by Lee Jung-seop of a fisher being welcomed home by his family is an unfulfilled dream: this artist became a migrant in the war and died before ever seeing his family again. Another roughly drawn work by him shows naked bodies tied up in a chilling glimpse of the horrors of that time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPast beauty and modern violence … Do Ho Suh, Self-portrait, 2019.Photograph: Trustees of the British MuseumThat grief, chaos and cultural loss – with Korea still divided today – is only slightly evoked. What stays with you is the lost harmony of the past, when scholars and monks meditated on nature and its beauties. The work of art that most gloriously responds to Korea’s landscapes is Jeong Seon’s hanging scroll Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang. Done in ink on paper in 1751, this more than metre-wide view takes you into a fresh, atmospheric encounter with nature: a dark mass of mountain hangs over the scene while trees are evoked as rapid moist blurs. It is not idealised but spontaneous. You wonder what Jeong and his faraway contemporary Thomas Gainsborough might have made of each other.Perhaps the broken feeling of the show, in which there is no link between past beauty and modern violence, tells us a tragic truth. The very last object implies this.Do Ho Suh’s 2019 self portrait, owned by the British Museum, depicts the artist as a tiny figure under a cascade of multicoloured threads streaming down from a floating image of a traditional Korean house. The grace of this world holds you in this exhibition and you feel its vanishing as a personal loss, wherever you come from.At theBritish Museum, London, 1 October-31 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArtSouth KoreaNorth KoreaBritish MuseumCeramicsIllustrationPaintingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’ | Books | The Guardian
description: Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novel
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novel
Content: ‘I’m proud of my resilience’ … Tomi Adeyemi.Photograph: Caroline FlissView image in fullscreen‘I’m proud of my resilience’ … Tomi Adeyemi.Photograph: Caroline FlissBooksTomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novelEmma LoffhagenSun 27 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing.Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her.“It was an intense choice, and I think it’s because I needed people to see me in this one,” she says. “I’ve had so much success, but it was also done in a way where so many people’s interpretations were put on to who I was.”The recent public fallout from the forthcoming film adaptation may have drawn attention, but the 33-year-old Nigerian American author had already spent much of her adult life being watched. Children of Blood and Bone, her 2018 debut, became a publishing phenomenon, netting a major seven-figure deal and debuting at No 1 on the New York Times young adult bestseller list. Its story of Zélie, a young woman fighting to restore magic to the kingdom of Orïsha, was inspired by West African mythology and offered something Adeyemi had craved as a child: a dark-skinned Black girl at the centre of an epic fantasy.The success brought its own mythology. Adeyemi was not merely a successful young writer; she became, she feels, a symbol of what the next generation of Black YA literature might be, something she felt the weight of acutely.double quotation markI felt pressure to be the perfect dark‑skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’“I felt pressure to be the perfect dark-skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’,” she says. “This was the biggest YA book deal in history, not just for a female or Black author. And so few of us are given a shot at all, so for the last 12 years there’s been this sense of carrying everyone.”Readers would tell her what the book had meant to their children. “You have no idea what this did for me,” they would say. Such responses were moving, but also difficult to know what to do with.Now, with The Siren, Adeyemi has moved from epic fantasy to something more contemporary. The standalone novel follows Emery, a Black student arriving at Dartmouth College determined to leave her troubled past behind. She is drawn into a mysterious sorority of “Sirens” and desperate to fit in. In some ways, Adeyemi says, the book is deeply personal. “[Emery] is my inner teen,” Adeyemi says. “I just want to give her a hug.”She may have found success, but in the beginning Adeyemi’s career never looked certain. She wrote her first story at five – a Parent Trap fan fiction because, she says, she “wanted a twin and a horse”. She then spent years trying not to become a writer. Her parents had moved to Chicago from Nigeria in their early 20s, and Adeyemi grew up with the ethos of relentless achievement that often comes with first-generation immigrants – one that does not take kindly to creative pursuits. She considered medicine, investment banking and consulting, but kept coming back to writing. “Being called to be an artist is terrifying,” she says. “It’s not a logical choice.”After studying English at Harvard, Adeyemi won a fellowship to study West African mythology and culture in Salvador, Brazil, an experience that would later inspire Children of Blood and Bone. She moved to California and began working part time at a film production company in Los Angeles, alongside writing her first novel.View image in fullscreenThat first attempt took four and a half years to write and received 63 rejections. She decided to drop the manuscript and wrote Children of Blood and Bone instead. When it was finally published in 2018 it quickly became one of the most talked about YA novels of the year. For a writer who had spent years being turned down, the speed and scale of what followed were dizzying. “I never really adjusted, because there was so much work still to do,” she says. “It’s been 12 to 14 years of intense grinding.”And then came the film. On paper, it was the stuff of a writer’s dreams: her novel was to be transformed into a major Hollywood production, with an impossibly starry cast including Viola Davis, Idris Elba, Regina King, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg and Cynthia Erivo, premiering in January 2027. Adeyemi co-wrote the screenplay, but as the adaptation progressed, she became increasingly unhappy with the process.In July, Adeyemi posted a five-minute video on TikTok in which she described the adaptation process as “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”. She said she had left the set “hyperventilating and sobbing”, and that afterwards she experienced severe physical pain and panic attacks. “I never want to hear about this project again,” she said.She says she had little hesitation about speaking publicly. “I understood that if I didn’t speak up, I couldn’t move forward,” she explains. “I can’t really worry about the response, because I don’t have to live with how people respond to me – I have to live with me, every day.”When I ask what exactly happened on set, however, Adeyemi hesitates. “I won’t go into the specifics,” she says carefully. “[But] the whole journey of the trilogy and the adaptation felt biblical … It took all of me.”There has, though, been public discussion around the film’s casting of Amandla Stenberg, who is mixed race, and questions around colourism: Stenberg’s character is described in the book as having “dark copper skin”. Adeyemi’s July TikTok also appeared to show messages she sent to Stenberg in February 2025, around the time Stenberg responded to the colourism backlash, telling the actor: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”When I ask Adeyemi whether she wants to clarify anything about the casting, she demurs. “With a film, the director makes every decision,” she says. “With my book I can talk about every choice down to the commas, because that’s truly in my hands. So there’s nothing for me to add, other than the clarity that these aren’t my choices.”She is clear, though, about one thing. When I ask her if she would ever adapt another one of her books for screen she responds simply: “Never.” She has no desire to watch the upcoming film either. “I still don’t plan to watch it, but it’s not really for me to watch,” she says.Instead, she is trying to leave the world of Children of Blood and Bone behind, and focus on what she has achieved. “I’m proud of my strength, resilience, and grace,” she says.She is also proud of what she believes her debut set in motion: the fact that she can now walk into a bookshop and see shelves of dark-skinned protagonists across fantasy, romance, thrillers and mysteries. “The girls who grew up after me will never have that experience,” she says. As her publisher told her: “You changed things.”The Siren by Tomi Adeyemi is published by First Ink on Thursday. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
