title: NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiere | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor defend findings on Israel’s killing of Palestinians amid threats from Israeli officials
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor defend findings on Israel’s killing of Palestinians amid threats from Israeli officials
Content: Rachel Szor (left) and Yuval Abraham on stage at the NAZA premiere in New York City on Saturday.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for FLCView image in fullscreenRachel Szor (left) and Yuval Abraham on stage at the NAZA premiere in New York City on Saturday.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for FLCNAZANAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiereYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor defend findings on Israel’s killing of Palestinians amid threats from Israeli officialsAdrian HortonSat 26 Sep 2026 20.48 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 20.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe film-makers behindNAZA, the award-winning documentary on Israel’s systemic mass killing of Palestinians in Gaza, defended their findings at the film’s North American premiere in New York on Saturday, amid protests in Israel and escalatingthreatsfrom Israeli officials to strip them of their citizenship.Thecritically acclaimed film, directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, features the testimony of 24 anonymized Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, who describe the AI-poweredsystemsused to select their targets. The project takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicatehow many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike, which are often conducted at night in private homes, killing many family members, including children, at once.“Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audienceat the New York film festivalin a Q&A that followed the film’s premiere. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”“These crimes that you saw are ongoing,” Abraham said. “They’re ongoing because it’s what our country is doing, and because of what your country is supporting and funding.”1:55NAZA - official trailerThe 80-minute documentary, filmed in secret on rooftops in Tel Aviv, builds on reporting published from 2023 to 2025 in the Guardian; +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication; and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call. It held its world premiere earlier this month at the Venice film festival, where it received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record – and went onto win the special jury prize.The film has been met with fierce derision from Israeli officials as well as threats to the film-makers, amid a tense election season largely focused on Benjamin Netanyahu’s ongoing campaign in Gaza, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians to date and has beendeclared a genocideby numerous international agencies, including theUnited Nations.A couple dozen protesters gathered outside the film’s premiere at the Lincoln Center on Saturday afternoon, brandishing Israeli flags and signs calling for viewers to “learn the facts” of the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas on Israeli civilians. At least one truck with LED screens accusing NAZA of being “propaganda dressed up as a documentary” circled the theater.NAZA’s New York City premiere came just a day after the Israeli prime minister offered anaggressive defenseof Israel’s use of deadly force in Gaza just across Central Park to the UN general assembly. As hundreds of protesters gathered outside and dozens of diplomats inside walked out in solidarity with Palestinians, Netanyahu called Israel’s war in Gaza the “opposite of genocide” and denounced Israel’s critics. Netanyahu had previously said he wouldseek new laws to strip citizenshipfrom people who “smear” Israeli soldiers in response to NAZA.“So, to all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor ofNew York, I say this: shame on you!” he said Thursday.On Friday, Netanyahureiteratedhis plan to advance legislation revoking the citizenship of Abraham and Szor, two of the four film-makers behindNo Other Land, an unstinting look at the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.In an interview with the conservative Israeli outlet Makor Rishon, he likened NAZA to “launching dozens of ballistic missiles” at Israel.Abraham addressed the missile comment directly in the post-screening Q&A, referring to such a characterization as “the criminalization of journalism and of this kind of work”.He also defended the film’s use of anonymous sources as necessary to expose systems of mass killing hidden by the Israeli state. “Throughout the history of investigative journalism, very often granting confidentiality to sources is a means to pursue the truth,” he said. “This film could not have been made any other way and because the crimes are ongoing, we felt that it was important to make it.”Along with Netanyahu, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, has called for the film-makers’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of “treason against the state”. The IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow IDF soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.Rightwing activists have gone even further, calling for violence against the pair. Earlier this month, dozens of agitatorssurroundedSzor’s parents’ home in central Israel, with one protester calling for the “death penalty for traitors”.More than 1,500 Israeli film professionals, 43 Israeli human rights organizations and the directors of major international festivals havedefendedAbraham and Szor, as have numerousinternational press freedom organizations. The film is currently set for release next month in cinemas in 55 countries, before a digital global release, for free, on the Guardian’s website in November, as part of the organization’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.But the US premiere Saturday held particular resonance, given the country’sannual $3.8bn in military assistanceto Israel – a connection the film-makers noted to the New York City crowd.“These soldiers are talking about what has been done with the taxpayer money of the people sitting here,” said Abraham.He also responded to the protesters outside the theater invoking the attacks of October 7. “It’s in the film and it’s completely unjustified,” he said of the massacre, which killed 1,200 Israelis, most of them civilians. “But it also cannot justify what you’ve seen in the film. It doesn’t justify the slaughter of so many civilians inGaza.”“I don’t want to live in a world where rightful empathy to Israeli victims is weaponized by leaders like Netanyahu – cynical people who promise nothing other than perpetual occupation and war,” he added. “It’s weaponized to mean a lack of empathy to Palestinians, to mean this continuous killing and murder of people. I don’t think we should want to live in such a world. I think we should all refuse to play this zero-sum game.”Explore more on these topicsNAZANew York film festival 2026Israel-Gaza warDocumentary filmsBenjamin NetanyahuNew YorkIsraelShareReuse this content

title: What’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?  | Brian Logan | The Guardian
description: The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed, says the Guardian’s comedy critic Brian Logan
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed, says the Guardian’s comedy critic Brian Logan
Content: David Mitchell and Robert Webb on stage during Amnesty International’s Secret Policeman’s Ball at the Royal Albert Hall, London, October 2008.Photograph: Ian West/PA Wire/PA PhotosView image in fullscreenDavid Mitchell and Robert Webb on stage during Amnesty International’s Secret Policeman’s Ball at the Royal Albert Hall, London, October 2008.Photograph: Ian West/PA Wire/PA PhotosOpinionTV comedyWhat’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?Brian LoganThe deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changedSun 27 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTShare“Are we the baddies?”, asked the comedy double actMitchell and Webbin theirmost famous sketch, in which two uniformed SS officers look one another up and down and arrive at that inescapable conclusion. And lo, it turns out they are, if this week’s news about the supposed offensiveness of the duo’s back catalogue is to be believed.Their newfound unpalatability made headlines last Monday,when 11 of the pair’s sketcheswere pulledfrom the rerelease of That Mitchell and Webb Look on iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary – a move that led to loud condemnation from the keyboard cavalry in Britain’s never-ending, and never much fun, culture war.Was the BBC right to expunge the skits? There’s an argument that in this instance, a warning or disclaimer might have been sufficient. The sketches in question variously involve jokes about Jimmy Savile,Robert Webbplaying a rude Gandhi (seemingly wearing skin-darkening makeup) and two further scenes in which the comedians wear blackface. In neither sketch are they doing so to depict people of colour, but instead to depict white people (in one scene, re-enactors of historic battles having a go at an African skirmish) who themselves wear blackface. In both, they are alert to their own indelicacy: “Are you sure,” asks Webb repeatedly throughout one, “that this isn’t racist?”Some have argued that sketches such as these – satires on chauvinism, not examples of it – should therefore be spared the editor’s scissors. But that’s missing the point, which is that blackface (and indeed the N-word, which caused the standup comic Alfie Brownso much troublerecently when he used it in his own anti-racist routine) is considered beyond the pale, irreducibly hurtful to a portion of the BBC’s audience, regardless of context.Is it right that it is so considered? There’s no question these terms and behaviours are associated with very real harms. Perhaps the corporation focus-grouped that question – or perhaps it is pre-empting criticism, erring on the side of caution and care. Is it so outrageous that they should do so? The BBC is, as the comedy producer Jimmy Mulville statedthis weekin the most sensible comment yet made on the controversy, “in an impossible position”.For my part, I can’t get too exercised by the removal of a handful of sketches – one of them, which jokes about therecently deceased Bill Oddie, for reasons of common decency, and others on the same basis that 70s sitcomIt Ain’t Half Hot Mumhas long been withheld, without great controversy, from our screens. It feels important, mind you, that the episodes in question should be prominently marked as abridged, much as those Roald Dahl books adjusted for modern sensitivities were marketed as “updated texts”, in a move even more contested than this one. (Interestingly, David Mitchellresponded very cynicallyto Dahl’s “updating”.)View image in fullscreenStill from Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping, with Stevie Martin and David Mitchell.Photograph: Channel 4That act of bowdlerism felt more extreme because it affected (some would say diluted) the entire text, leaving readers uncertain what was Dahl and what was edited Dahl. (On the other hand, unlike in the case of Mitchell and Webb, the unexpurgated versions remained freely available.) In sketch comedy, by contrast, individual sketches can be removed wholesale, leaving the others unmolested. And yet in both cases, there’s a risk the public will be misled into thinking the past was just like the present, and a chance missed to consider that values – and the boundaries of the acceptable – are perpetually shifting and up for grabs.Do measures such as these give comedians the collywobbles? Mitchell and Webb themselves have apparently sanctioned the sketches’ withdrawal. In 2017,Matt Lucas disavowedhis sketch series Little Britain (“I wouldn’t make that show now. It would upset people”) and didn’t sound as if he were doing so just to stay employable; three years later, the show wasremoved from iPlayer and Netflixfor its egregious use of blackface. In my experience, comics don’t tend to consider anything sacrosanct, least of all old episodes of comedy shows. No one is more aware than a comedian of the shifting of social attitudes over time.But equally, comics are – or should be – constitutionally averse to piety. None would wish to see abridgements to vintage comedy become commonplace, nor for what is sayable to be any more strictly policed. All would defend the space for comedy to be uncomfortable, to tease at cultural faultlines, probing what we think and feel about ourselves, one another and the world.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI doubt many comics will expend outrage on this isolated instance of pruning that renders a well-loved series palatable on a mainstream, licence fee-funded platform in 2026. What they will, and what we should, care more about is that the BBC invests in new comedy. And empower it to explore and address the issues that define and discomfit our times as irreverently as Mitchell and Webb did theirs.Brian Logan is the Guardian’s comedy critic, and the artistic director of A Play, a Pie and a PintDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyOpinionComedyTelevisionDavid MitchellRobert WebbcommentShareReuse this content

title: Godzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streak | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects
Content: A still from Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: Courtesy of GKidsView image in fullscreenA still from Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: Courtesy of GKidsFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewGodzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise’s winning streakNew York film festival:The follow-up to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effectsJesse HassengerSat 26 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 20.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago.Godzilla Minus One, the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in aseriesof Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn’t just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Now. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and theToho-made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. Arguably the artsiest, brainiest of the major fall fests is playing unexpected host to a truly spectacular monster battle royale, packaged alongside some of the same thoughtful historical context that informed the previous film.‘In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs’: the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson’s new filmRead moreWriter, director and VFX maestro Takashi Yamazaki returns for the sequel, bringing his lead characters back with him. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience withGodzillato overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to “zero”, hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to “minus one”. Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn’t seen directly in trailers, this isn’t a spoiler; he’s featured from the very first scene of the film.)Ghidorah’s appearance obviously sends off alarms in the disaster-response agency that now employs Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), also from the previous film. Noda is joined by Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist who introduces less artillery-heavy defense mechanisms for this new threat. Of course, there is a natural Ghidorah deterrent last seen disintegrating into the sea but known for his adaptability – if only the big guy could be called upon and steered in the right direction.In the older Godzilla films, Ghidorah-Godzilla battles can sometimes make whatever humans who might fit into the picture seem all the more insignificant; the monsters are so fearsome and, in their way, charismatic, that they level anything else in their way. In the tradition of its emotionally involving predecessor, Godzilla Minus Zero grapples more directly with humans’ attempts to assert some control over forces that initially seem impossible to harness. It’s no accident that one of its new heroes attempts to predict the weather – and has faced natural disasters despite her accurate predictions. The characters wield technology that is more science-fictionally advanced than in the previous movie while still relying on a sense of impromptu can-do scrappiness and determination to protect their country. With decreased puny-human helplessness comes greater dangers and new dilemmas.View image in fullscreenMasami Nagasawa in Godzilla Minus Zero.Photograph: Courtesy of GKidsThe film’s version of the US military, for example, is willing to provide planes but not troops to aid in the fight, which is partially how Kōichi and Noriko are drawn back into the conflict despite the pleading of young Akiko. The partners’ skill sets make them valuable assets, perpetuating some of the previous film’s questions about what kinds of sacrifices might be expected or required when sending citizens into the thick of battle. There’s also an element of body horror used intriguingly, but perhaps not to its fullest potential, given the shiver of anticipation that shoots through the audience when it’s introduced.There’s some value in sidestepping expectations; Yamazaki mentioned at a NYFF press conference that he sought to avoid conforming to any fan guesswork about how various kaiju business in a sequel to Minus One might proceed. True to his word, the movie seems determined to stay true to the human melodrama that proved so surprisingly effective in the previous film, rather than going into all-out monsters-attack mode. That approach works well for the film’s new characters as well as for Noda (Yoshioka is especially good reprising the role), but sometimes falters when it comes to the family-soap parts of the story, which manage to be both more tearful (onscreen) and less (in the audience, though obviously some mileage will vary). The restrained relationship between Kōichi and Noriko made sense last time; in a movie two years later, their nominally romantic partnership seems weirdly glum, even anti-sexual, in a state of co-parenting stasis. There’s little sense of time’s passage for this makeshift family.The Love Hypothesis review – hit BookTok romcom lacks spark on screenRead moreThat’s not to say that the monster-attack stuff falls by the wayside in favor of the humans. In fact, the movie’s extended climax features some of the most majestic CG monster action put to film; if the fun American MonsterVerse series tends toward pro-wrestling kaiju, Godzilla Minus Zero cross-breeds its fight-to-the-death grappling with disaster-movie scope and horror-movie teeth. Yet it also doesn’t go in for the overkill; like its predecessor, the movie favors quality of visual effects over quantity. Little-yet-huge details like Ghidorah’s lightning-like attack beams have a jagged beauty that makes them both cooler and scarier than so many obligatory effects-movie laser shows.It’s a fittingly judicious use of computers, given that the world of Godzilla Minus Zero often appears perched on the verge of a post-war technology boom, and on the precipice of the further global disasters that could be invited by the collision of humankind’s supposed innovations and unknowable forces of nature. (Minus One came out the same year as Oppenheimer; was this one, like Nolan’s The Odyssey, conceived in its wake?) If Yamazaki’s previous Godzilla movie ultimately allowed crowd-pleasing thrills to punch through its mid-century anxieties, this one lands a bit more ambiguously. Maybe that’s why the melodrama stuff isn’t quite so satisfying this time around; attentive as the movie is to its human cast, it’s increasingly clear that we’re living in a world of monsters.Godzilla Minus Zero is screening at theNew Yorkfilm festival and will be released in Australia on 5 November and in the US and the UK on 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewGodzillaAction and adventure filmsNew YorkFestivalsVisual effects (VFX)JapanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Doors Down review – outrageously sharp, joyously sweary return of the Latimer Crescent favourites | Stage | The Guardian
description: Ahead of the sitcom’s new series in 2027 the full TV cast reunite for a masterclass in comfort comedy, adding musical interludes to the familiar suburban bedlam
Author: Arusa Qureshi
Headline: Ahead of the sitcom’s new series in 2027 the full TV cast reunite for a masterclass in comfort comedy, adding musical interludes to the familiar suburban bedlam
Content: Amped up absurdity … from left, Jamie Quinn, Kieran Hodgson, Arabella Weir, Doon Mackichan and Jonathan Watson in Two Doors Down, at OVO Hydro, Glasgow.Photograph: Ian Georgeson/Ian Georgeson PhotographyView image in fullscreenAmped up absurdity … from left, Jamie Quinn, Kieran Hodgson, Arabella Weir, Doon Mackichan and Jonathan Watson in Two Doors Down, at OVO Hydro, Glasgow.Photograph: Ian Georgeson/Ian Georgeson PhotographyStageReviewTwo Doors Down review – outrageously sharp, joyously sweary return of the Latimer Crescent favouritesOVO Hydro, GlasgowAhead of the sitcom’s new series in 2027 the full TV cast reunite for a masterclass in comfort comedy, adding musical interludes to the familiar suburban bedlamArusa QureshiSun 27 Sep 2026 05.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may have started as a one-off special in 2013, but seven series and five Christmas specials in, Two Doors Down has become a Scottish institution of sorts. Created and written by Simon Carlyle and Gregor Sharp, the BBC Scotland sitcom set in aGlasgowsuburb is comfort comedy at its very best, with endlessly quotable quips and characters that are masterfully crafted – simultaneously far-fetched and remarkably familiar.The premise of every episode is essentially the same: longsuffering couple Beth and Eric Baird (played by Arabella Weir and Alex Norton) spend their days being hassled by their eccentric neighbours, who continuously abuse their hospitality and turn trivial moments into drama-fuelled bedlam. While the story follows the same structure in this stage adaptation, we soon learn that big changes are afoot, which threaten to upturn the entire ecosystem of Latimer Crescent as we know it.View image in fullscreenProsecco o’clock … Kieran Hodgson, Doon Mackichan and Alex Norton in Two Doors Down.Photograph: Ian Georgeson/Ian Georgeson PhotographyThe beauty of Two Doors Down is that very little ever happens in a single episode, so the question of how this translates to the mammoth stage of Glasgow’s OVO Hydro is a fair one to ask. But the intimacy of Simon Higlett’s suburban set design, with the addition of some creative and extravagant touches, transports you seamlessly to Beth and Eric’s living room, with its pressure cooker-like atmosphere amplified by the arrival of each guest.The entire cast are on fine form and their camaraderie and clear synergy is what allows this adaptation to work so well. Elaine C Smith is predictably, and gloriously, ludicrous as the ever-critical and no-holds-barred Christine, and Jonathan Watson and Doon Mackichan amp up the absurdity with each glass of prosecco as the unfiltered and highly inappropriate couple Colin and Cathy. Playing the usually polite and eager-to-please Gordon, Kieran Hodgson is finally let loose and elicits some of the biggest laughs of the night, while Graeme “Grado” Stevely’s deadpan Alan offers up a barrage of terrific one-liners.There are nods to the TV series throughout: callbacks to fan-favourite lines (“I’ll tell you who does a nice paracetamol – Morrisons.”) and memorable moments from episodes, including Cathy and Colin’s cringe-inducing wedding dance, but it never feels stale. Instead, the addition of musical interludes and purposely exaggerated Scottish cliches and in-jokes makes this production feel like a warm hug from someone you’ve missed. There is no expectation of anything profound occurring, but there are snippets of tenderness in the gentle reminder of the power of community and the strong pull of home. Ultimately though, with its outrageously sharp punchlines and joyously sweary cheek, this version of Two Doors Down is a great way to tide everyone over until the series returns in 2027.AtOVO Hydro, Glasgow, 9-11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageGlasgowTheatreComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Eva Longoria laps up butter on a French foodie tour | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The actor sets off on a culinary adventure, starting in Paris. Plus: ridiculous but addictive reality show Apocalypse. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The actor sets off on a culinary adventure, starting in Paris. Plus: ridiculous but addictive reality show Apocalypse. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Know your onions … Eva Longoria: Searching for France on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdView image in fullscreenKnow your onions … Eva Longoria: Searching for France on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Tv Productions LtdTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Eva Longoria laps up butter on a French foodie tourThe actor sets off on a culinary adventure, starting in Paris. Plus: ridiculous but addictive reality show Apocalypse. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hannah J Davies,Ali CatterallandPriya ElanSun 27 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEva Longoria: Searching for France7.15pm, BBC Two“Don’t you have any wine in this joint?” Even if Eva Longoria’s foodie tour of France sometimes feels stylish at the expense of content, she doesn’t hold back and her relish carries the day. The actor begins in Paris, where she tries an Asian version of the classic croque madame, enjoys a sit-down with the don of French cuisine Alain Ducasse, and discovers the secret of truly decadent cookery: basically, nothing isn’t improved by a few (dozen) cubes of butter.Phil HarrisonThe Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down7.45pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenCracked it? … Fatiha El-Ghorri on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down on Channel 4.Photograph: Channel 4The formula may be very familiar at this point but this pottery challenge is still a warmly good-natured indulgence. From Paul Merson’s bumbling charm to Lucy Beaumont’s eccentricity, the contenders all bring something welcome to the table. This time, it’s raku week and the newbie potters attempt animal sculptures – with inevitably mixed results.PHThe Split Up9pm, BBC OneMore of the hammy (if highly watchable) spin-off from Abi Morgan’s ratings hit The Split, centred on a British-Asian law firm in Manchester. Aria (Ritu Arya) deals with a demanding client, while also wondering what secrets her boss and dad Dhruv (Sanjeev Bhaskar) is hiding.Hannah J DaviesWilderness With Simon Reeve9pm, BBC TwoReeve explores Mexico’s extraordinary Sea of Cortez, nicknamed the “aquarium of the world”, where he joins conservationists striving to restore its fragile ecosystem. Diving with endangered sharks delivers some truly heartstopping images: a whirling mass of hammerheads results, as Simon says, in “a moment of almost ethereal beauty”.Ali CatterallThe Blame9pm, ITV1The addictive Line of Duty-ish six-parter continues, as Emma (Michelle Keegan) and Tom (Douglas Booth) attempt to solve the case of Sophie, the murdered 16-year-old figure skater. Convinced it’s an inside job, can they obtain enough evidence to get the case under the nose of the chief superintendent and, even better, find a motive?Priya ElanApocalypse9pm, Channel 4As watchable as it is ridiculous, this challenge show, which attempts to maroon its participants in an end-of-days thriller, continues to generate its own cheesy plotlines. This time, a fragile peace is on the horizon after the incident with the chickens. But a gun has gone missing, which could mean a resumption of hostilities.PHLive sportOne-Day International Cricket: England v Sri Lanka, 10am, Sky Sports Main EventThe final match from the Oval.Women’s Super League Football: Liverpool v Everton, 2pm, Sky Sports Main EventChelsea v Arsenal follows at 5.15pm.Uefa Nations League Football: Denmark v Wales, 4.45pm, BBC OneWales v Norway is on Thu at 7.30pm on BBC Two.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Catherine Bohart: Borrowing Trouble review – obsessive compulsion to overshare is captivatingly funny | Stage | The Guardian
description: This latest bulletin from the Irish standup’s fraught life delves deep into her OCD and dismay at her own foibles
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: This latest bulletin from the Irish standup’s fraught life delves deep into her OCD and dismay at her own foibles
Content: Irrepressible … Catherine Bohart in Borrowing Trouble at Soho theatre, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIrrepressible … Catherine Bohart in Borrowing Trouble at Soho theatre, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStageReviewCatherine Bohart: Borrowing Trouble review – obsessive compulsion to overshare is captivatingly funnySoho theatre, LondonThis latest bulletin from the Irish standup’s fraught life delves deep into her OCD and dismay at her own foiblesBrian LoganSun 27 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople talking about their mental health is boring, saysCatherine Bohart. Even listening to herself do so frays the patience. So how to justify Borrowing Trouble, a new standup hour from the Irishwoman delving deep into her OCD? Well, the justification here is the humour, rich and hard-won. But it also comes down to Bohart’s trademark candour. This is a condition so all-consuming, on this evidence, that to not address it might feel like dishonesty – which, for the 38-year-old, would be intolerably off-brand.In this latest bulletin from Bohart’s fraught life, we find her fulfilling an ambition close to all Irish hearts, she tells us, and buying her first home. This entails moving in with her girlfriend too, a process that applies pressure on her compulsion to control. But what’s a girl to do? Move on to her fifth therapist, after the underachievement of the preceding four? Try coming off antidepressants? Her doctor’s response to that suggestion does not inspire confidence. Seek refuge with her family? Well that won’t work, as illustrated by an ill-advisedly long visit home to her parents – AKA her symptoms. Here we see mum fret intrusively on Catherine’s behalf and (in one eye-opening anecdote) dad display the type of behaviours that might, just might, suggest that obsessive compulsions run in the family.This all comes at us in a torrent from the irrepressible Bohart, who channels real-world neurosis into a wonderfully uptight and oversharing stage persona. Her dismay at her own foibles is matched only by alarm at the inexplicable conduct of others – see her routine about disliking lesbian weddings, or the later one in which it dawns on her that her girlfriend’s masculine stylings are underpinned by no practical domestic skills whatsoever. Then there’s the section on women’s health, which argues, amusingly contrary to the received wisdom, that we all need to know and hear a lot less about it.You might think the same of comedians’ neurological disorders; Bohart certainly does. But Borrowing Trouble proves that, in the right hands, even the most tormenting of mental afflictions can be captivatingly funny.AtSoho Theatre, London, until 3 October;then touringExplore more on these topicsStageComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)Soho theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream review – Munya Chawawa bewitches in lovingly juiced-up 90s rave | Stage | The Guardian
description: A narcotic, orgiastic woodland party clashes with the traditional values of John Major’s Tory party in Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss’s exuberant production
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: A narcotic, orgiastic woodland party clashes with the traditional values of John Major’s Tory party in Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss’s exuberant production
Content: Showstopping … Munya Chawawa as Bottom in A Midsummer Night’s Dream at Chichester Festival theatre.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenShowstopping … Munya Chawawa as Bottom in A Midsummer Night’s Dream at Chichester Festival theatre.Photograph: Manuel HarlanStageReviewA Midsummer Night’s Dream review – Munya Chawawa bewitches in lovingly juiced-up 90s raveChichester Festival theatreA narcotic, orgiastic woodland party clashes with the traditional values of John Major’s Tory party in Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss’s exuberant productionMark LawsonSun 27 Sep 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Shakespearean canon contains the term “love juice” twice, both in A Midsummer Night’s Dream. So, though purists might be furious, that druggy usage – and Fairie King Oberon’s access to potions that “make eyes roll” – offer textual justification for Justin Audibert and Hannah Joss staging the play around a narcotic, orgiastic woodland party in the summer of 1994.At that time, prime minister John Major was introducing legislation to ban “illegal raves”. Egeus (Henry Everett), an Athenian courtier in the source, becomes Chief Constable of West Sussex, surnamed Anderton, an allusion to Sir James, a Thatcher ally whose Bible-inspired policing saw him called God’s Copper. Duke Theseus becomes MP for Chichester, a seat held by the Conservatives for a century from 1924. With one character wearing Major rosettes on her breasts, a PM often derided as dull is becoming a theatre star: the National next year stages a James Graham bio-drama, Major.High-concept Shakespeare risks bits not fitting, a jeopardy increased in A Midsummer Night’s Dream by a plot divided between courtiers, artisans and faeries. But, in this version, the substances consumed by the first two groups may lead them to hallucinate the third: reports of a woman snogging a donkey or Technicolor creatures filling forests can be attributed to the pharmacopeia of Oberon (David Sturzaker), here a DJ running a rave-based cult.View image in fullscreenRaving crew … Eve Ponsonby (centre) as Titania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.Photograph: Manuel HarlanWhile it’s unclear if he and his followers are from a higher sphere or merely high, the conceit, with word changes and some new speeches, accommodates most of the narrative. A hard part of the play to sell to modern audiences is the “law of Athens”, by which a woman who refuses her father’s choice of husband must opt for death or the convent. But this religious misogyny seems plausible enough amid the moral hardening in the 90s Tory party that led to three Labour terms and Conservatives defecting further right. Lysander becoming Lysanda (Ellie Larkin), adding bisexuality to the youthful romantic quadrangle, increases the moral jeopardy at this Tory court.The “rude mechanicals”, who have taken over the local Tory party’s am dram group, are the new working-class Tories of the era, including Nick Bottom, a video shop owner, bewitchingly played, in his full theatrical debut, by comedian Munya Chawawa. He is verbally (“prologue” mispronounced prow-log-wee) and physically energetic: his slapstick gymnastics in the often lumberingly unfunny Pyramus and Thisbe playlet stop the show with earned applause.Female characters are given additional agency, sometimes violent. Kieran Taylor-Ford’s swaggering Demetrius is regularly doubled over in pain after being thumped in the crotch by Hermia or Helena, potentially interchangeable characters who Angela Sant’Albano and Freya Parks make vividly distinct. Hippolyta (Celeste Dodwell) keeps guys in line with a riding crop.A play that can become tedious through repertoire regularity is lovingly juiced up by Audibert and Joss with resonances local and national. Chichester is now Liberal Democrat, while this production’s Bottom, Theseus and Egeus, you suspect, would have defected to Reform or Restore, a period when mainstream Conservatism seemed extreme now feeling like a dream.AtChichester Festival theatreuntil 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreA Midsummer Night's DreamChichester Festival theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: I’ll Be Seeing You review – Simon Russell Beale’s Liberace is a life force too great to be tamed  | Stage | The Guardian
description: Martin Sherman’s meta new work sees Fra Fee’s writer struggling to turn out a play about the flamboyant pianist while despising everything the showman stands for
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Martin Sherman’s meta new work sees Fra Fee’s writer struggling to turn out a play about the flamboyant pianist while despising everything the showman stands for
Content: Milking it … Simon Russell Beale as Liberace in I’ll Be Seeing You at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tiu MakkonenView image in fullscreenMilking it … Simon Russell Beale as Liberace in I’ll Be Seeing You at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tiu MakkonenStageReviewI’ll Be Seeing You review – Simon Russell Beale’s Liberace is a life force too great to be tamedPitlochry Festival theatreMartin Sherman’s meta new work sees Fra Fee’s writer struggling to turn out a play about the flamboyant pianist while despising everything the showman stands forMark FisherSun 27 Sep 2026 06.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSimon Russell Bealemakes his entrance in mid-air, appearing some way above the stage in a heavenly haze of smoke and light. He flashes a voluminous silver cape and spangly waistcoat, his eyes wide and imploring as if he cannot believe it either. It is flashy and flamboyant and it is a problem for Fra Fee.In this headily meta new play by Martin Sherman, still provocative and unexpected at the age of 87, Fee plays a writer commissioned byPitlochry Festival theatreto turn out a play about Liberace. The only thing is, he despises everything the American showbiz pianist stands for.Russell Beale has smashed into designer Tim Hatley’s previously orderly front-room set with the kind of over-the-top flourish that onlyLiberacecould pull off. And that is what infuriates the writer.As a young gay man, he is embarrassed by the innuendo, the materialism and the deceit. He is hung up in particular by the entertainer’s successful 1959court action against a Daily Mirror columnistwho had implied he was a homosexual (more precisely, a “quivering, giggling, fruit-flavoured, mincing, ice-covered heap of mother love”).View image in fullscreenEmbarrassed by the innuendo … Simon Russell Beale and Fra Fee in I’ll Be Seeing You.Photograph: Tiu MakkonenNot only the young writer but also, it would seem, Sherman himself is dismayed by Liberace’s willingness to lie on oath, denying his sexuality just as he would deny the HIV diagnosis at the end of his life.But the more the writer obsesses about that lie, the less Liberace’s court-room denial seems to be the issue. Sherman, the elderly playwright looking back on his life – and making his stage debut to do so – sees in Liberace the frivolous opposite of himself.The man who made his name withBent, a play about gay persecution during the Holocaust, has nothing in common with the pianist’s rhinestone-and-candelabra escapism. Yet, in a merrily wayward production co-directed by Ben Occhipinti and Alan Cumming, Russell Beale keeps barging in, demanding the limelight, milking the applause.Liberace’s life force is too great to be tamed. In a struggle between the earnest and the ephemeral, he might well be the victor. By the end, the pianist is spoon-feeding ice-cream into the mouth of the playwright, a man infantilised by a hopeless battle.AtPitlochry Festival theatre,until 11 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreSimon Russell BealeLiberacePitlochry Festival theatreMartin ShermanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: 15 great cottages and cabins for an autumn escape in the UK | Cottages | The Guardian
description: Get inspiration for your next short break with our pick of self-catering accommodation, from a sleek Highlands retreat to a cabin with a hot tub on a Somerset vineyard
Author: Rhiannon Batten
Headline: Get inspiration for your next short break with our pick of self-catering accommodation, from a sleek Highlands retreat to a cabin with a hot tub on a Somerset vineyard
Content: A cabin at Thornfalcon Winery in SomersetView image in fullscreenA cabin at Thornfalcon Winery in SomersetCottages15 great cottages and cabins for an autumn escape in the UKGet inspiration for your next short break with our pick of self-catering accommodation, from a sleek Highlands retreat to a cabin with a hot tub on a Somerset vineyard15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UKRhiannon BattenSun 27 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 04.57 EDTSharePen BoncMoelfre, Ynys Môn (Anglesey)View image in fullscreenAs close to the sea as you can get without setting sail, this newly renovated cottage is moored up between a little shingle beach and the village of Moelfre, with its lifeboat station, pub, fish and chip shop, cafe and parlour serving locally made ice-cream. A former fisher’s cottage, it’s decorated in nautical blues and whites, their cool tones warmed by antique chests and an inglenook fireplace once used for smoking herring. An unusual circular garden spins out towards the sea; hop over its low stone wall and you’re right on the Anglesey Coastal Path, soaking up cinematic views of Puffin Island, and Eryri beyond.Sleeps eight, twonights from £746,boltholesandhideaways.co.ukHeronden LodgeEastry, KentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Nathan ShepherdThis doll’s house-like, red-brick cottage sits sheltered by trees in a quiet corner of the Kent countryside, 10 minutes’ drive from Sandwich and 20 from Deal. Newly spruced up, it’s restfully low-key, with buttermilk walls and wooden floors. Upstairs are two bedrooms (one a king, the other a twin) and a bathroom with a tub: perfect for dunking mud-splattered children after days at the beach or trailing along footpaths. Downstairs, there’s a simple country kitchen, a double-windowed dining room and a sitting room with an open fireplace. Walks lead straight into the surrounding farmland and to the village pub, 20 minutes’ away. There are also two farm shops within 10 minutes’ drive.Sleeps four, twonightsfrom £472,keeperscottages.co.ukTy BachBeulah, PowysView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kayleigh DoyleMid Wales is at its moody best in the autumn, the hillsides glowing auburn beneath squally skies. If your walking boots are calling, this recently launched holiday cottage just north of Llanwrtyd Wells is a good base for exploring the trails of the Cambrian Mountains or the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons). The smaller of two cottages on a site that was once a busy village school, it had been empty for more than three decades when the current owners took it on. It took them eight years to restore it, and now it’s a vision of flagstone-floored, putty-walled, slate-roofed comfort, cosied up with a plush raspberry sofa and copper kitchen appliances. This is a place for being rather than doing. Add-ons range from gourmet grazing boards to massage treatments.Sleepsfour, twonightsfrom £260,tosholidayhomes.co.ukBasecamp North LakesTroutbeck, Lake DistrictView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ruth BurgessA few miles west of Penrith, this farm shop, cafe, community garden and wetland restoration site juggles more plates than a Barcelona tapas bar on a Saturday night. It’s also home to a charitable enterprise,Alpacaly Ever After, which rescues llamas and alpacas and offers meets, walks and even camping experiences with them, accessible to all. This summer it added one more item to the menu, launching seven smart new cabins beside the site’s lake. Kitted out with glossy green-tiled shower rooms, galley kitchens, wood-burning stoves and private outdoor baths, they each have one bedroom but can sleep two more on a sofa bed in the lounge.Sleeps four,twonightsfrom £300,basecampnorthlakes.co.ukPeatlands RetreatBallybogey, County AntrimView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gareth AndrewsSitting in the countryside between Ballymoney and Portrush, the two restful shepherds’ huts here come with en suite shower rooms and king-size beds. You’re within easy reach of Old Bushmills Distillery, the Giant’s Causeway, Dunluce Castle and a string of some of the most stunning sandy beaches in the UK, but many guests don’t venture beyond the site’s gardens, meadow and woodland, staying to spot resident hares and light wood-burning stoves. The owners also run an artisan micro-bakery on site; Saturday sourdough workshops can be booked (£90pp), bakery breakfasts can be delivered to your door (£16pp) and twice a week there’s a hyper-local pizza-to-hut delivery service (£15 each).Sleeps two, twonightsfrom £320 (discounts for solo stays),peatlandscausewaycoast.comPippin CottageBude, CornwallView image in fullscreenRun by a former Vogue producer, her chef partner and their farming family, Pippin is one of three cottages set on a working orchard outside Bude. Mixing heirloom pieces with Studio Ore taps and Hay lighting, it’s a lesson in understated, soulful style. Works by local artists cheer the walls (many are for sale) and in the kitchen you’ll find apple juice pressed straight from the orchard’s trees. This autumn, the site has opened a new custom-built sauna and cold plunge, and guests can book add-on wellness experiences such as yoga and sauna sessions that end with hot cocoa around a fire pit.Sleeps four, twonightsfrom £256,cannorchard.comMontagu CottageDrumlanrig, Dumfriesand GallowayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alix McIntosh PhotographyBuilt in the 19th-century as the laundry for the Queensberry estate, Montagu Cottage has been scrubbed up for modern-day guests. A peppermint cream colour scheme cosies up its lofty living area and three bedrooms, there’s a clawfoot bath for post-hike soaks and a double-aspect wood burner blazes in the cottage’s heart.Drumlanrig Castleis easily reached on foot (guests get free access to the gardens and adventure playground until the end of October); spectacular woodland and valley walks lead out from the door; and you’re close to the village of Thornhill for pubs, bakeries, shops, cafes and, if you time it right, a live gig or film screening at theOld School.Sleeps six, three nights from £750,drumlanrigcastle.co.ukMolly’s CabinSutton Bonington,NottinghamshireView image in fullscreenTucked into the field-woven gap between Nottingham and Leicester, beneath the approach to East Midlands airport, Bonington Farm’s four distinctive holiday cottages include a blackened timber cabin with sociable, dorm-style bedrooms, a circular grain store, a pretty brick farmhouse and a corrugated former hay barn. The latter, Molly’s Cabin, is a gallery-walled, salvage-speckled hideaway that’s about to undergo a gentle refurb. Single-night Sunday stays include a private movie night in the farm’s cute grain silo cinema. Or, stay for the whole weekend and go leaf-crunching along the trails ofThe Outwoods, a 110-acre woodland around 20 minutes’ drive away.Sleeps two, onenightfrom £200,boningtonfarm.comFjordUllapool, the HighlandsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lukas RambousekA minimalist counterpoint to the rugged maximalist scenery beyond, Fjord is one half of Corylus Retreats, the twin self-catering apartments opened just outside Ullapool in May. Conceived and run by the team behind nearbyEcotone Cabins, it was designed sustainably with stripped-back timber walls, and floor-to-ceiling windows maximise natural light and have views of neighbouring Loch Broom. On clement days, the pretty harbour and restaurants of Ullapool are easily reached, and there are craggy hikes around Assynt, Coigach and the Summer Isles. If it rains, hunker down inside, enjoying the luxury of underfloor heating or curling up on the covered deck to watch scudding clouds.Sleeps four, threenightsfrom £661,premiercottages.co.ukHafod GwylltCwmystwyth, CeredigionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lou ArchellIts name translates as “wild summer dwelling” but this renovated cottage deep in the Cambrian mountains is equally good for an autumn escape. On the Hafod Estate, deep in the Ystwyth valley, it has no neighbours besides ponies, and has easy access to hiking and wild swimming. Newly available as a holiday rental, it’s stylishly understated inside, with whitewashed walls, slate and wood floors and a collection of ruffled lampshades, tapestry blankets and old pine dressers in soothingly subdued shades. Outside, there’s a wood-fired hot tub with rugged mountain views and the owners can arrange dark skies photography sessions or visits to local potters.Sleeps four, threenightsfrom £690,sandandstoneescapes.comCae’n y BwlchTalsarnau, Eryri (Snowdonia)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Polly LovegroveGetting away from it all is a given at this newly launched cottage in a secluded mountain setting north-east of Harlech. Owned by a ceramicist and an artist, its slate floors and limewashed walls are warmed by glowing fires and a colourful collection of antique dressers, jaunty art, textiles and carved wooden love spoons. While you could drive down the hillside for a windswept walk along the beach at Black Rock Sands, or to explore the legacy of Clough Williams-Ellis at Portmeirion and Plas Brondanw, it would also be tempting to arrive fully supplied and squirrel yourselves away, soaking up the views or hiking straight out into the rugged wilds of Eryri national park.Sleeps six,threenightsfrom £509,underthethatch.co.ukRiders LodgeBallycastle, County AntrimView image in fullscreenStay Lagom is a small estate set around a Georgian rectory on the fringes of Ballycastle. With bike hire on site and a new programme of add-on wellness experiences (think yoga and seaside saunas), it’s popular with visitors coming to hike, surf or cycle the Causeway Coast. Hotel-style bedrooms and boutique dorms can be booked and there are two self-catering cottages, including Riders Lodge, where a sofa-bed stretches capacity to six. Popular with families and small groups of friends, it’s a sociable space with surfboards and bikes suspended on the walls, its own courtyard hot tub and a stash of board games for evenings around the wood burner.Sleeps six, twonightsfrom £524,staylagom.comHoolet BothyBeauly, the HighlandsView image in fullscreenIf Mrs Tiggy-Winkle retrained as an architect, she might come up with something like Hoolet Bothy. A remote, off-grid farm cottage in the hills above Beauly, 12 miles west of Inverness, it’s the epitome of cosy, with timber-panelled walls, a log-burning stove, a double bed tucked into the eaves and a wood-fired Rayburn for cooking and supplying hot water to a small cast iron bath. Guests have access to a fridge and a charging point down at the farm, three minutes’ walk away, and a cool box is supplied for essentials, but there’s no electricity on site so hunker down for days of walking among deer-speckled hills and red kite-dotted skies, and evenings spent storytelling by candlelight.Sleeps two, threenightsfrom £477,airbnb.co.ukLabour in Vain CottageWest Bexington, DorsetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: National TrustSet back from the 18-mile swoosh of shingle along Chesil Beach, this semi-detached rental (there’s another next door for holidaying apart together) has been newly renovated by the National Trust. Its name, like the lane beside it, is thought to refer to a year of crop failures in the middle ages – but there won’t be much labouring, in vain or otherwise, while staying here. Hike a stretch of the South West Coast Path, go swimming or fossil-hunting, watch the skies for migratory brent geese and head into nearby Bridport for shops, cafes and pubs. As well as a snug ground-floor lounge, the attic has been converted into a games room with a TV, telescope and space to spread out jigsaws or toys.Sleeps four, twonightsfrom £561,nationaltrust.org.ukThornfalcon WineryTaunton, SomersetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Felicity MillwardOne of two wooden cabins on a working vineyard (there’s also a more spacious barn conversion suitable for families), the Vine Hut blends rustic timber walls with apple green paintwork and a red gingham sofa to give a cheery, gingerbread cottage feel. It comes with its own outdoor copper bathtub and firepit, plus access to the neighbouring swimming lake and Finnish sauna (pictured). Earlier this year the owners of Thornfalcon renovated a barn on site and have launched a wine school there, plus a series of monthly supper clubs, pairing the vineyard’s wines and juices with seasonal menus; October’s is a culinary caper through the hedgerows, fields and waves via pheasant, hake, mussels, squash, radicchio, puntarelle and quince (from £65pp).Sleepstwo, twonightsfrom £340,thornfalcon.comPrices are for October-November and were correct at time ofpublication

title: How to make cornbread – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: While it’s ideal for mopping up chilli and soup, this Southern US staple can be made substantial enough for a main meal with a few simple additions
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: While it’s ideal for mopping up chilli and soup, this Southern US staple can be made substantial enough for a main meal with a few simple additions
Content: Felicity Cloake’s cornbread.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s cornbread.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make cornbread – recipeWhile it’s ideal for mopping up chilli and soup, this Southern US staple can be made substantial enough for a main meal with a few simple additionsFelicity CloakeSun 27 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike banana bread, a rather less ancient North American creation, cornbread isn’t a loaf in the conventional sense. Though it’s perfect for soaking up chilli, brothy bean soups and the like, it’s actually substantial enough to be the main event, rather than something you might reach for to mop the plate after it. (It’s also gluten-free, should that be a consideration.)Prep10 minSoak2 hrCook25 minServes6200g coarse cornmeal, or polenta, preferably stoneground240ml buttermilk(see step 3)2 tbsp bacon grease, or butter or oil½ tsp salt2 eggs, beaten1 tsp baking powder¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda2 tsp soft light brown sugar(optional)1 A note on the cornmealThe best, most flavourful cornmeal is stoneground but, depending on where you’re based, it may not be that easy to find, so you may have to compromise on the stoneground element of things. Coarse cornmeal is often found in the world food sections of larger supermarkets, usually from Caribbean brands, but if you do see stoneground polenta, grab that.View image in fullscreen2 Toast the cornmealEither way, you can enhance the flavour of your cornmeal by toasting it before use. Put a large, dry frying pan on a medium-high flame and, when it’s hot, add the cornmeal and toast, shaking constantly so it doesn’t catch and burn, until fragrant but not browned; this should take only a couple of minutes.3 Soak half the cornmealTip half the cornmeal into a large bowl and add the buttermilk (if you can’t find buttermilk, use the same amount of milk instead, and add a teaspoonful of lemon juice or vinegar in step 6). Leave to soak for at least a couple of hours, if possible (though you can use it immediately), or overnight if you’re making this for breakfast.4 Get everything else readyView image in fullscreenOnce you’re ready to cook, get all the ingredients ready, because, once the bicarb meets the buttermilk in step 6, it’ll get straight to work. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. For a really crisp base, you’ll need a roughly 20cm ovenproof frying pan, though you could use a (not loose-bottomed) cake or tart tin, greased with hot fat in step 7.5 A note on the fatIf you eat pork, cornbread is particularly delicious cooked in bacon fat, so it’s worth saving drippings or even wiping a piece of fat from a rasher of bacon around the warm pan to grease it before adding another fat. Put the drippings, butter or oil in the pan and heat until sizzling and, in the case of butter, browning.View image in fullscreen6 Finish the batterMeanwhile, stir the remaining toasted cornmeal into the bowl of buttermilk-soaked cornmeal, then mix in the salt, beaten eggs, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda and sugar (that last is sure to horrify those from the American South, but,according to Serious Eats, corn used for milling is traditionally ripened for longer, which makes it sweeter and more flavourful, so unless you have some really good cornmeal, a pinch of sugar will help replicate that).7 Add the fatStir the hot fat into the batter bowl, then turn up the heat under the pan. Pour in the batter – it should sizzle as it hits the pan (or quickly grease a tin and pour the batter in there instead) – level it out, then bake for about 20-25 minutes, until golden and firm. Serve warm. Cornbread reheats well in a moderate oven; it’s good to freeze, too.8 Or flavour with chilli and cheese …View image in fullscreenThis is a very adaptable recipe. Try stirring 70g grated cheddar or red leicester cheese and two-thirds of a chopped jalapeño chilli into the batter in step 7, then sprinkle 10g more cheese on top, plus the rest of the chilli, before baking (you can also use another variety of mild chilli or jarred pickled jalapeños, if you prefer).9 … or bacon, beans or vegOther good things to include: cooked drained beans, crumbled fried bacon, chunks of feta, cured chorizo, drained tinned corn, chopped chives, spring onions or caramelised onions, cooked peppers – if it goes with corn, it’ll probably work here. I especially like to serve mine with room-temperature butter whipped with hot honey (two to four teaspoons per 100g butter).Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassBakingBreadVegetablesAmerican food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sebb’s, Glasgow G1: ‘A delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: Little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, from a chef who wants to deliver maximum joy
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: Little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, from a chef who wants to deliver maximum joy
Content: Sebb's, Glasgow: ‘The distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSebb's, Glasgow: ‘The distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewSebb’s, Glasgow G1: ‘A delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns’ – restaurant reviewLittle bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, from a chef who wants to deliver maximum joyGrace DentSun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSebb’s is a basement restaurant on Miller Street in Glasgow with a door that’s perilously easy to miss, even though it’s bright red. The first time I tried to find it, I waltzed past and almost ended up in the pants department of TK Maxx. I was luckier the second time around, and soon found myself descending a set of stairs into a room with the distinct vibe of a beatnik diner inside a bowling alley: there’s no natural light, there are booths that are perfect for conspiring in, a DJ playing psychedelic rock and food served in brown paper bags. The13th Floor Elevatorsat noon on a Thursday?! Absolutely – as well as the globally ranging delights of sobrassada and ancho honey pitta, tandoori pork belly with tamarind chutney, barbecued squid withzhougand preserved lemon aïoli, and trout ceviche with habanero, mango and tequila. It’s as ifthe Big Lebowskitook up cooking.Sebb’s opened in late 2024, and just over a year later, head chefDanny Carruthers’ food had already snagged the place a Michelin bib gourmand – to my mind by far the most interesting part of the whole tyre company’s advertising hoopla. Bibs are designed to reward places just like Sebb’s: odd, informal, intriguing – the type of place where you can pop out to for lunch without needing four spare hours, a booking months in advance and a decorative Patek Philippe watch on your wrist.View image in fullscreen‘The best pakora in Britain’: Sebb’s are served with piccalilli and grated sheep’s cheese.Instead, I’m a solo lunchtime walk-in on a summer’s day. And they treat me beautifully, settling me at my table with an alcohol-freeCrossipcooler cocktail – bitter, long and with an olive in it, this is the kind of no-alcohol build that makes you forget to miss the gin – and a round of pakoras with cheese and piccalilli. I order coronation cauliflower, aware it sounds like the sort of thing with which Mrs Dooms-Patterson might torment Jerry onThe Good Life. And it turns out this cauliflower is an absolute stonking triumph: tiny, nutty florets, blackened but still sweet and crunchy, in a slick of silky, cashew-based sauce that’s fragrant with coconut and scattered with plump sultanas. As it happens, directly above Sebb’s, at street level, isMargo, a smarter, more composed restaurant that, like Sebb’s, is run by Scoop, the team also behind the city’sOx & FinchandKa Pao. Which basically means that Margo Leadbetter is upstairs, while downstairs is where the people who actually enjoy themselves are.Sebb’s menu is a delicious bombardment of continents, cuisines and cultural trickledowns, and the dishes are a testament to a chef who has learned little bits of loveliness from Sauchiehall Street to the Silk Road, and who wants to deliver maximum joy. Atom dip arrives first: sweet, smoky, mashed aubergine, red pepper, earthy hazelnut dukkah and strained yoghurt, with a warm pitta served unceremoniously in a brown paper bag. The humble aubergine, elevated.View image in fullscreen‘An absolute stonking triumph’: Sebb’s grilled coronation cauliflower with cashews and raisins.Then those pakoras: will I make friends by declaring that the best pakora in Britain is in a Glasgow basement, even though the place reminds me of nothing so much as turning up mid-soundcheck for some sort of music event? These pakoras are thoroughly crisp outside with a gloriously squidgy interior, paper-thin onion that’s properly fried through, and all dotted with creamed piccalilli and blanketed in grated sheep’s cheese.Rump fillet comes seared yet blushing pink, sliced thinly, beautifully arranged and served with cowboy butter – a Glasgow spin onbeurre maître d’hôtelthat features shedloads of garlic, herbs, mustard and chilli – sweetness, sharpness and umami. For me, this dish pretty much sums up Sebb’s, because it’s a riot of unbridled tastiness with a huge nod to French gastronomical technique. You can have spiced fries with garlic and herb aïoli alongside, or Isle of Wight tomatoes with urfa pepper, capers and pine nuts, which, on a menu this far-ranging, lands like a postcard from somewhere unexpectedly close.View image in fullscreen‘One of the best things I’ve eaten all year’: Sebb’s chocolate sorbet.Mimicking just about every Maccy D’s from Land’s End upwards, Sebb’s soft-serve machine is broken the day I go, so instead they offer me chocolate sorbet, which remains one of the best things I’ve eaten all year: a culinary sleight of hand, andsowithout the bad stuff that it’s practically a health tonic.I ate lunch with one of my favourite people (me, on a day off) and enjoyed myself so much that I found myself recommending Sebb’s to random people at Glasgow Central Station, and again later on my travels in Leeds, Birmingham and London. Nowthatis the sign of a properly good little spot.Sebb’s68 Miller Street, Glasgow G1, 0141-739 9381. Open all week, noon-9.45pm (last orders). From about £30 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsFrench food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks’ | Food | The Guardian
description: It has taken me decades to get over the vegetarian cookbooks of my past
Author: Ruby Tandoh
Headline: It has taken me decades to get over the vegetarian cookbooks of my past
Content: Illustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianFood‘I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks’It has taken me decades to get over the vegetarian cookbooks of my pastRuby TandohSun 27 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt would be unwise to overstate things, the world being as it is, but what happened in the UK with stuffed peppers is a tragedy. You know the ones I mean: traffic light bell peppers stuffed with a cupboard raid of rice, breadcrumbs, lentils, nuts and veg – 70s stuffed peppers. The kind you might find in a wholefoods cookbook, cheerfully distended and jaunty of cap, with the physiognomy of PC Plod. I used to make them at university sometimes, my sensibilities being, as ever, several decades out of touch. I think I was trying to channel the vegetarian cookbooks my parents once had – in the years before discovering pesto, these peppers were the vegetarian’s lot. The recipes I concocted bore things like buckwheat groats, curly leaf parsley and yeast extract. To this day, I cannot hear “stuffed vegetables” without flashbacks to such peppers and their generous cargo of junk.It’s a shame, because stuffed vegetables so obviously do not have to be this way. Takechiles rellenos: think about what it takes not just to stuff a poblano, but to blacken it over flame, then to peel off its skin, fill with cheese, secure the seam with a toothpick, coat in flour, dip in fluffy whisked egg, and fry until the batter is crisp and puffed.I recently decided it was time for me, too, to get on the stuffed vegetable beat. (It only took a couple of decades of recovery post my vegetarian spell.) It was late summer, and I was running out of ways to cook squash. Any allotment tender will know the feeling: the delight of the first little speckled courgette, the beauty of the flowers, the wonder that the earth could provide such riches. Then, the second wave of courgettes, then the third, then the panic of stewing, souping, roasting, baking, and pickling through the glut. You end up grating courgette into dishes it has no business being in; smuggling it into cakes, or, as I found myself thinking: “stuff these courgettes”.So, partly because I wanted to learn how to honour nature’s bounty, and partly because aubergines were yellow-stickered in the shop, I applied myself to the stuffed vegetable arts. For help, I went cap in hand to the cookbooks of the dolma belt – an area of stuffed-vegetable excellence, which maps nicely on to the contours of the Ottoman empire, from the Balkans across Turkiye and Palestine, through West Asia and to Iran. Calling this a region doesn’t exactly make sense – it spans time zones, languages and continents. But across this swath, there has been a Cambrian explosion of stuffed peppers, aubergines, summer squash, courgettes, cabbage and vine leaves. It makes the British stuffed pepper seem like a half-formed thought.So, I learned a little about texture, construction and contrast. I fried onions and minced beef, and mixed them with spiced maftoul, then spooned this into halved, hollowed-out peppers. I repurposed a few little globe squash, the size of closed fists, and filled them with lamb, bulgur and handfuls of soft herbs. I learned from Palestinian cookbooks (nowhere does stuffed vegetables quite like Palestine) that a specialmanakra– a long, curved blade, great for coring things and much easier to use than a knife – provides a first line of defence against mid-cook meltdowns. And crucially, I learned that no matter the fateful and seemingly inherent vegetarian-ness of stuffed vegetables over here, meat is probably the best stuffing you can use. So much pain could have been avoided, I think, if the ancestry of British stuffed veg came through the dolma belt, and not through macrobiotic cookbooks.The downside of all this, of course, is that such dishes take for ever. But now that the evenings are longer and summer FOMO is thankfully done, it’s a good time for such kitchen projects. In previous years, it’s been starting on the Christmas cake or ill-advisedly trying to reverse engineer a Mr Kipling fondant fancy. This year, it’s the seemingly modest – and actually momentous – challenge of stuffed veg dishes which, under ideal circumstances, require an entire production line of volunteer peelers, corers, rollers, folders, idlers, pot watchers and gossipers to produce.Top of the list: Kurdishyapraxi silq– the Noah’s ark of stuffed vegetables: an elaborate layering of simmered, translucent, onion layer sheaths; tiger-striped and hollowed out courgettes; aubergines and tomatoes, their bellies gouged; and rolled up swiss chard leaves. I found the recipe in Pary Baban’s delightfulNandên. I’ve already made one of her other yaprax (stuffed vegetable) recipes: aubergine and cucumber filled with rice and minced lamb, then – gorgeously, surgically – sewn shut with needle and thread. This is the level we’re at. I will report back when I have finished constructing this yapraxi silq, in this lifetime or the next.Explore more on these topicsFoodVegetablesEastern European food and drinkBritish food and drinkVegetarian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
